Language models (LMs) have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, underpinning applications ranging from speech recognition and machine translation to text generation and information retrieval (Bengio et al., 2003;Mikolov et al., 2010;Brown et al., 1992). Traditionally, LMs operate by predicting the probability of a word given its preceding context. While substantial progress has been made in developing increasingly sophisticated LMs – notably with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) – a persistent challenge remains: accurately modeling infrequent words, and particularly, named entities. Named entities (NEs) – representing people, organizations, locations, dates, and more – are ubiquitous in many real-world texts. However, by their very nature, NEs often exhibit low frequencies in typical training corpora. This scarcity poses a significant hurdle for traditional LMs, which struggle to assign reliable probabilities to these vital elements of language. A naive LM may assign a low probability to a perfectly valid, yet uncommon, entity name, leading to suboptimal performance in downstream tasks. For example, consider a recipe generation task. An LM trained on a general corpus might struggle to predict specialized ingredients like “harissa paste” or “saffron threads” accurately, despite their relevance in the recipe domain. Similarly, in code generation, uncommon API names or class identifiers can pose a similar challenge. Prior work has attempted to address the issue of rare words in LMs through various techniques. Smoothing methods (Kneser and Ney, 1995) alleviate the problem of zero probabilities, while byte-pair encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2016) and WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016) decompose rare words into subword units. However, these approaches often fail to fully capture the semantic and contextual information associated with named entities. While subword methods can represent the characters of the entities, they don’t leverage the knowledge about *what* kind of entity it is—a person, a location, an organization, etc. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to building discriminative language models that explicitly integrates entity type information to improve the prediction of named entities. Our model leverages the constraint that entity names are often predictable given their associated type. For example, knowing that a word is a ‘city’ greatly narrows down the possible options and increases the probability of valid city names. We incorporate this knowledge by augmenting the standard LM framework with an entity type embedding layer, allowing the model to learn representations that are sensitive to both the word itself *and* its entity type. To evaluate our approach, we introduce two novel benchmark datasets: one based on recipes, and another on Java programming code. These datasets are specifically chosen for their rich presence of named entities – ingredients in recipes and API names/class identifiers in code, respectively. Our experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art language models, achieving a 52.2% improvement in perplexity on the recipe generation task and a 22.06% improvement on the code generation task. These findings highlight the effectiveness of our approach in leveraging entity type information to build more robust and accurate language models for text containing named entities.

Understanding language necessitates considering its context, a principle gaining increasing traction within both linguistic theory and computational linguistics. The study of discourse and information structure, traditionally a core area within linguistics, is now demonstrably impacting the performance of various natural language processing (NLP) applications. For example, the explicit identification of discourse relations has been shown to improve the accuracy of Short Answer Assessment systems (Ziai & Meurers, 2014), highlighting the practical benefits of incorporating contextual understanding. A critical component of information structure is *focus*, the linguistic mechanism by which speakers signal which part of an utterance carries the new or salient information. Identifying focus – whether it's contrastive, exhaustive, or otherwise – is crucial for accurately interpreting meaning and capturing the speaker’s intent. Previous work has laid a solid foundation for studying focus through detailed annotation guidelines, enabling the manual analysis of information structural concepts in both written (Dipper et al., 2007; Ziai & Meurers, 2014) and spoken language data (Calhoun et al., 2010). However, manual annotation is a time-consuming and expensive process, limiting the scalability of these analyses to large, authentic datasets. This bottleneck hinders broader investigations into the role of focus in real-world language use. To address this limitation, we present the first approach to automatically annotate focus in authentic written data. Our work builds upon the established annotation schemes, aiming to bridge the gap between theoretical insights and large-scale computational analysis. The central challenge lies in capturing the subtle cues that signal focus, which can be lexical (e.g., contrastive stress indicated through capitalization or punctuation), syntactic (e.g., word order variations), and semantic (e.g., a focus-sensitive item implying a specific focus structure). To tackle this complexity, we employ a classification approach combining a rich set of features representing these different linguistic levels. These features range from basic lexical properties to more sophisticated syntactic dependencies and semantic indicators. Through rigorous experimentation, we demonstrate that our approach achieves an accuracy of 78.1% in identifying focus, marking a substantial step towards automating the analysis of information structure in real-world language data. This automated analysis holds the potential to unlock new insights into the dynamics of discourse and improve the performance of NLP applications that rely on a deeper understanding of communicative intent. By “bringing formal pragmatics alive” in the analysis of authentic data, this work contributes to a more nuanced and robust understanding of human language processing. The automatic identification of semantic orientations, often referred to as sentiment analysis or opinion mining, has emerged as a crucial task in natural language processing. A wide range of applications, including market research, social media monitoring, and political analysis, relies on accurately determining the affective tone expressed in text. Many successful approaches to this problem leverage the structure of lexical networks – graphs where nodes represent words and edges signify semantic relationships – to propagate polarity information (e.g., Turney, 2002; Kanayama et al., 2006). These methods operate on the assumption that words with similar meanings tend to share similar polarities, and that this shared information can be exploited to infer the sentiment of previously unseen words. A particularly promising line of work utilizes concepts from statistical physics, specifically the Ising spin model, to model the propagation of polarity in a lexical network (Yan et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2011). In this framework, words are represented as spins that can be either positive or negative, representing their respective polarities. The connections between words in the lexical network determine the interaction strength between the spins, and the overall system evolves towards a stable configuration where neighboring spins tend to align. Notably, Yan et al. (2010) reported an intriguing observation: the performance of this model exhibits a distinct phase transition as the temperature parameter is varied, peaking at an optimal temperature. This observation suggests that the model’s ability to accurately infer semantic orientations is highly sensitive to its underlying physical parameters. However, the underlying mechanism behind this phase transition remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we delve into a statistical mechanical analysis of this phenomenon, aiming to elucidate the principles governing the model’s behavior. We demonstrate that the phase transition is linked to the spectral properties of the weight matrix representing the lexical network’s connectivity. Specifically, we find that the largest eigenvalue of this matrix plays a dominant role in shaping the system’s dynamics and limiting its performance. Based on this analysis, we propose a novel scheme for improving the extraction of semantic orientations: removing the largest eigenvalue component from the weight matrix. This seemingly simple modification effectively mitigates the influence of a dominant mode that hinders accurate polarity propagation. Experimental results demonstrate that our scheme significantly enhances the accuracy of semantic orientation extraction, outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms while incurring minimal additional computational cost. Furthermore, we investigate the origins of this performance gain through a detailed analysis of the matrix eigenvalues and a linearized model, providing further insights into the mechanisms driving the model’s behavior. Our work not only provides a deeper understanding of the statistical mechanics underlying lexical network-based sentiment analysis but also offers a practical and effective method for improving its performance. The demand for sentiment analysis has rapidly grown with the proliferation of social media and online reviews. Businesses and organizations increasingly rely on understanding public opinion to inform decision-making, track brand reputation, and improve customer service. While substantial progress has been made in sentiment classification for English text, performing the same task across multiple languages presents significant challenges. A primary hurdle is the scarcity of labeled data for most languages beyond English. Creating large, high-quality datasets for each language is costly and time-consuming, hindering the development of effective multilingual sentiment analysis systems. Traditional approaches to multilingual sentiment classification often involve resource-intensive methods such as machine translation to convert all input text into a single language (typically English), followed by sentiment classification using existing English-centric models. While this approach leverages the availability of English resources, it introduces errors from the translation process and fails to fully capture language-specific nuances in sentiment expression. Another approach involves building language-specific models, but this necessitates substantial labeled data for each language, which is often unavailable. Recent research has explored cross-lingual transfer learning (Glorot et al., 2011;Socher et al., 2013) and multilingual embedding spaces (Mikolov et al., 2013;Chung et al., 2013) to address the limited resource problem. These approaches aim to learn shared representations across languages, enabling knowledge transfer from resource-rich languages to resource-poor ones. However, these methods often require sophisticated training procedures and can still suffer from performance degradation in languages substantially different from the source language. In this paper, we propose a simple and effective approach for multilingual sentiment classification that leverages the wealth of resources available in English. Our key idea is to translate words from the input language into their English equivalents and then utilize pre-trained English word embeddings to represent the input text. This projection into the English space provides a uniform framework for processing text from diverse languages. This approach sidesteps the need for resource-intensive machine translation of entire sentences and allows us to directly leverage the rich semantic information encoded in English word embeddings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique that incorporates polar words (words with strong positive or negative connotations) along with their associated polarities during training. This augmentation enhances the classifier's ability to recognize and utilize sentiment cues, resulting in significant performance gains. The intuition behind leveraging English resources is that English word embeddings capture a broad range of semantic and sentiment information. By translating words into English, we can map text from different languages into a common semantic space, enabling a single classifier to effectively process and analyze sentiment across multiple languages. This seemingly simple approach proves remarkably effective, consistently achieving performance improvements of 7-10% over traditional classifiers on various languages and text genres, even with limited training data. Textual entailment (TE), the task of determining whether the meaning of one text fragment (the text) is logically entailed by another (the premise), has emerged as a crucial paradigm for evaluating and driving research in natural language understanding (Bentivogli et al., 2009; MacMillan et al., 2009). Its appeal lies in its generality – successful TE systems necessitate robust capabilities in lexical semantics, compositional semantics, and pragmatic reasoning. Initial approaches to TE largely focused on sentence-level entailment, treating the text and premise as isolated units of meaning. However, human comprehension rarely occurs in a vacuum; rather, texts are routinely interpreted within the broader context of the surrounding discourse. Understanding the relationships between sentences, identifying implicit assumptions, and resolving ambiguities often require considering the entire communicative situation. The importance of discourse in natural language understanding is well-established. Discourse processing techniques, such as coreference resolution, rhetorical structure theory (RST), and discourse relation recognition, have proven beneficial in a variety of tasks including question answering (Pradeep et al., 2017), summarization (Hirschberg and Manning, 2015), and machine translation (Popescu et al., 2010). While acknowledging the value of discourse, current TE systems typically incorporate discourse information in a rather limited fashion. A common strategy involves employing off-the-shelf coreference resolution systems to identify mentions referring to the same entity, and then feeding this information as features into a TE classifier (e.g., Schneiderman et al., 2005). However, this approach often falls short of capturing the full richness of discourse phenomena relevant to entailment. For instance, discourse relations beyond coreference—such as elaboration, contrast, or cause-effect—can significantly influence how we interpret a text and determine whether it entails another. Similarly, background knowledge activated by the discourse context can play a crucial role in bridging inferences. Consider the example: “John bought a new car. He drove it home.” Determining whether “John drove a car” is entailed requires recognizing the coreference between “it” and “a new car,” but also understanding the common-sense relationship between car ownership and driving. In this paper, we investigate the impact of various discourse aspects on textual entailment. We aim to go beyond simple coreference and explore how other discourse features – specifically, discourse relation information and discourse-level background knowledge – can contribute to improved entailment performance. We propose initial solutions for incorporating these aspects into a TE framework and present experimental results demonstrating that leveraging discourse information yields significant improvements over baseline systems relying solely on sentence-level analysis and standard coreference resolution. Our findings underscore the need for future TE systems to more effectively address discourse considerations to achieve human-level reasoning capabilities. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Compositionality is a cornerstone of linguistic theory and a guiding principle in natural language processing (NLP). The principle posits that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rule by which they are combined (Fodor & Lepore, 1999). Translating this principle into computational models has been a central challenge in NLP for decades, leading to a diverse landscape of approaches. Early work focused on symbolic representations, notably using context-free grammars (CFGs) and lambda calculus (Montague, 1973) to explicitly define compositional semantics. However, these approaches often struggle with the inherent ambiguity and robustness of natural language, requiring extensive hand-engineered rules and lexicons. More recently, distributional semantic models (DSM) – or word space models – have gained prominence, leveraging statistical co-occurrence information to represent word meanings as vectors in a high-dimensional space (Lund & Burgess, 1996; Turney & Pantel, 2010). These models have demonstrated impressive performance in capturing semantic similarity but traditionally lack explicit mechanisms for compositionality. Attempts to overcome this limitation have explored various vector operations, such as addition, multiplication, and concatenation, to combine word vectors and derive phrase representations (Mitchell & Lapata, 2008; Yagiz et al., 2010; Baroni et al., 2014). While successful to a degree, these approaches often lack a firm theoretical grounding in compositional semantics and can be sensitive to the choice of combination operator. In this paper, we present Compositional Matrix-Space Models (CMSMs), a novel framework for compositional NLP that bridges the gap between symbolic and distributional approaches. CMSMs are based on matrix multiplication, offering a principled and flexible mechanism for combining representations at different levels of linguistic structure. The core idea is to represent both lexical items and grammatical rules as matrices, and to compute the composition of expressions by multiplying these matrices. This simple yet powerful operation naturally embodies the compositional principle, allowing for the systematic derivation of complex meanings from simpler components. We argue that CMSMs possess several key advantages over existing approaches. First, they provide a unifying framework that can cover and combine a broad range of compositional models, from simple word space operations to sophisticated grammar formalisms. Second, the matrix-based representation lends itself to efficient computation and can be readily integrated with existing linear algebra libraries. Third, CMSMs offer a plausible cognitive interpretation, suggesting that matrix representations may align with neural mechanisms for compositional processing. Finally, and importantly, CMSMs offer a natural and principled way of incorporating syntactic information into distributional semantic models. We demonstrate the versatility of CMSMs by showing how they can be used to reproduce and extend existing compositional NLP models. We discuss the structural and cognitive plausibility of the model, and highlight its potential for further research in areas such as semantic parsing, question answering, and machine translation. This paper lays the groundwork for a new line of investigation into compositional modeling, exploring the power of matrix multiplication as a fundamental operation for representing and processing natural language.

Automatic summarization has become increasingly important with the explosive growth of online information. The goal of automatic summarization is to produce a concise and fluent summary that retains the crucial information from the source document(s). Summarization techniques can broadly be categorized into two main approaches: extractive summarization and abstractive summarization. Extractive methods select key sentences or phrases directly from the source document(s) to form the summary (e.g., Luhn, 1958; Salton et al., 1968), while abstractive methods generate a summary by paraphrasing and synthesizing information from the original text, often employing natural language generation techniques (e.g., Rush et al., 2015; See et al., 2017). While abstractive summarization has the potential to produce more human-like summaries, it remains a challenging task due to the complexities of language understanding and generation. Consequently, extractive summarization remains a popular and effective approach in many practical applications. Most extractive summarization methods rely on scoring the importance of individual sentences and selecting the top-ranked sentences to form the summary. Common features used for sentence scoring include term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) (Salton and Buckley, 1988), sentence position (Baxendale, 2007), sentence length, and the presence of cue phrases (e.g., “in conclusion,” “importantly”). More advanced approaches utilize graph-based methods (e.g., LexRank (Erkan and Radev, 2004), TextRank (Mihalcea and Tarau, 2004)), which model relationships between sentences and rank them based on their centrality in the graph. Machine learning techniques, such as supervised learning and reinforcement learning, have also been applied to sentence scoring and selection (e.g., Lin and Bilmes, 2011; Ryu et al., 2015). However, a significant challenge in extractive summarization is ensuring the *coherence* of the generated summary. Simply selecting the most important sentences without considering their relationships can result in a disjointed and difficult-to-understand summary. Several studies have highlighted the importance of coherence for summary quality (e.g., Barzilay and Lapata, 2008; Celikyilmaz et al., 2018). Recent work explores methods to explicitly model coherence during summary generation, often by leveraging discourse relations or topic models. In this paper, we introduce a novel single-document summarization method based on a discriminative Hidden Semi-Markov Model (HSMM). The HSMM is a natural fit for the summarization problem because it allows us to explicitly model the sequential selection of sentences, and thus to optimize for summary coherence. Our model frames summarization as an optimization problem of selecting the best sequence of sentences under a given knapsack constraint (representing the desired summary length). Unlike many previous approaches that treat sentence selection independently, our model considers the relationships *between* selected sentences, thereby promoting coherence. Furthermore, the model can integrate sentence compression techniques to refine the selected sentences and enhance summary quality. Through extensive experiments on a large-scale corpus, we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms competitive baselines in terms of ROUGE evaluation and linguistic quality, and achieves a high degree of overlap with human-written reference summaries. Named Entity Recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text, such as person names, organizations, and locations – is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Supervised NER systems, typically relying on machine learning classifiers trained on large, manually annotated datasets, have achieved impressive performance. However, the creation of such datasets is expensive and time-consuming, and the performance of these systems often degrades significantly when applied to new domains or genres that differ from the training data. This phenomenon, known as domain adaptation, is a major challenge in deploying NER systems in real-world applications. A common scenario is the availability of a labeled dataset from a *source* domain, coupled with a large volume of unlabeled data from a *target* domain. Transferring knowledge from the source to the target domain is key. Several approaches have been investigated including domain adaptation techniques that attempt to learn domain-invariant features (Blitzer et al., 2006; Daumé III, 2007), and transductive learning methods that leverage the unlabeled target domain data directly (Ben-David et al., 2010). Another promising approach is bootstrapping (Rosenfeld et al., 1988), an iterative self-training process where a model initially trained on labeled data is used to label unlabeled data, which is then added to the training set for retraining. While bootstrapping is attractive due to its simplicity and potential to leverage abundant unlabeled data, it often struggles in domain adaptation scenarios. The discrepancy between the source and target domains can lead the initial classifier to make inaccurate predictions on the target domain data, thereby introducing noise into the training set and hindering performance improvement. Standard bootstrapping algorithms frequently select instances that are confidently, but incorrectly, labeled, reinforcing existing biases and failing to effectively bridge the gap between domains. In this paper, we propose a novel domain adaptive bootstrapping algorithm that addresses this challenge. Our key idea is to identify “bridge” instances – unlabeled data points from the target domain that are both informative about the target domain’s characteristics *and* relatively easy for the current classifier to label correctly. By selectively adding these instances to the training set, we aim to guide the classifier towards adapting to the target domain without being overwhelmed by noisy labels. We achieve this by combining confidence scores with measures of instance diversity and representativeness, ensuring that the added data provides new information and reflects the underlying distribution of the target domain. We evaluate our approach on a standard NER task, demonstrating its superior performance compared to fully supervised learning, transductive methods, and traditional bootstrapping algorithms. Our results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of our bridge-based selection strategy in overcoming the challenges of domain adaptation in NER. We further present an analysis of the selected bridge instances illustrating their role in facilitating effective knowledge transfer from the source to the target domain. The ability to understand language hinges on our capacity to compose meaning – to derive the meaning of a complex expression from the meanings of its parts and the way those parts are combined. This compositional principle is a cornerstone of linguistic theory and a fundamental requirement for achieving true language understanding in artificial intelligence. While recent advances in neural network-based language models have yielded impressive results on a variety of NLP tasks, a critical question remains: to what extent do these models actually *understand* compositionality, or are they merely exploiting statistical correlations in the training data? A central obstacle to answering this question is the inherent “black box” nature of the distributed representations learned by these models – namely, sentence vectors. These vectors encode a sentence’s meaning in a high-dimensional space, but offer little direct insight into how that meaning is structured or the extent to which compositional principles are being captured. Simply achieving high performance on downstream tasks does not necessarily demonstrate understanding of compositionality; a model could, for example, memorize frequent phrases and their associated vectors without truly grasping the underlying semantic relationships. Therefore, a crucial step towards building genuinely intelligent language processing systems is developing methods to *assess* the degree to which sentence vector representations reflect compositional meaning. This requires designing diagnostic tools and tasks that can selectively probe for specific aspects of compositional understanding with precision and control. Existing approaches to evaluating compositional generalization often rely on manually constructed datasets or synthetic languages, which may not fully capture the complexities of natural language. Furthermore, generating datasets that target specific compositional skills – such as understanding the effect of negation, quantification, or coordination – is a significant challenge. In this paper, we present a novel methodology for assessing compositionality in sentence vector representations. Our approach centers around the creation of controlled tasks designed to directly target compositional meaning information. To facilitate the construction of these tasks, we developed a specialized sentence generation system capable of producing large-scale, annotated datasets adhering to precise syntactic, semantic, and lexical constraints. The system allows us to systematically manipulate sentence structure and meaning, creating datasets that isolate specific compositional operations. We then leverage these datasets to probe sentence embeddings generated by a range of established sentence composition models, evaluating their ability to accurately represent the intended compositional relationships. Our experiments reveal meaningful differences in the compositional capacities of these models, shedding light on their strengths and weaknesses. We believe that this work makes a significant contribution to the ongoing effort to understand and improve the compositional abilities of neural language models. The datasets and generation system developed as part of this research are publicly available, providing a valuable resource for future work in this area. By offering a more nuanced and targeted approach to evaluating compositionality, we hope to inspire the development of models that truly understand the meaning of language, rather than simply mimicking its patterns. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) and Entity Linking (EL) are fundamental tasks in Natural Language Processing, critical for bridging the gap between textual representation and semantic understanding. WSD aims to identify the correct meaning (sense) of a word in a given context, while EL seeks to map named entities mentioned in text to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) such as Wikipedia or Freebase. Both tasks, though traditionally treated separately, are deeply intertwined. The correct interpretation of a noun often hinges on knowing whether it refers to a common noun sense or a specific entity, and similarly, accurately linking an entity requires understanding the context in which it appears to determine its intended sense. For example, consider the noun "Washington" in the sentence “Washington is the capital of the United States.” Resolving its sense necessitates linking it to the “Washington, D.C.” entity in a knowledge base, rather than to individuals named “Washington.” Recent years have seen significant progress in both WSD and EL, largely driven by the application of machine learning techniques. Early WSD systems relied heavily on supervised learning with manually annotated sense inventories (Lesk, 1986; Yarowsky, 1990). However, the creation of such inventories is both time-consuming and plagued by subjectivity. Modern approaches increasingly utilize knowledge-based WSD (Agirre and Soroa, 2009) or unsupervised methods leveraging large text corpora (Lin, 1998; Chevalier and Srinivasa, 2010). Similarly, EL has transitioned from feature-based methods (Gaizauskas et al., 2008) to neural network approaches (Yang et al., 2015; Petrov et al., 2017) that learn entity embeddings and contextual representations. Despite these advancements, existing systems often fall short of achieving high accuracy, particularly in ambiguous contexts. A key limitation lies in the independent treatment of WSD and EL. Joint models (Picca et al., 2016; Ji et al., 2017) have begun to address this issue, demonstrating that incorporating information from both tasks can lead to improved performance. However, most existing joint models rely on a single objective function, typically maximizing a single metric such as accuracy or F1-score. This approach inherently involves trade-offs and may not fully capture the complementary strengths of WSD and EL. In this paper, we present a novel approach to joint WSD and EL that moves beyond single-objective optimization. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective optimization task, combining several complementary objectives designed to capture different aspects of disambiguation quality. These objectives include maximizing the likelihood of correct senses and entities, promoting consistency between WSD and EL decisions, and encouraging sparsity in the learned representations. Our system performs continuous optimization to refine probability distributions over candidate senses, guided by these multiple objectives. We demonstrate through comprehensive experiments on standard corpora that our multi-objective approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods for both nominal WSD and EL, demonstrating the significant benefits of combining complementary objectives in a robust joint disambiguation model.

Natural language generation (NLG) systems often face the challenge of choosing among multiple valid surface realizations of an underlying semantic representation. Realization ranking, the task of ordering these candidate realizations based on their fluency and naturalness, has become a crucial component of many NLG pipelines (White, 2004;Langkilde & Knight, 2000;Toutanova et al., 2008). Traditionally, realization ranking models have relied on features encoding linguistic properties such as grammaticality, lexical cohesion, and syntactic well-formedness. However, recent work suggests that more subtle principles, such as dependency length minimization, play a significant role in human sentence production and comprehension (Gibson et al., 1998;Futrell & Levy, 2018). The principle of dependency length minimization posits that humans prefer syntactic structures where dependencies between words are short, as shorter dependencies are easier to process. This preference manifests in various linguistic phenomena including constituent ordering, agreement agreement, and pronoun resolution (Gibson, 2000). Corpus studies have demonstrated a clear inverse correlation between dependency length and frequency in natural language (Temperley, 2008), suggesting that shorter dependencies are more common and thus more natural. Motivated by these findings, we investigate the incorporation of dependency length minimization into discriminative realization ranking. Our central hypothesis is that explicitly favoring realizations with shorter dependencies can improve ranking performance, both by eliminating particularly egregious ordering errors and by better aligning the generated text with the distributional characteristics of natural language. We focus on the task of sentence realization from meaning representation (MRS) – the output of a semantic parser – as used in commercially deployed Spoken Dialogue Systems (SDS) (Popović & Hulden, 2015). We contribute a comprehensive evaluation of dependency length minimization within a state-of-the-art realization ranking model. Using a large corpus of news text, we demonstrate that incorporating dependency length as a ranking feature yields statistically significant improvements in BLEU scores, a standard metric for evaluating NLG quality. More importantly, we show that this feature significantly reduces the occurrence of “heavy/light” ordering errors – a type of error where the order of constituents clashes with the relative heaviness of their heads, resulting in highly disfluent utterances. Furthermore, we investigate the interaction between dependency length minimization and other linguistic preferences, such as canonical word order, finding that richer models are better able to balance these competing factors than simpler ones. We observe that with less expressive models, overly aggressive dependency length minimization can lead to unnatural constructions that prioritize short dependencies at the expense of more conventional phrasing. Our work extends beyond simply adding a feature to an existing model. It provides insights into how cognitive principles can be effectively integrated into NLG systems and highlights the importance of model complexity in capturing nuanced linguistic preferences. The findings underscore the potential of dependency-based features to improve not only the overall fluency of generated text but also its adherence to underlying cognitive processing constraints.

Argumentative essay writing is a cornerstone of secondary and higher education, serving as a crucial measure of a student’s critical thinking, research, and communication skills. Beyond simply presenting information, effective argumentative essays require students to articulate a clear position – their *stance* – with respect to a given proposition. Understanding this stance is not merely about identifying agreement or disagreement, but also gauging the *degree* to which an author holds a particular viewpoint. This nuanced understanding of stance is vital for educators assessing argumentation quality, and for automated essay scoring systems seeking a deeper comprehension of student work beyond surface-level features like grammar and vocabulary. Despite its importance, computational modeling of essay stance remains a surprisingly under-explored area within the broader field of argumentative essay analysis. Prior work has largely focused on identifying argumentative components like claims and premises (e.g., Toulmin et al., 1958; Stede, 2007; Rousseau & Branting, 2018), or assessing the overall quality of argumentation (e.g., Page, 1966; Shermis & Burstein, 2013). While these components contribute to a holistic understanding, they do not directly address the author’s perspective *towards* the central proposition. Existing stance detection research has primarily centered on social media (e.g., Somasundaran & Wiebe, 2009; Hasan & Mihalcea, 2009) or news articles (e.g., Blair-Early & Zibrek, 2012), domains with substantially different linguistic characteristics than formal academic writing. Furthermore, applying existing stance detection techniques directly to student essays often proves challenging. The language used in student writing tends to be less polished and more complex, exhibiting a wider range of stylistic and rhetorical strategies. Previous work *specifically* targeting stance in student essays (e.g., Dutt et al., 2016) has served as a valuable starting point, but relies on feature engineering that may not fully capture the subtle linguistic cues indicative of stance. To address these challenges, we introduce a new corpus of argumentative student essays, meticulously annotated with fine-grained stance labels reflecting the author’s degree of agreement or disagreement with a given proposition. This corpus provides a crucial resource for developing and evaluating computational models of essay stance. We then propose a novel approach to automatically predicting essay stance, leveraging recent advancements in neural network architectures to capture complex linguistic patterns. Through a comprehensive evaluation on this new corpus, we demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms several strong baselines—including a reimplementation of the previously published feature-based system—achieving substantial improvements in stance classification accuracy. This work contributes to the field by (1) providing a publicly available, annotated corpus to facilitate future research on stance detection in student writing, and (2) presenting a robust and effective computational model capable of accurately determining essay stance, paving the way for more sophisticated automated essay assessment systems and educational tools.

FrameNet (Baker et al., 1998) is a lexical resource based on Frame Semantics, which aims to describe the meaning of words in terms of “frames,” conceptual structures representing stereotypical situations, objects, or events. Each frame defines a set of “frame elements” (FEs) representing the semantic roles played by participants in the described scenario, and a set of “lexical units” (LUs) – words or phrases that evoke the frame. While FrameNet provides a rich and structured representation of lexical semantics, its construction is a laborious and time-consuming process, requiring substantial linguistic expertise. As of today, FrameNet covers a limited portion of the English lexicon, and its expansion to other languages is even more challenging due to the availability of linguistic resources and trained annotators. In recent years, a growing body of work has focused on automatically extending lexical resources. Techniques range from bootstrapping approaches that iteratively refine the mapping between resources (e.g., Mihalcea et al., 2006) to leveraging distributional similarity based on large text corpora (e.g., Baroni et al., 2009). However, these methods often struggle with ambiguity and require careful post-processing to ensure the quality of the acquired data. This paper explores a novel approach to automatically extending FrameNet by exploiting the vast knowledge repository that is Wikipedia. Wikipedia, a collaboratively edited online encyclopedia, contains articles covering a wide range of topics and written in multiple languages. Its structure, based on interconnected articles and rich internal linking, makes it an ideal source for augmenting lexical resources like FrameNet. Specifically, we address the task of linking FrameNet and Wikipedia. Given a frame *F* and a lexical unit *l* evoking that frame, we aim to identify the Wikipedia page that best represents the meaning of *l* within the context of *F*. This mapping allows us to automatically acquire valuable information from Wikipedia, including new example sentences illustrating the frame usage and potential LUs for the frame, both in English and in other languages where Wikipedia is available. Our approach leverages a word sense disambiguation (WSD) system to identify the most appropriate Wikipedia page for a given (F, l) pair. The core idea is that the Wikipedia article that best captures the meaning of the LU in the context of the frame will also exhibit a high degree of semantic similarity to the frame’s definition and example sentences. This work is particularly relevant for facilitating the creation of FrameNet in resource-poor languages. By bootstrapping from English FrameNet and leveraging multilingual Wikipedia, we can efficiently acquire initial training data for annotators, accelerating the development of FrameNet in new languages. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work on lexical resource expansion and knowledge-based WSD. Section 3 details our proposed approach for linking FrameNet and Wikipedia. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and evaluation results for both monolingual and multilingual expansion of FrameNet. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has seen remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by advances in phrase-based models (Koehn et al., 2003). However, a key challenge remains: adapting these systems to perform well on new domains or text types different from those they were originally trained on. Domain adaptation (DA) techniques aim to address this challenge, and a substantial body of work has focused on improving translation quality in these scenarios. Traditionally, the majority of DA research in SMT concentrates on two primary components: the translation model (TM), which learns the probabilistic relationship between source and target phrases, and the language model (LM), which assesses the fluency of the generated target language. The RM is responsible for learning the preferred source-target phrase reordering patterns, and its performance is often critical, particularly for language pairs with substantial differences in word order. Different domains can exhibit vastly different reordering preferences. For instance, legal documents often employ more complex sentence structures and require different reordering patterns compared to news articles. Therefore, it seems intuitive that adapting the RM to a new domain could yield significant improvements in translation quality. This paper addresses this gap in the literature by investigating the impact of reordering model adaptation on phrase-based SMT performance. We demonstrate, through extensive experimentation, that mixture model adaptation of a lexicalized RM can lead to substantial gains, even when the system already incorporates domain-adapted TMs and LMs. Our findings reveal a surprising disconnect: the optimal mixture weights for the TM, LM, and RM are not necessarily correlated. A corpus ideally suited for training a strong TM might be suboptimal for training the RM, and vice versa. This necessitates independent estimation of mixture weights for each component. Furthermore, we propose two novel improvements to the mixture model adaptation approach: smoothing the in-domain sample to mitigate overfitting and weighting training instances by document frequency to emphasize more representative reordering patterns. We show that these techniques, particularly smoothing, lead to significant and consistent performance gains across our experiments. This work provides a critical step towards more robust and adaptable SMT systems, highlighting the importance of considering the reordering model in domain adaptation efforts. The ability to translate natural language instructions into executable code is a long-standing goal in artificial intelligence, with applications ranging from automated programming assistants to more general forms of human-computer interaction. Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence learning (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014) and neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017) have led to promising results in code generation, particularly in scenarios where the task is relatively constrained (e.g., generating SQL queries from natural language questions (Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005; Iyer et al., 2017)). However, a critical aspect of real-world programming that has received limited attention in existing work is the significant influence of *programmatic context*. Source code rarely exists in a vacuum. It is deeply interwoven with the surrounding codebase, relying on class structures, existing functions, and defined variables. The meaning of a seemingly simple instruction, such as "return the smallest element," can change drastically depending on the class it’s implemented within - does the class already have a sorting method? What data structure is used to store the elements? Existing code generation models often overlook these crucial contextual cues, operating instead on isolated instructions without access to the broader program environment. To address this gap, we introduce a novel task focused on generating class member functions given both natural language documentation *and* the programmatic context provided by the rest of the class. This setting forces models to reason about the interaction between linguistic intent and existing code, mirroring the cognitive processes involved in real-world software development. It is significantly more challenging than previous code generation tasks because the desired code is highly sensitive to the functionality already implemented within the class. To facilitate research in this area, we created CONCODE, a new large-scale dataset comprising over 100,000 Java examples sourced from publicly available code repositories. CONCODE consists of Java classes, their method documentation, and the corresponding method implementations. We then develop a new encoder-decoder architecture designed to effectively model the interplay between the method documentation and the surrounding class environment. Our architecture integrates context-aware embeddings with attention mechanisms, enabling the model to selectively focus on relevant parts of the class definition during code generation. We present comprehensive experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and providing a detailed error analysis that highlights remaining challenges and opportunities for future work. This analysis reveals that current models struggle with complex logic and require improved reasoning capabilities to generate code that seamlessly integrates with the existing class structure. The explosive growth of online opinion platforms—ranging from product reviews and social media posts to forum discussions—has created an unprecedented need for automated methods to distill this vast collection of perspectives into concise, informative summaries. Summarization techniques aim to address this challenge, broadly categorized as either extractive or abstractive. Extractive summarization identifies and concatenates salient sentences directly from the source documents, while abstractive summarization attempts to generate novel sentences that capture the core meaning of the input. While extractive methods are relatively straightforward to implement and often yield grammatically correct summaries, they frequently lack fluency and can suffer from redundancy, especially when dealing with highly repetitive opinionated text. Abstractive summarization, on the other hand, promises more human-like summaries, but remains a significantly more challenging task due to the inherent complexities of natural language generation. Existing abstractive summarization approaches largely rely on sequence-to-sequence models, often employing attention mechanisms and recurrent neural networks (Rush et al., 2015; Chopra et al., 2016). These models have demonstrated success in various summarization tasks, but often struggle with redundancy in opinionated text. User reviews, for instance, frequently contain repetitive phrases or opinions expressed in similar wording, leading to summaries that, while abstractive, are still verbose and lack conciseness. Furthermore, many approaches treat each sentence independently, failing to explicitly model the relationships between different opinions and perspectives. To address these limitations, we introduce Opinosis, a novel graph-based framework for abstractive summarization of highly redundant opinions. Opinosis constructs a graph representation of the input opinions, where nodes represent individual opinion units (e.g., clauses or phrases) and edges encode semantic relationships between them. By leveraging graph structures, Opinosis captures the underlying network of opinions, identifies key themes, and reduces redundancy during the summarization process. Unlike sequential models, the graph-based approach allows for a more holistic understanding of the opinion landscape. Specifically, Opinosis employs a two-stage process: first, it constructs a semantic graph using a novel scoring mechanism that prioritizes opinion units with high information content and strong connections to other opinions. Second, it utilizes a graph traversal algorithm to select a representative subset of nodes, which are then fed into an abstractive sentence generator to produce the final summary. This generator is based on a sequence-to-sequence model pre-trained on a large corpus of text, enabling it to generate fluent and grammatically correct summaries. We evaluate Opinosis on a dataset of user reviews and demonstrate that it generates summaries that exhibit better agreement with human-written summaries compared to a strong baseline extractive method. Furthermore, our findings indicate that Opinosis summaries are readable, reasonably well-formed, and effectively convey the major opinions expressed in the input text. This work represents a significant step towards building more effective and concise abstractive summarization systems for opinionated text. <!-- I have tried to create an introduction that is around 400-500 words, setting the context, explaining the problem, highlighting existing limitations, and introducing the proposed solution (Opinosis) along with a brief overview of its key features. -->

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has made significant progress in recent years, achieving impressive results on a variety of language pairs (Koehn et al., 2003; Chiang, 2005; Philippsen et al., 2003). However, reordering words and phrases to match the target language’s grammatical structure remains a fundamental challenge, particularly for language pairs with substantial structural differences, such as Chinese and English (Och et al., 2003; Knight et al., 2003). Traditional phrase-based SMT systems often rely on distortion models to capture these reordering phenomena, but these models are limited in their ability to generalize to long-distance reorderings or account for linguistic constraints (Koehn, 2002). More recently, hierarchical phrase-based (Hiero) translation systems (Chiang, 2005) have emerged as a powerful framework for capturing longer-range dependencies and incorporating syntactic information. Reordering constraints derived from syntactic analysis have been shown to be particularly effective in improving translation quality. Previous work has explored various approaches to incorporating syntactic reordering constraints, including tree transposition (Yamada and Knight, 2001), dependency-based reordering (Nießen and Vogel, 2009), and synchronous tree alignment (Liu et al., 2010). However, these approaches often focus on specific aspects of syntactic structure and may not generalize well to other types of reordering phenomena. They may also require complex training procedures or specialized parsing tools. In this paper, we present a unified framework for incorporating soft linguistic reordering constraints into a hierarchical phrase-based translation system. Our approach leverages two complementary models: a syntactic reordering model based on context-free grammar (CFG) rules and a semantic reordering model based on predicate-argument structures. The syntactic model captures reorderings that are motivated by changes in phrase structure, such as moving prepositional phrases or auxiliary verbs. The semantic model focuses on reorderings that are driven by the relationships between predicates and their arguments, such as moving subjects or objects to different positions in the sentence. We develop novel features based on both models and use them as soft constraints to guide the translation process. This allows the system to leverage both syntactic and semantic information without imposing rigid reordering restrictions. Experiments on Chinese-English translation demonstrate that our reordering approach can significantly improve the performance of a state-of-the-art hierarchical phrase-based translation system. However, we also observe that the gain achieved by the semantic reordering model is limited in the presence of the syntactic reordering model. We provide a detailed analysis of the behavior differences between the two models to shed light on their complementary strengths and weaknesses. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work; Section 3 describes our unified reordering model; Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results; and Section 5 concludes the paper with a discussion of future work.

Event extraction (EE) – the task of identifying event triggers and their corresponding arguments from text – is a core component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, including information retrieval, question answering, and knowledge base construction (Grishman et al., 2013;Mani, 2011). While substantial progress has been made in single event extraction (SEE) (Li et al., 2013;Miwa & Bansal, 2016), real-world text frequently contains multiple, interacting events within a single sentence. Jointly Multiple Events Extraction (JMEE) addresses this complexity, posing a significant challenge due to the intricate relationships between events and the need to disambiguate overlapping triggers and arguments. For example, consider the sentence: “After the bombing in Baghdad, the Red Cross sent a team to help the victims.” This sentence contains two events – a ‘Bombing’ and an ‘Aid’ event – which are semantically related, with the ‘victims’ argument being shared between the two events. Effectively capturing these inter-event relationships is crucial for accurate JMEE. Existing approaches to JMEE can be broadly categorized into pipeline-based methods and joint modeling methods. Pipeline methods typically perform SEE independently and then resolve conflicts or merge overlapping events (e.g., Punyageri et al., 2009). However, these methods often suffer from error propagation and fail to effectively capture the contextual dependencies between events. Joint modeling methods, on the other hand, directly attempt to model the relationships between multiple events, often leveraging sequential models like recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (e.g., Nguyen & Grishman, 2015;Xiao et al., 2017). While showing improvements over pipeline approaches, these sequential models struggle to efficiently capture long-range dependencies between distant events within a sentence. Information regarding distant events is crucial for understanding inter-event relations, especially in complex sentences. The vanishing gradient problem inherent in RNNs further exacerbates this issue. To address the limitations of existing sequential models, we propose a novel JMEE framework that leverages graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to effectively model the relationships between events. Our key idea is to construct a graph representation of the sentence, where nodes represent words and edges represent syntactic dependencies. We then introduce “syntactic shortcut arcs” to augment the dependency graph, facilitating information flow between distant nodes and enhancing the representation of long-range dependencies. Finally, we employ attention-based GCNs to aggregate information from neighboring nodes, enabling the model to selectively focus on the most relevant contextual cues for each event trigger and argument. This attention mechanism allows the model to capture the relative importance of different words and their relationships to the events being extracted. Our experiments on a benchmark JMEE dataset demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach in capturing long-range dependencies and modeling inter-event relationships. We further conduct ablation studies to validate the contribution of each component of our framework, highlighting the importance of both the syntactic shortcut arcs and the attention-based GCNs.

The historical relationships between languages – how they have diverged from common ancestors over time – are a fundamental area of study in linguistics. Reconstructing these relationships allows us to understand the migration patterns of peoples, the evolution of thought, and the deep structures underlying human language itself. A central concept in this reconstruction is that of *cognates*: words in different languages that share a common origin, stemming from a single word in their ancestor language, often referred to as a *proto-word*. Identifying cognate sets – groups of cognates across multiple languages – is therefore a crucial step in comparative linguistics. Traditionally, this has been a painstaking manual process, requiring expert knowledge of the languages involved, historical sound changes, and semantic shifts (Lehmann, 1992). The advent of large, readily available dictionaries, both in print and digital form, provides a rich resource for automated cognate detection. However, simply identifying words with similar forms is insufficient. False friends—words that *look* similar but have different meanings and origins—are common and can easily mislead automated systems. Similarly, phonetic changes over time can obscure the relationship between cognates. Previous computational approaches to cognate detection have employed a variety of techniques, ranging from simple string comparison metrics (Dyvik, 1994) to more sophisticated methods incorporating phonetic algorithms (Kondrak, 2003; Bouchard-Côté et al., 2004) and probabilistic models (List, 2012; Dunn et al., 2013). While these methods have achieved some success, they often struggle to balance precision (avoiding false positives) and recall (identifying true cognates). This work introduces a novel system for identifying cognate sets across dictionaries of related languages, designed to address these challenges. Our approach leverages a comprehensive set of features combining phonetic similarity (using the Soundex algorithm and edit distance), semantic similarity (based on word embeddings), and crucially, the presence of *regular sound correspondences* – patterns of consistent sound changes that are characteristic of language families. We hypothesize that explicitly modeling these regularities is essential for accurately identifying cognate sets. We evaluate our system on a challenging dataset derived from the Algonquian language family, a well-studied group with complex historical sound changes. Our results demonstrate that the system achieves a significant improvement over previous approaches, detecting 63% of cognate sets while maintaining a cluster purity of 70%. This work represents a step towards automating the laborious task of cognate identification and unlocking new insights into the history of human languages. Probabilistic models have become dominant in natural language processing (NLP) over the last two decades. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) (Rabiner, 1989) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Lafferty et al., 2001) are widely used for sequence labeling tasks like part-of-speech (POS) tagging and word segmentation. While probabilistic models excel at capturing statistical regularities in language, they often struggle to enforce hard linguistic constraints. For example, in English, a determiner must be followed by a noun; in Chinese, words are typically composed of characters following well-defined compositional rules. These constraints are often not adequately captured by probabilistic models trained solely on raw text, leading to occasional but noticeable errors. One approach to address this is to incorporate constraints into the decoding process. Constrained decoding aims to find the most probable sequence that *also* satisfies a given set of constraints. Earlier work in constrained decoding often relied on dynamic programming algorithms or integer linear programming (ILP) (Roth & Yih, 2004). However, naively imposing a large number of constraints can become computationally expensive, hindering practical application. Recently, there’s been growing interest in *learning* constraints directly from data (Chang et al., 2012; Smith, 2014). The key idea is to identify frequently occurring patterns in the training data and formulate them as constraints that guide the decoding process. This approach has the potential to automatically discover and enforce relevant linguistic regularities without requiring extensive manual feature engineering. In this paper, we explore the use of deterministic constraints learned from training data for two distinct sequence labeling tasks: English POS tagging and Chinese word segmentation. We demonstrate that a surprisingly large number of constraints can be effectively learned, and leveraging these constraints leads to both improved accuracy and, surprisingly, efficiency in decoding. Our approach differs in how these constraints are applied. For POS tagging, we directly integrate the learned constraints into the Viterbi decoding algorithm, enhancing its ability to find the optimal label sequence. However, applying similar character-based tagging constraints to Chinese word segmentation is less effective when implemented directly on a character-based model. Instead, we present a novel integer linear programming (ILP) formulation that allows us to effectively apply the learned constraints to a word-based segmentation model. Our results demonstrate that both approaches – constrained Viterbi decoding for English POS tagging and ILP-based constrained segmentation for Chinese – significantly outperform their unconstrained counterparts. Furthermore, we show that the constrained solutions are often more efficient than those obtained through naive exhaustive search or other constraint satisfaction techniques. This work highlights the potential of learning and incorporating deterministic constraints as a powerful technique for improving the performance and efficiency of sequence labeling models in NLP. Understanding public opinion is a crucial task with broad applications, ranging from market analysis and political campaigning to public health monitoring. With the explosion of user-generated content on platforms like social media and online review sites, automatically extracting opinions from text has become increasingly important. Traditionally, opinion mining, or sentiment analysis, focused on determining the overall polarity (positive, negative, or neutral) of a given text. However, a more nuanced understanding of opinions requires not only *what* people think, but also *who* holds the opinion, *about what* they hold it, and *how* they express it. This has led to the development of fine-grained opinion extraction (FGOE), a task focused on identifying the key components of an opinion: opinion expressions (the words or phrases expressing an opinion), opinion holders (the individuals or entities expressing the opinion), and targets (the entities or aspects that the opinion is about), as well as the relationships between these components. For example, in the sentence “John thinks the new iPhone is overpriced,” the opinion expression is “overpriced,” the opinion holder is “John,” and the target is “the new iPhone.” Identifying these elements and their relationships is significantly more complex than simply classifying the sentiment of the entire sentence. Existing approaches to FGOE have largely relied on pipelined methods. A typical pipeline might first identify opinion expressions, then identify potential opinion holders and targets, and finally link them together based on syntactic relationships or predefined rules (Wilson et al., 2006; Li et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2011). While straightforward to implement, these pipeline approaches suffer from several limitations. The primary drawback is that they treat each subtask – opinion expression extraction, opinion holder identification, target identification, and relation extraction – as independent problems, ignoring the inherent interdependencies between them. For instance, knowing the target can help identify opinion expressions (e.g., searching for adjectives near the target), and identifying the opinion holder can clarify the intended meaning of ambiguous expressions. Errors made in earlier stages of the pipeline propagate to later stages, leading to a compounded reduction in overall performance. More recently, researchers have begun to explore methods that address these subtasks individually using machine learning techniques, including Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) and Support Vector Machines (SVMs) (Li et al., 2010; Xia and Li, 2012). However, even these approaches largely maintain a pipeline structure or treat each component extraction task in isolation, failing to capture the crucial interactions between the different aspects of fine-grained opinion information. Therefore, a unified, holistic approach is needed to exploit the synergies between these interconnected subtasks. In this paper, we propose a novel joint inference model for FGOE that aims to overcome the limitations of existing pipeline-based and individual-task approaches. Our model leverages predictors trained for each subtask – opinion expression, opinion holder, and target extraction, as well as relationship classification – within a globally optimized framework. By jointly considering all components and their relationships, our approach can effectively capture the dependencies between them and achieve a more accurate and robust solution for fine-grained opinion extraction. We demonstrate through comprehensive experiments that our joint inference model significantly outperforms traditional pipeline methods and baseline approaches that tackle the subtasks in isolation.

Traditional approaches to text summarization have predominantly focused on generating static, one-size-fits-all summaries. These methods typically operate on a collection of documents and produce a single summary intended to be informative for a general audience (Mani, 2001; Nenkova & McKeown, 2012). However, this approach overlooks a crucial aspect of information consumption: user individuality. Different readers approach the same source material with distinct information needs, prior knowledge, and inherent preferences (Belkin et al., 1992). Consequently, a universal summary, while potentially comprehensive, may fail to adequately address the specific interests of individual users. This limitation motivates the development of personalized summarization techniques, aiming to tailor summaries to the unique characteristics of each reader (Allan, 2005; Li et al., 2017). Recent advances in interactive systems have opened avenues for dynamically adjusting summaries based on user feedback. Interactive summarization allows users to actively guide the summarization process through explicit signals, such as relevance judgments or query refinement (White, 2002; Zhang et al., 2007). By incorporating user interaction, these systems can generate summaries that are more focused and relevant to the user's immediate goals. However, existing interactive summarization approaches often lack a robust mechanism for modeling long-term user preferences. In this paper, we introduce the problem of Interactive Personalized Summarization (IPS), a novel task that combines the benefits of both personalization and interactivity. IPS seeks to generate summaries that dynamically adapt to user interests, learned through explicit interaction with the system. Given a set of source documents, IPS captures user preferences by observing their clicks and interactions within the resulting summaries and leverages these preferences to personalize subsequent summary generations. This process aims to mimic a natural reading experience, where a user progressively refines their understanding of a topic through iterative exploration and feedback. To investigate IPS, we develop an optimization framework and implement five competing algorithms. These algorithms are rigorously evaluated on four diverse datasets comprising a total of 5197 documents. Our experiments demonstrate that IPS achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art summarization methods in terms of ROUGE metrics. More importantly, subjective evaluations reveal significantly higher user satisfaction with summaries generated by IPS, and a low ROUGE consistency among user-preferred summaries corroborates the effectiveness of personalization. The automation of legal tasks has garnered increasing attention in recent years, driven by advancements in natural language processing and machine learning. One crucial task within this domain is charge prediction – the process of determining appropriate criminal charges given a description of the facts of a case. Accurate charge prediction can be immensely valuable for legal professionals, assisting in case evaluation, legal research, and the development of legal arguments. It also forms a core component of legal assistant systems, where a user can input a factual scenario and receive informed suggestions regarding potential charges. Traditional approaches to charge prediction often rely on expert systems and rule-based methods, requiring extensive manual effort to encode legal knowledge. More recently, machine learning techniques, particularly those based on text classification, are being explored (Krämer et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018). However, a significant challenge in this task lies in the inherent complexity and ambiguity of legal language, and the critical role of legal context in determining appropriate charges. We argue that a critical, yet often overlooked, aspect of charge prediction is the identification of *relevant legal basis* – i.e., the specific law articles that support a given charge. A charge is rarely, if ever, justified in isolation; rather, it is grounded in specific legal statutes and precedents. Consequently, accurately predicting charges requires not only understanding the factual description but also identifying the legal principles that apply to that situation. Furthermore, providing the supporting legal articles alongside the charge prediction enhances the transparency and explainability of the system, making it more trustworthy and useful for legal professionals. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to charge prediction that explicitly integrates the task of relevant article extraction. We develop an attention-based neural network model that jointly learns to predict charges and identify the corresponding legal basis. Our model leverages the relationships between the factual description of the case and the text of the relevant law articles, allowing it to capture nuanced legal reasoning and accurately determine appropriate charges. Critically, our approach frames both tasks as interdependent – the identified legal articles inform charge prediction, and conversely, the predicted charge provides context for identifying relevant articles. We evaluate our model on a real-world legal dataset, demonstrating that incorporating legal basis significantly improves charge prediction performance. Beyond simply improving accuracy, the identified articles offer valuable justification for the predicted charges and provide a clear audit trail for legal professionals. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that the model is robust to variations in case expression styles, indicating its generalizability and practical utility. This work represents a step towards more intelligent and transparent legal assistant systems, capable of providing informed and legally sound recommendations. Sentence Semantic Equivalence Identification (SSEI) – the task of determining whether two sentences convey the same meaning – is a fundamental problem in Natural Language Processing with broad applications in information retrieval, question answering, and dialogue systems. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promise in tackling SSEI tasks, yet these models often require large, high-quality datasets for effective training and evaluation. While numerous datasets exist for SSEI in English, resources for the Chinese language, particularly within specific domains, remain comparatively limited. This scarcity hinders the development and benchmarking of Chinese SSEI models, and complicates cross-lingual transfer learning efforts. Existing Chinese SSEI datasets are typically smaller in scale, often focused on general domains, or constructed through machine translation from English resources. These limitations restrict their applicability to real-world scenarios where domain specificity and nuanced linguistic properties are crucial. For example, models trained on general-domain data may struggle to accurately identify semantic equivalence within the specialized vocabulary and phrasing common in technical support interactions or financial services. To address this gap, we introduce the Bank Question (BQ) Corpus, a large-scale, domain-specific Chinese corpus specifically designed for SSEI research. The BQ Corpus comprises 120,000 question pairs extracted from one year of online logs from a major Chinese bank’s customer service platform. This focus on a single, well-defined domain – banking – allows for a more controlled evaluation of SSEI models and fosters the development of systems tailored to practical applications in the financial industry. The creation of a corpus of this size poses significant annotation challenges. Manually labeling 120,000 question pairs is both time-consuming and expensive. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel clustering-based annotation method. This approach leverages the inherent redundancy within the customer service logs, where users often express the same intent using different phrasing. We first identify and cluster similar questions based on their textual similarity, using Word Mover’s Distance (WMD) and Affinity Propagation (AP) to group questions with consistent intended meaning. Human annotators then categorize these clusters, assigning them to specific intent categories. Finally, positive and negative question pairs for SSEI are selected based on whether they fall within the same or different intent categories. We present baseline SSEI performance on the BQ Corpus utilizing several state-of-the-art algorithms, providing a benchmark for future research. As the largest publicly available, manually annotated Chinese SSEI corpus in the banking domain, the BQ Corpus provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners. It not only facilitates advancements in Chinese question semantic matching, but also serves as a foundation for cross-lingual and cross-domain SSEI studies.
