Knowledge Base Population (KBP) is a critical task in natural language processing, aiming to automatically populate knowledge bases (KBs) with facts extracted from unstructured text. Populating KBs is crucial for a wide range of applications, including question answering, information retrieval, and reasoning. The task typically involves identifying entities, relations, and their corresponding values within text, and then linking these extracted pieces of information to existing entities in a KB. Two prominent tasks within KBP are Cold Start Slot Filling (CSSF) and Tri-lingual Entity Discovery and Linking (TEDL). CSSF addresses the challenge of predicting values for slots of entities that have limited prior information in the KB – the “cold start” problem. TEDL, on the other hand, focuses on discovering new entities mentioned in text across multiple languages and linking them to existing entities in a multilingual KB. Both CSSF and TEDL represent significant challenges for NLP systems. CSSF necessitates robust generalization capabilities to infer slot values for entities with sparse KB entries, often relying on contextual clues and distant supervision. TEDL, further complicated by multilingual data, requires effective cross-lingual entity alignment and disambiguation. In recent years, a diverse range of approaches have been explored for these tasks, spanning rule-based methods, supervised machine learning models, and distant supervision techniques (Riedel et al., 2013; Mintz et al., 2009; Hoffart et al., 2011). A common strategy for improving performance on KBP tasks is to combine multiple systems, effectively leveraging the complementary strengths of different approaches. Ensembling, a technique that aggregates predictions from multiple models, has consistently demonstrated its effectiveness in various NLP tasks (Dietterich, 2000). Traditional ensembling methods include averaging predictions, weighted averaging, and stacking (Wolpert, 1992). However, designing effective ensembling strategies can be non-trivial, particularly when integrating systems with varying levels of performance and differing underlying assumptions. In this paper, we present a novel algorithm for combining supervised and unsupervised methods to ensemble multiple systems for both CSSF and TEDL. Our approach moves beyond simple averaging or stacking, and intelligently leverages the outputs of both explicitly trained systems and systems derived from unsupervised learning techniques. We demonstrate that our combined approach significantly outperforms the best system from the 2015 KBP competition, several standard ensembling baselines, and a sophisticated state-of-the-art stacking method. The consistent success across two distinct and demanding KBP tasks highlights the power and generality of our technique. This work contributes a new and effective ensembling method for KBP, showcasing the potential of strategically integrating supervised and unsupervised learning for enhanced knowledge base construction. Distributed representations of words, also known as word embeddings, have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP). Introduced initially by (Bengio et al., 2003; Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), these representations map words from a high-dimensional, sparse space (e.g., one-hot encoding) to a lower-dimensional, dense vector space. This mapping captures semantic and syntactic relationships between words, enabling effective generalization and improved performance on a plethora of NLP tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis. A key advantage of distributed representations is their ability to mitigate data sparsity issues inherent in supervised learning. Traditional methods relying on discrete features often struggle when encountering unseen or rare words. Word embeddings, trained on large amounts of unlabeled text, provide a means to represent even infrequent words within a meaningful semantic space. The effectiveness of these representations hinges on the availability of substantial unlabeled text data for training. Fortunately, such data is readily accessible for many languages, fueling the rapid adoption of word embeddings across diverse NLP applications. However, the majority of research has focused on inducing representations for individual languages in isolation. This presents a challenge for crosslingual NLP, where the goal is to leverage knowledge learned in one language to improve performance in another—particularly important for low-resource languages where labeled data is scarce. Traditional approaches to crosslingual NLP often rely on machine translation (MT) to bridge the linguistic gap. Style transfer, the task of automatically altering the stylistic characteristics of text while preserving its semantic content, has emerged as a vibrant area of research within natural language processing. This capability holds promise for a diverse range of applications, including personalized communication, text simplification, and creative writing assistance. For instance, one might wish to transform a casual online comment into a more professional email, or to adapt a complex scientific article for a broader, less technically-inclined audience. While the potential benefits are significant, progress in style transfer has been hampered by a critical bottleneck: the scarcity of well-constructed datasets, robust evaluation benchmarks, and reliable automatic metrics. Existing datasets for style transfer often focus on narrow domains or employ relatively small corpora, limiting the generalizability of learned models. Furthermore, the subjective nature of style makes evaluation particularly challenging. Human evaluation, while the gold standard, is expensive and time-consuming, hindering rapid iteration and comparison of different approaches. Automatic metrics, while offering a scalable alternative, frequently fail to correlate well with human judgments, leading to misleading conclusions about the effectiveness of style transfer systems. The specific task of formality style transfer – adapting text to be either more formal or informal – presents a particularly interesting case study. Formality impacts numerous linguistic features, including vocabulary choice, sentence structure, and the use of contractions and politeness markers. Effectively capturing these subtleties requires sophisticated modeling techniques and a comprehensive understanding of the nuances of language use in different social contexts. Previous work on formality transfer has been limited by small, often artificially constructed, datasets and a reliance on simplistic evaluation measures. To address these limitations, we introduce the GYAFC (Gentle Yet Academic Formal-Casual) dataset, the largest publicly available corpus specifically designed for formality style transfer. This dataset comprises a substantial collection of parallel sentences, each representing a pair of formal and casual stylistic variants conveying the same underlying meaning. Beyond simply providing data, we establish clear evaluation benchmarks based on both human and automatic metrics. We also critically examine the limitations of commonly used automatic metrics for assessing the quality of formality style transfer, identifying key challenges and suggesting avenues for future research. Furthermore, we demonstrate that powerful techniques originally developed for machine translation—specifically sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanisms—serve as strong, competitive baselines for formality style transfer, offering a foundation for subsequent advancements in the field. This work aims to accelerate progress in formality style transfer by providing the necessary resources and a critical framework for evaluating and comparing different approaches. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The meaning of words is far from static. While traditional lexical resources like WordNet offer a foundational understanding of word senses, they often fall short when applied to the dynamic and nuanced language used within specific communities or domains (Kulkarni et al., 2013). The same term can carry drastically different connotations and semantic weight depending on the context of its usage. For instance, the word “sick” in general English denotes illness, but within certain online communities, it's a positive expression denoting something impressive or cool. Similarly, “shade” in mainstream usage refers to partial darkness, but in online discourse, it signifies subtle, indirect disrespect. Recognizing and capturing these domain-specific semantic variations is therefore crucial for numerous NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and information retrieval. Existing approaches to address this challenge often rely on sentiment analysis techniques or the creation of domain-specific lexicons (Liu, 2012;Turney, 2002). While effective for polarity detection, these methods frequently overlook the broader spectrum of semantic dimensions beyond simply positive or negative. More sophisticated techniques leverage distributional semantics, representing words as vectors in high-dimensional space where semantic similarity is reflected in proximity (Mikolov et al., 2013;Pennington et al., 2014). However, these vector spaces often encode a general-purpose semantics, requiring adaptation or fine-tuning for specific domains. In this paper, we introduce SEMAXIS, a lightweight and intuitive framework for characterizing domain-specific word semantics. SEMAXIS departs from the reliance on single sentiment axes, instead advocating for the identification and quantification of *multiple* semantic axes within word vector spaces. The core idea is to project word embeddings onto various directions, each representing a distinct semantic dimension relevant to a particular domain or community. This allows for a much richer and more granular understanding of how word meanings shift across contexts. We demonstrate that SEMAXIS is capable of capturing nuanced semantic representations in diverse online communities, revealing subtle differences in word usage that would be missed by traditional methods. Furthermore, we show that focusing on the sentiment axis *within* the SEMAXIS framework yields superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches for building domain-specific sentiment lexicons. Our contribution lies not in developing novel embedding techniques or complex learning algorithms, but rather in offering a simple yet powerful methodology for *interpreting* and *utilizing* existing word vector representations to understand domain-specific semantic variations. We believe that SEMAXIS provides a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners seeking to bridge the gap between general language models and the specific needs of diverse applications. Paraphrase generation, the task of expressing the same meaning using different words, is a core problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from text simplification and machine translation to dialogue systems and information retrieval. Traditionally, paraphrase generation has relied on rule-based systems utilizing lexical resources like WordNet (Lavie, 2008; Ganitlar & Lam, 2009). However, these approaches often struggle with scalability and require extensive manual effort. More recently, statistical machine translation (SMT) techniques have been applied to paraphrase generation, treating the source sentence as a “foreign” language and the target paraphrase as its translation (Zhao et al., 2008; Wubben et al., 2012). While showing improvement over rule-based systems, SMT approaches are limited by their reliance on parallel corpora of paraphrases, which are scarce. The advent of deep learning, particularly sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014), has revolutionized machine translation and, subsequently, paraphrase generation. These models learn to map input sequences to output sequences, making them well-suited for generating paraphrases. However, a crucial limitation of these models is their tendency to *memorize* patterns from the training data rather than genuinely *understanding* the underlying semantics (Lipton et al., 2016). This memorization manifests as a propensity to generate grammatically correct but semantically inappropriate paraphrases—essentially, repeating phrases or structures from the training set without capturing the original sentence's meaning. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel encoder-decoder framework named the Word Embedding Attention Network (WEAN). Unlike conventional seq2seq models that predict words directly from a fixed vocabulary, WEAN generates words by *querying* distributed word representations. Specifically, the decoder uses the encoded sentence representation to query a space of pre-trained word embeddings (e.g., GloVe, Word2Vec) for words that are semantically appropriate in the context of the current decoding step. The core idea is that by operating in a continuous embedding space, the model can better capture semantic relationships and generate more meaningful paraphrases. This approach moves beyond simple word-level predictions and encourages the model to truly reason about the meaning of the words it generates. We evaluate WEAN on two prominent paraphrase-oriented tasks: text simplification and short text abstractive summarization. Text simplification aims to reduce the complexity of a sentence while preserving its meaning, while abstractive summarization generates concise summaries that capture the key information from a longer text. Our experimental results demonstrate that WEAN consistently outperforms a strong seq2seq baseline, achieving significant improvements in both BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004) scores across multiple datasets. Notably, WEAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in generating high-quality paraphrases.

Sentiment classification, the task of determining the emotional tone expressed in text, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its broad range of applications, including opinion mining, market research, and customer feedback analysis (Pang and Lee, 2008;Liu, 2012). Traditional sentiment classification approaches typically rely on supervised learning techniques trained on labeled datasets, often specific to a particular domain, such as movie reviews, product reviews, or social media posts. However, acquiring large, labeled datasets for every domain is expensive and time-consuming. This limitation motivates research into cross-domain sentiment classification, where models trained on one or more source domains are applied to a new, unseen target domain. A key challenge in cross-domain sentiment classification is domain adaptation—addressing the discrepancy between the source and target domains. This discrepancy can manifest in various forms, including differences in vocabulary, topic distribution, and sentiment expression. Several approaches have been proposed to tackle this challenge, including feature adaptation (Blitzer et al., 2006;Glorot et al., 2011), instance weighting (Dai et al., 2014), and domain-invariant representation learning (Glorot et al., 2011;Chen et al., 2013). Recently, joint sentiment-topic (JST) modeling has emerged as a promising approach for sentiment analysis (Lin and He, 2009;Morsy et al., 2014;Blei and Ng, 2009). JST models aim to simultaneously discover latent topics and sentiment orientations within a corpus, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of the underlying text structure. Importantly, many JST models require limited supervision, relying primarily on domain-independent polarity word priors – lists of words known to express positive or negative sentiment. This characteristic renders JST models particularly appealing for cross-domain scenarios where labeled data in the target domain is scarce. In this work, we build upon the Joint Sentiment-Topic (JST) framework and propose a modification that enhances its ability to extract polarity-bearing topics. We integrate word polarity priors directly into the topic-word Dirichlet priors of the JST model, effectively guiding the topic discovery process towards topics with clearly defined sentiment orientations. We hypothesize that these polarity-bearing topics capture essential aspects of sentiment expression and can improve both in-domain sentiment classification accuracy and cross-domain transfer performance. We study the topics extracted by our modified JST model and demonstrate that augmenting the original feature space with these topics significantly boosts the performance of in-domain supervised classifiers. Specifically, we achieve state-of-the-art results on a movie review dataset, and competitive performance on a multi-domain sentiment dataset. Furthermore, for cross-domain sentiment classification, we propose a feature augmentation and selection strategy based on information gain, allowing our approach to outperform or match existing techniques while maintaining simplicity and requiring minimal parameter tuning.

Dependency parsing has become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, providing a valuable structural representation for a wide range of downstream tasks including semantic role labeling (Taieb et al., 2008), relation extraction (Nivre and Nilsson, 2004), and machine translation (Nießen and Vogel, 2009). The traditional evaluation of dependency parsers, largely driven by the CoNLL shared tasks (Nivre et al., 2007; Buchholz and Marsilli, 2008), relies heavily on the Parseval metric (Black et al., 1991). While Parseval has proven useful for comparing the performance of different parsers on readily available benchmark datasets, it primarily focuses on *projective* dependencies – those where edges do not cross. This emphasis on projectivity neglects a crucial aspect of natural language: non-projectivity, manifested in unbounded dependencies. Unbounded dependencies arise when a head and one of its dependents are not locally adjacent in the sentence, and often involve long-distance relationships mediated by other constituents. These constructions, encompassing phenomena like relative clauses, wh-movement, and scrambling, are common across many languages, despite their relatively low frequency in typical corpora (Nivre et al., 2010). Consequently, standard evaluation metrics may underestimate the true parsing capability of a system, as they inadequately assess the handling of these more complex structural relationships. Existing treebanks often lack comprehensive annotation of these non-projective, unbounded dependencies, or have annotation schemes which are inconsistent with modern linguistic theory. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a novel corpus specifically designed for evaluating dependency parsers on unbounded dependencies. The corpus consists of approximately 700 sentences, meticulously annotated with seven different grammatical constructions known to elicit these dependencies, carefully chosen to represent a diverse set of linguistic phenomena. We present a benchmark evaluation of several state-of-the-art dependency parsers on this new corpus, revealing a surprisingly low performance range of 25% to 59% accuracy in recovering unbounded dependencies. These results raise serious concerns about the generalizability of Parseval scores as a comprehensive indicator of parsing performance. We further analyze the types of errors made by one of the highest performing parsers, shedding light on the specific challenges posed by these constructions. By highlighting the limitations of current parsing technology in handling unbounded dependencies, this work aims to stimulate further research into robust and accurate parsing models capable of capturing the full structural complexity of natural language. Understanding and improving the parsing of these constructions is crucial not only for theoretical linguistic understanding, but also for building more reliable and accurate NLP applications. The corpus and analysis presented here offer a valuable resource for researchers in this area. The demand for automated writing assistance tools has grown significantly with the increasing number of non-native English speakers participating in global communication. A key component of such tools is the ability to automatically detect and correct grammatical errors in learner writing. While substantial progress has been made in the development of such systems, challenges remain, specifically in achieving robustness and accuracy when dealing with the varied and often unpredictable errors produced by language learners (Polio, 2010). Traditional approaches to grammatical error correction (GEC) often rely on large, natively written corpora to build language models (LM) or train error-specific classifiers. Language models, for example, can identify grammatically implausible sequences by assigning low probabilities to incorrect phrases. Similarly, classifiers can be trained to recognize specific error types, such as incorrect article usage or preposition choices (Lee & Seneff, 2004). However, these approaches can struggle to generalize to the unique error patterns exhibited by learners, which often differ substantially from the types of errors found in native writing. Learners frequently make errors rooted in their L1 interference, overgeneralization of rules, or a lack of understanding of nuanced grammatical concepts, mistakes rarely seen in native speech or writing. Recent work has explored the use of error-annotated learner corpora for GEC (Foster et al., 2011; Han et al., 2013). However, the creation of such corpora is a time-consuming and expensive process, limiting the amount of training data available. This paper investigates a novel meta-classification approach that aims to bridge the gap between leveraging the abundance of natively written data and effectively adapting to the characteristics of learner writing. Our core idea is to combine the strengths of both language models and error-specific classifiers, trained primarily on native data, with a meta-classifier trained on a smaller corpus of error-annotated learner data. The language model and classifiers serve as feature extractors, providing evidence regarding the likelihood of various corrections, while the meta-classifier learns to optimally weight and combine this evidence to make accurate error detection and correction decisions specifically for learner writing. We focus specifically on two common error types—article and preposition errors—and evaluate our approach on a large, publicly available corpus of learner English. We compare the performance of our meta-classification approach to two baselines: a traditional language model approach and a system relying solely on error-specific classifiers. Our results demonstrate that the meta-classification approach consistently outperforms both baselines, achieving substantial gains in both error detection and correction accuracy. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the size of the error-annotated learner corpus used to train the meta-classifier, determining the minimum amount of data required to observe significant improvements in performance. This investigation provides valuable insights into the trade-off between annotation cost and system accuracy, guiding future efforts in the development of effective GEC systems for non-native speakers. Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) remain a cornerstone of natural language parsing, offering a principled framework for modeling syntactic structure (Charniak, 2001). However, learning accurate PCFGs from treebanks is notoriously difficult, particularly for languages with complex, long-distance dependencies. The automatically induced latent variable grammars of Petrov et al. (2006) offer a compelling alternative, framing the PCFG learning problem as an instance of unsupervised parameter estimation. These grammars utilize a latent variable to model the ambiguity inherent in natural language, effectively smoothing parameter estimates and improving generalization. While demonstrably effective, a critical observation remains largely unexplored: the latent variable grammars learned via Expectation-Maximization (EM) are sensitive to initialization. Different random seeds during initialization lead to significantly different learned grammars, each representing a plausible, but distinct, model of the underlying syntactic structure. This sensitivity presents a significant challenge. Which grammar is “best”? Relying on a single, arbitrarily chosen grammar may result in suboptimal performance, failing to fully capture the nuances of the language. In this paper, we leverage this inherent variability to our advantage. Instead of selecting a single “best” grammar, we propose a novel approach: combining multiple automatically learned grammars into an unweighted product model. The intuition is that each grammar, while potentially flawed in isolation, captures a unique aspect of the syntactic structure. By combining them, we can mitigate the weaknesses of individual grammars and achieve a more robust and accurate parsing model. Our approach is remarkably simple. We estimate the probability of a constituent by taking the product of posterior probabilities obtained from multiple grammars, each learned with a different random seed. Crucially, we do *not* introduce any learning or tuning of combination weights. The model is entirely non-parametric, relying solely on the diversity of the independently learned grammars. This simplicity belies the effectiveness of our approach. We demonstrate substantial improvements on both English and German parsing tasks. Specifically, a product of eight automatically learned grammars improves parsing accuracy from 90.2% to 91.8% on English, and from 80.3% to 84.5% on German, establishing a new state-of-the-art for these languages using the latent variable grammar formalism. These results highlight the benefits of embracing the inherent stochasticity of the EM algorithm and demonstrate the power of combining diverse models, even without explicit optimization. N-gram language models (LMs) are a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, serving as crucial components in a wide range of applications, including speech recognition (Jelinek, 1976), machine translation (Brown et al., 1993), and text generation (Rosenblatt, 2011). At their core, these models estimate the probability of a sequence of words, allowing systems to predict the likelihood of various continuations given a context. However, the efficacy of N-gram LMs is inextricably linked to the size of the corpus used for training. As the training corpus grows – a trend driven by the increasing availability of text data – the size of the language model itself swells dramatically. This growth in model size poses significant challenges, particularly in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices or embedded systems. Large models demand substantial memory for storage, and their computational complexity can hinder real-time performance. Traditional implementations of N-gram LMs often rely on tree-based structures, like tries or suffix trees, to efficiently store and retrieve N-gram probabilities. However, these structures can become excessively large as the vocabulary size and N-gram order increase. Recent research has explored alternative data structures and compression techniques to mitigate these issues. For example, quantitative variable precision (QVP) (Goodman, 2001) and Bloom filters (Bloom, 1970) have been employed to reduce model size, although they may introduce approximation errors. Weighted finite-state transducers (WFSTs) (Mohri, 1997) offer a powerful framework for representing and composing LMs, but can be complex to implement and manage. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to N-gram LM implementation based on double-array structures. Double-array structures, initially developed for representing dictionaries (Nakano and Bunke, 1995), offer a compact and efficient representation of sequential data. We leverage this structure to build a representation of backwards suffix trees, exploiting its inherent efficiency to minimize model size and accelerate query speeds. Beyond the core representation, we introduce two key optimization methods. The first method embeds N-gram probabilities directly into unused spaces within the double-array structure, effectively minimizing external storage requirements. The second optimization dynamically tunes word IDs within the language model, further compacting the representation and enhancing query performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to construct large-scale language models using a division method, enabling scalability to massive datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach, utilizing both optimization techniques, significantly outperforms existing methods—including those based on recent related works—in terms of both model size and query speed. This improvement is critical for deploying N-gram LMs in resource-limited scenarios and unlocking the potential of large-scale language modeling. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Understanding how the meanings of words evolve over time – a phenomenon known as semantic shift – is a core problem in historical linguistics, cognitive science, and increasingly, computational linguistics. The study of semantic shift provides insights into cultural change, the dynamics of language use, and the cognitive processes underlying meaning construction. Traditionally, historical linguists have relied on meticulous manual analysis of texts across different time periods to trace these changes (Haspelmath, 2004). However, the advent of large historical corpora has opened up new avenues for investigating semantic shift using quantitative methods. Diachronic distributional semantics (Michel et al., 2005; Hamilton et al., 2016) has emerged as a prominent approach in this domain. These models leverage the distributional hypothesis – the idea that words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings – but extend it to consider context *across time*. By analyzing changes in a word’s distributional profile over time, researchers can identify shifts in its semantic usage. Early work often involved comparing distributional representations at discrete time slices, analyzing changes in nearest neighbors, or modeling word embeddings as time series (Hamilton et al., 2016). However, existing approaches face several limitations. Treating time as discrete can lead to a loss of information about the gradual nature of semantic change. Modeling semantic shifts as time series requires careful selection of time intervals and can struggle to capture non-linear changes. Moreover, evaluating the performance of diachronic models and quantitatively assessing their ability to capture the intricacies of semantic trajectories has proven challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel deep neural network framework for modeling semantic shift. Our approach departs from traditional time series modeling by representing time as a *continuous* variable and modeling a word’s usage as a function of time. Specifically, we employ a neural network that maps a word’s context to a latent semantic space, while simultaneously incorporating temporal information to predict the semantic representation at any given point in time. This allows us to capture nuanced and potentially non-linear patterns of semantic change. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we introduce a new synthetic task designed to specifically measure a model’s ability to reconstruct the semantic trajectory of a word. This task allows us to quantitatively assess how well our model captures the dynamic evolution of word meaning. Beyond simply detecting change, our model provides a continuous representation of semantic space across time, opening possibilities for analyzing the *speed* of lexical change. We investigate whether the derivatives of our model’s output can be meaningfully correlated with the rate at which a word’s meaning is shifting. Through experiments, we demonstrate that our deep neural model consistently outperforms existing diachronic distributional models on our novel synthetic task, and shows promising results in capturing known patterns of semantic shift in historical text. These findings highlight the potential of deep learning to provide a more nuanced and accurate understanding of how language evolves over time. --- I've aimed for a length and style suitable for an ACL paper introduction - providing context, outlining current limitations, explicitly stating the contribution, and hinting at the results.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has remained the dominant paradigm in machine translation for over a decade (Koehn et al., 2003). Phrase-based SMT (Koehn et al., 2003; Marcu et al., 2006) specifically, has proven remarkably effective, leveraging phrases as the fundamental unit of translation, and achieving state-of-the-art results for many language pairs. However, a fundamental limitation of phrase-based systems lies in the independence assumption amongst phrases. Each phrase is modeled independently of its surrounding context, hindering the system's ability to capture long-range dependencies and leading to disfluent or inaccurate translations, especially when dealing with complex sentence structures or ambiguous words. Recent advances in neural network modeling have demonstrated significant potential for addressing the shortcomings of SMT (Cho et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), in particular, excel at processing sequential data and capturing contextual information. Sequence-to-sequence models with attention mechanisms have achieved compelling results, often surpassing phrase-based systems in terms of translation fluency. However, these end-to-end neural machine translation (NMT) systems still grapple with challenges related to rare words and the ability to effectively leverage existing phrase tables painstakingly constructed over years of research. In this work, we aim to bridge the gap between the strengths of phrase-based SMT and the contextual modeling capabilities of RNNs. We propose a Recurrent Neural Network-based Tuple Sequence Model (RNNTSM) designed to augment traditional phrase-based systems. RNNTSM models bilingual tuples—pairs of phrases and their translations—in a continuous space, allowing the system to capture contextual dependencies between tuples during translation. By representing tuples as vectors, we allow the model to generalize to unseen tuple combinations and learn more nuanced translation probabilities. However, the modeling of tuples introduces a significant data sparsity problem. The space of possible bilingual tuples is vast, while the amount of available parallel training data is often limited. This sparsity hinders the effective training of RNNTSM and limits its ability to generalize. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce two key improvements. First, we propose a factorization of the bilingual tuples into independent source and target representations, drastically reducing the number of parameters and improving generalization. Second, we decompose phrasal tuples into word-level representations, further refining the model and providing richer contextual information. Our experiments on the IWSLT2012 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Compared to state-of-the-art phrase-based systems and RNN language models, our RNNTSM consistently achieves significant improvements in translation quality, as measured by BLEU score. Understanding the impact of central bank communication on financial markets has become increasingly important in recent decades. In particular, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) – the monetary policymaking body of the Federal Reserve System – has adopted a more transparent approach to communication, releasing detailed statements following each meeting, as well as minutes and transcripts of those meetings. This increased transparency is predicated on the idea that clear communication can shape market expectations, and thereby enhance the effectiveness of monetary policy (Bernanke, 2004; Yellen, 2015). However, precisely *how* the content of FOMC communications affects market behavior remains a subject of active research. Early work focused on the impact of changes in the *tone* of FOMC statements, often employing ‘dichotomous word counts’ – counting the occurrences of optimistic versus pessimistic words (Ehrmann and Fratzscher, 2006; Pyun et al., 2008). More recently, researchers have employed more sophisticated text analysis techniques, including topic modeling, to identify the underlying themes discussed in FOMC communications and assess their influence on asset prices (Lustig et al., 2011; Lai and Morse, 2015). While these studies have demonstrated a link between FOMC statements and market movements, many rely on relatively broad measures of textual content and may not fully capture the nuanced relationship between specific policy signals and specific segments of the yield curve. A key challenge in this line of inquiry lies in the fact that FOMC communications are multifaceted, addressing a range of economic conditions, policy objectives, and potential future actions. The words and phrases relevant to influencing short-term interest rate expectations are likely to differ from those that affect longer-term rates. For example, signals regarding the immediate path of the Federal Funds Rate will directly impact short-term Treasury yields, while discussions of long-run economic growth and inflation expectations are more likely to influence longer-term yields. Consequently, a unified topical structure applied to all maturities may obscure important distinctions and reduce predictive power. This paper addresses this limitation by adopting a supervised learning approach to identify distinct sets of topics relevant to different segments of the yield curve. Specifically, we learn topic models tailored to predict movements in the Target and Effective Federal Funds Rates, as well as in longer-term Treasury rates. We utilize a dataset spanning the period from 1999 to 2016, covering a period of significant monetary policy shifts and evolving communication practices. We generate predictive models both with and without controlling for other macroeconomic and market factors known to influence interest rate movements, providing a robust assessment of the incremental contribution of FOMC communication content. Our results demonstrate high predictive accuracy – averaging 93% and 64% for short-term rates, and 38%-40% for longer-term rates – highlighting the significant information contained within FOMC communications and the value of a disaggregated, supervised approach to its analysis.

Vector space models (VSMs) have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP), enabling a wealth of applications from information retrieval to machine translation (Manning et al., 2008). These models represent words as dense vectors in a high-dimensional space, where semantic similarity is mirrored by closeness in vector space—i.e., words used in similar contexts tend to have similar vector representations (Pennington et al., 2014; Mikolov et al., 2013). However, a fundamental limitation of standard VSMs is their inability to effectively differentiate between synonymous and antonymous relationships. In a purely distributional setting, words appearing in opposing contexts (e.g., “good” and “bad”) can exhibit high vector space similarity due to the shared presence of certain words (e.g., modifiers such as "very", "not"). This limitation hinders tasks requiring nuanced semantic understanding, such as sentiment analysis and text classification. Existing approaches to address this problem often involve incorporating external lexical resources, such as WordNet (Miller, 1995), into VSMs. These methods typically augment the vector representation of a word with information about its synsets and hypernyms, or use lexical relations to refine similarity measures. However, such approaches can be limited by the coverage and accuracy of the external resource, and may struggle to capture subtle semantic distinctions not explicitly encoded in the lexicon. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic word clustering that leverages the strengths of both distributional and lexical information. We cast the problem as a signed spectral clustering task, where edges between words in a graph are weighted based on both their distributional similarity (positive weights) and their antonymous relationship (negative weights). This allows us to simultaneously capture synonymy and antonymy, leading to more coherent and informative word clusters. Specifically, we introduce a “signed clustering” algorithm that overlays existing thesauri—providing information about antonyms—onto distributionally derived vector representations of words. This creates a signed graph, where positive edge weights represent semantic similarity, and negative weights represent opposition. The core of our approach is a new signed spectral normalized graph cut algorithm tailored to this signed graph structure. We effectively extend standard spectral clustering techniques to handle negative edge weights, resulting in clusters that reflect both semantic relatedness and opposition. Furthermore, we employ randomized spectral decomposition (Halko et al., 2011) and sparse matrix representations to ensure that our method is both fast and scalable to large vocabularies. We validate our approach on standard datasets of human judgments of word pair similarities, demonstrating that our method consistently outperforms existing techniques. We further demonstrate the utility of our word clusters for sentiment prediction, showing that incorporating our clusters as features improves sentiment classification accuracy. Our contributions are thus threefold: (1) we propose a novel signed spectral clustering framework for semantic word clustering, (2) we introduce a new algorithm for signed spectral normalized graph cuts, and (3) we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation tasks.

The ability to understand and execute natural language instructions is a cornerstone of intelligent systems. While significant progress has been made in areas like speech recognition and natural language understanding, a critical gap remains in bridging the semantic gap between human intention, expressed as high-level instructions, and the concrete actions required to fulfill that intention within a dynamic environment. Consider the simple instruction: “Bring me the book on the table.” A human effortlessly understands this instruction, recognizing the implicit sub-goals – locating the table, identifying the book, navigating to the book, grasping the book, and transporting it to the speaker – and the appropriate sequence of actions to achieve them. However, for a robotic agent or software assistant, directly translating this instruction into a sequence of executable commands is a substantial challenge. Existing approaches to instruction following often rely on pre-defined templates or hand-crafted rules that map specific keywords to predefined actions. These methods, while effective in limited domains, struggle with the inherent flexibility and ambiguity of natural language. Furthermore, they necessitate extensive manual effort to adapt to new environments or tasks. Statistical machine translation techniques, treating instructions as source language and commands as target language, have shown promise, but they typically require large parallel corpora of instruction-command pairs – a resource that is often unavailable or expensive to create. Crucially, these methods lack the ability to *reason* about the environment and infer the missing steps necessary to achieve a given goal. The core difficulty lies in the fact that high-level instructions typically specify *what* needs to be done, not *how*. They leave unstated the necessary preconditions, intermediate steps, and the effects of actions within the environment. To bridge this gap, a system must possess an internal model of the environment that allows it to predict the consequences of its actions and plan a sequence of commands that will lead to the desired outcome. In this paper, we present a novel approach to mapping high-level instructions to commands that addresses these challenges. Our method learns to infer missing information by constructing an *environment model* – a probabilistic representation of the states, transitions, and commands within a given environment. This model is learned automatically from interactions with the environment, eliminating the need for manual specification. We integrate this learned environment model into a policy gradient reinforcement learning framework for text interpretation, enabling the agent to learn a policy that maps instructions to optimal command sequences. This approach allows the agent to handle high-level instructions even without explicit instruction-command pairings, a capability that distinguishes it from many existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a simulated task, showcasing its ability to learn complex policies from minimal supervision. Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) (Banarescu et al., 2013) is a semantic representation designed to capture the meaning of a sentence in a graph-based format. Unlike traditional syntactic parse trees, AMR focuses on “who is doing what to whom,” representing concepts as nodes and semantic relations as directed edges. This rich semantic structure makes AMR a valuable resource for a variety of natural language processing tasks, including machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. However, automatically constructing AMR graphs from raw text is a challenging problem. The task requires not only accurate syntactic analysis but also a deep understanding of semantic roles and relationships. Early approaches to AMR parsing relied heavily on feature engineering and complex graph alignment techniques (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2000; Kyle and Van Genuchten, 2008). These approaches often struggled to scale to large datasets and suffered from limited generalization ability. More recently, neural network models have shown promising results in AMR parsing (Li et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016). However, these models often require significant amounts of labeled AMR data for effective training, and achieving high accuracy remains a considerable challenge. Furthermore, many neural approaches still treat AMR parsing as a direct graph construction problem, neglecting the strong connection between syntactic structure and semantic representation. We argue that leveraging syntactic information can significantly improve AMR parsing performance. Sentences possess an underlying syntactic structure that inherently reflects semantic relationships. Dependency parsing, a well-established NLP task, provides a relatively accurate and readily available representation of this syntactic structure. Consequently, we propose a two-stage framework for AMR parsing that separates the syntactic analysis stage from the semantic graph construction stage. In this paper, we present a novel approach that utilizes a dependency parser to generate an intermediate syntactic representation, followed by a transition-based algorithm to transform this dependency tree into an AMR graph. The key insight behind our approach is that by decoupling syntactic and semantic processing, we can benefit from the advancements in both fields. Specifically, we can train a high-performance dependency parser on a large corpus of syntactically annotated data – much larger than the available AMR training data – and then focus on learning a targeted transformation from the dependency tree to the AMR graph. This two-stage framework not only improves the overall parsing accuracy but also allows for a more linguistically informed design of the transition system. Our experiments demonstrate a 5% absolute improvement in F-measure over the previously reported state-of-the-art results, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficiency of our transition-based algorithm, which operates in nearly linear time despite a theoretical quadratic worst-case complexity. This paper makes the following contributions: (1) We propose a novel two stage framework for AMR parsing that leverages the strengths of dependency parsing and transition-based graph construction. (2) We design a linguistically motivated transition system that effectively transforms dependency trees into AMR graphs. (3) We demonstrate a significant performance improvement over existing AMR parsing methods, achieving a new state-of-the-art result on the benchmark dataset.

The automatic generation of concise and informative summaries, particularly in the form of headlines, remains a challenging problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP). News headlines serve a critical function: to distill the core meaning of an article (or collection of articles) into a succinct and engaging phrase. Traditional approaches to headline generation have largely fallen into two categories: extractive and abstractive. Extractive methods (e.g., Lead-3, Goldberg et al., 2010) simply select existing phrases from the source text, offering simplicity and fluency but often lacking the ability to truly *abstract* the key information. Abstractive methods, on the other hand, aim to paraphrase and re-write the content, potentially producing more informative and fluent headlines, but at the cost of increased complexity and a greater risk of grammatical errors or semantic incoherence (Rush et al., 2015; Chopra et al., 2016). Recent advances in neural sequence-to-sequence models have yielded promising results for abstractive summarization (See et al., 2017; Nallapati et al., 2017), including headline generation. However, these methods often require large, parallel corpora of articles and corresponding human-generated headlines for training, a resource often unavailable or costly to create, particularly for rapidly evolving news topics. Furthermore, open-domain abstractive models struggle with factual consistency and frequently generate generic or uninformative headlines (Kryściński et al., 2019). In this paper, we introduce HEADY (Headline Abstraction through Event pattern clustering), a novel abstractive approach for headline generation that leverages a large-scale corpus of news data *without* requiring paired article-headline examples. Our core idea is to identify and cluster recurring *event patterns* present within news collections, and then use these patterns to generate succinct headlines. Unlike many existing abstractive methods that directly model the mapping from article text to headline, HEADY operates at a higher level of abstraction, focusing on the underlying semantic events described in the news. We mine syntactic patterns from a web-scale news corpus and generalize them into event descriptions using a Noisy-OR model. At inference time, given a new collection of news articles, we query this model with the patterns observed in the collection, identifying the event that best characterizes the overall narrative. Finally, we retrieve the most appropriate syntactic pattern associated with that event to construct a headline. Our approach offers several key advantages. First, it bypasses the need for large, parallel training datasets, making it suitable for low-resource scenarios. Second, by operating at the event level, HEADY is able to capture the gist of a collection of articles more effectively than methods that focus solely on individual documents. Third, the reliance on syntactic patterns ensures that generated headlines are generally fluent and grammatical. We demonstrate through comprehensive evaluations on multiple datasets that HEADY significantly improves upon a state-of-the-art open-domain title abstraction method, and achieves performance comparable to human-generated headlines as measured by ROUGE metrics.

Understanding the structure of text is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing. While content-based approaches have dominated much of the field, focusing on the semantic meaning of words and phrases, a growing body of work recognizes the importance of *structural* cues in determining how humans understand and process text (Mann and Thompson, 1988;Halliday and Hasan, 1976). These cues, often manifested in rhetorical relationships between sentences and paragraphs, provide a scaffolding for interpretation, enabling readers to navigate and comprehend even lengthy and complex documents. Traditional methods for analyzing text structure, such as Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988), require extensive manual annotation, are computationally expensive, and don’t scale effectively to large corpora. Consequently, automated techniques for identifying and leveraging structural information remain a significant area of research. Existing approaches to identifying important textual units often rely on content-driven metrics like Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) (Robertson, 2004). While TF-IDF effectively captures the statistical importance of words in a corpus, it fundamentally overlooks the role of structural features. A word might frequently appear in a document, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s structurally important—it might simply be a common function word or a frequently used topic-specific term. Similarly, while topic modeling (Blei et al., 2003) can uncover latent thematic structure, it rarely explicitly models the rhetorical relationships that organize a text. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to measuring structural importance, termed the Rhetorical Structure Index (RSI). RSI aims to identify words and phrases that act as structural cues within a document, independent of their specific semantic content. Our core idea is that words or phrases that consistently appear at the beginning or end of segments, or in positions that signal transitions in thought, are likely to be structurally important. Unlike TF-IDF, RSI doesn’t depend on term frequency or document prevalence, but instead focuses on positional patterns within the text. We hypothesize that these structurally motivated features are more informative for tasks requiring understanding of document organization – such as segmenting unstructured lecture transcripts into coherent sections. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RSI through experiments on the task of lecture transcript segmentation. Lecture transcripts, often lacking clear formatting or explicit section headings, present a particularly challenging test case for structural analysis. We show that incorporating RSI features significantly improves segmentation accuracy compared to using TF-IDF features alone. This improvement suggests that explicitly modeling structural cues can overcome the limitations of purely content-based approaches, offering a more robust and accurate means of understanding the underlying organization of unstructured text. Our results highlight the value of attending to the “how” of writing—the rhetorical structure—in addition to the “what” of writing—the content itself. These initial findings pave the way for further exploration into the broader applications of RSI and the development of more sophisticated techniques for extracting and utilizing structural information from text.

Computational Argumentation Mining (AM) is the task of automatically identifying and analyzing argumentative structures within text. This burgeoning field draws from natural language processing, artificial intelligence, and logic, offering potential applications in areas ranging from legal reasoning and policy analysis to online debate moderation and persuasive technology. Historically, approaches to AM have relied heavily on hand-engineered features derived from linguistic theory and argumentation schemes (e.g., Toulmin’s model of argument – Toulmin, 1958). These features often target the identification of argument components – claims, premises, and their relationships – and require significant domain expertise to design and implement effectively. More recent work has explored machine learning techniques, including support vector machines and conditional random fields, leveraging features such as lexical cues, syntactic patterns, and discourse relations (e.g., Habernal and Gabel, 2016; Lauscher et al., 2013). However, these methods still largely depend on carefully crafted feature sets. The success of deep learning in various NLP tasks has spurred a growing interest in applying neural networks to AM. Initial efforts focused on representing arguments as distributed vectors and employing these embeddings for classification tasks (e.g., Niculae and Banea, 2017). However, these approaches often operate at the argument component level, requiring a pre-defined segmentation of the text into claims and premises, a task in itself prone to error. Furthermore, they may struggle to capture the intricate relationships between argumentative elements and the long-range dependencies inherent in complex arguments. In this paper, we explore the potential of neural end-to-end learning for AM, moving away from feature engineering and component-level analysis. We investigate two distinct neural formulations: framing AM as a token-based dependency parsing problem and as a token-based sequence tagging problem. The dependency parsing approach attempts to directly model the hierarchical relationships between argument components, leveraging the expressive power of graph-based neural networks. Conversely, the sequence tagging approach frames AM as a classification task, assigning labels to individual tokens indicating their argumentative role. We hypothesize that a more localized, sequence-based approach might prove more robust, given the challenges of capturing long-range dependencies and complex structural information with current neural architectures. Our experiments reveal a surprising result: framing AM as dependency parsing, despite its theoretical appeal, leads to suboptimal performance. In contrast, simpler BiLSTM-based sequence tagging models demonstrate robust performance across various AM classification scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a multi-task learning setup, incorporating auxiliary ‘natural’ subtasks, further enhances the performance of these models. This suggests that leveraging related linguistic information can provide valuable inductive biases for learning argumentative structures. This work therefore presents a compelling case for shifting focus towards more localized, sequence-based neural models for computational argumentation mining, paving the way for more effective and scalable AM systems. Large Vocabulary Continuous Speech Recognition (LVCSR) systems have reached a remarkable level of accuracy in recent years (Schuster et al., 2013; Hinton et al., 2012). However, performance still suffers considerably when encountering words not present in the system's vocabulary – so-called Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) words. These OOV words are a persistent challenge, arising from proper nouns, newly coined terms, misspellings, and diverse accents, amongst other sources. Recognition errors on OOV words don’t exist in isolation; they propagate through downstream Natural Language Understanding (NLU) components, significantly degrading the performance of end-to-end applications such as dialog systems, information retrieval, and voice search (Hain et al., 2015; Scherer et al., 2018). Therefore, robust OOV detection is vital for building reliable speech-enabled systems. Traditionally, OOV detection has been approached as a binary classification problem: for each hypothesized word or word region in the ASR output, a classifier determines whether it represents an OOV word or not (Fiscus, 1997; Lai et al., 2012). These classifiers typically leverage acoustic features, language model scores, and lexical features – effectively relying on *local* information about the hypothesized word itself. While effective to a degree, this localized approach overlooks crucial contextual cues that can indicate the presence of an OOV word. For instance, a word preceded by “newly appointed” or following “Dr.” is more likely to be an OOV term. Recent work has explored incorporating contextual information into OOV detection, primarily through recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Karaoğlu et al., 2017). However, these methods often treat OOV detection as an independent task for each word region, without explicitly modeling the dependencies *between* regions. We hypothesize that jointly predicting OOV regions, and explicitly leveraging contextual information from neighboring regions, provides a more holistic and accurate solution. In this paper, we present a novel approach to OOV detection that addresses these limitations. We formulate OOV detection as a sequence labeling problem, employing a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network to model the relationships between consecutive hypothesized word regions. Crucially, we augment the BiLSTM with rich contextual features derived from the surrounding speech and text, allowing the model to make informed decisions based on a broader understanding of the utterance. Through experiments on a challenging benchmark dataset, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art OOV detection systems, reducing the missed OOV rate by a substantial margin while maintaining a reasonable false alarm rate. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 details our proposed model. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

The burgeoning availability of data from online social media platforms has opened up exciting new avenues for understanding human behavior, both online and offline. This data provides a unique window into individual preferences, interests, and lifestyles, offering unprecedented opportunities for both academic research and commercial applications. In particular, the ability to accurately predict user attributes – such as demographics, personality traits, and, crucially, spending habits – holds significant value for diverse areas, ranging from social science analysis to targeted marketing and personalized recommendations. A particularly compelling application lies in the realm of consumer behavior, where predicting a user’s propensity to spend, or their consumption level, can inform restaurant marketing strategies, optimize resource allocation, and enhance customer experiences. Existing research has explored the correlation between online activity and various offline behaviors. Studies have demonstrated the predictive power of social media data for attributes like political affiliation (Bakshy et al., 2015), personality traits (Youyou et al., 2015), and even health risks (Eichstaedt et al., 2018). However, predicting actual monetary spending, particularly in a specific domain like restaurant consumption, remains a significant challenge. Often, research relies on aggregated and anonymized transaction data, lacking the richness of individual user profiles and lacking the link to expressed preferences and opinions. Furthermore, limited work has focused on leveraging the unique characteristics of social media platforms prevalent in different cultural contexts. This paper addresses the gap by presenting a systematic approach for predicting restaurant consumption level using user-generated content from two popular Chinese platforms: Dianping and Sina Weibo. Dianping is a widely used platform for restaurant reviews and recommendations, akin to Yelp, while Sina Weibo is a microblogging service similar to Twitter. Crucially, we leverage the increasingly common practice of “social login,” which allows users to seamlessly connect their accounts across different platforms, providing a valuable bridge between online social expression and offline spending behavior. By exploiting this connection, we create a unique dataset of 8,844 users linked across Dianping and Sina Weibo, complemented by self-reported consumption data on Dianping. Our methodology focuses on both raw textual features from Weibo posts, and, importantly, latent features extracted using topic modeling and celebrity cluster analysis. We hypothesize that users’ expressed interests, topical concerns, and social connections provide valuable signals regarding their offline spending habits. We demonstrate that online social media content possesses substantial predictive power for offline spending, achieving strong performance with various predictive models. Beyond the quantitative results, we provide a qualitative analysis of feature importance, revealing specific differences in language usage, topical interests, and following behavior across different consumption level groups, offering valuable insights into the link between online expression and real-world spending patterns. The WordNet lexicon (Fellbaum, 1998) has long served as a cornerstone resource for natural language processing, providing a structured representation of lexical semantics through synonym sets (synsets) linked by semantic relations such as hypernymy (is-a) and meronymy (part-of). However, even this extensive resource is inherently incomplete. The lexicon lacks coverage for emerging concepts, particularly those arising in specialized domains, and often suffers from a lack of fine-grained attributes that would allow for more nuanced semantic understanding. Manually extending WordNet remains a labor-intensive and expensive process, necessitating the development of automated approaches. Previous efforts to augment WordNet have explored a range of techniques, often relying on distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics (Lin et al., 1998; Pantel and Hovy, 2003; Gabrilovich and Markovitch, 2007). These approaches typically identify potential attributes – or “properties” – based on patterns observed in large text corpora. For instance, one method might identify “has_color: red” as an attribute of “apple” by observing frequent co-occurrence of those terms. While successful to a degree, these heuristic methods often struggle with precision, generating numerous irrelevant or noisy attribute suggestions. A fundamental limitation is the reliance on surface-level co-occurrence, without a robust probabilistic framework to model the underlying relationship between concepts and attributes. In this paper, we address the problem of concept-attribute attachment by introducing a suite of Bayesian models based on Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003). LDA has proven remarkably effective in topic modeling, uncovering latent semantic structure in text collections. We leverage this capability to model the relationship between WordNet concepts and a broad range of potential attributes, framing the problem as one of discovering latent topics that connect concepts to their properties. Our models allow us to both rank candidate attributes for a given concept – providing a prioritized list for potential manual review – and directly assign attributes to concepts with associated probabilities. We evaluate our approach along two key dimensions: the precision of the ranked attribute lists, and the overall quality of the learned attribute assignments to WordNet concepts. By comparing our LDA-based methods against previously proposed heuristic approaches (Pantel and Hovy, 2003), we demonstrate substantial improvements in both areas. Specifically, our results indicate that the probabilistic modeling inherent in LDA leads to a significant increase in the specificity of attributes associated with each concept, enabling a more nuanced and informative extension of the WordNet ontology. Statistical machine translation (SMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, largely driven by the phrase-based approach (Koehn et al., 2003). These systems learn to translate phrases – sequences of words – from a source language to a target language, composing the final translation from these learned phrase pairs. However, a key limitation of standard phrase-based SMT, particularly when translating *into* morphologically rich languages, is the issue of data sparsity (Knight et al., 1999;Nelken & Yarowsky, 2005). Morphologically rich languages, such as Arabic, Turkish, and Finnish, generate a large number of distinct word forms from a relatively small number of morphemes. This leads to a combinatorial explosion of possible word forms in the target language, which standard SMT models struggle to adequately represent due to insufficient parallel training data. A common approach to alleviate this sparsity is morphological segmentation (Creutz & Lagus, 2005;Popović & Ney, 2015), where words are broken down into their constituent morphemes. This dramatically reduces the vocabulary size and allows the model to generalize more effectively to unseen word forms. However, introducing segmentation also necessitates a *desegmentation* step – reassembling the morphemes into surface-level words – to produce fluent, readable output. Traditionally, this desegmentation is performed as a post-processing step, typically using a 1-best segmentation approach (e.g., using Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation). While conceptually simple, this post-hoc desegmentation introduces several drawbacks. Firstly, it restricts the search space during decoding, preventing the decoder from exploring alternative segmentations that might lead to a better overall translation. Secondly, the decoder is unable to directly optimize for the quality of the final, desegmented output, as the scoring function only considers the segmented forms. For example, a word-level language model (WM) – a crucial component in modern SMT systems – cannot be applied to the final, fluent target sentence if the decoder only has access to segmented morphemes. In this paper, we present a novel approach to address these limitations: *decoder-integrated desegmentation*. Our method incorporates the desegmentation process directly into the phrase-based decoding search, allowing the decoder to explore different segmentation options and score them based on features that consider the final, desegmented target. This enables the use of powerful features, such as a surface-level word language model, throughout the entire search process, leading to improved translation quality. We achieve this by extending the standard phrase-based decoder to handle multiple segmentation hypotheses simultaneously, scoring them based on both translation model scores and a desegmentation model that favors fluent, grammatical word forms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a large-scale English to Arabic translation task. Our experiments show a significant improvement over a strong 1-best desegmentation baseline, highlighting the benefits of integrating desegmentation directly into the decoding process. Our results confirm the importance of considering the final, desegmented target during the search process and pave the way for more sophisticated approaches to handling morphological complexity in statistical machine translation.

Automated essay scoring (AES) has a long history in educational testing and assessment. For decades, AES systems have been used to provide rapid, consistent, and cost-effective feedback on student writing. Early AES systems relied heavily on hand-crafted features – measures of essay length, vocabulary richness, grammatical correctness, and rhetorical structure – combined with linear regression models. While these systems achieved reasonable levels of agreement with human raters, their performance was fundamentally limited by the quality and completeness of the hand-engineered features. The process of feature engineering is time-consuming, requiring substantial domain expertise in both natural language processing and educational assessment. Furthermore, the features that prove most predictive of essay quality can vary across different writing prompts, genres, and educational levels, necessitating a continuous cycle of feature refinement. More recently, machine learning techniques, such as Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Gradient Boosting, have been applied to AES, often leveraging larger feature sets and more sophisticated learning algorithms. However, these systems still rely on expertly designed features and struggle to generalize to unseen prompts or essay populations. The recent resurgence of deep learning has opened up new possibilities for AES. Deep neural networks, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), are capable of learning complex patterns and representations directly from raw text data, without the need for explicit feature engineering. This is particularly appealing for AES, where the nuances of writing quality are often difficult to capture with traditional features. The ability of RNNs to process sequential data makes them well-suited for modeling the structure and coherence of an essay, capturing dependencies between sentences and paragraphs. In this paper, we present a novel approach to AES based on recurrent neural networks, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Our goal is to demonstrate that a deep learning model, trained directly on essay text and associated scores, can achieve state-of-the-art performance without relying on manually engineered features. We explore several variations of RNN architectures, and provide an analysis of the learned representations to gain insights into how the model perceives and evaluates essay quality. Our experimental results, evaluated on a standard AES dataset, demonstrate that our LSTM-based system significantly outperforms a strong baseline system relying on traditional features, achieving a noteworthy improvement in inter-rater agreement as measured by Quadratic Weighted Kappa. This work contributes to a growing body of research suggesting that deep learning offers a promising path toward more accurate, robust, and adaptable automated essay scoring systems.
