Domain adaptation has emerged as a crucial research area in natural language processing, particularly as models trained on readily available, large-scale datasets often exhibit performance degradation when applied to new, unseen domains. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in open-domain scenarios where the characteristics of the text can vary significantly. Traditional supervised learning methods typically require substantial labeled data in the target domain, a resource that is often limited or costly to obtain. Consequently, techniques that leverage unlabeled data from both source and target domains, alongside limited labeled data from the source domain, have gained considerable attention. Recent advances have focused on representation learning, aiming to discover informative feature representations that generalize well across domains. Unsupervised representation learning approaches, such as those based on autoencoders and word embeddings (Bengio et al., 2013; Mikolov et al., 2013), have demonstrably improved performance in numerous NLP tasks. However, these methods often fail to fully exploit the valuable information contained within the limited labeled data available in the source domain. This paper proposes a semi-supervised representation learning approach, leveraging both labeled data from the source domain and unlabeled data from both source and target domains to learn more robust and transferable feature representations. Specifically, we introduce a Dynamic Dependency Network (DDN) model, designed to capture complex dependencies between data points across domains. The DDN model dynamically adjusts its connections based on data similarity, allowing it to effectively integrate information from diverse sources. Importantly, the model’s structure and parameters are learned in a semi-supervised fashion, maximizing the utilization of available training signals. Our key contribution lies in the development of a framework that seamlessly integrates task-specific knowledge (via source domain labels) with the power of unlabeled data. Unlike purely unsupervised methods, the DDN model benefits from the guidance of labeled examples, leading to improved generalization performance. Furthermore, the dynamic network structure allows for adaptation to the nuances of the target domain, reducing the domain gap. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed DDN model on two widely used NLP tasks: part-of-speech (POS) tagging and syntactic chunking. Extensive experiments using the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) and MEDLINE corpora for POS tagging, and the WSJ and Brown corpora for chunking, demonstrate that the DDN model consistently outperforms existing unsupervised and semi-supervised representation learning techniques. The results highlight the benefits of exploiting both labeled and unlabeled data in a dynamic and adaptive framework for domain adaptation. In the remainder of this paper, we first discuss related work in domain adaptation and representation learning (Section 2). We then elaborate on the details of the proposed Dynamic Dependency Network model (Section 3). We present our experimental setup and results (Section 4), followed by a detailed analysis and discussion (Section 5). Finally, we conclude with a summary of our contributions and outline potential avenues for future research (Section 6). . . . . . . .

Semantic parsing, the task of mapping natural language utterances to formal meaning representations, is a core problem in natural language processing. It serves as a crucial component for various applications including question answering (Popescu et al., 2013), database querying (Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005), and robot control (Tellex et al., 2011). Traditionally, semantic parsing has been approached using grammar-based methods (Kate and Mooney, 2006;Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005), which rely on handcrafted grammars and complex feature engineering. These methods often struggle with the compositional nature of language and require significant domain expertise for grammar construction and maintenance. More recently, statistical machine learning methods, particularly those based on semantic role labeling (SRL) (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002), have gained popularity. However, these methods often operate on linearized representations of meaning, which can limit their ability to capture complex semantic relationships effectively. In the past few years, neural network models have demonstrated remarkable success in a variety of NLP tasks, including machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015) and image captioning (Vinyals et al., 2015). These successes have inspired a wave of work applying neural networks to semantic parsing (Dong and Lapata, 2016;Iyer et al., 2016;Yu et al., 2017). While promising, many of these approaches still rely on intermediate representations like logical forms or abstract syntax trees, which can be challenging to learn and may not fully capture the richness of natural language meaning. A particularly appealing alternative is to directly represent the meaning of a sentence as a semantic graph. Semantic graphs offer a natural way to encode entities, relations, and attributes, and their tight coupling with knowledge bases (KB) allows for effective reasoning and knowledge integration. Several recent works have explored this direction (Guo et al., 2018;Herzig et al., 2018). However, generating accurate semantic graphs remains a challenging task, requiring the model to simultaneously identify entities, predict relations, and resolve coreference. In this paper, we propose Sequence-to-Action, a novel neural semantic parsing approach that models semantic parsing as an end-to-end semantic graph generation process. Our method leverages the strengths of both semantic graph representations and sequence-to-sequence neural networks. Specifically, we employ a recurrent neural network (RNN) to map sentences to action sequences that define the steps for building a semantic graph. Each action in the sequence corresponds to a specific operation, such as adding a node, defining an edge, or specifying an attribute. This action-based approach allows the model to explicitly control the graph generation process and to learn complex dependencies between different graph components. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three benchmark datasets – OVERNIGHT, GEO, and ATIS – achieving state-of-the-art performance on OVERNIGHT and competitive results on the other two datasets. Our results demonstrate the potential of Sequence-to-Action for building robust and accurate semantic parsers.

Community-based Question Answering (cQA) platforms, such as Yahoo! Answers, Stack Overflow, and Quora, have emerged as invaluable resources for knowledge sharing and problem-solving. These platforms enable users to pose questions on diverse topics and receive answers from a community of knowledgeable individuals. The sheer volume of questions posted daily on these platforms presents both an opportunity and a challenge. Efficiently locating relevant questions is crucial for both users seeking information and experts seeking to contribute their knowledge. A key component of effective question retrieval in cQA is accurate *question detection* – the ability to reliably identify question sentences within a potentially noisy stream of online text. While question detection in well-structured corpora, like news articles or academic papers, is relatively straightforward due to the prevalence of linguistic cues such as question marks and interrogative words (5W1H – Who, What, When, Where, Why, How), applying these techniques to cQA data proves considerably more difficult. Online text, particularly in cQA forums, is often characterized by informality, grammatical errors, and a lack of conventional punctuation. Users frequently omit question marks, employ slang, and construct complex, rambling sentences that blur the boundaries between questions and statements. Traditional question detection methods, heavily reliant on these surface-level features, consequently suffer from low precision and recall in this domain. Existing approaches to question detection often leverage machine learning techniques, utilizing features such as part-of-speech tags, syntactic parse trees, and word embeddings (Huang et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007). However, these methods often require extensive feature engineering and struggle to generalize to the diverse and evolving language patterns found in cQA platforms. Furthermore, they may not effectively capture the underlying *salient patterns* that distinguish questions from other types of sentences in this context. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to question detection that focuses on identifying these salient patterns within cQA data. We hypothesize that questions, even in informal online language, exhibit characteristic lexical and syntactic properties that can be exploited for detection. Specifically, we investigate features related to verb usage, syntactic structure, and contextual information to build a robust and accurate question detection model. Our approach is designed to be automated, minimizing the need for manual feature engineering and capable of handling the inherent noise present in online communication. We evaluate our model on a large-scale dataset of questions and non-question sentences extracted from a popular cQA platform. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional methods in detecting online question sentences, achieving substantial improvements in both precision and recall. Importantly, we also demonstrate that accurate question detection directly translates to improved performance in the downstream task of question retrieval, highlighting the critical role of this component in building effective cQA systems. This work contributes a practical and effective solution for question detection in the challenging domain of community-based question answering, enabling more efficient information access and facilitating knowledge sharing within these valuable online communities.

Distributed word representations, also known as word embeddings, have revolutionized Natural Language Processing (NLP) in recent years (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). These representations capture semantic and syntactic information about words in a continuous vector space, enabling more effective performance in a wide range of downstream tasks, including machine translation, sentiment analysis, and question answering. The success of word embeddings, particularly models like Word2Vec and GloVe, has largely focused on languages with clear word boundaries, most notably English. However, applying these techniques directly to languages like Chinese presents unique challenges. Chinese is a morphologically rich language where words are often formed by combining multiple characters, each carrying semantic meaning. Unlike English, where a single word generally corresponds to a single semantic unit, a Chinese character can function as an independent morpheme and contribute to the overall meaning of a compound word. Consequently, simple word-based embeddings often fail to fully capture the nuanced semantics inherent in Chinese text. Existing approaches to handle this complexity often rely on segmenting Chinese text into words before applying word embedding techniques. However, word segmentation is itself a non-trivial task, prone to errors, and can lose valuable information contained within individual characters. Recognizing this limitation, we propose a novel approach to learning Chinese character embeddings that explicitly leverages the compositional nature of Chinese characters. Our core idea is to enhance traditional embedding models by incorporating information about the individual components, or radicals, that constitute each character. Chinese characters are not arbitrary glyphs; they are largely constructed from a set of fundamental components, often representing core semantic concepts. For example, the radical “氵” (water) frequently appears in characters related to water, such as 河 (river) and 海 (sea). By explicitly representing these components and their relationships within characters, we aim to create embeddings that are more semantically rich and capable of capturing the underlying structure of the Chinese language. In this work, we introduce two component-enhanced Chinese character embedding models: a Component-Aware Embedding (CAE) and a Component-Interaction Embedding (CIE). CAE directly incorporates component embeddings into the character embedding space, while CIE models the interactions between components within a character. We further extend both models to utilize bigram information, capturing sequential dependencies between adjacent characters and components. Our experiments on both word similarity and text classification tasks demonstrate that our component-enhanced models consistently outperform baseline character embedding methods and achieve competitive results compared to existing word embedding techniques for Chinese. These results highlight the effectiveness of leveraging the compositional structure of Chinese characters to improve semantic representation learning. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: * We propose two novel component-enhanced Chinese character embedding models, CAE and CIE, that explicitly incorporate information about the constituent components of Chinese characters. * We extend both models to utilize bigram information, capturing sequential dependencies between characters and components. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of our models through comprehensive evaluations on both word similarity and text classification tasks, showcasing improvements over existing methods.

Multiword expressions (MWEs) pose a significant challenge to natural language processing systems, particularly those involving syntactic analysis. These expressions – idioms, collocations, named entities, and other lexical chunks – exhibit non-compositional semantics and often violate standard syntactic rules. Consequently, accurately identifying and representing MWEs is crucial for robust parsing and downstream applications like machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Previous research has demonstrated the benefits of incorporating MWE knowledge into parsing systems. For example, studies have shown that artificially providing a parser with pre-identified MWEs can lead to improved parsing accuracy (Dasgupta and Ng, 2009; Zhou & Neubig, 2012). However, these idealized scenarios often fail to reflect the complexities of real-world applications where MWE recognition itself is a non-trivial task prone to errors. This paper investigates practical strategies for integrating MWE recognition and parsing in a constituency parsing framework. We aim to determine whether and how incorporating MWE knowledge can genuinely improve parsing performance when MWEs are not perfectly known *a priori*. Our work builds on the observation that effective MWE integration requires addressing two key challenges: accurately identifying MWEs within the input text, and efficiently incorporating this information into the parsing process. We explore two distinct empirical approaches. First, we examine a *pregrouping* strategy, wherein we employ a state-of-the-art MWE recognizer to identify and pre-segment candidate MWEs *before* parsing. The resulting segmented text is then fed to a standard constituency parser. This approach aims to leverage the strengths of dedicated MWE recognition modules while allowing the parser to operate on a modified input. Second, we investigate a *grammar integration* strategy, wherein we augment the parser’s grammar with rules specifically designed to handle identified MWEs, followed by a reranking step that prioritizes parses consistent with MWE boundaries and semantic interpretations. Our evaluation, conducted on a standard benchmark dataset, reveals nuanced results. While pregrouping improves MWE recognition accuracy and unlabeled attachment score, the overall impact on parsing F-score is not statistically significant, suggesting that errors in MWE recognition can negatively impact parsing performance. Conversely, integrating MWEs into the parser grammar and subsequent reranking yields modest, yet consistent, improvements across all evaluation metrics. These findings highlight the importance of considering error propagation in MWE integration strategies and suggest that a sophisticated integration approach that accounts for potential recognition errors is key to achieving substantial gains in parsing accuracy. Our contributions lie in providing a realistic assessment of MWE integration in a practical parsing context, elucidating the trade-offs associated with different integration strategies, and offering insights for future research in this area. We believe our work provides a valuable stepping stone for developing more robust and accurate NLP systems capable of handling the complexities of multiword expressions. Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is a challenging natural language processing task with broad applications, ranging from language learning tools to writing assistance software. The goal of GEC is to automatically identify and correct grammatical errors in a given text, encompassing a wide range of issues including incorrect word choice, improper tense usage, spelling mistakes, and flawed sentence structure (Lee & Schuler, 2012; Ng et al., 2014). Traditionally, GEC systems relied on rule-based approaches or statistical machine translation (SMT) techniques (Skerritt-Miller et al., 2009; Dahlmeier et al., 2012). However, these methods often struggle to generalize to unseen error types or capture the complex contextual dependencies that characterize natural language. Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have spurred a surge of interest in applying similar techniques to GEC, treating the task as a translation problem from erroneous text to correct text (Juncen et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016). These neural models demonstrate promising performance, largely due to their ability to learn complex patterns and long-range dependencies directly from large corpora of parallel erroneous and corrected sentences. Despite their success, existing neural GEC models often exhibit limitations in accurately correcting both *global* errors – those affecting sentence structure and word choice – and *local* errors – such as spelling mistakes and incorrect inflections. Global errors often require understanding the broader context of a sentence, while local errors frequently involve subtle changes to individual words. To address these limitations, we propose a novel hybrid neural model for GEC that incorporates information at both the word and character levels, interwoven through a nested attention mechanism. Our model builds upon the strengths of sequence-to-sequence architectures leveraging attention, but extends it to consider both word-level and character-level representations simultaneously. This allows the model to effectively capture both global contextual dependencies and fine-grained local details often missed by traditional word-level models. Specifically, our approach employs a nested attention layer where a word-level attention mechanism guides the model's focus on relevant parts of the input sentence, and a separate character-level attention mechanism is applied within each word to pinpoint specific character-level errors (e.g., spelling corrections or inflectional changes). This nesting allows the model to refine its attention based on both contextual information and fine-grained orthographic details. We evaluate our model on the widely used CoNLL-14 benchmark dataset and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms existing neural GEC models in terms of standard evaluation metrics. Further analysis reveals that the nested attention mechanism is particularly effective in correcting local errors, thereby contributing significantly to the overall performance improvement. We believe this is the first work to demonstrate the effectiveness of nested attention for GEC and provides a valuable step forward in developing more robust and accurate error correction systems. Natural language generation (NLG) systems frequently require the ability to inflect words, including pluralizing nouns, to produce grammatically correct and contextually appropriate text (Reiter & Dale, 2000). This capability is crucial for applications ranging from user interfaces that dynamically adapt their language to the user’s input (Lau et al., 2011) to broader NLG tasks like story generation and machine translation (Manning & Schütze, 1999). While effective pluralization techniques exist for many well-resourced languages like English (e.g., adding ‘-s’ or ‘-es’), this remains a significant challenge for low-resource languages, particularly those with complex morphological systems. The Bantu language family, comprising over 500 languages spoken across sub-Saharan Africa, presents a particularly complex case for morphological inflection, including pluralization. These languages are typically agglutinative, meaning that words are formed by stringing together multiple morphemes, each carrying a specific grammatical meaning. Noun classes, a central feature of Bantu languages, play a crucial role in determining the appropriate pluralization strategy. Historically described by Meinhof (1948), these noun classes are prefix-driven, influencing agreement patterns throughout the sentence. Previous work on pluralization in Bantu languages has demonstrated promising results for individual languages, such as isiZulu (Louwrens & van Niekerk, 2016) and Runyankore (Niyomugabo et al., 2019). These studies highlighted the need to integrate morphological, syntactic, and even semantic information to accurately predict plural forms. Interestingly, despite belonging to different Guthrie language zones (zones E and F respectively), isiZulu and Runyankore displayed shared characteristics in their pluralization mechanisms, suggesting the potential for cross-linguistic bootstrapping and generalization. This paper systematically investigates the feasibility of generalizing pluralization techniques across multiple Bantu languages. We examine seven languages spanning three distinct Guthrie language zones (E, F, and G) - namely, isiZulu, Runyankore, Kinyarwanda, Kirundi, Luganda, Sukuma, and Swahili. Our investigation reveals fundamental limitations in the traditional Meinhofian noun class system for computational applications, stemming from inherent non-determinism in the application of noun class prefixes. We address this by refining the noun class tables, expanding from Meinhof’s original 29 classes to a more granular 53-class representation. Furthermore, we present a generic pluralization model that achieves high accuracy—over 93% in coverage testing and over 94% on a random sample—comparable to the performance of language-specific pluralizers developed for isiZulu and Runyankore. This demonstrates the potential for building broadly applicable pluralization systems for the Bantu language family, addressing a critical gap in low-resource language technology. Machine transliteration, the task of converting words from one script to another while preserving their pronunciation, is a crucial component in many multilingual natural language processing (NLP) applications. These applications range from cross-lingual information retrieval and machine translation to speech recognition and spoken language understanding in scenarios with code-switching or mixed scripts (Knight and Graehl, 1998; Kang and Glass, 2000; Jose et al., 2006). Traditional approaches to machine transliteration have largely focused on modeling the relationship between the source and target scripts based on phonetic similarity, often relying on hand-crafted rules or statistical models trained on parallel transliteration corpora (Khoo et al., 1999; Zhou and Li, 2003; Bilmes and Kirchhoff, 2004). However, a significant limitation of these existing approaches is their reliance on solely phonetic information. While pronunciation is undoubtedly critical in transliteration, the spelling of a word also plays an important role, particularly in languages where spelling conventions reflect historical phonetic evolution or morphological structure. For example, the English word “knight” is often transliterated into languages that approximate its spelling, despite its unconventional pronunciation. Similarly, loanwords frequently retain elements of their original spelling even when adapted into a new language. In this paper, we argue that effective machine transliteration requires a model that jointly leverages both spelling and pronunciation information. We propose a novel framework for transliteration generation that explicitly incorporates both representations of the source word and learns to generate the target transliteration based on a combination of these features. Our approach moves beyond solely phoneme-based alignment and allows the model to capture interactions between spelling patterns and phonetic mappings. Furthermore, we generalize this model to include information from multiple source languages, recognizing that transliterations are often mediated through intermediary scripts rather than directly between two languages. This capability allows our model to benefit from the larger and more readily available transliteration resources across multiple language pairs. We further enhance the system with a reranking stage and the incorporation of lexicon features derived from existing transliteration dictionaries. We evaluate our proposed model on several benchmark datasets for machine transliteration, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art systems. Our results highlight the importance of considering both spelling and pronunciation and the benefits of leveraging multilingual resources in machine transliteration. Quantifier scope disambiguation (QSD) – the task of determining the correct logical relation between quantified noun phrases within a sentence – remains a significant challenge in natural language processing. Consider the classic example: "Every farmer owns a cow." This sentence is ambiguous between two possible logical forms: (1) ∀x (Farmer(x) → ∃y (Cow(y) ∧ Owns(x,y))), meaning every farmer owns at least one cow, and (2) ∃y (Cow(y) ∧ ∀x (Farmer(x) → Owns(x,y))), meaning there exists a cow that every farmer owns. While formal semantics provides the tools to represent these ambiguities, resolving them requires more than purely syntactic or compositional analysis. Humans readily resolve such ambiguities based on contextual knowledge, common sense reasoning, and pragmatic inferences. It is widely acknowledged that pragmatic knowledge plays a vital role in QSD (Breheny, 2008; von Fintel, 2008). For example, our understanding of typical scenarios – farmers generally owning cows, rather than a single cow being universally owned by all farmers – strongly favors the first interpretation of the example above. However, explicitly representing and computationally accessing such pragmatic knowledge is notoriously difficult. Traditional approaches rely heavily on hand-crafted rules, lexical databases, or manually annotated corpora (e.g., Lascarides & Hunter, 2000; White, 2004), which are expensive to create and may not generalize well to novel contexts. Recently, there has been growing interest in leveraging distributional semantics and machine learning techniques to acquire pragmatic knowledge automatically (e.g., Lin et al., 2009; Clark et al., 2013). This paper aims to contribute to this line of research by presenting a novel open information extraction (OpenIE) technique for automatically extracting a specific type of pragmatic knowledge relevant to QSD. Our approach focuses on identifying common relational triples pertaining to typical states of affairs. For instance, extracting triples like “(farmer, owns, cow)” and “(cow, associated with, farm)” provides hints about the likely relationship between farmers and cows in typical scenarios. We integrate this extracted pragmatic knowledge into a Markov Logic Network (MLN) – a probabilistic logic programming language that combines first-order logic with probabilistic graphical models (Richardson & Domingos, 2006). The MLN allows us to encode both the syntactic constraints of QSD and the pragmatic preferences derived from our OpenIE system. Preliminary experiments demonstrate that our model, incorporating the automatically extracted pragmatic knowledge, significantly improves performance on benchmark QSD datasets compared to models relying solely on syntactic information. While these results are preliminary, they suggest promising avenues for incorporating pragmatic reasoning into computational models of natural language understanding. This work builds on the observation that truly robust QSD requires not merely *representing* logical possibilities, but *ranking* them according to their plausibility in the real world. Our aim is to begin to bridge the gap between formal semantics and the messy realities of human language use.

Microblogs, such as those found on Twitter and Sina Weibo, have become a popular platform for information dissemination and social interaction. However, the informal nature of microblog text presents several unique challenges for natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Unlike formal written text, microblogs often contain a high degree of noise, including a lack of explicit word boundaries, grammatical errors, and non-standard language use. These characteristics make traditional NLP tools, designed for well-formed text, less effective when applied to microblog data. Specifically, three core subtasks become particularly challenging: word segmentation (determining where words begin and end), part-of-speech (POS) tagging (assigning grammatical tags to each word), and text normalization (mapping non-standard words and phrases to their standard forms). Traditional word segmentation methods rely on predefined dictionaries or statistical models trained on large, annotated corpora (Xie and Lai, 2003;Schmidhuber, 1994). However, the open-vocabulary nature of microblog text and the frequent use of neologisms and slang render these methods inadequate. While seemingly straightforward, ECV is complicated by the practical reality that claims are rarely assessed in a vacuum. Instead, verification often requires sifting through potentially vast collections of documents to locate relevant evidence. This initial evidence retrieval step is itself a significant hurdle, particularly given that the ideal evidence supporting a claim might be drastically different from that which would refute it. Traditionally, approaches to ECV have largely treated evidence retrieval and claim verification as largely independent pipeline stages (e.g., identifying candidate evidence first, then scoring their relevance and entailment strength). These pipeline systems often rely on pre-defined heuristics or separate models for each stage. While simplifying the problem, this decoupling can lead to suboptimal performance. For instance, a system might retrieve a large set of superficially relevant documents, only to find that none actually provide conclusive support or refutation for the claim. Conversely, relevant evidence might be overlooked if the retrieval stage is too restrictive. Furthermore, pipeline approaches typically operate with a fixed-size evidence set, limiting their flexibility to adapt to the varying amount of supporting information available. TWOWINGOS offers two key advantages over existing approaches. Topical segmentation – the task of automatically dividing a text into sections, each addressing a distinct topic – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from document summarization and information retrieval to meeting analysis and textbook structuring. This intuition suggests that identifying changes in word usage can reveal the boundaries between distinct topical segments. Consequently, many existing topical segmenters leverage lexical cohesion – the degree to which words in a text are related to one another – as a key indicator of topical consistency. However, relying solely on lexical similarity, measured primarily through word repetition or semantic relatedness, often proves insufficient, particularly when dealing with text genres exhibiting complex discourse structures or nuanced topical transitions. Literary narratives, for example, frequently employ coreference chains and sustained thematic development that can obscure clear lexical shifts, while lecture notes, characterized by a high density of specialized terminology, may exhibit limited vocabulary variation even across distinct subtopics. This paper investigates a complementary signal for identifying topical shifts: the characteristics of referring expressions and their relationship to antecedent accessibility. We hypothesize that *how* an entity is referred to – whether through a full noun phrase, a pronoun, or another type of expression – provides valuable information about the ongoing topical context. Specifically, we posit that shorter, less informative referring expressions (e.g., “he,” “it”) indicate a highly accessible antecedent, suggesting that the topic under discussion has remained relatively constant. Conversely, longer, more descriptive expressions (e.g., “the renowned astrophysicist Dr. Eleanor Vance”) imply a lower degree of accessibility, potentially signaling a shift in topic or the introduction of a new entity into the discourse. This intuition rests on principles of information structure and cognitive processing, where shorter expressions leverage shared knowledge, reducing the need for explicit re-identification. We introduce a novel similarity metric that incorporates this information, augmenting a traditional lexically-based topical segmenter. By considering both lexical relatedness and the types of referring expressions used, we aim to improve the accuracy and robustness of topical segmentation, particularly in challenging genres. We evaluate our hypothesis on two distinct datasets: literary narratives and lecture notes, representing a spectrum of discourse styles and topical coherence. The results demonstrate that our similarity metric consistently improves upon, or maintains the performance of, a baseline lexically-based segmenter. Furthermore, analysis reveals that certain types of referring expressions, particularly pronouns and demonstratives, are more informative than others in identifying topical shifts. This work contributes a new dimension to the study of lexical cohesion and provides a promising avenue for enhancing topical segmentation systems. Our findings show that jointly optimizing multiple objectives consistently improves parsing performance and, crucially, leads to enhanced performance on downstream applications. This suggests that leveraging a broader range of signals during training can result in parsers that are not only more accurate in isolation, but also more effective at supporting other NLP tasks. STMs incorporate document-level labels, allowing the model to learn topic distributions that are predictive of these labels. These models typically define a likelihood function that combines a multinomial likelihood for word generation with a logistic likelihood for the document labels. However, two key challenges hinder the broader adoption of Bayesian logistic STMs: a potential imbalance in the influence of the word counts and document labels, and the computational difficulties associated with inference. The first issue arises from the scale difference between document word counts and the binary label indicators. Typically, word counts are significantly larger than label values (0 or 1), which often leads to the response variables (labels) being effectively overshadowed by the document word counts during model training. This imbalance can result in the model prioritizing the fit to the word distributions over accurately predicting the document labels. The second challenge concerns the computational cost of performing Bayesian inference in these models. Furthermore, VI can be sensitive to initialization and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters. To address these limitations, we propose an improved Bayesian logistic STM. This augment-and-collapse Gibbs sampling method possesses analytical forms for all conditional distributions, eliminating the need for restrictive mean-field assumptions. Moreover, the algorithm is inherently parallelizable, significantly reducing computation time compared to traditional VI methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets, showcasing substantial improvements in prediction performance and computational efficiency. This work aims to provide a more robust and scalable solution for Bayesian logistic STMs, expanding their applicability to a wider range of supervised topic modeling tasks.

Dependency parsing provides a structured representation of sentence syntax, explicitly revealing the grammatical relationships between words. By analyzing the dependency structure of the source sentence, we can identify key relationships, particularly those involving the subject, object, and verb, and use this information to guide the reordering process. This allows the decoder to estimate the likelihood of a partially completed parse tree and guide the search for the best translation. Computing prefix probabilities efficiently and accurately is thus essential for practical SCFG-based translation systems. Previous approaches to prefix probability computation in SCFGs have often relied on approximations or have been limited in their applicability to certain grammar formalisms (Knight & Alshawi, 1997; DeNelle & Klein, 2004). Furthermore, many require the grammar to be in a specific normal form, often necessitating complex and potentially lossy transformations. The core challenge lies in the inherent complexity of the synchronous nature of the grammar. Traditional techniques for computing prefix probabilities in context-free grammars (CFGs) do not directly translate to the synchronous setting, as the dependencies between the source and target languages must be carefully considered. In this paper, we present a novel and general method for the computation of prefix probabilities for synchronous context-free grammars. Our approach is based on a combination of a simple, yet effective, grammar transformation and standard techniques to bring grammars into a suitable normal form for efficient probability computation. The key contribution is a transformation that allows us to leverage existing algorithms for CFG prefix probability calculation while correctly accounting for the synchronous dependencies encoded in the SCFG rules. This transformation does not introduce any approximations or require the use of complex data structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results. By providing a robust and efficient method for prefix probability calculation, we aim to facilitate the development of more practical and performant SCFG-based machine translation systems. Structured prediction – the task of predicting a structured output, such as a parse tree or a sequence of labels – has become increasingly important in natural language processing and machine learning. Unlike traditional classification problems producing a single label, structured prediction requires modeling dependencies between the output variables. A common approach to structured prediction is the structured perceptron (Taskar et al., 2003;McCallum and Nigam, 1998), an online learning algorithm which iteratively updates model parameters to correct misclassifications. However, a fundamental assumption underlying much of the theory surrounding structured perceptrons, and structured prediction in general, is the ability to perform *exact* inference – finding the globally optimal structure according to the model’s scoring function. Unfortunately, exact inference is often computationally intractable for non-trivial structured prediction problems. This is particularly true in models with complex dependencies or large output spaces, as encountered in tasks like parsing, machine translation, and speech recognition. As a result, practical implementations routinely rely on approximate inference techniques such as beam search (Lowerre, 1976), Viterbi approximation, or sampling methods. These approximations trade off accuracy for computational efficiency, but come at the cost of theoretical guarantees. While effective in practice, the behavior of structured perceptrons trained with approximate inference has remained largely unexplored from a theoretical perspective. The convergence behavior is unknown, and the practical heuristics used – such as determining when to update parameters – are often justified empirically rather than theoretically. This paper addresses this gap by providing a theoretical framework for analyzing structured perceptrons trained with *inexact* search. We propose a general “violation-fixing” perceptron framework, extending the standard structured perceptron update rule to accommodate approximate inference. Our framework introduces new separability conditions that guarantee convergence even when the model is unable to find the globally optimal structure. Importantly, this framework naturally subsumes and provides a theoretical justification for the widely used “early-update” heuristic (Collins and Roark, 2004) commonly employed with beam search in sequence labeling tasks. Beyond simply justifying existing practice, our framework allows us to explore new update methods. We propose several novel update strategies within this framework, and demonstrate that one method, termed “max-violation,” dramatically reduces training time – achieving a 3x speedup – without sacrificing performance on state-of-the-art part-of-speech tagging and incremental parsing systems. This improvement in training efficiency is crucial for scaling structured perceptrons to larger datasets and more complex models. Our contributions, therefore, are threefold: (1) a theoretical framework for analyzing structured perceptrons with inexact inference; (2) a justification of the commonly used early-update heuristic; and (3) the introduction of a novel update method that significantly improves training speed. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate the practical benefits of our framework for improving the efficiency and scalability of structured prediction algorithms. Statistical machine translation (SMT) has rapidly advanced in recent years, becoming a dominant paradigm for automated translation. Early SMT systems relied heavily on word-based models (Brown et al., 1993), but these struggled to capture non-local dependencies and handle phrases. Phrase-based SMT (Koehn et al., 2003) significantly improved performance by translating phrases, rather than individual words, and introduced distortion models to account for differences in word order. More recently, hierarchical phrase-based translation (HPBT) (Chiang, 2005) has emerged as a powerful extension, allowing for the representation of hierarchical syntactic structures and more complex reordering phenomena. HPBT models translate syntactically structured phrases, offering greater expressiveness and flexibility than standard phrase-based models. However, the effectiveness of HPBT heavily relies on the quality of the extracted grammar rules. Traditionally, these rules are extracted using Viterbi alignment – selecting the single most probable alignment between source and target sentences. While often effective, Viterbi alignment can be overly restrictive, discarding potentially valuable alignments that contribute to a more robust and generalizable grammar. Moreover, Viterbi alignments are susceptible to error propagation, and a single incorrect alignment can invalidate an otherwise useful rule. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach to grammar extraction – utilizing the full posterior distribution over alignments, rather than relying solely on Viterbi. We propose a method for extracting hierarchical phrase-based translation grammars based on rules weighted by their posterior probabilities derived from the HMM word-to-word alignment model. This approach allows us to consider multiple plausible alignments, capturing a broader range of translational relationships and potentially mitigating the errors inherent in Viterbi alignment. We hypothesize that by incorporating information from the entire posterior distribution, we can build more robust and accurate translation grammars. We investigate the impact of these posteriors on various levels of grammar complexity, progressively adding rule classes to a baseline phrase-based system. We evaluate these grammars both intrinsically – by assessing their ability to align the training data – and extrinsically – by measuring the quality of the translations they produce. Our experiments on Chinese-to-English translation demonstrate that grammars extracted from posterior distributions yield significant improvements in translation quality. Notably, we find that even relatively simple grammars consisting of rules with a single nonterminal, when extracted from posteriors, can outperform more complex grammars extracted using Viterbi alignments. Furthermore, we demonstrate the benefits of combining systems built from source-to-target and target-to-source alignment models, showcasing an effective method for leveraging complementary information. This work contributes to the field of SMT by providing a novel approach to grammar extraction that leverages the full information available in the alignment posterior distribution, leading to improved translation performance and a deeper understanding of the characteristics of effective hierarchical phrase-based translation grammars. . . . . . .

The notion that individuals modify their communication patterns to align with those of their interlocutors – a phenomenon known as communication accommodation theory (CAT) – has been a cornerstone of interdisciplinary research for decades (Giles et al., 1991). Originally conceived within the fields of linguistics, psychology, and communication, CAT posits that humans instinctively adjust their linguistic style to either converge towards, or diverge away from, their conversational partners. Convergence, often driven by a desire for social solidarity or to enhance understanding, involves adapting speech rate, vocabulary, accent, and other linguistic features to resemble those of the other person. Divergence, conversely, highlights differences, potentially signaling social distance or emphasizing group identity. Over the years, CAT has expanded beyond face-to-face interactions, finding applications in analyses of nonverbal cues like gesture (Kendon, 1981), backchannels (Yngve, 1970), and even broader social dynamics. More recently, the increasingly pervasive nature of online communication has spurred interest in extending CAT to digital environments. Preliminary studies have begun to explore communication accommodation in social media platforms such as Twitter (Ireland et al., 2011), examining how users adapt their language use in response to trending topics or the styles of influential accounts. However, a nuanced understanding of accommodation processes in online *debates* – environments characterized by explicit disagreement and often heightened emotionality – remains largely unexplored. Online debates present a particularly intriguing test case for CAT. While convergence might be expected to facilitate constructive dialogue, the adversarial nature of the setting could also incentivize divergence as participants seek to assert their positions and differentiate themselves. Furthermore, identifying accommodation in textual data, where cues like prosody and nonverbal behavior are absent, requires innovative analytical approaches. In this work, we address these gaps by conducting a rigorous analysis of linguistic style accommodation in online debates. Our contribution is two-fold. First, to enable controlled study of accommodation dynamics, we introduce a Joint Topic Expression (JTE) model, designed to generate synthetic debate posts exhibiting varying degrees of agreement or disagreement on specified topics. This allows us to create a unique dataset specifically engineered for investigating accommodation phenomena. Second, we propose a formal framework for analyzing accommodation in online debates, incorporating quantifiable linguistic features and defining metrics to measure the extent to which debaters adjust their style relative to their opponents. We apply this framework to a large collection of real-life debate posts, revealing insightful patterns concerning the interplay between agreement/disagreement, linguistic convergence/divergence, and the overall dynamics of online debate. Our findings offer valuable insights into the complex psycholinguistic processes underlying online interaction and contribute to a broader understanding of how individuals navigate conflict and build (or dismantle) rapport in digital spaces. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) provides a powerful and expressive formalism for natural language parsing, allowing for a concise and elegant representation of grammatical structure (Steedman, 2000). However, the very expressiveness that makes CCG attractive also contributes to its computational complexity. Parsing with CCG can be significantly more challenging than parsing with simpler formalisms like context-free grammar (CFG), leading to considerable research focused on improving parsing efficiency. Traditional CCG parsing algorithms, such as the CKY algorithm (Cocke, Younger, and Kasami, 1984), exhaustively explore the parse space, resulting in high computational costs, particularly for longer and more complex sentences. To address this computational bottleneck, various approximation and optimization techniques have been developed. One prominent strategy is *supertagging*, which aims to reduce the search space by pre-assigning lexical categories to each word in the input sentence (Bang-Jensen and Johansson, 1991). This significantly reduces the number of parses considered by the main parser, leading to substantial speedups. *Adaptive supertagging* (Roark, 2001) further enhances this approach by learning to predict lexical categories based on contextual information, adapting to the specific characteristics of the input text. Another line of research explores refining the search process itself. A* search is a classic informed search algorithm that prioritizes the exploration of promising parse candidates based on a heuristic function. While A* has been successfully applied to parsing in other formalisms, its application to CCG—with its richer rule set and potential for ambiguity—has received comparatively less attention. A crucial question remains: can A* effectively guide the search process in CCG and achieve substantial performance gains? Moreover, how does A* compare to established approximation techniques like adaptive supertagging in terms of both parsing effort (a hardware-independent metric) and actual CPU time (a more practical and stringent evaluation measure)? In this paper, we present a systematic comparison of adaptive supertagging and A* search for efficient CCG parsing. We investigate several variants of A* specifically tailored to the complexities of CCG, and evaluate their performance against a standard CKY baseline. Importantly, we introduce a methodology for evaluating A* parsing based on CPU time, providing a more realistic assessment of its practical benefits. Our results demonstrate that while A* reduces parsing effort, this does not always translate directly to reduced CPU time. However, by *combining* A* with adaptive supertagging, we achieve a further 15% reduction in CPU time over our best individual models, highlighting the potential of integrating these two orthogonal approaches for truly efficient CCG parsing. The increasing volume of email communication presents a significant challenge for information management. Manually sorting and prioritizing emails is time-consuming and often inefficient. Automatic topic segmentation – the task of dividing a document (in this case, an email conversation) into segments each covering a distinct topic – offers a promising solution. This allows for more efficient browsing, summarization, and retrieval of relevant information within email threads. While topic segmentation has been extensively studied in the context of single documents, such as news articles and research papers, applying these techniques to email conversations requires addressing unique characteristics inherent in this communication medium. Email threads are not simply concatenations of independent messages; rather, they embody a dynamic conversation structure, with replies building upon previous statements, introducing new subtopics, and shifting the overall focus. Existing topic segmentation models, like the Lexical Chain Segmenter (LCSeg) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), primarily rely on lexical similarity and often fail to capture these crucial conversational dynamics. These methods treat each email as an independent unit, disregarding the inherent relationships and dependencies between messages within a thread. Consequently, they often struggle to accurately identify topic boundaries and can generate incoherent or fragmented segments. To address this gap, we present a systematic investigation of topic segmentation in email conversations, including the creation of a novel, manually annotated corpus of email threads. To our knowledge, this is the first publicly available dataset specifically designed for evaluating topic segmentation models in the email domain. The corpus includes detailed annotations specifying topic boundaries within email threads, allowing for robust evaluation of different approaches. We begin by evaluating the performance of standard topic segmentation models – LCSeg and LDA – on this corpus, highlighting their limitations when applied to email conversations. Based on this analysis, we identify key considerations for an effective email topic segmentation model, including the need to incorporate conversation flow, identify topic shifts, and account for the inherent hierarchical structure of email threads. Motivated by these observations, we propose two novel extensions to LCSeg and LDA that explicitly exploit conversation structure, leveraging information such as reply-to relationships, sender information, and message ordering to improve segmentation accuracy. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that LCSeg outperforms LDA as a baseline for email topic segmentation, and that incorporating conversation structure into both models yields substantial performance improvements. This work contributes a valuable resource for the research community and provides a foundation for developing more sophisticated and effective topic segmentation techniques tailored to the unique challenges of email communication. Sentiment analysis, the computational task of determining the emotional tone expressed in a piece of text, has garnered significant attention in recent years. Its applications are widespread, ranging from monitoring brand reputation and understanding customer feedback to gauging public opinion and predicting market trends (Pang and Lee, 2008;Liu, 2012). A plethora of approaches have been proposed for sentiment classification, including lexicon-based methods, machine learning algorithms, and deep learning techniques. Among machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVMs) have consistently demonstrated strong performance and remain a popular choice for baseline sentiment classification systems (Pang et al., 2002). A common practice in establishing these baselines is to represent text as a bag-of-words, utilizing binary or frequency-based weighting schemes for individual terms (unigrams). While effective, this approach often overlooks the nuances of language and the varying importance of different terms in conveying sentiment. The field of Information Retrieval (IR) has a long and rich history of developing sophisticated weighting schemes designed to capture the relevance of terms within document collections (Salton and McGill, 1983; Manning et al., 2008). These schemes aim to identify terms that are both discriminative and representative of a document’s content. Given the inherent connection between identifying relevant terms and discerning sentiment – where certain words carry more emotional weight than others – a natural question arises: can we leverage the established methodologies of IR to improve the accuracy of sentiment analysis models? This paper investigates precisely this question. We hypothesize that by incorporating more nuanced feature weighting schemes from IR, specifically variants of the widely used tf-idf (term frequency-inverse document frequency) scheme, we can enhance the performance of a standard SVM classifier for sentiment analysis. Our work systematically explores several modifications to the traditional tf-idf weighting scheme, including the application of sublinear term frequency scaling and various document frequency smoothing techniques. We perform extensive experiments on a diverse collection of sentiment analysis datasets, encompassing product reviews, movie reviews, and social media posts. The results demonstrate that carefully tuned tf-idf variants consistently outperform the baseline binary unigram weighting scheme, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on several benchmark datasets. To the best of our knowledge, the presented techniques yield the highest reported accuracy for sentiment classification using an SVM-based approach. This research highlights the potential for cross-disciplinary innovation, bridging the gap between Information Retrieval and Sentiment Analysis to yield significant improvements in practical applications. Negative reviews are more likely to mention specifically the defects, whereas positive reviews are likely to focus on the merits of the product. Hence, word weights can be crucial to accurately determining the sentiment of a document; while simple binary weighting schemes capture the presence or absence of a word, they do not capture its relative importance to the overall sentiment bearing. This motivates the study of IR weighting schemes. In the following sections, we will detail the IR weighting schemes investigated, describe the experimental setup, present the results, and discuss the implications of our findings.

Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to analyze the grammatical structure of a sentence by establishing relationships between words. Accurate dependency parsing is crucial for a wide range of downstream NLP applications, including machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Traditionally, dependency parsing has been approached using graph-based (McDonald & Nivre, 2007; Kübler, McDonald, & Nivre, 2009) and transition-based methods (Nivre, 2007; Covington, 2001). Graph-based parsing attempts to build the entire dependency tree simultaneously, often employing complex algorithms for optimization. Transition-based parsing, on the other hand, constructs the dependency tree incrementally through a series of well-defined actions, or transitions. Recent advances in neural networks have significantly improved the performance of both graph-based and transition-based dependency parsing. Neural network models excel at learning rich representations of words and sentences, which can then be used to guide the parsing process. Specifically, transition-based dependency parsing has benefited from the development of neural architectures that can effectively model the history of transitions and predict the next action to take. However, training these neural network-based transition systems remains a challenge. Standard approaches such as backpropagation through time can be computationally expensive and may suffer from vanishing gradients, especially for long sequences. In this work, we present a novel structured training approach for neural network transition-based dependency parsing. Our method combines the strengths of neural networks and structured perceptron learning, leveraging large amounts of data to achieve state-of-the-art performance. We begin by training a neural network representation using a combination of a gold corpus and a large number of automatically parsed sentences. This allows us to learn robust and generalizable word and sentence embeddings. Critically, we keep this neural network representation fixed and then learn a final linear layer using the structured perceptron algorithm (Collins, 2002) with beam-search decoding. This structured learning step allows us to optimize the model directly for parsing accuracy, taking into account the dependencies between transitions. Our experiments on the Penn Treebank demonstrate that our approach achieves exceptional results, reaching 94.26% unlabeled and 92.41% labeled attachment accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the highest accuracy reported to date on the Stanford Dependencies dataset. Furthermore, we provide a detailed ablative analysis to identify the key components of our model that contribute most to its strong performance. This analysis reveals the importance of both the neural network representation and the structured perceptron training procedure. Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has emerged as a powerful formalism for representing the semantic content of sentences (Banarescu et al., 2013). Unlike traditional syntactic parse trees, AMR focuses on “what” is being said rather than “how” it is said, representing concepts and their relationships in a directed, acyclic graph. The resulting graphs capture the core meaning of a sentence, abstracting away from surface-level variations in wording and syntactic structure. A wealth of research has demonstrated the utility of AMR for tasks such as machine translation (Song et al., 2018), information extraction (Faruqui et al., 2015), and question answering (Popescu et al., 2018). However, the vast majority of AMR resources and associated research has focused on single-sentence semantics. Real-world information processing frequently requires understanding the semantic content of entire documents, not just isolated sentences. Consider a multi-sentence news article or a complex scientific report; the meaning is often distributed across multiple sentences, with subtle connections and dependencies that are not immediately apparent from analyzing each sentence in isolation. Representing document-level semantics is a long-standing challenge in natural language processing, requiring mechanisms to handle phenomena such as coreference resolution, implicit roles, and bridging anaphora – all of which contribute to a coherent understanding of the overall document meaning. Existing approaches to document-level semantic analysis often rely on heuristics or shallow methods that do not capture the full richness of semantic relations. In this paper, we present the Multi-Sentence AMR (MS-AMR) corpus, a resource designed to address this gap. MS-AMR extends the traditional single-sentence AMR framework to incorporate annotations that capture the semantic relationships *between* sentences. Specifically, we annotate coreference links to track entities across sentences, as well as implicit roles and bridging relations to represent subtle semantic connections that are not explicitly stated. The corpus is built upon existing gold-standard AMR annotations, providing a solid foundation for semantic analysis. We detail the methodology employed in developing MS-AMR, including the annotation guidelines and quality control measures used to ensure consistency and accuracy. We also present an initial analysis of the corpus, highlighting key characteristics and providing statistics on annotation density. Finally, we establish a plausible baseline for comparison and discuss the potential applications of MS-AMR for downstream tasks such as information extraction and question answering. It is our hope that MS-AMR serves as a valuable resource for the research community and illustrates a feasible approach to developing rich representations of document meaning. Semantic similarity – the degree to which concepts are related – is a fundamental concept underpinning numerous areas of cognitive science, linguistics, and increasingly, computational fields like Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Establishing robust and accurate methods for measuring semantic relatedness between words is, therefore, critically important. Such measurements provide essential foundations for a wide range of downstream tasks, including information retrieval (Voorhees & Harman, 2000), text summarization (Mani, 2001), word sense disambiguation (Yarowsky, 1990), synonym extraction (Budanitsky & Cotton, 2004), and document clustering (Steinbach et al., 2000). Historically, approaches to determining semantic similarity have relied heavily on manually constructed lexical resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995), which organizes words into synsets—groups of synonymous terms—and defines relationships between these synsets, such as hypernymy/hyponymy (is-a relationships). While WordNet provides a valuable foundational resource, its construction is labor-intensive, and its coverage is limited, particularly for specialized domains or emerging terminology. More recently, there has been a significant shift towards leveraging the vast amount of textual data available on the web to automatically estimate semantic similarity. These web-based approaches typically exploit distributional semantics – the idea that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings (Harris, 1954; Firth, 1957). Methods based on co-occurrence statistics (e.g., Latent Semantic Analysis, LSA; Deerwester et al., 1990) and explicit semantic analysis (ESA; Gabrilovich & Markovitch, 2007) have demonstrated promising results. However, these methods often struggle to capture nuanced semantic relationships beyond simple co-occurrence and can be sensitive to data sparsity. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to semantic similarity assessment that builds upon the principles of distributional semantics but seeks to go beyond simple co-occurrence by explicitly modeling *relational* information between words. Specifically, we propose a model that automatically extracts lexical patterns from the web and clusters them to identify recurring semantic relations. For example, patterns like “X causes Y,” “X is a type of Y,” or “X is used for Y” reveal specific types of relationships between words. By representing words not just by their individual contexts, but by the *types* of relations they participate in, we aim to capture a richer and more accurate representation of semantic similarity. This relational information is then used within a Mahalanobis distance framework to compute the similarity score. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by evaluating it on two widely used benchmark datasets, the Miller-Charles dataset (Miller & Charles, 1991) and the WordSimilarity-353 collection (Finkelstein et al., 2002), showing significant improvements over existing web-based measures, achieving a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.867 on the Miller-Charles dataset. This work presents a significant advancement in automatic semantic similarity measurement, harnessing the power of web-scale data and relational modeling to provide a more nuanced and accurate representation of word meaning.

Recommender systems have become ubiquitous in the digital age, assisting users in navigating the ever-expanding landscape of online content. A crucial component of many recommender systems is the ability to accurately measure the similarity between items, enabling the suggestion of relevant and engaging content. In the context of television programming, this translates to identifying programs that are likely to appeal to viewers based on their past preferences or the characteristics of other watched programs. Traditionally, similarity assessments have relied heavily on statistical measures applied to textual descriptions of the programs, typically sourced from Electronic Program Guides (EPGs). These methods often utilize techniques like Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) to create vector representations of program summaries, and subsequently employ cosine similarity to quantify the resemblance between vectors (Salton and McGill, 1983). However, these approaches often fall short when dealing with the nuanced and often concise nature of TV program summaries. A key limitation of purely lexical approaches is their sensitivity to surface-level differences in wording. Two programs with highly similar thematic content may employ distinct vocabulary, resulting in low similarity scores despite their conceptual overlap. For instance, a documentary about “wildlife conservation” and a show focused on “protecting endangered species” would likely exhibit limited lexical overlap, even though they address the same core subject matter. This issue is particularly pronounced in short summaries, which are common in EPGs and often lack sufficient textual information for reliable statistical analysis. Consequently, there is a pressing need for methods that can capture semantic relationships beyond simple word co-occurrence, allowing for a more robust and accurate assessment of program similarity. The advent of large-scale knowledge bases and semantic web technologies has opened new avenues for addressing this challenge. Resources like WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998) and DBpedia (Lehmann et al., 2015) provide structured representations of concepts and their relationships, offering the potential to enhance semantic understanding. Furthermore, automated methods for extracting semantic relations from the web have become increasingly sophisticated, enabling the creation of knowledge graphs that capture complex connections between entities. This paper proposes a novel approach to measuring TV program similarity that leverages the power of semantic relations. Instead of relying solely on word-based statistics, we construct a graph structure where nodes represent both TV programs and the key nouns appearing in their summaries. Edges in the graph represent semantic relationships extracted from web-based resources, effectively capturing the conceptual connections between programs. We then employ a random walk algorithm on this graph to quantify the relativeness of two programs, providing a similarity score that reflects their semantic proximity. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches based on TF-IDF, highlighting the benefits of incorporating semantic knowledge in TV program similarity assessment. This work contributes to a more nuanced and reliable approach to TV program recommendation, enhancing the user experience and facilitating content discovery. Hierarchical phrase-based translation (HPBT) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in statistical machine translation (SMT), offering a compelling blend of the advantages of both phrase-based and syntax-based approaches (Chiang, 2005). HPBT models leverage the expressive power of mildly context-sensitive formalisms to capture non-local dependencies and long-distance reordering phenomena that are challenging for traditional phrase-based models. This is achieved by representing phrase translations as tree fragments governed by synchronous context-free grammar (SCFG) rules. However, despite its strengths, HPBT suffers from a critical limitation: its capacity to distinguish between linguistically plausible and implausible syntactic structures. The generative nature of SCFG rules allows for the derivation of numerous syntactically invalid or semantically nonsensical parse trees, leading to a proliferation of spurious translation candidates. Previous attempts to address this issue have largely focused on enriching HPBT models with syntactic information derived from annotated corpora. These approaches typically involve constraining the SCFG rules to adhere to pre-defined syntactic constraints, learned from parallel treebanks (Resnik and Collins, 2006;Hajič et al., 2009). While these methods can yield performance improvements, they necessitate large-scale syntactic annotations, which are expensive and time-consuming to create, and often unavailable for low-resource language pairs. In this paper, we propose an alternative strategy that leverages the inherent linguistic properties of *function words* to constrain the search space of HPBT models, without relying on explicit syntactic annotations. Function words – such as prepositions, determiners, conjunctions, and auxiliary verbs – play a pivotal role in structuring syntactic dependencies and signaling grammatical relationships. Their relative order and co-occurrence patterns are remarkably consistent across languages, reflecting underlying universal grammatical principles. We hypothesize that imposing soft constraints on the topological ordering of function words can significantly reduce the number of implausible syntactic structures considered by the HPBT decoder, thereby improving translation quality. Specifically, we introduce a novel log-linear feature function that penalizes reorderings which violate typical function word dependencies. This feature does not represent a hard constraint—allowing for flexibility in cases where linguistic context warrants deviations from the norm—but rather biases the model towards more plausible syntactic configurations. Our approach builds upon the established framework of HPBT, seamlessly integrating the function word-based constraints into the existing log-linear model. We evaluate our approach on both Chinese-English and Arabic-English translation tasks, demonstrating consistent and substantial gains in performance, as measured by BLEU score. These results highlight the effectiveness of leveraging function word information as a principled means to guide the search process in HPBT models, while avoiding the challenges associated with annotation-driven syntactic modeling. Our contribution offers a practical and effective approach to addressing a fundamental problem in SMT, paving the way for more robust and accurate translation systems. In the following sections, we will detail our proposed topological ordering model (Section 2), describe the experimental setup (Section 3), present and analyze the results (Section 4), and conclude with a discussion of future work (Section 5).

Character relationships are a cornerstone of narrative, driving plot, shaping reader engagement, and reflecting complex social dynamics. In literary studies, understanding *how* these relationships evolve – the shifts from affection to animosity, trust to betrayal – offers critical insight into character motivations, thematic development, and the author’s intent. Traditionally, such analysis has been a manual, qualitative process, reliant on close reading and expert interpretation. However, the increasing availability of digitized literary texts presents an exciting opportunity to leverage computational methods to automatically track and model relationship dynamics at scale. Recent work in computational literary studies has begun to address this challenge, primarily by focusing on identifying relationships and characterizing their overall sentiment (e.g., Goodfellow, 2018; Piper, 2010). However, these approaches often rely on pre-defined categories or require laborious manual annotation of plot events associated with each relationship, limiting their scalability and introducing potential biases. Furthermore, they often fail to capture the nuanced *trajectory* of change – the specific sequence of events and emotional shifts that define the arc of a relationship. Our work addresses these limitations by proposing a novel unsupervised approach to modeling dynamic fictional relationships directly from raw text. We argue that relationship trajectories can be understood as a sequence of states defined by underlying events and emotional contexts. To capture these states without relying on pre-defined labels, we draw upon the principles of dictionary learning within a neural network framework. This allows our model to automatically discover a set of interpretable “relationship descriptors” – latent representations that correspond to recurring patterns of interaction and sentiment – and then learn a trajectory through this descriptor space for each character pairing. Unlike topic modeling approaches, which often struggle to capture dynamic shifts (Boyd-Graber et al., 2017), our model is specifically designed to model temporal sequences. Our key contribution lies in the joint learning of both the global descriptor space *and* the relationship-specific trajectories. This allows the model to benefit from shared knowledge across all relationships in the dataset while still capturing their individual nuances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a corpus of novels, showing that the learned descriptors meaningfully represent both plot events (e.g., marriage, conflict) and interpersonal states (e.g., love, hostility). Through two crowdsourced evaluation tasks, we demonstrate that our model outperforms traditional topic model baselines in predicting relationship changes. We further validate our findings by analyzing correlations between the learned descriptors and existing annotated datasets, providing further evidence of its interpretability and accuracy. Ultimately, we aim to empower digital humanities scholars with a tool for uncovering hidden patterns in character interactions and gaining a deeper understanding of narrative structure.
