Recommender systems have become increasingly important in various online platforms, helping users discover relevant items from a vast catalog. Traditional collaborative filtering (CF) methods (Koren et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2008) rely solely on user-item interaction data, often suffering from data sparsity and the cold-start problem – where new users or items lack sufficient interaction history. To address these limitations, content-based recommendation has emerged as a promising approach, leveraging auxiliary information about users and items, such as their profiles, descriptions, and associated images. Recent advances in multimodal learning have showcased the potential of integrating multiple modalities – including text, images, and audio – to enhance recommendation performance (He et al., 2016; McAuley et al., 2015). By jointly modeling information from different modalities, these methods can capture richer representations of users and items, leading to more accurate and personalized recommendations. For instance, incorporating item images into a recommendation model allows it to understand visual features that might not be explicitly mentioned in the textual description. However, a critical challenge often overlooked in multimodal recommendation is the issue of incomplete and missing modalities. In real-world scenarios, it's common for some users or items to have only partial information available. A user might not provide a profile description, or an item might lack associated images. Existing multimodal recommendation methods typically assume complete data and struggle to handle such scenarios, leading to performance degradation and biased recommendations. Simple imputation techniques like filling missing values with averages are often insufficient to capture the underlying relationships between modalities. In this paper, we address the problem of missing modalities in multimodal recommendation by proposing LRMM (Learning to Recommend with Missing Modalities), a novel framework designed to mitigate not only data incompleteness but also the broader cold-start problem. Our core idea is to learn robust multimodal representations that can effectively complement and impute missing information. To achieve this, we introduce two key components: *modality dropout (m-drop)* and a *multimodal sequential autoencoder (m-auto)*. M-drop randomly masks out modalities during training, forcing the model to learn representations that are less reliant on any single modality. M-auto then leverages the remaining available modalities to reconstruct the missing ones, enhancing the model’s ability to infer information from partial data. Through this process, LRMM learns to build more comprehensive and resilient representations of users and items. We evaluate LRMM extensively on a real-world Amazon dataset, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on rating prediction tasks. Importantly, our results show that LRMM is significantly more robust to data sparsity and the cold-start problem, offering improved recommendations for new users and items with limited interaction history. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the LRMM framework; Section 4 presents experimental results; and Section 5 concludes the paper.

Determining the semantic similarity between pieces of text is a core problem in natural language processing, with applications spanning a diverse set of tasks. These include identifying instances of plagiarism (Lancaster, 2007), ranking documents based on relevance to a query (Manning et al., 2008), recognizing paraphrases (Madnani et al., 2010), and determining textual entailment (Bentivogli et al., 2009). The effectiveness of these applications frequently hinges on the quality of the underlying text similarity measure employed. Traditionally, approaches to this problem have relied on various heuristics, including calculating overlap in n-grams (Commission, 2003), representing text as vectors based on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) (Robertson, 2004), or utilizing kernel methods with string or syntactic features (Lodhi et al., 2002). More recently, advancements in deep learning have yielded powerful new methods for text representation, particularly through the use of word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). While these models demonstrate impressive performance in natural language generation, existing text similarity measures often fail to fully leverage the inherent sequential nature of language. Many approaches, such as n-gram and skip-gram overlap, work with discrete slices of the input texts, potentially losing valuable information about the continuous flow of meaning and context. They may struggle to capture subtle semantic relationships that are expressed through word order and the dynamic interaction between words. Inspired by techniques used in bioinformatics, particularly DNA sequence alignment algorithms, we introduce TextFlow, a novel text similarity measure designed to address these limitations. In DNA sequence alignment, continuous curves are used to represent sequences and identify regions of similarity based on both the position of elements and the patterns of their arrangement (Durbin et al., 1998). We adapt this concept to the domain of natural language, representing text pairs as continuous curves in a multi-dimensional space constructed from word embeddings. The similarity between texts is then computed by considering both the spatial proximity of corresponding words and the degree of alignment between the underlying sequences. Our approach aims to capture not only *what* words are present in the text but also *how* those words are organized and related to one another. Through extensive experimentation on eight diverse datasets encompassing paraphrase detection, textual entailment recognition, and ranking relevance, we demonstrate that TextFlow consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art text similarity measures. These results highlight the benefits of incorporating the sequential nature of language into the similarity computation process and offer a promising new direction for research in this critical area of NLP. ### References Bentivogli, L., Dagan, I., Lascarides, S., & McLaren, M. Task-oriented dialogue systems are rapidly gaining prominence as effective interfaces for a variety of applications, ranging from customer service to personal assistance (Bohus & Rudnicka, 2017; Young et al., 2013). A crucial component of such systems is the language understanding (LU) module, responsible for accurately interpreting user utterances and extracting their underlying semantic intent (Gao et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019). However, the performance of LU modules is often severely hampered by the scarcity of labeled training data, particularly for complex and nuanced dialogue domains. Acquiring sufficient labeled dialogue data is expensive and time-consuming, necessitating the development of effective data augmentation techniques. Data augmentation, a standard practice in many machine learning tasks (Shorten & Khoshgoftaar, 2019), aims to artificially increase the size of the training set by generating new samples from existing ones. In the context of dialogue systems, previous data augmentation approaches have largely focused on augmenting individual utterances in isolation (e.g., back-translation, synonym replacement). While these methods can be beneficial, they often fail to capture the intricate relationships between utterances within a dialogue context, potentially introducing inconsistencies or diluting the semantic meaning. For example, simply replacing words in an utterance with synonyms doesn’t guarantee the augmented utterance remains a valid and coherent response within the broader conversational flow. In this work, we argue that effective data augmentation for dialogue LU requires leveraging the inherent semantic diversity present *within* the training data itself. Specifically, we observe that many utterances often have multiple, semantically equivalent paraphrases present in the training set. By leveraging these existing paraphrases, we can generate new, diverse augmentations that preserve the original semantic intent while expanding the training data coverage. To this end, we propose a novel sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) generation-based data augmentation framework explicitly designed for dialogue LU. Our framework employs a seq2seq model to generate novel utterances conditioned on a given input utterance, guided by the semantic relationships captured within the training data. Importantly, we introduce a novel diversity rank incorporated into the utterance representation, encouraging the model to produce diverse and semantically valid augmentations. This diversity rank helps overcome the tendency of seq2seq models to produce degenerate or repetitive outputs. We evaluate our framework on two challenging dialogue datasets: the Airline Travel Information System (ATIS) dataset and a newly created semantic frame annotation on the Stanford Multi-turn, Multidomain Dialogue Dataset (SMD). Our experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves significant improvements in LU performance, particularly in low-data scenarios where only a few hundred labeled utterances are available. Case studies further confirm that our method generates diverse, meaningful, and contextually appropriate augmentations. This suggests our approach successfully addresses the limitations of previous data augmentation techniques and paves the way for more robust and data-efficient dialogue systems. Requirements engineering is a critical phase in the software development lifecycle. Poorly defined or ambiguous requirements are a major source of project failure (Boehm and Basili, 2003), leading to cost overruns, delays, and ultimately, software that does not meet user needs. Traditionally, requirements are documented using natural language, which is prone to imprecision and misinterpretation. To address this, researchers have explored formal methods for requirements specification, such as using model-based notations and executable specifications. One promising approach involves the use of live sequence charts (LSCs) (Schärf et al., 1994), a visual, scenario-based language for describing the dynamic behavior of systems. LSCs offer a balance between formality and understandability, making them suitable for communication between stakeholders and for automatic code generation. However, the creation of LSCs is often a manual and time-consuming process. Automating the translation of natural language requirements into formal LSC specifications would significantly streamline the development process and reduce the risk of errors. This task falls under the umbrella of semantic parsing – the process of converting natural language text into a formal, machine-understandable representation of its meaning (Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005). Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep learning, have shown promising results in semantic parsing for various domains, including question answering (Berant et al., 2013) and database querying (Zhong et al., 2017). Despite these advances, semantic parsing applied to requirements documents poses unique challenges. Requirements documents often consist of multiple sentences that are interconnected and depend on each other for complete understanding. A single sentence may be ambiguous or incomplete in isolation but becomes clear when considered in the context of the surrounding discourse. Therefore, a semantic parsing system for requirements must be able to effectively integrate both sentence-level and discourse-level information. Existing semantic parsing approaches often focus solely on individual sentences (e.g., Liang et al., 2011), neglecting the valuable contextual cues present in requirements documents. In this paper, we present a novel model for the automatic semantic analysis of requirements elicitation documents, specifically targeting the generation of LSC specifications. Our approach addresses the challenges of discourse-level understanding by integrating sentence-level and discourse-level processing within a generative probabilistic framework. We demonstrate empirically that our discourse-based model consistently outperforms a sentence-based baseline in constructing a complete and accurate LSC representation of the requirements document, encompassing both static (entities, properties) and dynamic (behavioral scenarios) aspects. Our contribution lies in demonstrating the effectiveness of a unified, probabilistic model that leverages both content and context for accurate semantic parsing in the requirements engineering domain. This work builds upon previous efforts in LSC generation from text (e.g., Finkel et al., 2009), but significantly improves upon them by employing a more sophisticated discourse-aware model and a rigorous empirical evaluation.

Argument extraction, the task of identifying the arguments of a predicate in a sentence, is a core component of many natural language processing pipelines, including information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. Traditional approaches to argument extraction have largely focused on *explicit* arguments – those that are directly linked to their predicates through syntactic relations such as subject-verb or object-verb dependencies (Gildea & Jurafsky, 2002; Surdeanu et al., 2008). However, a significant portion of semantic roles are expressed *implicitly*, meaning they lack these direct syntactic connections. For instance, in the sentence “John went to the store,” the agent ‘John’ is explicitly linked to the verb ‘went,’ but in the sentence “The storm damaged the bridge,” the agent—the cause of the damage—is not explicitly stated. Identifying these implicit arguments is crucial for a complete understanding of events described in text. The difficulty of implicit argument prediction stems from its inherent ambiguity and the reliance on background knowledge and inference. Previous work has tackled this problem with feature-rich models that incorporate a variety of lexical, syntactic, and semantic cues (Chung & Penning, 2002; Gonzalez-Carriedo et al., 2009). These models often leverage hand-crafted features designed to capture subtle relationships between predicates and potential arguments. However, the construction of such features is labor-intensive and requires significant domain expertise. Furthermore, the evaluation of these systems has been hampered by the limited availability of large, annotated datasets for implicit argument prediction. Existing datasets, such as PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) and FrameNet (Baker et al., 1998), predominantly focus on explicit arguments, leaving implicit argument identification under-resourced. In this paper, we explore a novel approach to training models for implicit argument prediction, leveraging the power of large-scale automatically generated data. We frame the task as a cloze-style prediction problem, where the model is presented with a sentence containing a predicate and must identify the missing implicit argument from a candidate set. This allows us to generate training data at scale, bypassing the bottleneck of manual annotation. Our approach utilizes a neural model that effectively captures narrative coherence and entity salience, crucial aspects of understanding implicit relationships. Unlike traditional feature-based approaches, our model learns representations directly from the data, eliminating the need for extensive feature engineering. We demonstrate that our model, trained on automatically generated data, achieves superior performance on both synthetic and natural datasets, suggesting the efficacy of our approach and the potential of large-scale cloze task training for implicit argument prediction. Notably, our results highlight the importance of learning contextualized representations and leveraging narrative structure to accurately infer missing arguments. --- **References (for context - not explicitly mentioned in the abstract but appropriate for an introduction):** * Baker, C. Named entity recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying mentions of real-world objects in text – is a cornerstone of many natural language processing applications, and its importance is amplified within the medical domain. In healthcare, accurate NER on electronic medical records (EMRs) enables a wide range of downstream tasks, including disease detection, treatment outcome prediction, and patient cohort identification (Savova et al., 2010; Denny et al., 2015). However, applying NER systems to EMRs presents unique challenges compared to general-domain text. The highly specialized vocabulary, complex medical terminology, and variable writing styles of clinicians create significant obstacles for traditional NER approaches. These challenges are further compounded by the inherent heterogeneity of medical data, as records are often created by physicians specializing in different fields – cardiology, oncology, radiology, and so on – each with their own distinct lexicon and documentation conventions. The specialization of medical practice poses a critical problem for developing robust, generalized medical NER systems. A model trained on data from one specialty may perform poorly when applied to records from another due to domain shift (Pan & Yang, 2010). Obtaining sufficient labeled data to train high-performing, specialty-specific NER models is costly and time-consuming, requiring specialized expertise and extensive manual annotation. This annotation bottleneck severely limits the scalability of NER systems across the diverse landscape of medical specialties. Transfer learning (Pan & Yang, 2010) has emerged as a promising solution to address the data scarcity and domain adaptation challenges in medical NER. Previous studies have explored techniques for transferring knowledge from general-domain NER (Plank et al., 2015) or from one medical specialty to another (Habibi et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018). Fine-tuning pre-trained language models, such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), on limited annotated data has shown considerable success. However, most existing transfer learning approaches treat all labels equally, neglecting the inherent relationships between medical entities across specialties. For example, concepts like “disease” or “treatment” are fundamental to all medical domains, while others, like “imaging modality” may be significantly more prominent in radiology than in cardiology. In this paper, we address the limitations of existing approaches by introducing a novel label-aware double transfer learning framework (La-DTL) specifically designed for cross-specialty medical NER. Our approach leverages the principle that knowledge transfer should be guided by the semantic relationships between labels, ensuring that relevant information is effectively shared across specialties while minimizing the impact of domain-specific noise. We achieve this through two key components: (i) label-aware Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) for transferring feature representations, and (ii) parameter transfer informed by a theoretically grounded upper bound on transfer loss, also leveraging label similarities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of La-DTL through extensive experiments on 12 cross-specialty NER tasks, consistently outperforming strong baseline methods. Furthermore, we show the generalizability of our framework by achieving promising results on non-medical NER scenarios, suggesting its potential applicability to a wider range of NER problems.

Automatic text summarization has become a central task in Natural Language Processing, driven by the ever-increasing volume of online information. The goal of summarization is to produce a concise and fluent abstract of a source text (or texts) that conveys the most important information. Over the past two decades, a significant body of research has been dedicated to developing and evaluating automated summarization systems (Mani, 2001;Nenkova and McKeown, 2012). Evaluating the quality of summaries, however, remains a challenging problem. While automatic metrics like ROUGE (Lin, 2004) offer a computationally efficient means of assessment, they often exhibit limited correlation with human judgments (Holt and Lachishik, 2014). Consequently, human evaluation remains the gold standard for summarization assessment. The Text Analysis Conference (TAC) evaluation campaign has played a vital role in advancing the field of summarization. Since its inception, TAC has provided a standardized platform for comparing the performance of different summarization systems on a common set of documents, evaluated by human assessors. A key component of the TAC evaluation methodology is the ranking of participating systems based on their average score across multiple document sets. This aggregated score is used to identify the top-performing summarization approaches. However, the statistical validity of this simple averaging approach has not been rigorously examined. We hypothesize that the standard TAC ranking metric may not accurately reflect the true differences in performance between human and machine-generated summaries. Several factors contribute to this concern. First, the variance in human judgments is often substantially lower than the variance in machine-generated summaries. Second, the distribution of scores for human summaries may be systematically different from that of machine summaries. These differences can lead to a biased ranking and an underestimation of the performance gap between human and automated systems. In this paper, we investigate the statistical appropriateness of the current TAC ranking methodology. We analyze the human evaluation data from past TAC summarization tasks, focusing on the distributions of scores awarded to human and machine summaries. We demonstrate that the assumptions underlying the standard averaging approach – namely, that all systems are evaluated on the same scale and that the variances are comparable – are often violated. Based on this analysis, we propose an alternative ranking metric that accounts for the differences in variance and distribution between human and machine evaluations. We show, through empirical analysis, that this alternative metric provides a more nuanced and accurate assessment of system performance, better distinguishing between the strengths and weaknesses of human and machine summarization systems. Our results have implications not only for the design of future TAC evaluations but also for the interpretation of results from other summarization campaigns. References: Holt, D., & Lachishik, L. The longstanding goal of Artificial Intelligence (AI) – to create systems capable of understanding and interacting with the world in a manner akin to humans – fundamentally relies on bridging the gap between perception and communication. This necessitates the integration of vision and language, two cornerstones of human cognition. For decades, researchers have pursued this ambition, initially through rule-based systems and, more recently, propelled by the advancements in deep learning. The past two years have seen a particularly rapid acceleration in this field, marked by a prolific surge in research aimed at jointly reasoning about visual and linguistic information – spanning tasks from image and video captioning to visual question answering and grounded language understanding. This remarkable progress would not have been possible without the development of large-scale, high-quality datasets. These corpora provide the necessary training and evaluation resources for algorithms to learn the complex relationships between visual scenes and their corresponding linguistic descriptions. The growth in dataset availability has directly fueled innovation, allowing researchers to move beyond simple image-sentence pairings to more intricate scenarios involving videos, dialogues, and complex reasoning. However, the rapid proliferation of datasets also presents challenges. The datasets vary significantly in their size, annotation style, task focus, and intrinsic biases. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to compare the performance of different models objectively and to identify the key factors driving progress. A principled understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of these datasets is therefore crucial for guiding future research and establishing a solid foundation for building truly intelligent vision-and-language systems. This paper aims to address this need by providing a comprehensive survey of current datasets for vision and language research. We move beyond a simple listing of available resources and instead propose a set of quality metrics for evaluating and analyzing these datasets along several key dimensions. These metrics encompass aspects such as dataset size, linguistic complexity, visual complexity, annotation quality, and task difficulty. By applying these metrics, we categorize and compare existing datasets, revealing trends in dataset design and highlighting their respective strengths and weaknesses. Our analysis reveals that recent datasets are increasingly employing more complex language structures and focusing on more abstract visual concepts, demonstrating a push towards more challenging and realistic scenarios. However, we also identify persistent issues – such as biases in annotations, limitations in vocabulary coverage, and a lack of standardized evaluation protocols – that require attention. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers in the field, providing a critical assessment of the current landscape and informing the development of future datasets that can further advance the state-of-the-art in vision and language research. The ability to automatically learn grammatical structure directly from raw text – grammar induction – has long been a central goal in computational linguistics (Gildea, 2001; Clark & Lappin, 2000). This task is particularly challenging, as it requires simultaneously discovering both the lexicon (the set of words) and the grammar (the rules that combine these words into larger structures). While supervised parsing, which relies on manually annotated treebanks, has achieved remarkable success (Kübler et al., 2009; Martins et al., 2011), the creation of such resources is expensive, time-consuming, and often language-specific. Therefore, unsupervised grammar induction remains crucial for enabling language technology in resource-scarce settings and for understanding the principles governing natural language acquisition. Early approaches to dependency grammar induction largely relied on lexicalized probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) (Matsuzaki et al., 2005; Klein & Manning, 2004). These methods, however, often struggled to generalize beyond the training data and produced grammars that were overly complex. More recent work has focused on simpler, non-lexicalized models (Hall et al., 2011; Bansal & Klein, 2014), achieving reasonable performance but lacking the expressiveness of their supervised counterparts. A key limitation of these models is their inability to capture long-range dependencies and complex phrase structures. They often represent grammar rules as simple binary splits, failing to encode the rich hierarchical structure present in natural language. To address these limitations, we propose an approach to dependency grammar induction based on tree substitution grammars (TSGs) (Dessì & Lasagna, 2006). TSGs are a powerful formalism capable of representing large dependency fragments as single grammar rules, allowing for a more compact and expressive representation of grammatical structure. By learning these fragments, our model can better capture the hierarchical organization of dependency trees and improve parsing accuracy. However, directly inducing a TSG from raw text poses significant challenges. Without supervision, the search space for possible grammars is vast, and naive approaches can easily lead to overfitting and the discovery of spurious patterns. To address this challenge, we introduce a hierarchical non-parametric Bayesian prior based on the Pitman-Yor Process (PYP) (Pitman & Yor, 1997). The PYP is a stochastic process that naturally biases towards sparse, hierarchical structures, favoring grammars with a small number of rules and simple productions. This prior effectively regularizes the learning process, preventing overfitting and promoting generalization. We demonstrate, through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, that our approach significantly improves the state-of-the-art in unsupervised dependency grammar induction, achieving substantial gains in head attachment accuracy compared to existing methods. This improvement highlights the benefits of leveraging the expressive power of TSGs and the effectiveness of our hierarchical prior in guiding the grammar induction process.

The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced explosive growth in the 21st century, fueled by advancements in deep learning and the increasing availability of data. Alongside this growth, however, concerns have been raised regarding equity, diversity, and inclusion within the community. While anecdotal evidence suggests potential barriers to advancement for certain groups, rigorous quantitative analysis has been lacking. The concept of a “glass ceiling”—an invisible barrier preventing qualified individuals from rising to upper-level positions within an organization—is well-documented in other fields, yet its presence within NLP has remained largely unaddressed by systematic investigation. This paper aims to provide empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that a glass ceiling *has* developed within NLP, effectively limiting the representation of certain demographic groups in positions of increasing power and influence since approximately the mid-2000s. Our investigation stems from observations of authorship trends in top-tier NLP conferences – specifically, ACL, EMNLP, and NAACL – over the past two decades. Initial examination of author lists revealed a notable shift in the demographic composition of the research community around 2005. While early years showed a relatively diverse, albeit imperfect, distribution, subsequent years witnessed a diminishing representation of women and underrepresented minorities in lead author positions and on program committees. Simple correlation, however, is insufficient to establish a causal link or demonstrate the existence of systematic barriers. To address this limitation, we employ a novel mathematical model inspired by the study of bi-populated networks. This model, detailed in Section 2, simulates the dynamics of researcher collaboration and advancement, incorporating key parameters such as publication rate, citation patterns, and network centrality. Critically, the model allows us to introduce subtle biases – reflecting potential discriminatory factors in review processes, funding allocations, or mentorship opportunities – and observe their impact on the long-term distribution of researchers across different levels of influence within the network. These biases are not explicitly *assumed* but rather *tested* for their ability to reproduce the observed trends in the real-world NLP community. Our simulations, described in Section 3, demonstrate that even small, seemingly innocuous biases introduced into the model consistently lead to the emergence of a glass ceiling effect. Specifically, we find that a slightly higher bar for acceptance for researchers belonging to historically disadvantaged groups, or a tendency for established researchers to preferentially cite work from within their own network, drastically reduces their ability to accumulate influence and achieve positions of leadership over time. The model’s predictions align remarkably well with observed authorship trends in the aforementioned conferences, specifically the declining participation of certain groups in high-impact publications and conference organization roles. Importantly, this work does not aim to assign blame or identify individual perpetrators of bias. Rather, our goal is to provide a quantitative, data-driven analysis that illuminates systemic issues within the NLP community. The implications of these findings are significant, suggesting that continued attention to issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion is crucial to ensure the continued growth and innovation of the field. Section 4 discusses potential remedies and future research directions to dismantle these barriers and create a more inclusive and equitable NLP community.

Wikipedia, a collaboratively edited online encyclopedia, represents a unique corpus for studying human text revision. Millions of edits are made daily, ranging from simple spelling corrections to substantial content rewrites and, unfortunately, acts of vandalism. Understanding the *nature* of these edits – classifying them into categories like “Spelling Error Correction,” “Content Addition,” or “Vandalism” – is crucial for various applications. These applications include automated quality control, identifying constructive contributors, and improving the overall reliability of the encyclopedia (Potts et al., 2007; Halfaker et al., 2009; Suh et al., 2009). Traditionally, edit categorization relies on manual annotation, a process that is both time-consuming and expensive, particularly given the sheer volume of revisions. Consequently, automatic edit category classification has emerged as a significant research area within the fields of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). Early work in this area focused on leveraging textual features of the edit itself to predict its category (Sorokin and Forsyth, 2008; Greenwood and Hotho, 2011). These methods often employed techniques like bag-of-words and n-grams, combined with machine learning classifiers. However, recent research suggests that a more holistic approach, incorporating not only the textual changes but also metadata about the edit and the document’s history, can yield significantly improved performance (Bryant et al., 2016). For instance, information about the editor, the revision timestamps, and the size of the edit can provide valuable clues about the edit’s intent. In this paper, we contribute to the field of automatic edit category classification by presenting a novel set of features designed to capture various aspects of the revision process. These features span three primary categories: metadata relating to the edit and its author; textual properties quantifying the changes made; and linguistic features assessing the quality and style of the revised text, including markup characteristics. We hypothesize that the interplay between these features provides a more comprehensive representation of the edit, allowing for more accurate categorization. We evaluate our approach on a publicly available corpus of edits from the English Wikipedia, annotated with a 21-category taxonomy. Using a supervised machine learning framework, we demonstrate that our feature set achieves a micro-averaged F1 score of .62, representing a substantial improvement over existing approaches. Notably, a model trained on our data also exhibits state-of-the-art performance on the closely related task of *fluency edit classification,* suggesting the robustness and generalizability of our feature engineering. Furthermore, we explore the collaborative patterns within Wikipedia articles through pattern mining, revealing that high-quality articles tend to exhibit more homogeneous editing behavior. This suggests a connection between the nature of collaboration and the overall quality of Wikipedia content. Question answering (QA) has long been a central task in natural language processing, with applications ranging from information retrieval to virtual assistants. Early QA systems focused on factoid questions – those with short, precise answers – leveraging knowledge bases and information extraction techniques (Voorhees and Terveen, 1999; Moldovan et al., 2003). However, a significant portion of real-world questions, particularly those seeking explanations, fall into the category of non-factoid QA, requiring more complex reasoning and generation of longer, more descriptive responses. Among non-factoid questions, *why*-questions pose a unique challenge. Unlike questions asking “what,” “who,” or “where,” *why*-questions demand an understanding of causality and motivation. Answering them effectively requires not just identifying relevant information, but also inferring the underlying reasons behind events or phenomena. Existing approaches to non-factoid QA often rely on techniques like information retrieval, passage ranking, and answer extraction (Yamada et al., 2006; Suzuki et al., 2014). These systems typically rank potential answers based on their similarity to the question, utilizing features like term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf) and language modeling. More recent work has explored the use of neural network architectures, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers, to encode both questions and answer candidates, improving the ability to capture semantic relationships (Seo et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018). Despite these advancements, *why*-question answering remains a difficult problem. Many existing systems struggle to identify answers that provide a genuine explanation, often returning superficial or irrelevant information. We hypothesize that a key element missing from current approaches is an explicit consideration of the inherent *sentiment* and *semantic directionality* typically found in causal relationships. Specifically, we observe that a *why*-question and its corresponding answer frequently exhibit aligned sentiment – if the event described in the question is negative, the answer is likely to identify a negative cause, and vice versa. For example, “Why did the company’s stock price fall?” is likely answered with reasons pertaining to negative financial performance or unfavorable market conditions. Furthermore, understanding the semantic classes of words involved – whether they represent actions, states, entities or attributes – can provide crucial clues about the causal links at play. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to explicitly incorporate sentiment analysis and semantic word classes into a why-question answering system. We propose a novel approach that leverages these features to re-rank potential answers generated by a state-of-the-art QA system. Our experiments on a dataset of 850 *why*-questions demonstrate a substantial improvement in precision at the top-1 answer, achieving a 15.2% gain over the baseline system. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 discusses related work in QA and sentiment analysis; Section 3 details our proposed method; Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results; and Section 5 concludes the paper with a discussion of future directions.

Stance classification – determining whether a piece of text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral attitude toward a target – has emerged as a crucial task in analyzing online discourse. The ability to automatically identify stances is valuable in numerous applications, ranging from understanding public opinion on political issues (Hanson, 2005;Sobolev et al., 2018) to monitoring sentiment surrounding brands or events (Vilares et al., 2012;Qiu et al., 2017). Early work on stance classification treated it as a standard text classification problem, leveraging features extracted from the text itself to predict the stance (Mukherjee and Bhattacharyya, 2012;López et al., 2014). However, these approaches often neglected the rich contextual information inherent in social media conversations. More recent approaches have recognized the importance of considering the relationships between entities – such as users and posts – within a network (Guo et al., 2019;Baños et al., 2020), leading to the development of structured output prediction models like collective classification and sequence labeling. These methods leverage the network structure to improve stance prediction accuracy by propagating stance information across connected nodes. Twitter, with its public and interconnected nature, provides a particularly fertile ground for stance classification research. Users express opinions on diverse topics through tweets, often engaging in conversations centered around specific hashtags or events. Importantly, the platform’s social network structure – comprised of users, their followers, and the relationships between tweets (e.g., retweets, mentions) – offers valuable contextual cues that can aid in stance identification. Existing work has shown that integrating network information can significantly boost the performance of stance classification models (Agarwal et al., 2016;Sinha et al., 2018). However, obtaining large, labeled datasets for supervised stance classification can be a significant bottleneck. Manually annotating tweets with stance labels is often time-consuming, expensive, and requires careful consideration of nuanced language and context. To address this limitation, we explore a weakly supervised approach to stance classification on Twitter, leveraging the presence of stance-indicative hashtags or phrases as a source of limited supervision. Given the inherent interconnectedness of Twitter data, we propose a collective classification framework based on hinge-loss Markov random fields (HL-MRFs). This framework allows us to jointly model the stances of tweets and the underlying stances of users, incorporating network relationships as constraints. Our central hypothesis is that by enforcing consistency between predicted tweet labels and user stances, and by leveraging the network structure to propagate stance information, we can achieve accurate stance classification even with minimal labeled data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the stance-indicative tweets identified through our relational bootstrapping process can be used to train effective linear text classifiers, even in scenarios where the network structure is unavailable or computationally expensive to process. This provides a valuable path towards scalable and robust stance classification in real-world applications.

Traditional n-gram language models (LMs) have long served as a cornerstone of many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, due to their simplicity and effectiveness. However, these models fundamentally suffer from limitations in capturing long-range dependencies and generalizing to unseen data. While smoothing techniques like Kneser-Ney interpolation mitigate some of these issues, they largely operate at the surface level of word sequences, failing to explicitly model the underlying syntactic and semantic structure of language. Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in incorporating structured knowledge into language models. Approaches range from using parse trees as features (Chelba & Pereira, 2009) to directly modeling dependencies between words using probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) (Clark & Curran, 2007). These approaches, while promising, often require large, accurately parsed corpora, which are expensive to create and may not be available for all languages. Moreover, the accuracy of the parse trees themselves can significantly impact the performance of the resulting language model. In this paper, we introduce the Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM), a novel language modeling approach that aims to bridge the gap between n-gram models and structured linguistic representations. Unlike methods relying on pre-defined grammars or parse trees, LTLM *learns* a tree structure directly from the data, representing the syntactic and semantic roles of words within a sentence. The core idea is to encode a sentence as a tree, where each node represents a ‘word role’ – a generalized semantic or syntactic function of a word in that context. This allows the model to capture dependencies beyond the immediate n-gram window and implicitly encode information about sentence structure without explicitly relying on a full parse. The LTLM learning process is iterative, and utilizes Gibbs sampling to refine the tree structure associated with each sentence. This probabilistic framework enables the model to explore a space of possible tree structures, gradually converging towards arrangements that best explain the observed word sequences. We present two algorithms for tree inference: a fast Gibbs sampling approach and a slower, but more accurate, dynamic programming algorithm. A comparative analysis of these algorithms is provided, highlighting their respective strengths and weaknesses. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the LTLM, we combine it with a standard 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney language model via linear interpolation. Extensive experiments conducted on both English and Czech corpora demonstrate substantial perplexity reductions – up to 46% for English and 49% for Czech – compared to a standalone 4-gram Modified Kneser-Ney baseline. These results confirm the ability of LTLM to effectively capture linguistic structure and improve language modeling performance, offering a significant advancement over traditional n-gram approaches. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 details the LTLM framework. Section 4 presents the tree inference algorithms. Section 5 outlines the experimental setup and results. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

Question answering (QA) – the task of automatically providing answers to questions posed in natural language – is a cornerstone of Artificial Intelligence. Achieving human-level performance on QA demands robust mechanisms for knowledge representation and reasoning. Historically, approaches to QA have relied heavily on either unstructured text corpora or highly structured knowledge bases (KBs). Unstructured text, while readily available, presents significant challenges for automated reasoning due to its ambiguity and lack of explicit relationships between facts. Techniques like information retrieval (IR) and reading comprehension are commonly employed to extract answers from text, but often struggle with complex reasoning or questions requiring external knowledge. Conversely, highly structured KBs, such as those represented in RDF or Prolog, facilitate precise reasoning but are notoriously difficult and expensive to construct and maintain. Manually populating such KBs requires significant expert effort, and the process is often bottlenecked by the inherent complexity of representing real-world knowledge. This paper investigates an alternative: leveraging tables as a form of *semi-structured* knowledge for question answering. Tables represent a compelling middle ground between the accessibility of unstructured text and the reasoning power of structured KBs. They possess an inherent organization – rows and columns – that delineate relationships between entities and attributes, making them easier to parse and reason about than free-form text. Furthermore, tables are ubiquitous on the web and in many real-world applications, representing a readily available source of knowledge. However, exploiting tables for QA is not trivial. Existing methods often focus on retrieving relevant tables and then applying natural language processing techniques to extract answers, overlooking the rich structural information contained within the table itself. We propose a novel approach that explicitly incorporates table structure into a feature-driven QA model. A key contribution of this work is the creation of a large-scale, high-quality dataset of multiple-choice questions grounded in tables. Recognizing the difficulty of manually authoring such a dataset, we leverage crowd-sourcing, guided by the inherent structure of tables to efficiently generate over 9,000 question-answer pairs. Crucially, we obtain rich alignment annotations linking question phrases to specific table cells and columns, providing valuable supervisory signals for learning. Using this annotated data, we train a semi-structured QA model that combines features derived from both natural language and table structure. We demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms both a strong unstructured retrieval baseline leveraging dense passage retrieval, and a highly structured Markov Logic Network (MLN) model designed for reasoning over relational databases. These results highlight the benefits of our approach in effectively capturing and utilizing the semi-structured nature of tabular knowledge for question answering. This work demonstrates the potential of tables as a valuable and readily-accessible resource for building more robust and intelligent QA systems. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Phrase structure parsing remains a core task in natural language processing, serving as a crucial foundation for numerous downstream applications such as machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. While significant progress has been made in parsing algorithms and techniques, particularly for languages like English with relatively simple morphology, parsing morphologically rich languages presents unique challenges. These languages, characterized by complex inflectional systems and a high degree of word-form ambiguity, demand parsers capable of effectively leveraging morphological information to disambiguate syntactic structures. Traditional phrase structure parsers often struggle with this task, either due to limitations in their ability to represent and utilize morphological features or due to computational inefficiencies when dealing with the increased complexity of the grammar. Lexicalized parsing, as pioneered by Collins (2003), represents a significant advancement in this area. By incorporating lexical associations directly into the parsing process, it demonstrably improves accuracy, particularly for languages where lexical information strongly influences syntactic structure. However, standard lexicalized parsers often treat lexical items as atomic units, failing to fully exploit the rich internal structure inherent in morphologically complex words. This limitation is particularly pronounced in languages like French, German, or Russian, where a single word form can encode a considerable amount of grammatical information. This paper introduces a novel parsing algorithm designed to address this limitation. We present an LR-inspired parsing approach that generalizes lexicalized parsing by allowing for a structured representation of lexical items. Instead of treating each word form as a distinct lexicon entry, our system represents lexical items as compositions of morphological features, enabling the parser to effectively capture and utilize the intricate relationships between form and meaning. This structured lexical representation, combined with a discriminative weighting scheme (Collins, 2002) learned from treebank data, allows our parser to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on the French Treebank. Furthermore, our implementation is designed for efficiency. LR parsing, known for its speed and deterministic nature, provides a robust framework for handling the computational demands of morphologically rich languages. We demonstrate that our parser achieves considerably faster parsing times compared to existing state-of-the-art parsers on the French dataset, without sacrificing accuracy. Finally, we present a comparative analysis with parsing performance on English, a language with considerably simpler morphology, highlighting the benefits of our approach in the context of morphological complexity. This comparison provides insights into the generalizability of our method and its potential applicability to a wider range of languages. In essence, this work aims to bridge the gap between the efficiency of LR parsing and the representational power needed to accurately parse morphologically rich languages. By generalizing the concept of lexicalization and incorporating a sophisticated morphological representation, we offer a practical and effective solution for syntactic parsing in challenging linguistic environments. We believe that our contribution provides a significant step forward in the field of parsing, contributing to more accurate and efficient natural language processing systems for morphologically rich languages. . . . . . . .

The pursuit of artificial intelligence capable of human-level reasoning requires access to vast quantities of structured knowledge. While large text corpora offer a wealth of information, this knowledge is largely implicit and unstructured, making it difficult for machines to utilize effectively. A promising avenue for addressing this challenge lies in leveraging existing repositories of formalized knowledge, such as knowledge graphs and axiom sets. However, creating these resources from scratch is a laborious and time-consuming process. Consequently, there’s growing interest in automatically extracting structured knowledge from readily available sources, with textbooks representing a particularly valuable, yet largely untapped, resource. Textbooks, particularly in well-defined domains like mathematics, represent carefully curated and systematically organized knowledge. They provide a foundation for human learning and, crucially, often explicitly state foundational axioms and definitions. Harvesting this axiomatic knowledge represents a significant step towards equipping AI systems with the reasoning capabilities needed to tackle complex problems. However, extracting this knowledge automatically is not straightforward. Textbooks are written in natural language, which is inherently ambiguous, and the axioms are often embedded within lengthy explanations and proofs. This paper focuses on the specific challenge of harvesting axiomatic knowledge from math textbooks, specifically in the domain of geometry. Geometry, with its rigorous axiomatic foundation, provides an ideal testbed for developing and evaluating automated knowledge extraction techniques. Existing approaches to knowledge extraction often struggle with precision and recall, particularly when dealing with complex logical structures. Our core hypothesis is that by carefully considering the contextual and typographical features of textbook content, and by exploiting the redundancy and consistency of axioms across multiple sources, we can significantly improve the accuracy of axiom extraction. We propose an approach that combines sophisticated feature engineering with a robust rule-learning framework. We extract features related to the textual context surrounding potential axioms (e.g., surrounding keywords, sentence structure), as well as typographical characteristics (e.g., use of boldface, indentation, numbering). Furthermore, we leverage the fact that many fundamental geometric axioms are presented in multiple textbooks, using cross-validation between different sources to refine the accuracy of the extracted rules. The extracted axioms are then formalized as horn-clause rules, a standard representation in logic programming, enabling their application in automated reasoning systems. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply the harvested axioms to the task of automated geometry problem solving. We integrate the extracted knowledge into a state-of-the-art geometry problem solver and evaluate its performance on a challenging benchmark dataset. Our results demonstrate that the extracted axioms significantly improve the solver’s ability to correctly solve geometry problems, highlighting the value of automatically harvesting knowledge from textbooks. We further demonstrate that with increased textbook coverage, the performance continues to scale, highlighting the potential for building even more sophisticated reasoning systems. This work contributes to the growing body of research on automated knowledge extraction, with a specific focus on harnessing the power of educational materials. By bridging the gap between textbook content and machine-readable knowledge, we aim to unlock new possibilities for AI-powered educational tools and intelligent reasoning systems.

The field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) relies heavily on treebanks – annotated corpora providing syntactic and sometimes semantic information about language. These treebanks are invaluable resources for training and evaluating NLP models, yet they rarely align perfectly with the requirements of a specific task. Consequently, transforming one treebank structure into another is a common necessity. These transformations include, but are not limited to, projecting constituency trees onto dependency trees (Kübler et al., 2009), converting between different dependency schemes (McDonald et al., 2013), enriching trees with part-of-speech or named entity information, and modifying tree structures to suit specific linguistic theories or applications. However, describing these treebank transformations in a precise and unambiguous manner has proven challenging. Historically, treebank transductions have been detailed primarily through textual descriptions embedded within research papers. While such descriptions convey the *intent* of the transformation, they often lack the necessary rigor for independent replication or automated implementation. These descriptions are frequently ambiguous, relying on implicit assumptions about the source and target treebank formats and the underlying linguistic principles. This ambiguity leads to inconsistencies in implementations and hinders the reproducibility of research results. Furthermore, existing implementations are often tightly coupled with specific treebank formats and programming languages, making them difficult to adapt to new scenarios. The resulting “spaghetti code” is hard to maintain, extend, and share. The core problem lies in the absence of a formal, dedicated language for expressing treebank transductions. Existing formalisms, such as regular expressions or context-free grammars, are either insufficiently expressive for capturing the complexities of tree structures and their annotations, or they require significant effort to adapt to this specific domain. The need for a standardized approach became apparent as the complexity of NLP tasks grew and the demand for interoperable treebanks increased. A clearly-defined language would enable researchers to share their transformations easily, facilitate automated execution, and ensure that results are truly reproducible. This paper introduces a transduction language designed specifically for natural language treebank transformations. Our language aims to provide a clean, precise, and concise way to describe these complex operations, addressing the shortcomings of existing textual descriptions. The language’s design prioritizes clarity and expressiveness, allowing for a faithful representation of the desired transformation. Moreover, we have implemented a tree transduction tool based on this language, demonstrating its practical applicability. The primary goal of this work is not simply to present a new tool or language, but to foster a community-driven effort towards establishing a de facto standard for treebank transduction specification. We invite feedback from the NLP community to refine and enhance the language, ultimately promoting collaboration and reproducibility in the field. We believe that a shared language will significantly advance the development and utilization of treebank resources, accelerating progress in a wide range of NLP tasks. References: Kübler, S., McDonald, R., & Nivre, J. (2009). Dependency parsing. *Syntactic Natural Language Processing*, 763–826. McDonald, R., Nivre, J., Hall, Y., Sato, S., & Kumar, S. (2013). Universal dependency annotation for multilingual parsing. *Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics*, *1*, 245–258.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has become the dominant paradigm in machine translation (MT) over the past decade (Koehn et al., 2003; Och and Ney, 2004). The performance of SMT systems is heavily dependent on the quantity and quality of parallel corpora, i.e., collections of text segments (typically sentences) paired with their translations in another language. Traditionally, constructing parallel corpora has been a laborious and expensive process, often relying on human translators or meticulously aligned documents from international organizations like the United Nations or the European Parliament (Brown et al., 1993). However, the demand for MT systems for a wider range of language pairs and domains necessitates exploring alternative, more cost-effective methods for acquiring parallel training data. One promising avenue is the extraction of parallel sentences from comparable corpora – large collections of monolingual texts in different languages that cover similar topics (Gale and Church, 1993; Fung and Cheung, 2004). These approaches often leverage techniques like cross-lingual information retrieval and sentence alignment to identify potential translation pairs. While effective, this indirect method relies on the assumption that comparable texts contain significant overlap in content and structure, and the resulting parallel data is often noisy and requires extensive filtering. A more direct, though considerably more challenging, approach is to directly mine the Web for parallel sentences. The World Wide Web contains an immense amount of multilingual content, including mirrored web pages, translated documents, and discussions in multilingual forums. However, extracting high-quality parallel data from the Web is fraught with difficulties. The Web is inherently noisy and unstructured, making it difficult to identify true translation pairs amidst the vast amount of irrelevant and poorly aligned content. Existing efforts in Web mining of parallel data (e.g., Resnik and Smith, 2003; Freitag and Al-Onaizan, 2007) have often focused on identifying bilingual web pages and then applying sentence alignment techniques. These methods typically rely on heuristics based on HTML structure, anchor text, and character encoding, but often suffer from low precision and recall. This paper presents an empirical investigation into the challenges and opportunities of directly mining parallel corpora from the Web. Rather than relying on pre-existing comparable corpora, we explore the use of targeted Web searches to retrieve potential translation pairs. Our approach leverages “Learning to Rank” (Li, 2009) to formulate effective search queries that maximize the likelihood of retrieving high-quality parallel sentences. Furthermore, we employ the well-established IBM Model 1 (Brown et al., 1993) alignment score as a filtering mechanism to remove noisy document pairs and improve the accuracy of our extracted data. We present a comprehensive end-to-end evaluation that demonstrates the significant improvements in statistical machine translation performance achievable through the proposed approach. We argue that a carefully designed Web mining strategy, guided by machine learning principles and informed by statistical alignment models, can provide a viable and scalable solution for acquiring parallel data for MT.

Natural Language Generation (NLG) systems are increasingly employed in a variety of applications, ranging from report generation (Reiter & Dale, 2000) to dialogue systems (Lochbaum & Tomsett, 2017). A common goal in NLG is to produce text that is not only accurate and informative, but also natural and engaging. However, many NLG systems tend to generate repetitive and predictable text, lacking the stylistic variation characteristic of human language (Gatt & Krahmer, 2018). This lack of variation can lead to user dissatisfaction and a perception of artificiality. One key aspect of stylistic variation lies in the choice of referring expressions – the ways in which entities are referred to in text. For instance, consider referring to the same person: “John,” “the man,” “he,” “the individual,” or “my friend.” Human writers routinely vary their choice of referring expressions, influenced by factors like discourse context, grammatical preferences, and even individual style. This variation contributes significantly to the overall naturalness and readability of the text. Existing NLG systems often struggle to replicate this natural variation. Typically, they employ deterministic algorithms for referring expression generation (REC) (Dale, 1992), selecting a single, seemingly optimal form based on a set of predefined rules. While these rule-based approaches can ensure grammatical correctness and unambiguous reference resolution, they often result in repetitive and monotonous text. To address this limitation, we advocate for a nondeterministic approach to REC, one that allows for multiple plausible referring expressions to be generated for the same entity. In this paper, we introduce two probabilistic models designed to capture individual variation in the choice of referential form: a Naive Bayes model and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). These models are trained on the VaREG corpus (Krahmer et al., 2011), a unique resource specifically created for studying variation in referring expressions. The VaREG corpus provides multiple, manually authored references for the same referential situation, capturing the range of choices deemed acceptable by human annotators. We evaluate both models on their ability to predict human preferences for referring expressions within the VaREG corpus. Subsequently, we integrate the best-performing model into a full NLG pipeline, applying it to generate referring expressions within texts from the GREC-2.0 corpus (White et al., 2003). A human evaluation experiment assesses the impact of the generated variation on perceived text coherence and comprehensibility, comparing the output of our variation model against both the original reference texts and a random baseline model. Our results demonstrate that incorporating probabilistic variation models into NLG systems can significantly improve the perceived naturalness and quality of generated text. The increasing globalization of communication has led to a surge in code-switching, the practice of alternating between two or more languages within a single conversation or text. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent in online communication, such as social media posts, emails, and instant messaging, where users frequently mix languages to express themselves more effectively or efficiently. In the context of Chinese language processing, the integration of English words into Chinese text is becoming increasingly common, especially among younger generations and in informal writing styles. This mixing of languages presents significant challenges for traditional natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, named entity recognition, and syntactic parsing. Existing Chinese POS taggers typically perform poorly when encountering English words embedded in Chinese sentences, often misclassifying them as unknown words or assigning generic tags like "foreign word" (外来语). This lack of accurate POS tagging hinders downstream NLP applications that rely on well-annotated linguistic data. The primary difficulty in POS tagging for Chinese-English mixed texts lies in the scarcity of large-scale, manually annotated corpora that explicitly label the POS tags of English words within a Chinese context. Creating such a corpus is a time-consuming and expensive undertaking, limiting the availability of supervised learning resources. Furthermore, the inherent ambiguity of English words – a single word can have multiple POS tags depending on the context – adds to the complexity of the task. Traditional sequence labeling methods, such as hidden Markov models (HMMs) and conditional random fields (CRFs), rely heavily on statistical patterns observed in training data. Without sufficient labeled examples, these models struggle to generalize to the diverse range of English words and their possible POS tags in mixed texts. In this paper, we address the challenge of POS tagging for Chinese-English mixed texts by proposing a novel approach that leverages dynamic features extracted from the surrounding context. Our method aims to overcome the limitations of traditional sequence labeling techniques by incorporating information that helps to disambiguate the POS tags of English words. Specifically, we introduce a set of features that capture the syntactic and semantic relationships between English words and their Chinese neighbors. These dynamic features include dependency relations, word embeddings, and contextual cues derived from the surrounding text. We demonstrate through experiments on a benchmark dataset that our dynamic feature-based method significantly outperforms traditional sequence labeling approaches in terms of POS tagging accuracy for mixed texts. Notably, our approach also leads to improved performance in POS tagging for pure Chinese texts, indicating that the incorporation of dynamic features can benefit the overall tagging process. The contributions of this work are twofold: (1) We present a novel method for POS tagging of Chinese-English mixed texts that utilizes dynamic features to capture contextual information. (2) We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments and show that it improves both the accuracy of English POS tagging and the overall performance of Chinese POS tagging. The rapid growth of microblogging platforms like Twitter has created a wealth of data for analyzing public opinion, tracking emerging trends, and understanding user interests. Topic modeling, a statistical technique for discovering latent thematic structures within large text corpora, has become a prominent tool for tackling these challenges. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) is arguably the most widely used topic model, and it has been successfully applied to various Twitter-related tasks, including user profiling (Zhao et al., 2011), event detection and summarization (Mathioudakis & Koudas, 2010), and trend analysis (Petrovic et al., 2010). Traditional applications of LDA to Twitter often treat a collection of a user’s tweets as a single document. However, this approach overlooks the inherent characteristics of Twitter data, specifically the short, often single-topic nature of individual tweets. Recognizing this limitation, Yan et al. (2012) proposed Twitter-LDA, a topic model explicitly designed for Twitter. Twitter-LDA assumes each tweet focuses on a single topic, thereby better capturing the semantic coherence of the discovered topics compared to traditional LDA when applied to aggregated tweet collections. Empirical results demonstrated the superiority of Twitter-LDA in topic modeling on Twitter data. Despite its advantages, a crucial limitation of Twitter-LDA is its inability to perform online inference. Real-world applications on Twitter demand models that can adapt to the continuous stream of incoming data, allowing for dynamic updates to the estimated topics and user interests. Static, batch-based models like Twitter-LDA require retraining from scratch with each new influx of tweets, which is computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale deployments. Moreover, the dynamic nature of Twitter necessitates models capable of tracking the evolution of both user interests and topic trends over time. Users’ interests shift, and new topics emerge constantly, requiring timely adjustments to the model. To address these shortcomings, we propose an extension to Twitter-LDA that incorporates online inference capabilities and explicitly models the dynamics of user interests and topic trends. Our approach builds upon the strengths of Twitter-LDA while leveraging concepts from the Topic Tracking Model (TTM) (Fujiwara et al., 2011), originally developed for modeling consumer purchase behavior. Specifically, we introduce two key enhancements: First, we refine the generative process of tweets by estimating the ratio between topic-specific words and more general vocabulary terms for each user, providing a more nuanced representation of their topical engagement. Second, we adapt the TTM framework to enable online estimation of both individual user interest dynamics and the temporal evolution of topic trends within the Twitter stream. This allows us to track how users’ topical preferences shift and how the prominence of different topics waxes and wanes over time. Our contributions aim to provide a more robust and adaptable topic modeling solution for Twitter, capable of responding effectively to the platform’s fast-paced and dynamic nature.

Abstractive text summarization aims to generate concise and fluent summaries that capture the salient information from source documents. While significant progress has been made in this field with sequence-to-sequence models (Rush et al., 2015;See et al., 2017;Gehrmann et al., 2018), effectively representing the underlying *events* described in the text remains a core challenge, particularly for news summarization. News articles frequently revolve around specific events – such as political elections, natural disasters, or corporate mergers – and a successful summarization system must accurately identify and represent these events to produce a coherent and informative summary. Existing approaches to event representation in summarization often rely on predefined event schemas or ontologies (Barzilay and Lapata, 2008;Li et al., 2013), which require substantial manual effort to create and maintain. More recent work leverages Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) techniques (Banko et al., 2008;Etzioni et al., 2011) to identify event patterns directly from text, offering a more flexible and data-driven approach. These patterns can be viewed as different linguistic realizations of the same underlying event. For example, the event “marriage” might be expressed through patterns like “X married Y,” “X and Y tied the knot,” or “X wedded Y.” In this work, we explore different methods for extracting and representing these event patterns. We compare three distinct approaches: a heuristics-based method, a compression-based method, and a novel memory-based method. The heuristics-based approach, reminiscent of techniques used in earlier multi-document summarization systems (Mani, 2001), relies on predefined linguistic rules to identify event patterns. Compression-based methods leverage techniques from information theory to identify frequent and informative patterns (Teufel and von Zeska, 1994). While these methods have seen some success, we argue they often fail to capture the full richness and variability of event expressions. Our central contribution is the introduction of a memory-based method for extracting event patterns. This approach stores a vast collection of parse trees derived from a large corpus of grammatical utterances and then searches for subtrees within newly parsed sentences that match these stored patterns. This allows the system to extrapolate event representations from existing knowledge, even for novel sentence structures. However, searching this enormous space of parse trees – potentially hundreds of millions – is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel data structure and search method designed to efficiently identify matching subtrees. We empirically demonstrate that the memory-based method significantly outperforms both the heuristics-based and compression-based approaches in generating grammatical and informative sentences for abstractive summarization. While computationally more demanding, the enhanced pattern quality provided by the memory-based method leads to improvements in summary quality, highlighting the benefits of leveraging a rich memory of linguistic knowledge for event representation.

Narratives are fundamental to human communication and understanding. They structure our experiences, convey information, and facilitate reasoning about the world. A key element of narrative comprehension lies in recognizing recurring patterns of events, often referred to as narrative schemas or frames. These schemas represent abstract knowledge about typical sequences of actions and the roles played by different participants within those sequences. For example, the schema for an “Arrest” event might involve a police officer, a suspect, and a location, unfolding in a predictable manner. Automatically extracting these schemas from text has long been a goal in natural language processing (NLP), with applications ranging from story understanding and information retrieval to question answering and commonsense reasoning. Traditionally, approaches to narrative schema learning have relied heavily on supervised machine learning techniques (Pichler et al., 2012; Ruppert et al., 2014), requiring large, manually annotated datasets of events and their associated roles. While effective, these supervised methods are costly to develop and generalize poorly to new domains or languages. Alternatively, researchers have explored the use of hand-built knowledge resources, such as FrameNet (Baker et al., 1998) or PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005), to guide the learning process. However, these resources are often incomplete, limited in scope, and reflect the biases of their creators. Furthermore, many existing approaches treat event structure learning and semantic role induction as separate tasks, hindering the potential for synergy between the two. In this paper, we present a novel unsupervised system for learning narrative schemas and their constituent participant roles directly from raw text. Our approach eschews the need for supervised data, hand-crafted knowledge, or predefined event or role classes. Instead, we leverage the inherent structure of narrative text – specifically, the co-occurrence of verbs and their arguments within coreference chains – to simultaneously discover both rich event structure and fine-grained semantic roles. The core insight behind our method is that arguments which consistently appear together across multiple instances of a verb are likely to fulfill similar semantic roles within the corresponding narrative schema. By jointly addressing event structure learning and semantic role induction, our system benefits from a synergistic effect, improving upon previous results in both areas. Specifically, the discovered event structure provides valuable contextual information for refining semantic role assignments, while the induced semantic roles, in turn, strengthen the coherence of the learned schemas. The system's ability to operate entirely in an unsupervised fashion offers significant advantages in terms of adaptability and scalability, enabling it to learn schemas from a wide range of textual sources without the need for extensive manual annotation or expert knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a corpus of news articles, showcasing its ability to induce meaningful and interpretable narrative schemas with rich, frame-specific semantic roles.
