The ability for machines to comprehend natural language text remains a fundamental, yet persistently challenging, goal within the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). True comprehension necessitates not merely recognizing words and syntactic structures, but also inferring meaning, understanding context, and reasoning about the information presented – skills that are readily achieved by humans but remain elusive for even the most sophisticated computational models. A significant obstacle to progress in this area is the scarcity of large, high-quality, human-annotated datasets suitable for training and evaluating such systems. Obtaining this data is expensive, time-consuming, and often requires specialized expertise. Recently, Hermann et al. (2015) proposed a novel approach to address this data bottleneck, introducing a large-scale reading comprehension dataset constructed by pairing articles from CNN and the Daily Mail news sources with the corresponding bullet-point summaries. The rationale behind this approach is that the summaries can serve as “answers” to questions implicitly posed by the articles, effectively creating over one million training examples without the need for extensive human annotation. They demonstrated that a neural network architecture, when trained on this dataset, could achieve surprisingly good performance on question answering tasks related to the articles. This work marks a significant step forward in the pursuit of machine reading comprehension. However, the nature of the comprehension skills *actually* required to succeed on this task—and thus the extent to which it reflects true understanding—remains an open question. Is high performance achieved through deep semantic analysis and logical reasoning, or can it be attained through more superficial pattern matching and statistical associations? In this paper, we undertake a thorough examination of the CNN/Daily Mail reading comprehension task, aiming to shed light on this critical issue. Our investigation proceeds along two complementary axes. First, we perform a detailed hand analysis of a representative subset of the question-answer pairs, identifying the types of linguistic phenomena and reasoning processes involved. This qualitative analysis provides insight into the subtleties of the task and the challenges it poses to computational models. Second, we present a series of surprisingly effective, yet relatively simple, systems designed to exploit inherent characteristics of the dataset. These systems, built with carefully engineered features, achieve accuracies of 72.4% and 75.8% on the CNN and Daily Mail datasets respectively – exceeding current state-of-the-art results by over 5% and, we argue, approaching the practical upper limit of performance achievable with this particular data construction method. Through this combined qualitative and quantitative analysis, we aim to provide a nuanced understanding of the depth of language understanding required to perform well on the CNN/Daily Mail task, and to contribute to the development of more robust and genuinely intelligent reading comprehension systems. Recommender systems have become increasingly important in various online applications, ranging from e-commerce and social networks to news and music platforms. The fundamental goal of a recommender system is to predict the preferences of users for items they have not yet encountered, enabling personalized suggestions that can enhance user experience and drive engagement. Traditional approaches to recommendation, such as collaborative filtering (CF) (Sarwar et al., 2001) and matrix completion (MC) (Koren et al., 2009), predominantly rely on observed user-item interaction data – typically ratings or purchase history – to identify patterns and similarities between users and items. While effective in many scenarios, these methods suffer from several limitations. Chief among these is the “cold start” problem, where the system struggles to make accurate recommendations for new users or items with limited interaction data. Furthermore, CF and MC operate in a feature-scarce environment, effectively ignoring the rich textual information often associated with both users and items. Consider, for example, the vast amount of textual data generated in the form of product reviews, user comments, and item descriptions. These texts contain valuable insights into user preferences, item attributes, and the nuances of opinions that are simply untapped by traditional methods. Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in leveraging textual data for recommendation. Opinion mining techniques (Liu, 2012) can be employed to extract sentiment and subjective information from text, providing valuable features for users and items. However, these methods often rely on hand-crafted features and lexicons, and may struggle to capture the complex relationships between words and concepts. Furthermore, the extracted features are often used as input to separate machine learning models, lacking the benefit of a unified representation framework. Another line of work focuses on utilizing topic modeling (Blei et al., 2003) to discover latent topics from text data, representing users and items based on their topic distributions. While these approaches can effectively capture semantic information, they often treat text as a bag-of-words, ignoring the sequential structure and contextual relationships within sentences. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn distributed representations of users and items directly from text comments, addressing the limitations of existing methods. Our core idea is to construct low-dimensional vector representations – embeddings – that capture the semantic meaning and contextual nuances of both users and items. We achieve this through a unified framework that maximizes the likelihood of observing words in user comments given the learned representations. By learning joint embeddings for users and items in this manner, we can predict scores for unobserved user-item pairs based on the similarity of their vector representations. Our approach is fully data-driven, requiring no hand-crafted features or external knowledge sources. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, showing that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline systems. This work not only offers a robust solution to the recommendation problem but also contributes to the broader field of representation learning by showcasing the power of distributed representations for capturing complex relationships in textual data.

Anaphora resolution, the task of identifying what expressions refer to, is a crucial component of natural language understanding. While traditional anaphora resolution research has largely focused on coreference – where an anaphor (e.g., *he*, *she*, *it*) refers to a previously mentioned entity – human language frequently employs more subtle forms of reference. One such form is bridging anaphora, where the relationship between the anaphor and its antecedent is implicit, relying on world knowledge or inference. A particularly challenging instance of bridging anaphora is *associative anaphora*, observed prominently in languages like Japanese. In associative anaphora, the anaphor and its antecedent are not coreferent but are linked through a closely related concept. For example, in the Japanese sentence “*Kare wa kami o kaimashita. Kore wa ii desu.*” (“He bought paper. This is good.”), the pronoun *kore* (“this”) refers not to the *paper* itself, but rather to the act of *buying paper* or the *resulting product* of the purchase. This connection isn’t one of identity, making it distinct from coreference. Resolving such anaphora requires understanding the implicit association between the antecedent and the anaphor, presenting a significant challenge for computational models. Existing approaches to anaphora resolution often struggle with associative anaphora due to their focus on identifying direct entity matches. Techniques based on coreference chains or entity grids are ill-equipped to handle these implicit, conceptual links. Moreover, datasets for associative anaphora are limited, particularly for languages beyond English. Interestingly, associative anaphora shares characteristics with *zero anaphora*, where an anaphor is omitted but understood from context. For instance, in “*Kare wa kami o kaimashita. (Kotae wa) ii desu.*” (“He bought paper. (The result) is good.”), the subject of the second sentence is implicitly “the result of buying paper”. We hypothesize that treating associative anaphora as a form of zero anaphora – where the missing anaphor represents the associated concept – can provide a fruitful avenue for resolution. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic model for associative anaphora resolution in Japanese that leverages this connection to zero anaphora. Our model utilizes automatically acquired lexical knowledge to identify plausible associates between antecedents and potential anaphors. By framing the problem as a form of zero anaphora resolution, we can apply existing techniques developed for that task. Further, we demonstrate that resolving associative and zero anaphora simultaneously can lead to improved performance, due to the mutual constraints between the two phenomena. Our experimental results on a Japanese dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and highlight the benefits of joint resolution. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Taxonomy induction – the task of automatically building hierarchical classifications of concepts – has long been a central problem in natural language processing (NLP) and knowledge representation. Such taxonomies, like WordNet (Miller, 1995) or the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS), are crucial for a variety of downstream applications, including information retrieval, question answering, and semantic reasoning. Traditional approaches to taxonomy induction often relied on distributional semantics (Lin, 1998;Pantel and Eisenstein, 2008), where the semantic similarity between words is estimated from their co-occurrence patterns in large corpora. More recent work has explored leveraging structured knowledge resources like Wikipedia (Strang and Lin, 2009;Navigli and Ponzetto, 2010), by extracting hypernymy relations from the text surrounding category names. However, many existing methods treat hypernymy and siblinghood relations independently, failing to exploit the inherent structural constraints of a taxonomy. Moreover, the often noisy and incomplete nature of the evidence used for induction necessitates robust inference techniques capable of handling ambiguity and uncertainty. In this paper, we propose a structured learning approach to taxonomy induction that explicitly models both hypernymy and siblinghood relations within a probabilistic graphical model. Our model incorporates heterogeneous relational evidence derived from Web n-grams and Wikipedia abstracts, capturing semantic features indicative of hypernymy (e.g., patterns like “X, such as Y”) and siblinghood (e.g., co-occurrence in lists or definitions). Crucially, we formulate the problem as learning the parameters of this graphical model, allowing us to jointly reason about hypernymy and siblinghood constraints. A key challenge lies in efficient inference over the complex taxonomy structures that can emerge. To address this, we employ loopy belief propagation (BP), an approximate inference algorithm well-suited to graphical models. We incorporate a directed spanning tree structure to efficiently handle the core hypernymy factor within the BP algorithm, reducing computational complexity while maintaining accurate hypernymy predictions. To train the system, we adopt a discriminative learning approach, focusing on reproducing existing taxonomic structures derived from WordNet. We extract sub-structures from WordNet and utilize adaptive subgradient stochastic optimization to learn model parameters that minimize prediction error. This approach allows us to focus the learning process on accurately capturing the relationships present in well-established taxonomies. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on reproducing sub-hierarchies of WordNet. We achieve a significant 51% error reduction compared to a chance baseline, with a notable 15% error reduction attributed to the inclusion of non-hypernym-factored sibling features. Furthermore, we find up to 29% relative error reduction over previous work on ancestor F1 score, highlighting the benefits of our structured learning framework and efficient inference techniques. In summary, this work presents a novel and effective approach to taxonomy induction, leveraging structured learning, heterogeneous evidence, and efficient inference to build accurate hierarchical classifications of concepts.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as the dominant paradigm for machine translation, surpassing traditional Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) systems in both translation quality and fluency (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). The success of NMT stems from its ability to learn complex, non-linear mappings between source and target language sequences using deep neural networks, typically employing an encoder-decoder architecture with attention mechanisms. However, standard NMT models are fundamentally text-based and operate solely on textual information, neglecting potentially valuable supplementary modalities such as visual data. In many real-world scenarios, the meaning of a sentence is heavily influenced by its visual context. Consider image captioning, where a precise description requires understanding the content of the corresponding image, or visual dialog, where interactions are grounded in the visual environment. Similarly, in multi-lingual image description or translation, the ability to incorporate visual information can significantly improve the accuracy and relevance of the generated translation. Recent work has explored multi-modal machine translation, leveraging visual cues alongside textual inputs. Early attempts focused on concatenating image features with word embeddings (Flickr8k and Flickr30k datasets) (Cornia et al., 2014;Yang et al., 2015). However, these approaches often treat visual features as just another word in the input sequence, and do not fully exploit the rich, global information captured by images. More sophisticated approaches employ attention mechanisms to selectively focus on relevant image regions during translation (Xu et al., 2015; Luong et al., 2017). These models typically extract local image features using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and then use an attention mechanism to dynamically weigh these features based on the current decoding step. While promising, these models primarily focus on fine-grained regional attention and often overlook the importance of global visual context. In this paper, we investigate how to effectively incorporate global visual features into attention-based NMT models. We propose a novel approach that integrates global image representations, extracted using a pre-trained CNN, into various components of both the encoder and decoder. Specifically, we explore three strategies: (i) treating the global visual feature as an additional “word” in the source sentence, (ii) initializing the encoder hidden state with the global visual feature, and (iii) initializing the decoder hidden state with the global visual feature. We conduct comprehensive experiments on the Multi30k dataset (Elliott et al., 2016), a benchmark dataset for multi-modal machine translation, evaluating translations into both English and German. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of incorporating synthetic multi-modal, multilingual data, generated to augment the training set. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves translation performance, achieving new state-of-the-art results and, crucially, surpassing a strong PBSMT baseline on all evaluation metrics. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a purely neural model has consistently outperformed PBSMT on this dataset across all reported metrics.

Temporal relation extraction (TRE) is a crucial subtask of information extraction, aiming to identify the temporal relationships between events described in text. Accurate identification of these relationships – such as before, after, or overlap – is fundamental for applications spanning clinical decision support (Sartorio et al., 2018), event timeline construction (Chambers et al., 2016), and story understanding (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2009). In the biomedical domain, specifically, TRE plays a vital role in understanding patient histories from clinical narratives, enabling systems to build a chronological view of disease progression, treatment effects, and overall patient health. The challenges in TRE are multifaceted. Temporal expressions are often implicit, requiring reasoning about event order based on linguistic cues or world knowledge. The complexity of natural language introduces ambiguity, and the presence of negation or modality further complicates the task. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown promise in tackling these challenges. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been successfully applied to TRE, leveraging their ability to capture sequential dependencies and salient features from text (Yoshikawa et al., 2017;Lin et al., 2018). However, a common practice involves utilizing pre-trained word embeddings – such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) – as fixed input representations within these models. While pre-trained embeddings offer benefits by transferring knowledge from large unlabeled corpora, they may not be optimally suited for the specific nuances of the downstream TRE task. Simply initializing a model with these embeddings, or even fine-tuning them briefly, may not fully exploit their potential. Several approaches aim to address this limitation. Fine-tuning pre-trained embeddings during the training process is a common practice. However, substantial fine-tuning may lead to catastrophic forgetting – the loss of general semantic information encoded in the initial embeddings. Conversely, insufficient fine-tuning may not allow the embeddings to adapt sufficiently to the specific task. In this work, we propose a novel approach that extends the standard task-specific loss function with an unsupervised auxiliary loss at the word-embedding level. This allows for continuous refinement of the word representations, encouraging them to retain general semantic properties while simultaneously learning task-relevant features. By balancing the supervised task loss and the unsupervised embedding loss, we aim to produce word representations that are both informative for the TRE task and robust to domain-specific variations. Our key contribution lies in the introduction of this word-level loss extension, and its application to the challenging task of narrative containment relation extraction from clinical records. We demonstrate empirically, on the widely used THYME dataset (Uzuner et al., 2008), that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing methods while relying only on a general-domain part-of-speech tagger as a linguistic resource.

Determining the semantic similarity between sentences is a fundamental task in natural language processing with broad applications, including information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization (Agirre et al., 2016). In recent years, the task of Sentence Similarity (SS) has attracted significant attention, spurred by the introduction of benchmark datasets like the Stanford Semantic Textual Similarity (SSTS) dataset (Cer et al., 2017) and the Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STSbenchmark) (Cer and Dolan, 2017). While early approaches to SS relied heavily on feature engineering and hand-crafted rules (Marelli et al., 2014), the current state-of-the-art is dominated by distributed representation models, such as those based on word embeddings (Le and Mikolov, 2014) and recurrent neural networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). However, a key challenge in SS, particularly when compared to document-level semantic tasks, is the inherent sparsity of words within a sentence. A sentence, by definition, is a relatively short text unit, and consequently contains a limited vocabulary. This sparsity makes it difficult to reliably estimate the semantic representation of the sentence, as the model may not encounter sufficient contextual information for each word. Effectively capturing the semantic nuances of each word is, therefore, crucial for achieving high performance on SS tasks. Existing approaches often address this sparsity by leveraging large pre-trained word embeddings, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), which encode semantic relationships between words learned from massive text corpora. However, these embeddings primarily capture distributional semantics – that is, semantic similarity based on co-occurrence patterns. They often neglect crucial aspects of lexical semantics, such as the specific preferences a word has for certain semantic roles (selectional preference) or its relationships to closely related concepts (synonymy). We hypothesize that enriching the representation of individual words with explicit lexical semantic information can significantly improve the accuracy of sentence similarity models. In this paper, we propose a novel latent variable model that incorporates both corpus-based and knowledge-based lexical semantics. Specifically, we integrate selectional preference information, extracted from large corpora, to capture the typical semantic arguments a word takes, and leverage lexical resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995) to identify similar words that can provide additional contextual cues. By modeling these aspects of lexical semantics within a probabilistic framework, we aim to create a more robust and informative word representation, leading to better overall sentence similarity scores. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance among unsupervised systems on two benchmark SS datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach. The increasing adoption of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) presents a unique opportunity to leverage the wealth of clinical information for improving healthcare outcomes. However, a significant portion of this information is buried within unstructured text – clinical notes dictated by physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals. Extracting meaningful insights from this unstructured data is a critical step towards realizing the full potential of EHRs. A core task in this endeavor is medical event detection, the process of identifying mentions of medical events (e.g., diseases, medications, procedures) and their associated attributes (e.g., dosage, frequency, severity) within clinical text. Accurate medical event detection is foundational for a multitude of downstream applications, including pharmacovigilance (identifying adverse drug reactions), drug surveillance (monitoring drug usage patterns), clinical decision support, and population health management. Traditionally, medical event detection has been approached as a sequence labeling problem, where each word in the clinical note is assigned a label indicating its role in a medical event. Dominant approaches have relied on Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Lafferty et al., 2001), probabilistic graphical models that excel at structured prediction. These CRF-based systems typically employ a rich set of hand-crafted features derived from fixed-size context windows around each word – features capturing lexical information, part-of-speech tags, dependency parse information, and domain-specific knowledge resources. While effective, constructing and maintaining these feature sets requires significant human expertise and can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly in the area of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), offer a compelling alternative to traditional CRF-based approaches. RNNs are well-suited for processing sequential data like text, as they can capture long-range dependencies and contextual information without relying on hand-engineered features. This capability is particularly crucial in the clinical domain, where subtle nuances in language and complex medical terminology can significantly impact the meaning of a sentence. Furthermore, the ability of RNNs to learn representations directly from data eliminates the need for painstaking feature engineering. In this work, we explore the application of recurrent neural network frameworks – specifically, Bidirectional RNNs – to the task of medical event detection in EHR notes. Bidirectional RNNs process the input sequence in both forward and backward directions, allowing the model to consider both past and future context when making predictions. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation that Bidirectional RNNs significantly outperform state-of-the-art CRF models on a challenging medical event detection benchmark dataset. Our results highlight the potential of deep learning techniques to automate the extraction of valuable information from unstructured clinical text and pave the way for more intelligent and data-driven healthcare applications. Entity linking (EL), also known as named entity disambiguation, is a fundamental task in natural language processing with applications ranging from information retrieval and question answering to knowledge base population and text understanding. Given a mention of an entity in text, the goal of entity linking is to identify the corresponding entity in a predefined knowledge base (KB), such as Wikipedia or Freebase. While seemingly straightforward, EL presents a number of challenges, particularly regarding ambiguity – many entity mentions can refer to multiple entities – and scalability given the sheer size of modern KBs. For instance, the mention “Washington” could refer to the U.S. state, the city, or a person, and resolving this ambiguity requires careful consideration of the surrounding context. Early approaches to EL relied heavily on hand-engineered features and relied on comparing mention context with entity descriptions (Galárraga et al., 2011;Milne et al., 2008). These systems often struggled with performance on diverse datasets and required substantial feature engineering effort. More recently, neural network-based approaches have emerged, demonstrating improved performance and reduced reliance on hand-crafted features (Yamada et al., 2016;Shen et al., 2017). These models typically employ distributed representations of both mentions and entities, learning to map similar concepts closer together in a vector space. Despite the progress, many existing neural EL systems treat each information source—entity descriptions, mention context, and entity types—in relative isolation. Descriptions provide a succinct summary of an entity, but may not fully capture its nuances. Context, on the other hand, provides valuable clues about the specific meaning of a mention in its surrounding text, but can be noisy and incomplete. Furthermore, leveraging the structured information available in KBs, such as entity types, often requires separate modeling components. A key challenge is therefore to develop a unified framework that can effectively integrate these diverse sources of information. In this work, we present a novel neural entity linking system that addresses these challenges. Our system learns a joint dense representation for each entity, incorporating its textual description, the contextual information surrounding its mentions, and its fine-grained type information. We employ a modular architecture that allows for flexible combination of these sources. Crucially, our model is designed to be domain-agnostic, requiring no domain-specific training data or manually engineered features. We demonstrate that our system achieves competitive results on standard EL benchmarks, sometimes outperforming state-of-the-art systems, and exhibits strong performance on unseen entities, demonstrating its ability to generalize to novel situations. Our contributions lie in the design of a unified embedding space that effectively integrates multiple information sources and the evaluation demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of our approach. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving state-of-the-art results on numerous translation tasks (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). Traditional NMT models, however, typically process sentences independently, ignoring the broader contextual information available in a document. This often leads to inconsistencies in translation, especially with respect to pronoun resolution, terminology consistency, and discourse coherence (Popović, 2015). Consequently, there has been growing interest in incorporating document-level context into NMT systems. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge. One line of work extends the standard NMT architecture by concatenating previous hidden states to the current input (Cho et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016). Another approach involves explicitly modeling document-level representations using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or convolutional neural networks (CNNs) (Shen et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017). Hierarchical NMT (H-NMT) models (Gehrmann et al., 2018) have also gained prominence, leveraging a hierarchical encoder to capture both sentence-level and document-level information. While many of these systems improve upon sentence-level NMT, they often lack the flexibility to dynamically adapt to the changing context within a document and can struggle with long-range dependencies. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical attention model designed to capture document-level context in a more structured and dynamic manner for NMT. Our model extends the standard NMT architecture with an additional attention layer that operates over the hidden states of the encoder, effectively creating a hierarchical representation of the document. Crucially, this hierarchical attention mechanism *conditions on the NMT model's own previous hidden states*. This allows the model to selectively attend to relevant parts of the document context based on the current translation state, leading to more informed and coherent translations. Our approach differs from prior work in several key aspects. Unlike simply concatenating previous hidden states, our hierarchical attention layer provides a differentiable mechanism for weighting the importance of different parts of the document and facilitates the propagation of contextual information throughout the encoding and decoding processes. This allows the model to learn more complex relationships between sentences and adapt to the specific contextual demands of each translation step. We evaluate our model on a standard machine translation task, demonstrating that it significantly improves BLEU scores over a strong NMT baseline and outperforms current state-of-the-art context-aware methods. Our analysis also shows that both the encoder and decoder benefit from incorporating document-level context, and that these benefits are complementary, leading to further improvements in overall translation quality. The results indicate that our hierarchical attention mechanism effectively captures and leverages document-level context to generate more fluent and coherent translations.

The ability to automatically infer opinions expressed in text is a core task in sentiment analysis and opinion mining. Traditional approaches typically focus on identifying the sentiment polarity (positive, negative, or neutral) towards entities – people, products, organizations, etc. However, a growing body of work recognizes a more nuanced form of opinion expression centered around *events* that have a positive or negative *effect* on entities. For example, “The company’s new product launch delighted customers” expresses a positive opinion toward the company, but crucially, this opinion is mediated through the positive effect of the product launch event. Conversely, “The oil spill devastated the local wildlife” indicates a negative opinion toward the company responsible, stemming from the negative effect of the oil spill. We refer to these as +/-effect events – events that directly cause a positive or negative consequence for an entity. Inferring opinions regarding +/-effect events presents unique challenges compared to standard sentiment analysis. It requires not just identifying sentiment-bearing words, but also recognizing the causal relationship between the event and the entity, and determining whether the event has a positive or negative impact. This necessitates a focused lexicon of events annotated with their inherent effect polarity. Existing sentiment lexicons, such as SentiWordNet (Baccianella et al., 2010) and VADER (Hutto and Gilbert, 2014), primarily focus on the sentiment of individual words and are insufficient for identifying +/-effect events and their corresponding polarities. This paper addresses the task of building a sense-level lexicon specifically tailored for +/-effect event identification and opinion inference. A key motivation for a sense-level approach is the inherent ambiguity of words. Many words can participate in events with differing effects depending on the context and their specific sense. For instance, “break” can denote a positive event (e.g., “a breakthrough in research”) or a negative one (e.g., “a broken leg”). Consequently, assigning a fixed polarity to a word regardless of its sense can lead to inaccurate opinion inference. Our approach leverages both lexical-semantic resources, specifically WordNet, and textual gloss information to detect +/-effect senses automatically. We employ a graph-based method that propagates polarity information through WordNet’s semantic network, and a classifier trained on glosses (definitions) to identify event senses with positive or negative effects. A central contribution is a hybrid system that combines the strengths of both approaches, achieving significantly improved performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of our model in actively guiding manual annotation, enabling the discovery of +/-effect senses that were not included in our initial seed set. This active learning aspect allows for iterative refinement of the lexicon and expansion of coverage. Sentence compression – the task of shortening a sentence while preserving its essential meaning – has emerged as a valuable technique in natural language processing (NLP) with applications ranging from text summarization and machine translation to information retrieval and mobile computing. Traditionally, sentence compression has been largely investigated as a monolingual problem, focusing on reducing redundancy and streamlining sentence structures within a single language (Galley et al., 2006; Knight & Marcu, 2002). However, with the increasing demand for multilingual NLP applications and the growing availability of parallel corpora, extending sentence compression to a bilingual or multilingual setting presents a compelling research direction. In this paper, we explore the challenges and opportunities of *parallel* sentence compression – the simultaneous compression of corresponding sentences in a pair or set of languages. The potential benefits of parallel sentence compression are manifold. Firstly, it can facilitate cross-lingual information retrieval by providing shorter, more concise queries and document representations in multiple languages. Secondly, it can aid in machine translation by simplifying the input sentences, potentially reducing ambiguity and improving translation quality. Furthermore, compressed parallel sentences can serve as valuable training data for other multilingual tasks such as cross-lingual summarization and parallel text simplification. In essence, parallel sentence compression unlocks opportunities for creating more efficient and effective multilingual NLP pipelines. However, performing sentence compression in a bilingual context is not simply a matter of applying monolingual compression techniques independently to each sentence in a parallel pair. Maintaining semantic equivalence and structural alignment across languages requires careful consideration. A naive approach could lead to inconsistencies and loss of crucial information. Therefore, it is crucial to leverage the inherent relationships within a parallel corpus to guide the compression process. This paper investigates two distinct approaches to incorporating bilingual information into sentence compression. The first approach focuses on leveraging translation probabilities to identify phrases that are likely to be preserved during compression due to their importance in the target language. The second approach explores techniques for explicitly enforcing structural alignment between the compressed sentences. We evaluate the performance of these approaches on a parallel corpus of news articles, comparing their effectiveness in terms of compression ratio, semantic preservation, and structural similarity. Our goal is to provide insights into the most effective strategies for achieving high-quality parallel sentence compression and lay the groundwork for future research in this exciting area. Chinese natural language processing (NLP) presents unique challenges compared to many other languages. Unlike English, Chinese lacks explicit word boundaries, meaning that word segmentation is a necessary prerequisite for most downstream tasks. This initial stage introduces ambiguity, as a single string of characters can be segmented in multiple ways, each leading to potentially different interpretations. Following segmentation, parts-of-speech (POS) tagging is crucial for disambiguating words and providing grammatical information. Finally, dependency parsing aims to uncover the hierarchical relationships between words in a sentence, providing a structural representation of meaning. Traditionally, these three tasks – word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing – have been tackled sequentially in a pipeline fashion. However, this approach suffers from error propagation: errors made in earlier stages cascade through subsequent stages, negatively impacting overall performance. For example, an incorrect word segmentation can lead to incorrect POS tags, which in turn can hinder accurate dependency parsing. Recent work has explored joint models that address this error propagation problem by simultaneously learning to perform all three tasks. These joint models typically rely on graphical models such as Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) to capture dependencies between the tasks. However, these traditional graphical models often require extensive feature engineering, which is both time-consuming and requires expert knowledge. Furthermore, they often struggle to capture complex, non-linear relationships between words and their context. The rise of neural networks has revolutionized many areas of NLP, offering the potential to automatically learn complex features from raw data. Neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art results in individual tasks like word segmentation (Chou et al., 2015), POS tagging (Huang et al., 2015), and dependency parsing (Chen and Manning, 2014). However, applying neural networks to the *joint* Chinese analysis task has proven challenging. Existing neural joint models typically rely on word embeddings, which represent words as dense vectors capturing semantic and syntactic information. However, these word embeddings are often pre-trained on large corpora and may not generalize well to unseen words or to the specific requirements of a joint model. Moreover, they don’t directly address the fundamental challenge of segmenting the input character sequence in the first place. To address these limitations, we present a novel neural joint model for Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing. Our model is designed to prevent error propagation by learning the three tasks simultaneously within a single neural network architecture. Importantly, we introduce character string embeddings *in addition to* word embeddings. These character string embeddings allow the model to represent unseen words and capture morphological information, improving performance on both segmentation and downstream tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that our models consistently outperform existing systems on benchmark datasets for Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing. Furthermore, we show that our models can achieve competitive results even with fewer features, highlighting the effectiveness of our neural approach. Ontologies play a critical role in modern knowledge representation and reasoning, providing a formal and structured way to represent concepts, relationships, and axioms within a specific domain (Noy and McGuinness, 2001). They serve as the semantic foundation for numerous applications, including information retrieval, data integration, and knowledge discovery. However, the development of ontologies is often a decentralized process, leading to the emergence of multiple, independent ontologies covering the same or overlapping domains. This proliferation of ontologies, while beneficial in some respects, creates a pressing need for ontology matching – the process of identifying correspondences between entities (classes, properties, individuals) in different ontologies (Shvaiko and Euzenat, 2013). Successful ontology matching facilitates interoperability, knowledge sharing, and the creation of more comprehensive knowledge bases. Traditional ontology matching approaches relied heavily on linguistic similarity measures, structural comparison, and logical reasoning (Do and Rahm, 2002; Euzenat and Shvaiko, 2007). However, these methods often struggle to capture the subtle semantic nuances that distinguish related entities, leading to low precision and recall, particularly when dealing with entities represented by short labels or ambiguous terms. More recently, distributional semantic models (DSMs) have gained traction in ontology matching, leveraging the principle that words with similar meanings tend to occur in similar contexts (Turney and Pantel, 2010; Jimenez-Ruiz et al., 2011). DSMs represent entities as vectors in a high-dimensional space, allowing for the application of similarity measures like cosine similarity to identify potential alignments. Despite their success, existing DSM-based ontology matching approaches often rely on pre-trained word vectors derived from general-purpose corpora. These general-purpose embeddings may not adequately capture the specific semantic characteristics of the ontology domain, hindering their ability to differentiate between closely related entities. The core insight of this work is that refining pre-trained word vectors specifically *for* the ontology matching task can considerably improve alignment accuracy. We introduce DeepAlignment, a novel unsupervised entity alignment method that refines existing word vectors to generate entity representations tailored to the matching problem. Crucially, DeepAlignment achieves this refinement without requiring any manually labeled training data specific to ontology matching, making it broadly applicable and scalable. The key contribution is a process for deriving ontological entity descriptions that leverage the inherent structural information within the ontologies themselves to guide the vector refinement process. Our experiments on established ontology matching benchmarks demonstrate that DeepAlignment significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the power of representation learning techniques in this domain. The increasing digitization of healthcare has led to a wealth of clinical data, primarily in the form of unstructured text notes documenting patient encounters. These notes, meticulously crafted by clinicians, contain crucial information regarding a patient’s diagnosis, treatment, and overall medical history. Simultaneously, standardized medical codes – such as ICD (International Classification of Diseases) and CPT (Current Procedural Terminology) – are assigned to each encounter to facilitate billing, reporting, and research. While these codes offer a structured representation of the clinical narrative, their assignment is a labor-intensive, time-consuming, and often error-prone process. Perhaps more importantly, the *reasoning* behind a specific code assignment remains largely implicit within the clinical text, creating a disconnect between the structured code and the unstructured justification. This opacity hinders a deeper understanding of clinical decision-making, limits the utility of coded data for downstream tasks, and presents challenges for auditing and quality control. The task of automatically predicting medical codes from clinical text has garnered significant attention within the natural language processing (NLP) community (Shi et al., 2017; Li & Pushparajah, 2018). Existing approaches typically employ machine learning models trained on labeled clinical text and corresponding codes. However, many of these methods treat code prediction as a black-box classification problem, lacking the ability to provide insights into *why* a particular code was assigned. This is a critical limitation in the medical domain, where transparency and interpretability are paramount. Clinicians require not only accurate predictions but also clear explanations to validate the model’s reasoning and build trust in its suggestions. In this paper, we address the challenge of accurate *and* explainable medical code prediction from clinical text. We propose an attentional convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture designed to leverage the strengths of both convolutional processing for identifying relevant textual patterns and attention mechanisms for highlighting the specific segments of text that support each code assignment. Our model effectively aggregates information across the entire clinical document using a CNN, then employs an attention layer to dynamically weigh the importance of different text spans for predicting each of the thousands of potential medical codes. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a challenging medical coding dataset, significantly outperforming prior methods in terms of both precision@8 (0.71) and Micro-F1 (0.54). Crucially, we go beyond simply reporting accuracy metrics. We conduct a thorough interpretability evaluation, involving a physician review of the attention weights generated by our model. This evaluation confirms that the attention mechanism consistently identifies clinically meaningful phrases and sentences that justify the predicted code assignments, providing valuable insights into the model’s decision-making process. This focus on explainability differentiates our work and positions it as a valuable contribution to the field of clinical NLP. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The rapid adoption of smartphones and voice assistants has fueled a significant increase in voice search, especially for local business directory assistance. Users increasingly rely on voice commands – “Find me a pizza place nearby,” or “Call the closest dry cleaner” – to quickly access information about local businesses. However, despite advances in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), accurately transcribing business listing names remains a significant challenge. Unlike general-purpose speech, business names often contain uncommon words, proper nouns, and idiosyncratic spellings, leading to lower recognition accuracy and a frustrating user experience. A key reason for this difficulty lies in the limitations of traditional, nationwide language models (LMs). These models are trained on large corpora of general text, which are poorly suited to capturing the specific vocabulary and linguistic patterns associated with local businesses. For example, the probability of recognizing a business name like “Joe’s Crab Shack” will be significantly lower in a nationwide LM compared to a localized LM that has encountered this phrase frequently in queries originating from areas where the business operates. Previous approaches to address this issue have included augmenting nationwide LMs with business listing data (e.g., adding business names to the vocabulary). However, these methods often suffer from scalability issues, especially when dealing with a large and constantly evolving business directory. Furthermore, a uniform application of business listings to a nationwide model can introduce noise and degrade performance for general-purpose speech recognition. In this paper, we present a novel approach based on geo-centric language models for local business voice search. Our central idea is to dynamically generate language models tailored to the user's geographic location. This allows the ASR system to prioritize business names and related terms that are relevant to the user's current surroundings. Our algorithm offers several key advantages: First, it provides a language model for *any* user, leveraging geolocation data to adapt to their specific context. Second, the geographic area covered by each language model is dynamically adjusted based on local business density, ensuring high recognition accuracy even in areas with sparse business coverage. Finally, the language models can be pre-compiled offline, resulting in minimal latency during real-time speech recognition. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments using spoken business listing name queries from a real-world business directory assistance service. The results show a substantial 16.8% absolute improvement in recognition accuracy and a 3-fold speedup in recognition time compared to using a traditional nationwide language model. These findings highlight the potential of geo-centric language models to significantly improve the accuracy and responsiveness of local business voice search applications. Figure 1 illustrates the architecture of our proposed system and highlights the key components involved in generating and applying geo-centric language models for local business voice search. The system begins with the user’s speech input and corresponding geographic location, obtained via GPS or network triangulation. This location data is then used to target a specific geographic area for language model generation. Our algorithm dynamically determines the size of this area based on local business density, with smaller areas used in densely populated regions and larger areas in sparsely populated regions. The business listings within this area are then extracted from a database and used to create a customized language model tailored to the user’s surroundings. Finally, the generated language model is fed into the ASR system alongside the audio input, enabling more accurate and efficient recognition of business listing names.

Humans routinely encounter large numbers in everyday life – in news articles, financial reports, and scientific publications. However, comprehending the true scale of these numbers can be challenging. Abstract quantities like “131 million dollars” lack inherent meaning without contextualization. To bridge this gap, people naturally seek *perspectives* – relatable comparisons that ground the number in familiar terms. For instance, stating “$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period” provides a concrete and intuitive understanding of the sum. This ability to contextualize numbers is crucial for informed decision-making and effective communication. Current information access systems largely fall short in providing such contextualization. While calculators can perform arithmetic and search engines can retrieve information *about* numbers, they rarely offer comparisons that aid comprehension. Existing work on number understanding typically focuses on quantity extraction (Chang & Li, 2010), normalization (Kuhn, 2013), or reasoning about numerical values (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005). However, generating human-understandable perspectives – bridging the gap between an abstract number and a relatable concept – remains a largely unexplored area. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing the task of *compositional description generation* for numbers. Our goal is to automatically generate short, natural language descriptions – perspectives – that help users grasp the magnitude of a given number. We hypothesize that these perspectives can be constructed by composing readily available numeric facts from a knowledge base, combined with carefully formulated natural language generation. To facilitate research in this area, we introduce a new dataset of numeric mentions extracted from news articles, each annotated with multiple human-rated perspectives. This dataset allows for quantitative evaluation of perspective generation systems. We then present a system consisting of two core components: *formula construction* and *description generation*. The formula construction module leverages a knowledge base to compose numerical comparisons based on metrics like familiarity, numeric proximity, and semantic compatibility. The description generation module uses a sequence-to-sequence recurrent neural network to translate these formulas into fluent, natural language. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our compositional approach, achieving a 15.2% F1 score improvement over a non-compositional baseline for formula construction and a 12.5 BLEU point improvement over a baseline approach to description generation. These results highlight the importance of both compositional reasoning and natural language generation in creating effective number perspectives. We believe this work represents a significant step towards building more human-centric information systems that not only present data but also facilitate its understanding. References: Chang, C. Vector space models of word meaning have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP). These models, often learned via distributional methods (Harris, 1954; Firth, 1957), represent words as dense, low-dimensional vectors, capturing semantic relationships based on their contextual occurrences. However, a fundamental limitation of traditional word embeddings, such as those produced by Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), is their inability to represent polysemy – the phenomenon where a single word has multiple distinct meanings. For example, the word “bank” can refer to a financial institution or the land alongside a river. Standard word embeddings assign a single vector to “bank,” effectively averaging its different senses and losing crucial disambiguation information. Recent approaches have sought to address this limitation by learning *multi-sense* embeddings, where each sense of a word is represented by a separate vector (Rei & Briscoe, 2014; Chen et al., 2015; Pilehvar & Collier, 2016). These methods typically rely on word sense disambiguation (WSD) techniques to identify the appropriate sense in a given context, then assign the corresponding sense vector. However, WSD remains a challenging task, and errors in sense identification can propagate to the embedding space. Furthermore, many existing multi-sense embedding models are limited to monolingual data. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to learning multi-sense embeddings that leverages both monolingual and bilingual information. Our model is based on a discrete autoencoder architecture, which learns to encode a word’s context and a parallel sentence context into a discrete sense representation, and then decode this representation to predict surrounding words. This joint estimation of encoder and decoder allows for a more robust and accurate representation of word senses. Importantly, the use of parallel data provides cross-lingual constraints, enabling the model to learn more generalizable and consistent sense representations. We hypothesize that shared semantic space across languages helps to resolve ambiguities and refine the distinctions between different senses. Our key contribution lies in demonstrating that word representations induced from bilingual data significantly outperform those learned from monolingual data alone, even when evaluated on monolingual downstream tasks where cross-lingual information is not available at test time. This finding suggests that the cross-lingual signal provides valuable information for disambiguating word senses and learning more informative representations. We conduct experiments on a variety of evaluation tasks, including word similarity, word analogy, and relatedness, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. 1 Conceptual Semantics and Word Sense Disambiguation. 2 Bilingual Supervision for Multi-Sense Learning. 3 Experiments and Results. Section 4 describes the experimental setup and results, and Section 5 concludes with a discussion of future directions.

Linguistic alignment – the tendency for individuals to converge towards similar linguistic features during interaction – is a well-documented phenomenon in psycholinguistics and sociolinguistics (Levelt & Grommers, 1995; Clark, 1996). Numerous studies have demonstrated alignment across various linguistic levels, including lexical choice (Garrett, 1993), syntactic structures (Bock, 1986), and phonetic characteristics (Nielsen, 2003). While early research largely focused on the cognitive mechanisms underlying alignment – often attributing it to shared representations and ease of processing – more recent investigation has explored the role of social factors in modulating this process. Of particular interest are the effects of social power dynamics on linguistic alignment. A recurring claim in the literature is that individuals with higher social power tend to elicit greater linguistic alignment from their interlocutors compared to those with lower power (e.g., Ng & Kraus, 2012; Ireland et al., 2011). This observation has been interpreted as reflecting deference, accommodation, or attempts to build rapport with higher-status individuals. However, these interpretations often overlook the significant contribution of low-level linguistic features to alignment patterns. For example, utterance length is known to correlate with alignment likelihood (Chung & Pennebaker, 2008); longer utterances provide more opportunities for shared linguistic elements. Similarly, syntactic complexity, lexical diversity, and even phonetic articulation rate can all influence the probability of alignment, independent of social factors. Failing to account for these potentially confounding variables may lead to erroneous conclusions regarding the impact of social power on linguistic alignment. This work aims to re-examine the relationship between social power and alignment, explicitly controlling for a range of low-level linguistic features. We utilize logistic regression models to characterize alignment behavior in two distinct conversational datasets, rigorously assessing the predictive power of social power after accounting for factors such as utterance length, lexical overlap, and syntactic similarity. Our findings demonstrate that the often-reported influence of social power on alignment is substantially diminished, or even reversed, when these low-level features are considered. This suggests that linguistic alignment is primarily driven by cognitive and linguistic factors rather than a deliberate attempt to signal social deference or accommodation. We argue that future research on observational data must adopt a more comprehensive approach, acknowledging the complex interplay of cognitive, linguistic, and social variables when investigating the influence of social factors on language use. Ultimately, this work calls for a nuanced perspective on the relationship between power and alignment, highlighting the limitations of simplistic interpretations and emphasizing the need for rigorous methodological controls. Accurate identification of predicate-argument relationships is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing, impacting a wide range of downstream applications including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation (Dasgupta and Ng, 2009;Kate et al., 2011;Moschcowitz, 2013). These dependencies delineate *who* did *what* to *whom*, forming the semantic backbone of a sentence’s meaning. While much progress has been made in dependency parsing, a significant portion of these crucial relationships involve *unbounded dependencies* – those spanning arbitrary distances within a sentence, often involving phenomena like relative clauses, wh-movement, and topicalization. These long-range dependencies pose a substantial challenge to traditional parsing methods, frequently relying on heuristics or distant supervision to achieve reasonable accuracy (McDonald and Nivre, 2007;Kübler et al., 2009). One prominent approach to syntactic and semantic analysis is the use of formal grammars. Categorial Grammars (CGs), in particular, offer a compelling framework for reasoning about compositionality. They define syntactic and semantic categories, and combine them based on specific rules reflecting functor-argument relations. This compositional framework naturally captures the idea that the meaning of a complex expression is built up from the meanings of its parts, making them particularly well-suited for representing and recovering dependencies. However, traditional CGs can suffer from combinatorial explosion, requiring a potentially infinite number of categories and leading to computational intractability (Buszkowski and Copeland, 1982). To address this limitation, Generalized Categorial Grammars (GCG) introduce a crucial modification: they restrict the number of categories to only those strictly necessary for enforcing grammatical constraints. This curtailment, inspired by Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) (Pollard and Sag, 1994), results in a more manageable and efficient system. While GCG has shown promise in theoretical linguistics, its application to large-scale dependency recovery, particularly for unbounded dependencies, remains comparatively underexplored. This paper presents a novel GCG-based approach to accurate unbounded dependency recovery. Our grammar combines the compositional strength of CGs with the efficiency of GCG, while carefully balancing expressive power with grammatical constraints. A critical component of this work lies in the creation of a comprehensive resource for mapping existing treebanks, traditionally annotated following Government and Binding Theory (GB) (Chomsky, 1986), into our novel categorial representation. We developed a novel re-annotation system specifically designed for this task, allowing us to leverage the wealth of linguistic information already encoded in widely available resources such as the Penn Treebank (PTB) (Marcus et al., 1993). We evaluate our system on the established unbounded dependency recovery task defined by Rimell et al. (2009) and further studied by Nivre et al. (2010), demonstrating its ability to achieve competitive accuracy and offering a promising new direction for dependency parsing research.

The rapid growth of information available online has spurred significant interest in automated methods for knowledge acquisition. Traditional Information Extraction (IE) systems rely on carefully crafted patterns and pre-defined relation types, requiring substantial human effort and limiting their adaptability to new domains (Gaizauskas et al., 2008; Sarawagi, 2008). In contrast, Open Information Extraction (Open IE) aims to automatically discover relations from text without prior knowledge of the target schema (Banko et al., 2008; Yates et al., 2007). This paradigm shift offers the promise of scalability and flexibility, enabling the extraction of a vast amount of knowledge directly from unstructured text. Early Open IE systems, such as TEXTRUNNER (Banko et al., 2008) and WOEpos (Woo et al., 2010), have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach, achieving impressive coverage by extracting billions of relations from web-scale corpora. However, a critical limitation of these systems is the quality of the extracted relations. A significant portion of their output consists of uninformative, incoherent, or simply erroneous extractions. For example, consider the sentence “The president visited London.” A typical Open IE system might extract relations like “visited: president – London,” which, while syntactically valid, offers limited semantic insight. Furthermore, systems frequently generate noisy extractions like “contains: report – of,” stemming from overly permissive extraction patterns. This low precision severely hinders the practical utility of Open IE, as downstream applications require substantial filtering and cleaning of the extracted data. Existing approaches to improve Open IE precision have focused on techniques such as relation clustering (Milne et al., 2008), coreference resolution (Hoffmann et al., 2011), and leveraging external knowledge bases (Poon and Domingos, 2011). While these methods can yield improvements, they often introduce additional complexity and computational cost. In this paper, we argue that a substantial improvement in Open IE precision can be achieved through the application of relatively simple, yet effective, syntactic and lexical constraints on the binary relations expressed by verbs. We hypothesize that filtering extractions based on basic properties of the verb phrase – specifically, its transitivity and the semantic compatibility of its arguments – can significantly reduce the number of spurious extractions without sacrificing coverage. We integrate these constraints into the REVERB Open IE system (Fader et al., 2011), a state-of-the-art extractor based on a bootstrap-and-iterate learning approach. Our experimental results demonstrate that these constraints more than double the area under the precision-recall curve compared to previous extractors like TEXTRUNNER and WOEpos. Notably, REVERB generates a significantly higher proportion of high-precision extractions (precision ≥ 0.8) – over 30% – compared to virtually none for earlier systems. We also present a detailed error analysis of REVERB, identifying remaining challenges and suggesting avenues for future research.

Neural word embeddings have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing, providing dense vector representations of words that capture semantic and syntactic relationships (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). These embeddings have shown remarkable success in a diverse range of downstream tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. However, a persistent challenge relates to the dimensionality of these embeddings. The optimal dimensionality is often task-dependent and requires careful tuning. Selecting a dimensionality that is too low can lead to information loss, while a dimensionality that is too high can introduce noise and computational inefficiency. Traditionally, training a set of word embeddings requires a fixed dimensionality to be specified *a priori*. If the dimensionality proves insufficient for a new task, the embeddings must be retrained from scratch, which can be computationally expensive, especially with large vocabularies and corpora. Conversely, if a higher dimensionality is not needed for some applications, the extra dimensions represent wasted computational resources in storage and processing. In this paper, we propose a novel incremental learning strategy for generating neural word embeddings that addresses these limitations. Our approach, which we term “Right-truncatable Neural Word Embeddings,” iteratively constructs embedding vectors one dimension at a time. The key innovation lies in the property that any right-truncated version of a fully generated embedding vector maintains the optimal solution for the corresponding lower-dimensional embedding space. This means that a single set of embedding vectors can seamlessly adapt to varying dimensionality requirements without retraining. Specifically, we demonstrate how this incremental learning process can be seamlessly integrated with popular embedding algorithms such as Skip-Gram (Mikolov et al., 2013) and Global Vectors (Pennington et al., 2014). By iteratively adding dimensions and updating the embeddings, we create a hierarchy of representations where lower-dimensional embeddings are naturally embedded within higher-dimensional ones. This provides significant flexibility and efficiency, allowing users to select the appropriate dimensionality for their specific needs without incurring the cost of retraining or storing multiple sets of embeddings. We present empirical results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and highlighting the unique property of right-truncatability. Our experiments show that truncating a high-dimensional embedding to a lower dimension yields performance comparable to embeddings trained directly at that lower dimension, confirming the preservation of information. This work opens new avenues for efficient and adaptable word embedding generation and management, with potential implications for a wide array of NLP applications. Furthermore, by avoiding the need for separate training runs for different dimensionalities, our method contributes to reducing the overall computational footprint of word embedding models. Cross-lingual lexical substitution (XLS) is the task of finding equivalent words in different languages given a context. It’s a core component of many multilingual NLP applications, including machine translation (MT), cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR), and computer-assisted translation (CAT). Traditional approaches to XLS often rely on parallel corpora and bilingual dictionaries to identify translational equivalents (e.g., Vondrák, 2009; Ergun and Tür, 2011). More recent approaches have leveraged distributional semantics, learning vector representations of words and seeking nearest neighbors across languages (e.g., Ritter et al., 2011; Mikolov et al., 2013). These methods typically map words from different languages into a shared vector space, where semantic similarity is reflected in proximity. However, establishing a truly aligned semantic space remains a significant challenge. A key issue is that words can have multiple senses, and simple averaging of word embeddings often fails to capture this polysemy, leading to poor substitution quality. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) aims to identify the correct sense of a word in context, and integrating WSD into XLS has proven beneficial (e.g., Chan et al., 2007; Moreau et al., 2017). However, fine-grained WSD, which attempts to distinguish between subtly different senses, is computationally expensive and often requires large, manually annotated datasets, such as WordNet or SemCor. Furthermore, the gains from employing extremely granular WSD can be marginal, and often do not justify the added complexity. In this work, we explore a different avenue for improving XLS: leveraging word sense subjectivity. Our intuition is that the sentiment or emotional coloring associated with a particular sense of a word plays a critical role in ensuring a good cross-lingual substitution. A "good" substitution should not only be semantically equivalent but also convey the same affective tone. For example, substituting “happy” with a Mandarin equivalent should yield a word conveying positivity, whereas substituting “gloomy” should yield a negative-connotative word. We hypothesize that incorporating subjectivity information into the substitution process can lead to significant performance gains, particularly for words with both subjective and objective senses. We examine subjectivity as a relatively coarse-grained signal. Rather than attempting to pinpoint the precise emotional intensity, we simply categorize senses as being primarily subjective (expressing opinion, emotion, or judgment) or objective (describing factual information). We present experiments on English-Chinese XLS, demonstrating that incorporating word sense subjectivity does indeed improve performance, as measured by human evaluation of substitution quality. Notably, we find that utilizing subjectivity information alone can achieve comparable results to integrating fully-fledged, fine-grained WSD for words that exhibit both subjective and objective senses. These results suggest that subjectivity provides a valuable signal that reduces ambiguity and guides the selection of appropriate cross-lingual substitutions, and offers a more practical approach than relying solely on computationally intensive WSD techniques.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems typically perform best when trained on large quantities of in-domain data. However, acquiring such data can be expensive and time-consuming, particularly for specialized domains like medical or legal translation. Domain adaptation techniques aim to bridge the gap between readily available, large general-domain parallel corpora and the performance demands of specific target domains. Several approaches to domain adaptation have been proposed, including feature-based methods (Kuhn & De Neve, 2008), model adaptation techniques (Woehrle et al., 2009), and data selection methods (Isozaki et al., 2008; Freitag & Al-Onaizan, 2008). Among these, data selection focuses on identifying and utilizing only the most relevant subsets of the general-domain corpus for adaptation. Previous work in data selection has primarily focused on identifying sentences within the general-domain corpus that are lexically similar to the in-domain data (Isozaki et al., 2008). While intuitive, this approach often overlooks semantic relevance and may include sentences that superficially resemble the target domain but lack the necessary contextual information. Freitag & Al-Onaizan (2008) explored selecting data based on cross-entropy, aiming to identify sentences that minimize the perplexity when modeled by an initial in-domain language model. However, this method relies heavily on the quality of the initial language model and may be susceptible to bias. In this paper, we explore an efficient domain adaptation strategy based on extracting sentences from a large, general-domain parallel corpus that are most relevant to the target domain. We term these extracted sentences “pseudo in-domain data,” recognizing that they are not strictly in-domain but represent the closest approximation available within the general-domain corpus. Crucially, we investigate simple and scalable cross-entropy based methods for identifying these pseudo in-domain sentences, presenting three distinct variations. Our central hypothesis is that a carefully selected, small subcorpus of pseudo in-domain data can outperform models trained on the entire general-domain corpus, and that combining models trained on both in-domain and pseudo in-domain data will yield further performance gains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a statistical machine translation task. Our results show that selecting just 1% of the original general-domain corpus based on our proposed criteria can yield significant improvements over training on the full corpus. Furthermore, combining a system trained on pseudo in-domain data with a separate system trained solely on limited in-domain data consistently delivers state-of-the-art performance. This highlights a key finding: more training data is not always better, and strategically selecting domain-relevant data coupled with model combination during decoding is crucial for successful domain adaptation in SMT.
