Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, with applications ranging from information extraction and knowledge base construction to question answering and machine translation. Traditional NER systems primarily focused on identifying flat, non-overlapping entity mentions within text. However, real-world text often exhibits complex, nested structures where entity mentions can contain other entity mentions recursively. For example, in the sentence “The CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, announced a new product,” “Apple” is an organization, “Tim Cook” is a person, and “CEO of Apple” is also an organizational role – representing a nested structure. Recognizing these nested entities is crucial for accurate information extraction and a deeper understanding of the text. Existing approaches to nested NER can be broadly categorized into post-processing based methods and direct modeling methods. Post-processing approaches (e.g., Finkel et al., 2008;Stoyanov et al., 2010) first identify flat mentions and then employ rules or heuristics to discover nested spans. These methods often lack robustness and struggle with complex nesting patterns. Direct modeling methods, on the other hand, attempt to directly identify nested mentions during the recognition process. These methods include span-based approaches (e.g., Guo et al., 2018) and graph-based approaches (e.g., Wick et al., 2018). Span-based models enumerate all possible spans and classify them as entity or non-entity, which suffers from computational complexity, and graph-based methods struggle with the training of complex graph structures. In this work, we introduce a novel, scalable transition-based method for modeling nested mentions, aiming to address the limitations of existing approaches. Our approach leverages the power of neural networks and efficient transition systems. We first transform a sentence with nested mentions into a designated forest structure, where each mention corresponds to a constituent within the forest. The forest accurately represents the hierarchical relationships between nested spans. Our system then learns to construct this forest structure in a bottom-up manner, using a shift-reduce parsing strategy. This means we iteratively build the forest from the individual words, combining them into larger and larger constituents until the complete forest structure is created. The key benefit of our transition-based approach lies in its scalability. The length of the action sequence required to construct the forest is guaranteed to be linear with respect to the sentence length – specifically, a maximum of three times the sentence length. This limits computational costs significantly in comparison to span-based methods. Furthermore, we use a Stack-LSTM architecture (Goldwasser and Goller, 2014) to efficiently represent the states of the system during the transition process. Stack-LSTMs have been shown to be effective at capturing contextual information in sequential tasks. Finally, to better handle morphological variations and out-of-vocabulary words, we incorporate a character-based component that captures letter-level patterns. Through comprehensive experiments on the ACE datasets, we demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art results, highlighting its effectiveness in accurately detecting nested mentions.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has remained the dominant paradigm in machine translation for over a decade, achieving impressive results across numerous language pairs. However, the performance of SMT systems is heavily reliant on the quality of features used to represent source and target phrases. Traditionally, these features have been carefully engineered by human experts, leveraging linguistic knowledge, domain expertise, and intuition (Och & Ney, 2003; Chiang, 2005). This process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and often requires significant effort to adapt to new languages or domains. As a result, there is a growing interest in automatically learning effective features for SMT. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promising results in various NLP tasks, including machine translation (Cho et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). The ability of deep neural networks to automatically learn hierarchical feature representations from raw data offers a potential solution to the feature engineering bottleneck in SMT. One popular approach is to leverage deep autoencoders (DAEs) to learn useful representations for phrases (Li et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2016). DAEs are neural networks trained to reconstruct their inputs, forcing them to learn compact and informative feature representations in the hidden layers. However, directly applying unsupervised DAEs to SMT features can be challenging. Unsupervised learning can be unstable and may result in features that are not particularly effective for translation. Prior work has explored initializing DAEs with deep belief networks (DBNs) pre-trained in an unsupervised manner (Hinton & Salakhutdinov, 2006). While DBNs can provide a good starting point for DAE training, they often fail to fully capture the nuances of translation-specific features. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learning effective features for SMT using semi-supervised DAEs. Our key idea is to leverage the readily available original phrase features (e.g., word-based features, POS tags, etc.) as a “teacher” to guide the fine-tuning of the DAE. By incorporating a semi-supervised objective function, we encourage the DAE to learn representations that are both capable of reconstructing the input and consistent with the existing, well-established features. Furthermore, to tackle the limitations of learning high-dimensional representations with a single DAE, we introduce a method for horizontally composing multiple DAEs, effectively increasing the capacity of the model to capture complex relationships. We evaluate our approach on two Chinese-English translation tasks: IWSLT and NIST. Our results demonstrate that semi-supervised DAE features consistently outperform unsupervised DBN features and the baseline features, achieving statistically significant improvements in BLEU score. Specifically, we observe gains of 1.34/2.45 BLEU points on IWSLT and 0.82/1.52 BLEU points on NIST. These results highlight the effectiveness of our semi-supervised approach in learning robust and effective features for SMT, offering a promising avenue for reducing the reliance on manual feature engineering.

Neural response generation, the task of automatically generating relevant and coherent responses to a given input utterance, has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential applications in chatbots, virtual assistants, and social media interactions (Serban et al., 2016;Vinyals & Le, 2015). Early approaches relied on retrieval-based models, which selected responses from a pre-defined corpus (Ji et al., 2014). However, these models were limited by the diversity and creativity of the responses, as they could only choose from existing options. Generative models, particularly sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) architectures with attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2014;Luong et al., 2015), offered a potential solution by generating responses from scratch. Despite their promise, traditional Seq2Seq models for response generation often suffer from several drawbacks. A common issue is the generation of “safe” or generic responses, such as “I don’t know” or “That’s interesting,” which lack informativeness and engagement. This phenomenon arises because maximizing the likelihood of the training data often leads the model to favor common, high-probability responses, rather than more creative and contextually relevant ones. Another challenge lies in the non-differentiable nature of the decoding process during training. Seq2Seq models typically employ sampling-based decoding techniques (e.g., beam search) to generate responses, which prevents direct gradient propagation from the generated output back to the encoder. Recently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as a powerful framework for training generative models (Goodfellow et al., 2014). GANs pit a generator network against a discriminator network in a min-max game, where the generator aims to produce realistic samples that can fool the discriminator, while the discriminator tries to distinguish between real and generated samples. This adversarial training process encourages the generator to learn a more sophisticated distribution over the output space, leading to more diverse and realistic generations. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to neural response generation based on a GAN framework. The generator is a Seq2Seq model responsible for generating responses, while the discriminator is a classifier trained to differentiate between human-written responses and machine-generated responses. By training these two networks adversarially, we aim to overcome the limitations of traditional Seq2Seq models and generate more engaging and informative responses. Furthermore, we introduce an approximate embedding layer to address the non-differentiability problem caused by the sampling-based decoding procedure, enabling more effective gradient propagation during training. Our experiments on both Mandarin and English datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing neural response generation models in terms of diversity, while maintaining competitive relevance scores. Automatic induction of grammars from raw text remains a core challenge in natural language processing. A fully unsupervised approach promises broad applicability to resource-poor languages, circumventing the costly and time-consuming process of manual grammar construction. However, unsupervised grammar induction often suffers from low accuracy and struggles to capture the complexities of natural language syntax. Conversely, supervised approaches, relying on annotated treebanks, achieve high accuracy but are limited by data availability, particularly for less-studied languages. A promising middle ground lies in *bilingual projection*, where syntactic structure from a resource-rich language is transferred to a target language via machine translation (Yamada & Knight, 2001; McDonald et al., 2013). This approach leverages the availability of high-quality treebanks in languages like English to bootstrap grammatical knowledge for others. However, bilingual projection is not without its limitations. Translation errors can propagate syntactic inaccuracies, leading to a distorted and unreliable grammar for the target language (Tillmann et al., 2008). Furthermore, languages often exhibit significant typological differences, meaning that a direct transfer of syntactic structures may not be appropriate or even possible. For instance, word order variations (e.g., subject-verb-object vs. subject-object-verb) can directly impact dependency relations, and imbalances in grammatical features (e.g., rich morphology vs. analytic morphology) can pose additional challenges. In this paper, we propose a novel strategy for inducing monolingual dependency grammars that combines the benefits of bilingual projection with unsupervised learning. Our approach, *bilingually-guided monolingual dependency grammar induction*, leverages dependency information projected from a parsed counterpart language – English in our experiments – but simultaneously incorporates methods for discovering the underlying syntactic structure of the target language. This is achieved by moderately leveraging bilingual information as a soft constraint during the unsupervised grammar induction process, striking a balance between the guidance of projected dependencies and the discovery of inherent syntactic patterns. Our central idea is to utilize the projected dependencies as a regularization term in the unsupervised induction process, encouraging the induced grammar to align with the projected structures where appropriate, but allowing for divergence when linguistic considerations necessitate it. This differs from purely projection-based methods, which blindly transfer structures, and from purely unsupervised methods, which lack any external guidance. (See Figure 1 for an illustration of this process.) We induce grammars for five diverse languages – Czech, German, Hungarian, Japanese, and Chinese – guided by dependency structures projected from their English translations. Our experiments demonstrate that this bilingually-guided method achieves a substantial improvement of 28.5% over a strong unsupervised baseline and 3.0% over the best projection baseline on average, confirming the effectiveness of integrating bilingual information with unsupervised structure learning. Argumentation is a cornerstone of human communication, critical thinking, and knowledge construction. Effective arguments are rarely built on abstract principles alone; rather, they are frequently bolstered by concrete examples, illustrative stories, and relatable experiences. These narratives, often centered around individuals, serve not merely as decoration but as crucial evidence, offering persuasive insights and reinforcing key claims. We term these illustrative narratives “anecdotes” – brief, revealing accounts of individual experiences that impart a broader meaning or lesson. Recognizing and leveraging anecdotes presents significant opportunities across a range of applications, from enhancing argumentative writing to providing enriching contextual information for readers and facilitating more engaging learning experiences. However, identifying and accessing relevant anecdotes presents a considerable challenge. While anecdotes frequently appear in written text, particularly in forms like essays, opinion pieces, and narratives, they are rarely explicitly labeled as such. Extracting them requires nuanced understanding of discourse structure, identifying the interplay between a narrative event and its underlying message – its ‘implication.’ Furthermore, once identified, connecting these anecdotes to specific topics or arguments to facilitate recommendation demands a robust system for analyzing and matching semantic content. This paper introduces a novel task – Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation – designed to address these challenges. We propose a structured representation of anecdotes as triplets: <person, story, implication>. The ‘person’ denotes the individual at the center of the narrative, the ‘story’ is the account of events involving that person, and crucially, the ‘implication’ captures the overarching meaning or lesson conveyed by the anecdote. Our approach focuses on extracting these structured anecdotes from archived argumentative essays, leveraging insights from discourse analysis to pinpoint narratives and uncover their implicit connections to broader themes. Specifically, we hypothesize that understanding the *discourse role* of a passage—whether it serves as a thesis statement, supporting evidence, or a counter-argument—is critical for both anecdote recognition and identifying the anecdote’s intended implication. By identifying passages functioning as illustrative support, we can extract the associated narratives (the ‘story’) and infer the argumentative point they are meant to reinforce (the ‘implication’). Finally, we present an anecdote recommendation system built upon the identified anecdotes and their implications. This system can respond to user-provided topics by recommending relevant anecdotes, effectively bridging the gap between user interests and informative narratives. Our experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, showcasing the ability to automatically recognize informative and interpretable anecdotes and deliver relevant recommendations based on shared thematic resonance. This work opens new avenues for research at the intersection of argumentation mining, narrative understanding, and information retrieval. Sequence labeling – the task of assigning a label to each token in a sequence – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing (NLP), with applications spanning part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and semantic role labeling. Supervised sequence labeling has enjoyed considerable success thanks to powerful discriminative models like conditional random fields (CRFs) (Lafferty et al., 2001) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). However, the performance of these models relies heavily on the availability of large, manually annotated datasets, which are often expensive and time-consuming to create. This limitation motivates the exploration of semi-supervised learning (SSL) techniques that can leverage readily available unlabeled data to improve model performance. Existing semi-supervised approaches for sequence labeling often rely on techniques like self-training (Yarowsky, 1990) or co-training (Blum & Mitchell, 1998), which iteratively refine model predictions using pseudo-labels generated on unlabeled data. More recently, generative models have gained traction in SSL settings, offering a principled way to incorporate unlabeled data into the learning process. For instance, language models can be pre-trained on large corpora and then fine-tuned for sequence labeling tasks (Peters et al., 2018). However, many of these approaches treat the generative and discriminative components as separate entities, potentially limiting their synergy. In this paper, we introduce a novel family of multitask variational methods for semi-supervised sequence labeling. Our approach combines the strengths of both generative and discriminative modeling within a unified variational framework. Specifically, we propose a latent-variable generative model that learns to predict words given their context, echoing the objectives used in training word embeddings like word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013). Simultaneously, a discriminative labeler is trained to predict sequence labels, and is designed to guide the learning of the latent space in a manner that facilitates downstream sequence labeling. This interweaving of generative and discriminative objectives allows the model to leverage both the distributional information present in unlabeled data and the precise labeling information available in labeled data. Furthermore, we explore various configurations for the latent variables, including hierarchical structures that allow the model to capture both label-specific and word-specific variations. This design choice allows for a more nuanced representation of the underlying data distribution, potentially leading to improved performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods on eight standard sequence labeling datasets. Our results consistently outperform strong sequential baselines and demonstrate substantial improvements when incorporating unlabeled data, highlighting the benefits of our variational approach. We believe this work represents a significant step towards more effective and data-efficient sequence labeling models. ### References Blum, A., & Mitchell, T. (1998). Learning with weak labels. Morphologically rich languages pose a significant challenge to natural language processing (NLP) systems. Traditional approaches often rely on explicit segmentation – identifying morphemes (the smallest meaningful units of language) – as a crucial first step for tasks like machine translation, information retrieval, and text classification. However, for many languages, particularly those without explicit word boundaries (often termed “unsegmented languages”), this initial segmentation stage is remarkably difficult. Languages like Japanese, Chinese, Korean, and Thai present this challenge, where words are not clearly demarcated by spaces. Existing approaches to morphological analysis for unsegmented languages typically involve statistical machine learning techniques. These methods often rely on parallel corpora, where texts in the unsegmented language are aligned with texts in a morphologically richer language, allowing for the inference of segmentation and morphological rules (Knight & Graehl, 1998). Alternatively, unsupervised or semi-supervised methods attempt to learn segmentations directly from monolingual data, often employing Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) or Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Goldwater & Johnson, 2003; Sorensen, 2004). However, a key limitation of these statistical models is their reliance on observable word sequences. When applied to unsegmented languages, the inherent difficulty lies in the fact that even the training data – purportedly segmented – is likely to contain errors. Automatic segmentation procedures are rarely perfect, and the resulting noisy data contaminates the learning process. Consequently, language models trained on such data struggle to generalize and often perform poorly on unseen text. While language models are frequently incorporated as features in morphological analysis systems, their effectiveness is diminished when the underlying word sequences are unreliable. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to morphological analysis that addresses this issue by leveraging the power of recurrent neural network language models (RNNLMs). Unlike traditional n-gram language models that treat word sequences as discrete units, RNNLMs learn distributed representations of words, capturing semantic similarities and contextual relationships. This semantic generalization allows the RNNLM to model word sequences even in the presence of segmentation errors, effectively building a more robust and informative language model. Our core insight is that an RNNLM, trained to predict the next morpheme in a sequence, can indirectly encode information about plausible morphological structures. Rather than relying on exact word matches, the RNNLM's learned embeddings capture semantic plausibility, guiding the morphological analysis process towards more meaningful segmentations. We demonstrate this by integrating the RNNLM’s output probabilities into a morphological analysis model, specifically to score potential segmentations. We evaluate our approach on two Japanese corpora, a notoriously challenging unsegmented language. Our experimental results demonstrate a significant improvement over baseline models that utilize conventional n-gram language models or rely solely on statistical morphological analysis techniques. This improvement underscores the effectiveness of RNNLMs in capturing semantic plausibility and mitigating the impact of segmentation errors in morphological analysis for unsegmented languages. This work opens up new avenues for research in morphological analysis, particularly for low-resource languages where parallel data is scarce and segmentation is inherently ambiguous.

Automatic topical segmentation – the task of dividing a text into segments, each addressing a distinct topic – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from text summarization and information retrieval to discourse analysis and question answering. A key challenge in topical segmentation is determining the optimal granularity of the segmentation; that is, deciding how many segments a document should be divided into and where the boundaries between these segments should lie. Traditional approaches to topical segmentation often rely on either sliding window methods (e.g., Hearst, 1998) or iterative clustering algorithms (e.g., Yamada et al., 2003). Sliding window methods fix a window size and move it across the document, identifying segment boundaries based on changes in topic density within the window. These methods often require careful tuning of the window size to achieve optimal performance, and can struggle to capture topics that span multiple windows. Iterative clustering approaches, on the other hand, start with an initial set of segments and refine them iteratively, adding or merging segments based on similarity measures. These methods typically require specifying the desired number of segments in advance, which can be difficult to determine accurately. Furthermore, many existing methods focus on producing flat segmentations, dividing the document into a single level of segments without considering the inherent hierarchical structure of discourse. In this paper, we present a novel approach to hierarchical topical segmentation called Hierarchical Affinity Propagation for Segmentation (HAPS). HAPS builds upon the Affinity Propagation (AP) clustering algorithm (Frey and Dueck, 2007), extending it to construct a hierarchical topical tree. The nodes at the top level of the tree represent the most prominent topical shifts in the document, while nodes at lower levels represent finer-grained topical fluctuations. A key innovation of HAPS is its ability to identify *segment centres* – sentences or paragraphs that best encapsulate the content of each segment. These segment centres provide a concise summary of the segment’s topic and aid in interpreting the segmentation structure. Unlike many existing topical segmentation methods, HAPS does not require specifying the desired number of segments *a priori*. AP automatically determines the appropriate number of clusters (and thus segments) based on the data, adapting to the inherent topical structure of the document. Moreover, HAPS produces a hierarchical segmentation, capturing the nested relationships between different topics and allowing for multiple levels of granularity. We evaluate HAPS on a dataset of texts manually segmented by multiple annotators, and on a dataset of Wikipedia articles. The results demonstrate that the hierarchical segmentations produced by HAPS are superior to those obtained by iteratively applying several one-level segmenters. This suggests that HAPS is able to capture the hierarchical nature of discourse more effectively than flat segmentation methods. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work in topical segmentation. Section 3 describes the HAPS algorithm in detail. Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

Anaphoric shell nouns (ASNs), such as “this issue,” “this fact,” and “the problem,” function as placeholders for larger concepts introduced elsewhere in discourse. Accurately interpreting these ASNs – that is, identifying their referents – is crucial for achieving robust natural language understanding (NLU) and is a key component in tasks ranging from question answering to document summarization. Despite their pervasiveness in natural language, ASNs pose a significant challenge to automated interpretation systems. This is largely due to the abstract nature of ASNs; they lack inherent semantic content and rely entirely on context for meaning. Furthermore, the potential antecedents for ASNs can be distant, complex, and expressed in various ways, making reliable identification difficult. A major bottleneck in the development of ASN interpretation methods is the scarcity of annotated training data. Creating such datasets is a laborious and expensive process, requiring significant human effort to identify and link ASNs to their corresponding referents. Existing datasets, while valuable, are often limited in size and scope, hindering the performance of supervised learning approaches. Consequently, there is a pressing need for methods that can overcome this data scarcity issue and enable more effective ASN interpretation. In this paper, we explore a novel approach to address the data scarcity problem. We leverage the characteristics of *cataphoric* shell nouns (CSNs), which are shell nouns that *follow* their referent (e.g., “the fact that X”). Unlike their anaphoric counterparts, CSNs are comparatively easy to interpret because their referents are immediately adjacent. This inherent property allows us to automatically extract a wealth of training data by identifying the antecedents of CSNs in large, unlabeled corpora. Our core idea is to treat the automatically identified antecedents of CSNs as proxy training examples for interpreting ASNs. We hypothesize that the mechanisms governing the interpretation of cataphoric and anaphoric shell nouns are similar, and that learning from the readily available CSN data can generalize to the more challenging ASN interpretation task. We design a system that extracts these antecedent-CSN pairs and utilizes them to train a model capable of predicting the antecedents of ASNs. We evaluate our approach on a variety of shell nouns, comparing its performance to a baseline system. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving promising precision scores ranging from 0.35 to 0.72, depending on the specific shell noun being interpreted. These results highlight the effectiveness of leveraging cataphoric shell noun data to improve anaphoric shell noun interpretation, offering a cost-effective solution to the data scarcity problem. This work contributes a novel data augmentation technique for a challenging NLU problem and opens avenues for further research in leveraging linguistic structure to improve the performance of machine learning models. Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) has emerged as a powerful formalism for representing natural language syntax, offering a compelling balance between expressiveness and compositional semantics (Steedman, 2000). Unlike traditional phrase structure grammars, CCG elegantly handles non-local dependencies – a crucial feature for parsing complex sentences – through the use of combinatory rules that specify how constituents combine. However, a significant bottleneck in leveraging the benefits of CCG lies in the creation of large, annotated treebanks required for supervised parsing. Constructing such resources is a laborious and expensive undertaking, limiting the applicability of CCG to languages and domains with readily available treebanks. This motivates the pursuit of unsupervised grammar induction techniques, aiming to automatically learn CCG grammars directly from raw text corpora. Previous efforts in CCG induction have demonstrated promising, yet limited, success (Ferretti et al., 2009; Marton et al., 2010). A particularly influential approach, proposed by Bisk and Hockenmaier (2012), utilizes an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm to iteratively refine grammar rules and constituent annotations, achieving state-of-the-art results on English. This work serves as a strong baseline for further improvements. However, existing methods often struggle with issues of grammatical ambiguity and overgeneralization, leading to unwieldy grammars and suboptimal parsing performance. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing two key enhancements to the Bisk and Hockenmaier (2012) framework. First, we incorporate boundary Part-of-Speech (POS) tags – specifically, tags indicating the start and end of sentences – to provide valuable lexical information during the induction process. This allows the model to better disambiguate between different grammatical functions of words, particularly those that can occur at the beginning or end of a sentence. Second, we employ nonparametric Bayesian inference, specifically utilizing the Pitman-Yor process (PYP), to learn compact and well-structured grammars. The PYP allows for a flexible representation of grammar rules, favoring simpler grammars and avoiding overfitting to the training data. Our experiments on the English Penn Treebank demonstrate the significant effectiveness of both the boundary model and Bayesian learning. The proposed approach consistently outperforms the baseline, resulting in improved grammar precision and recall, and ultimately leading to more accurate parsing. This work represents a substantial step forward in unsupervised CCG induction, bringing us closer to the goal of building high-quality CCG parsers for a wider range of languages and domains without the need for extensive manual annotation. The incorporation of linguistic knowledge in the form of boundary POS tags, combined with the principled grammar regularization offered by Bayesian inference, prove to be a potent combination for tackling the challenges inherent in unsupervised grammar learning. The field of machine translation (MT) has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by the advent of neural machine translation (NMT) models (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). These models, leveraging deep learning techniques, have dramatically improved translation quality, particularly for high-resource language pairs. Indeed, a growing body of work now claims that NMT systems are approaching, and in some cases achieving, human parity on standard MT benchmarks (Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). Such claims have significant implications, suggesting that the long-standing goal of automated, high-quality translation is within reach. However, assessing translation quality is notoriously difficult. Traditionally, MT systems have been evaluated using automatic metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and more recently, learned metrics based on neural networks (Shen et al., 2019). These metrics, while useful for rapid iteration during development, are known to correlate imperfectly with human judgments of translation quality (Papineni et al., 2002). More reliable evaluations involve human assessment, typically through direct assessment (DA) or pairwise ranking (Pfizner et al., 2008). Recent work has focused on refining these human evaluation protocols to obtain more nuanced and accurate results. A central finding emerging from these evaluations is that the performance gap between state-of-the-art NMT systems and human translators is narrowing, leading to claims of human parity (Wang et al., 2020). However, most of these evaluations are conducted at the sentence level – that is, human raters are asked to assess the quality of individual translated sentences in isolation. We argue that evaluating MT systems at the sentence level alone is insufficient, particularly as translation quality improves. While a system might produce fluent and accurate sentences in isolation, coherence and consistency across a larger text—a document—are crucial for conveying the full meaning and intent of the original author. Errors that are subtle or difficult to detect at the sentence level, such as pronoun resolution errors, inconsistent terminology, or stylistic infelicities, can accumulate over the course of a document, significantly impacting overall readability and comprehensibility. This paper investigates the claim of human parity in MT by contrasting sentence-level and document-level human evaluations. We focus on the WMT Chinese-English news translation task, where recent results have been particularly encouraging. Through a carefully designed pairwise ranking experiment, we demonstrate that human raters consistently prefer human-produced translations over machine translations when evaluating entire documents, even when the sentence-level preferences are more balanced. Our findings underscore the importance of shifting towards document-level evaluation as MT technology matures, as it is at this level that the limitations of current systems become most apparent.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving state-of-the-art results on numerous language pairs (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). However, the success of NMT is heavily reliant on the availability of large, parallel corpora, typically consisting of millions of sentence pairs. This presents a significant challenge for low-resource language pairs, where such data is scarce or non-existent. Consequently, NMT systems trained on limited data often suffer from poor translation quality, hindering their practical application. A particularly difficult scenario arises when one of the languages involved is ‘rare’ – meaning that it has limited digital resources and little existing parallel data with other commonly translated languages. Direct training of an NMT model for a low-resource pair (X, Z), where Z is a rare language, often results in overfitting and poor generalization. Numerous approaches have been investigated to address this issue, including back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016), transfer learning (Luong et al., 2015), and pivoting (Chu et al., 2017). While these methods offer improvements, they often struggle to fully leverage available data and can be sensitive to the quality of the intermediate resources. In this paper, we propose a novel triangular training architecture (TA-NMT) for low-resource NMT, specifically designed to handle scenarios where one language (Z) is particularly rare. The core idea behind TA-NMT is to leverage a rich, pivot language (Y) to facilitate translation between the source language (X) and the rare target language (Z). Instead of directly training a (X, Z) model, we exploit existing bilingual corpora (Y, Z) – which may be small but are often more readily available than (X, Z) – and a rich (X, Y) corpus. Our approach positions Z as an intermediate latent variable, effectively decomposing the complex (X, Y) translation problem into two simpler steps: X → Z and Z → Y. We then jointly optimize these two translation models within a unified Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework. This framework maximizes the likelihood of translating from X to Y, while implicitly learning representations for the rare language Z. By treating Z as a hidden variable, we encourage the models to learn representations that are consistent across both translation steps. The main contributions of this work are: (1) the introduction of the triangular training architecture for low-resource NMT; (2) a novel bidirectional EM algorithm for jointly optimizing the translation models; and (3) comprehensive experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of TA-NMT on both the MultiUN and IWSLT2012 datasets, with significant improvements over baseline NMT models and even further gains when combined with back-translation techniques.

Entity Linking (EL), also known as Named Entity Disambiguation (NED), is a core task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that aims to map mentions of entities in text to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) such as Wikipedia or Freebase. This process is crucial for a wide array of downstream applications, including question answering, information extraction, and knowledge graph construction. The fundamental challenge in EL lies in the inherent ambiguity of entity mentions. A single mention, such as “Apple,” can refer to multiple entities – the technology company, the fruit, or even a record label. Resolving this ambiguity requires a deep understanding of both the context surrounding the mention and the characteristics of the candidate entities in the KB. Early approaches to EL relied heavily on handcrafted features and rule-based systems (Gaizauskas et al., 2008; Hoffart et al., 2008). While these methods achieved reasonable performance on limited datasets, they suffered from poor scalability and generalization ability. More recently, statistical machine learning techniques, particularly those based on language models, have gained prominence (Bekkerman & McCallum, 2005; Milne & Robertson, 2008). These approaches model the probability of an entity given its surrounding context, typically utilizing bag-of-words representations or more sophisticated feature engineering. However, a significant limitation of many existing EL systems is their reliance on local context alone. While the immediate surrounding words provide valuable clues, they often fail to capture the broader semantic relationships and world knowledge necessary for accurate disambiguation. For instance, consider the mention “Washington.” Without additional information, it’s impossible to determine whether it refers to the U.S. state, the city, or George Washington. Leveraging global knowledge, such as the entity’s associated topics and relationships within the KB, is therefore essential. In this paper, we present a novel approach to entity linking that addresses this limitation by integrating both local context and global world knowledge through query expansion. We formulate EL as a statistical information retrieval problem, where the goal is to retrieve the most relevant entity from the KB given a query representing the entity mention and its context. To enhance the query representation, we employ a language model-based approach, expanding the query with both local contextual terms and related terms extracted from the KB. We pay particular attention to the role of named entities within the local context, utilizing a positional language model to weight them differently based on their distance to the target mention. Our experiments on the TAC-KBP 2010 dataset demonstrate that incorporating such contextual information significantly improves entity linking performance, consistently outperforming baseline models and achieving competitive results compared to other participants in the KBP 2010 competition. The explosive growth of online content, particularly in languages like Chinese, has created a vast repository of opinions and sentiments. Analyzing this “evaluative information” – encompassing attitudes, opinions, and sentiments – is increasingly vital for understanding public perception, market trends, and societal dynamics. While significant progress has been made in sentiment analysis and opinion mining for English, resources and methodologies for Chinese remain comparatively limited. Existing Chinese sentiment analysis systems often focus narrowly on polarity detection (positive, negative, neutral) and struggle with the nuanced expression of evaluation prevalent in Chinese discourse. This is partly due to the linguistic complexities of the Chinese language, including its reliance on context, idioms, and implicit cues. This paper presents the Chinese Evaluative Information Analyzer (CEIA), a system designed to identify and analyze a wider spectrum of evaluative information present in Chinese text. Beyond simple polarity, CEIA aims to extract not only *what* is being evaluated, but *how* it is being evaluated – capturing the intensity, specific aspects, and underlying reasons for opinions. We view evaluative information as a unifying concept encompassing sentiment analysis, appraisal extraction, and opinion mining, offering a more comprehensive framework for understanding subjective expressions. To facilitate the development of CEIA and overcome the scarcity of labeled data, we have constructed a novel, annotated corpus specifically designed for Chinese evaluative information analysis. This corpus goes beyond simple sentiment labels, providing detailed annotations of evaluative expressions, their targets, and associated attributes. Alongside the corpus, we have compiled a large-scale sentiment dictionary, tailored to the nuances of Chinese language and culture. Leveraging these resources, CEIA employs a feature engineering approach incorporating syntactic dependency relations, semantic class information, and distance features to improve the accuracy and robustness of evaluative information extraction. This work makes three key contributions: (i) CEIA represents an advancement in identifying and analyzing a more diverse and richer set of evaluative information than previously demonstrated for Chinese; (ii) the newly created annotated corpus and large sentiment dictionary provide valuable resources for the research community; and (iii) we demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating syntactic, semantic, and distance-based features in improving the performance of evaluative information extraction from Chinese text. We evaluate CEIA’s performance on our annotated corpus, demonstrating the significant benefits of the proposed features through a series of rigorous experiments and comparative analysis. The aim of this work is to lay the foundation for more sophisticated and nuanced understanding of Chinese public opinion expressed online. Introducing the Chinese Evaluative Information Analyzer (CEIA) could significantly advance research in Chinese opinion mining and sentiment analysis, offering a blueprint for building more nuanced and accurate systems. Specifically, this research fits into a wider field of computational linguistics where accurate evaluation of texts is critical. It is vital to assess the overall perceptions on a given topic to cater for user needs, to predict future outcomes, or to understand the characteristics of the target population. The present research aims to deliver on this need by proposing a novel system that implements cutting-edge techniques and additional resources such as the annotated dataset.

Word embeddings, dense vector representations of words, have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). These embeddings capture semantic and syntactic regularities in language, enabling significant performance gains across a wide range of downstream tasks. However, traditional word embedding models, such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), produce a single vector representation for each word, effectively ignoring the phenomenon of polysemy – the existence of multiple meanings for a single word. This averaging of senses can lead to suboptimal performance in tasks that require fine-grained semantic understanding. For example, the word “bank” can refer to a financial institution or the land alongside a river. A single word embedding for “bank” will represent a blending of these two distinct meanings, potentially hindering performance in tasks such as word sense disambiguation or relation extraction. Consequently, a significant body of research has focused on learning *multi-sense* word embeddings – representations that assign a separate vector to each sense of a polysemous word (Rei & Briscoe, 2014; Huang et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014). Existing approaches to learning multi-sense embeddings generally fall into two categories: clustering-based and context-based. Clustering-based methods (e.g., Huang et al., 2012) first cluster word occurrences based on their contextual similarity and then learn a separate embedding for each cluster. Context-based methods (e.g., Rei & Briscoe, 2014) directly model the probability of a word sense given its context, and learn embeddings conditioned on the predicted sense. While effective, these methods often rely on external resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995) or require complex, non-differentiable optimization procedures. In this paper, we introduce the *disambiguated skip-gram model*, a novel neural probabilistic model for learning multi-sense word embeddings. Our model jointly estimates a skip-gram-like context word prediction model and a word sense disambiguation model within a single, end-to-end differentiable framework. This allows us to leverage the power of neural networks while avoiding the limitations of previous probabilistic approaches. Importantly, our model can be interpreted as a simple feed-forward neural network, simplifying training and enabling efficient implementation. We further introduce an effective pruning strategy that allows us to control the granularity of the learned representations, discarding senses with low predictive power. We demonstrate the effectiveness of disambiguated skip-gram through extensive evaluation on several word sense induction benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results. Our main contributions are threefold: (1) a novel end-to-end differentiable model for learning multi-sense word embeddings, (2) an effective pruning strategy for controlling the granularity of representations, and (3) strong empirical results demonstrating improved performance on standard word sense induction tasks.

Building intelligent conversational systems—agents capable of engaging in natural and meaningful dialogue with humans—remains a central challenge in Artificial Intelligence. Traditionally, approaches to dialogue systems have fallen into two broad categories: retrieval-based and generative. Retrieval-based systems (e.g., Serban et al., 2016) select responses from a pre-defined database, relying on techniques like information retrieval or machine learning to identify the most appropriate reply given the dialogue context. While often achieving high relevance, these systems frequently suffer from a lack of novelty and can become repetitive, limited by the diversity of their response database. Generative systems, on the other hand (e.g., Li et al., 2016), attempt to *produce* responses from scratch, learning to map dialogue contexts to natural language outputs. This approach has the potential for greater flexibility and creativity, but is significantly more challenging, often struggling with coherence, fluency, and factual accuracy. Perhaps more fundamentally, many successful dialogue systems, even those employing generative models, still rely heavily on hand-engineered rules, domain-specific knowledge, or carefully curated datasets. This limits their adaptability to truly open-domain conversations—interactions not constrained to a specific task or topic. The goal of creating a truly open-domain conversational system, able to seamlessly navigate a wide range of topics and engage in natural, human-like dialogue, is therefore a significant undertaking. This paper proposes an architecture for such a system, importantly, one constructed *entirely* from modules based on natural language processing (NLP) techniques. We eschew the need for hand-crafted rules, extensive domain-specific knowledge bases, or pre-defined response templates. Instead, we leverage recent advances in NLP, including sequence-to-sequence models, attention mechanisms, and language modeling, to build a system capable of understanding and generating natural language dialogue in a fully data-driven manner. The core idea is to create a pipeline of interconnected NLP components: a natural language understanding (NLU) module, a dialogue management (DM) module, and a natural language generation (NLG) module—all trained end-to-end using large-scale text corpora. We implemented a system based on this architecture and present a thorough evaluation, comparing its performance against a strong retrieval-based baseline and a well-established rule-based system. Our results, obtained through human evaluation, demonstrate that our proposed architecture achieves significantly better naturalness than the retrieval-based baseline, indicating a substantial improvement in dialogue quality. Furthermore, the naturalness of our system approaches that of the rule-based system—a system relying on a massive 149,000 hand-crafted rules—suggesting that a fully NLP-based approach can effectively compete with, and potentially surpass, traditional methods in open-domain conversational AI. This work represents a significant step towards realizing the vision of engaging, open-domain conversational agents powered solely by the power of natural language processing.

Sentiment analysis, the computational task of determining the emotional tone expressed in text, has witnessed significant advances in recent years, largely fueled by the proliferation of machine learning techniques and readily available labeled datasets (Pang and Lee, 2008;Liu, 2012). While substantial progress has been made in handling explicit sentiment expressions, a persistent challenge lies in accurately interpreting the sentiment conveyed by words whose polarity is context-dependent – particularly, dynamic sentiment ambiguous adjectives (DSAAs). Words like “large,” “small,” “high,” and “low” don’t inherently possess positive or negative sentiment; their polarity is determined by the noun they modify. For example, “large screen” typically evokes a positive sentiment, whereas “large debt” carries a negative connotation. This contextual sensitivity makes DSAAs particularly difficult for traditional sentiment analysis approaches that rely on static lexicons or pre-trained word embeddings. Existing work has attempted to address this challenge through various methods. Sentiment lexicons often assign multiple polarities to ambiguous terms (Turney and McKoon, 2002), but resolving ambiguity requires accurate contextual understanding. Machine learning models can learn to disambiguate based on surrounding words (Nagel et al., 2014), but performance is often limited by the availability of labeled data and the model's ability to generalize to unseen contexts. Furthermore, many approaches focus on determining the “semantic orientation” of ambiguous terms – a concept that often conflates inherent meaning with context-specific sentiment. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge-based approach to disambiguating DSAAs, framing the task not as identifying semantic orientation, but as determining the *sentiment expectation* associated with the noun being modified. We argue that this shift in perspective is crucial. Instead of trying to define the inherent polarity of “large,” we focus on understanding what sentiment is typically associated with things that are “large”—screens, salaries, opportunities, versus debts, risks, or problems. To achieve this, we leverage the vast amount of information available on the Web, employing lexico-syntactic patterns to automatically infer the sentiment expectation of nouns. Recognizing that web-mined data is often noisy, we further incorporate a character-sentiment model to effectively reduce noise and improve the reliability of sentiment estimations. Our method demonstrates promising results. At the sentence level, we achieve an f-score of 78.52%, significantly outperforming baseline models. More importantly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a real-world application: document-level sentiment classification of product reviews. Here, our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art techniques, highlighting the practical value of accurately disambiguating DSAAs. The rapid expansion of scientific literature presents a significant challenge for researchers and funding agencies alike. Keeping pace with the latest advancements, identifying burgeoning research areas, and anticipating future directions are crucial for maximizing impact and allocating resources effectively. Traditionally, identifying emergent research trends relied on manual literature reviews, expert opinions, or descriptive analyses of keyword frequencies. While valuable, these methods are often time-consuming, subjective, and struggle to scale with the ever-increasing volume of publications. More recently, automated approaches leveraging bibliometric data, text mining, and machine learning techniques have emerged as promising alternatives (Small, 1973; Chen, 2006; Bornmann & Mutz, 2015). However, existing automated methods often fall short in capturing the nuanced interplay between key concepts and influential researchers that truly define an emergent trend. Simple keyword analysis can identify frequently occurring terms, but fails to distinguish between established areas and genuinely novel directions. Citation-based approaches highlight influential papers, but may not reflect the evolving thematic landscape. Approaches focusing solely on textual centrality may identify important phrases but miss the crucial connection to the researchers driving the innovation. This work addresses these limitations by proposing a novel framework for identifying emergent research trends rooted in a *bijunctive hypothesis*: influential authors tend to write about important phrases, and conversely, important phrases are authored by influential scholars within a field. We posit that simultaneously considering author authority and phrase significance is essential for accurately detecting trends as they begin to coalesce. Our approach constructs a multigraph representation that integrates author networks and phrase co-occurrence patterns, allowing for joint ranking of both entities. We then leverage these rankings to create phrasal embeddings—vector representations of phrases that incorporate information about both their textual context and the authority of their authors. These embeddings are fed into a recurrent neural network (RNN) to compute a trend score for each phrase, capturing its trajectory over time and indicating its emergence as a prominent research topic. Through experiments on two large datasets of scientific articles – datasets from the arXiv and PubMed – we demonstrate that our method effectively identifies past research trends, surpassing baseline approaches that rely solely on text centrality or citation analysis. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay between authors and phrases in uncovering the dynamic evolution of scientific knowledge. The presented work offers a scalable and objective framework for identifying emergent research trends, providing valuable insights for researchers, funding agencies, and anyone seeking to understand the future of science. Event detection, the task of identifying event mentions in text alongside their corresponding types, is a core component of many natural language processing applications, including information extraction, knowledge base population, and news summarization. Traditionally, event detection has been approached as a sequence labeling or word-wise classification problem (Zhou et al., 2008; Miwa and Saigo, 2016). These methods strive to classify each word in a sentence as either belonging to an event trigger or not, and if so, to determine the event type. While effective in languages with clear word boundaries like English, this paradigm faces significant challenges when applied to languages like Chinese, where word segmentation is often ambiguous and word boundaries are not explicitly marked. This ambiguity leads to a mismatch between the granularity of words and the often multi-character nature of event triggers, hindering the performance of word-wise classification models. The inherent difficulties posed by Chinese’s morphological characteristics necessitate exploring alternative approaches to event detection. Existing work attempting to address this issue includes character-level models (e.g., Lample et al., 2016), which operate directly on characters bypassing the word segmentation step. However, these models often struggle to capture the structural and semantic information conveyed by words, leading to suboptimal performance. Furthermore, directly classifying individual characters as triggers often fails to account for the compositional nature of Chinese event triggers, which frequently span multiple characters. Recognizing that event triggers are often formed by coherent character sequences—"nuggets"—we argue for a paradigm shift toward directly proposing and classifying these nuggets rather than individual words or characters. In this paper, we introduce Nugget Proposal Networks (NPNs), a novel framework for Chinese event detection that directly addresses the word-trigger mismatch problem. NPNs operate in a character-wise paradigm, proposing potential event trigger nuggets centered around each character, completely independent of predefined word boundaries. A key innovation is the design of a hybrid character representation that effectively integrates both character-level and word-level information, capturing both fine-grained structural details and broader semantic context. Subsequently, we leverage the compositional structures inherent in Chinese event triggers to propose promising nuggets, which are then categorized using a dedicated classification layer. We evaluate NPNs on two benchmark datasets for event detection: ACE2005 and TAC KBP 2017. Experimental results demonstrate that NPNs consistently and significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods, establishing a new performance baseline for Chinese event detection. Our findings underscore the effectiveness of the proposed nugget-centric approach and highlight the importance of considering the unique characteristics of Chinese when designing event detection systems. Grammar induction – the task of learning a grammar from raw text without any explicit linguistic supervision – remains a central challenge in natural language processing (NLP). The ability to automatically discover the underlying structure of language would not only advance our fundamental understanding of linguistic principles but also enable the rapid development of NLP tools for low-resource languages where manually constructed grammars are unavailable (Klein & Manning, 2004; Bod, 2006). Existing approaches to grammar induction typically rely on distributional methods, clustering words based on their contexts to identify syntactic categories and infer dependencies between them (Pereira et al., 1992; Clark, 2001; Goldberg, 2006). While these methods have achieved considerable success, they often struggle to produce grammars that align well with established linguistic theory or yield high-quality parsing performance, particularly across diverse language families. A key limitation of purely data-driven approaches is their disregard for universal linguistic principles – the inherent properties and constraints shared by all human languages (Chomsky, 1965; Hawkins, 1988). These universals reflect fundamental cognitive biases and constraints on language processing, suggesting that incorporating them into grammar induction should lead to more robust and generalizable results. Previous work has attempted to leverage linguistic knowledge in grammar induction, primarily through the use of pre-defined syntactic categories or features (Johnson et al., 2007; Petrov et al., 2011). However, these approaches often rely on language-specific resources and do not fully exploit the potential of cross-linguistically valid principles. In this paper, we present a novel approach to grammar induction that explicitly incorporates syntactic universals to guide dependency parsing. Our method utilizes a single set of manually-specified, language-independent rules that identify common syntactic dependencies between pairs of syntactic categories frequently found across languages. These rules—expressed as constraints on the allowable attachments between categories like noun and adjective, or verb and adverb—implicitly encode universal linguistic patterns. During probabilistic model inference, we employ posterior expectation constraints to ensure that a minimum proportion of the dependencies we infer adhere to these established rules. Furthermore, we automatically refine the initial, coarsely-tagged syntactic categories based on distributional similarities, improving the accuracy of dependency parsing. We evaluate our approach across six languages, demonstrating consistent and significant performance gains over state-of-the-art unsupervised methods. Supervised machine learning models, particularly those leveraging Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and more recently, Large Language Models (LLMs), have become the workhorse for numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. However, the performance of these models often hinges on the quality and quantity of their features. A common strategy for improving performance involves utilizing *conjunctive features* – combinations of more basic, primitive features. These conjunctive features, while powerful in representing complex relationships within the data, introduce a significant computational burden. The core problem lies in the exponential growth of feature space as the number of primitive features increases. For instance, if we have *n* primitive features, the number of possible conjunctive features of degree *k* grows as O(n<sup>k</sup>). This necessitates substantial memory to store the model weights and equally substantial computational time during both training and, crucially, inference. While feature selection techniques can mitigate this issue, they often come at the cost of performance, discarding potentially valuable information. Recent research has explored hashing tricks to reduce memory requirements (Weinberger et al., 2009), but these methods can introduce collisions and degrade accuracy. This paper proposes a novel approach to address the computational bottleneck imposed by conjunctive features, without sacrificing accuracy. Our key insight is that in many NLP tasks, certain primitive feature vectors appear with high frequency. By precomputing the weights for these frequent partial results – prefixes of longer conjunctive features – we can significantly accelerate classification. We achieve this through the use of a *trie* data structure, a tree-like structure optimized for efficient prefix searching. The trie compactly stores primitive feature vectors along with their corresponding weights, enabling rapid retrieval of precomputed weight information during inference. Essentially, given an input feature vector, our system traverses the trie to identify the longest prefix that has a precomputed weight. This allows us to avoid redundant computations, effectively transforming what would have been a complex calculation involving potentially numerous primitive features into a simple lookup and addition operation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a challenging Japanese dependency parsing task. Our experimental results demonstrate a substantial speedup – a factor of 10.7 for SVM classifiers and 11.6 for LLM classifiers – without sacrificing accuracy. The parsers utilizing our optimized classification scheme achieve accuracy levels of 90.84% and 90.71%, respectively, showcasing that efficient computation and high performance are not mutually exclusive. This work contributes a practical and effective technique for deploying complex, conjunctive feature-based models in real-world NLP applications where speed and scalability are paramount. Coreference resolution – the task of identifying mentions that refer to the same real-world entity – is a fundamental problem in natural language processing. Accurate coreference is crucial for a wide range of downstream applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Traditional approaches to coreference have largely focused on pairwise comparison methods, where every pair of mentions is evaluated for compatibility, and then clustered based on similarity scores (Soon et al., 2001;Ng and Cardie, 2002;Daumé III, 2007). While these systems have achieved impressive results on benchmark datasets, they exhibit significant limitations when applied to large-scale text. The computational complexity of pairwise comparison scales quadratically with the number of mentions, rendering it impractical for documents containing thousands of entities. Furthermore, the representational capacity of pairwise models is often insufficient to capture complex coreference phenomena, such as long-range dependencies and subtle semantic relationships. As the size of text corpora continues to grow, and the demands for scalable NLP applications increase, the limitations of pairwise approaches become increasingly apparent. Analyzing the vast amounts of text available on the web, in news archives, or in scientific literature requires coreference systems that can process millions of mentions efficiently and accurately. Consequently, there is a pressing need for new coreference models that overcome the scalability bottlenecks and representational limitations of existing methods. Recent work has explored various avenues for improving coreference performance and scalability. Mention ranking models (Goldberg and Levy, 2014) aim to reduce the number of pairwise comparisons by prioritizing the most promising candidate antecedents. Cluster-based methods (Fernandez-Luna et al., 2005) iteratively merge mentions into clusters based on similarity scores. However, these approaches still rely on pairwise comparison as a core component, and are therefore limited in their scalability. In this paper, we introduce a novel discriminative hierarchical model for fast coreference at large scale. Our model departs from the traditional pairwise paradigm by recursively partitioning entities into trees of latent sub-entities. These trees provide a succinct and informative representation of the coreference structure, allowing us to reason about entity relationships and coreference uncertainty efficiently. The hierarchical structure enables a logarithmic scaling complexity, significantly improving performance for massive datasets. We demonstrate that our model achieves several orders of magnitude speedup compared to state-of-the-art pairwise approaches, allowing us to perform coreference on six million author mentions in under four hours on a single CPU. Moreover, we demonstrate that the hierarchical model achieves competitive accuracy, further highlighting its potential as a scalable and effective coreference resolution technique. Information Extraction (IE) is the task of automatically extracting structured information from unstructured text. A core component of many IE systems is event extraction, which focuses on identifying event triggers (typically verbs) and their associated arguments – the role fillers that participate in the event (e.g., Agent, Patient, Time, Location). Traditional approaches to event extraction often focus on identifying role fillers within the immediate phrasal context surrounding a potential event trigger (e.g., within a few words to the left or right of the trigger verb). While this local context is valuable, it often proves insufficient for accurately identifying all relevant role fillers. A significant challenge lies in the fact that role fillers are not always expressed in close proximity to the event trigger. Often, arguments are mentioned in clauses or sentences that are syntactically separated from the primary event expression. For example, consider the sentence: “Following the earthquake in Nepal, international aid organizations dispatched relief supplies to Kathmandu.” While “earthquake” is the event trigger, the role filler for the Location (“Kathmandu”) appears much later in the sentence and is connected to the event through a discourse marker ("Following"). Similarly, agents or instruments may be introduced earlier or later in a document and then referred to through pronouns or nominals. Existing event extraction systems often struggle with these non-local dependencies. Approaches based solely on local phrasal context may miss distant role fillers entirely. While some systems incorporate syntactic parsing to extend the context window, they may still be limited in capturing long-range dependencies and discourse relations. More sophisticated approaches utilize coreference resolution to link mentions, but this adds complexity and introduces potential errors. In this paper, we introduce a novel, unified probabilistic model for event extraction that explicitly addresses the challenges of both local and non-local evidence. Our model moves beyond the limitations of purely phrasal context by jointly considering the entire sentence in which a potential event occurs, as well as the relationship between sentences within a document. Specifically, our approach consists of two key components: a *sentential event recognizer* which identifies events within a sentence, and a *plausible role-filler recognizer* conditioned on the identified event sentences. This conditional dependency allows the system to leverage the broader sentential context to infer the likelihood of a phrase being a valid role filler for a given event. We hypothesize that considering the entire sentence provides crucial contextual information that aids in resolving ambiguities and identifying distant arguments. By modeling the interplay between the event and its surrounding context, our system can more accurately extract structured information from unstructured text. We evaluate our model on two standard IE datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over existing systems that primarily rely on local phrasal context. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our unified approach and highlight the importance of incorporating sentential evidence into event extraction systems. Sentiment analysis and connotation detection are fundamental tasks in natural language processing with broad applications ranging from opinion mining and market research to understanding emotional responses in text. Existing approaches often rely on lexicon-based methods, where words are assigned polarity scores (positive, negative, or neutral) to determine the overall sentiment or connotation expressed in a text (Wilson, 2005;Turney, 2002). However, a significant limitation of these methods is their inability to capture the nuances of word meaning, specifically the context-dependent connotation variations arising from polysemy – the property of having multiple meanings. For example, the word “bright” can have a positive connotation when describing intelligence (“a bright student”), but a negative connotation when describing colors that are overly intense (“a bright, glaring light”). Current sentiment lexicons typically assign a single, average polarity score to a word, failing to account for these semantic differences. Furthermore, most existing lexicons focus solely on word-level connotations, largely ignoring the rich relational information encoded within lexical resources such as WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998). WordNet organizes words into synsets – groups of synonymous terms representing distinct concepts (senses). These synsets are further interconnected through semantic relations such as hypernymy (is-a relation), hyponymy (has-a relation), and meronymy (part-of relation). Leveraging these relationships can potentially improve connotation prediction by propagating sentiment information across related concepts. For instance, if a particular sense of a word has a positive connotation, its related synsets might also be inclined towards positivity. In this paper, we introduce ConnotationWordNet, a novel connotation lexicon that explicitly addresses both the sense-level disambiguation and relational dependency issues. Our approach is unique in its formulation of lexicon induction as a collective inference problem over a pairwise Markov Random Field (MRF) defined on the WordNet network. This framework allows us to simultaneously determine the polarity of both word-level and sense-level connotations, exploiting the innate bipartite graph structure inherent in WordNet - a network of words connected via their various senses. We propose a loopy belief propagation algorithm to efficiently perform inference within this MRF, iteratively refining the polarity estimates based on the surrounding semantic relationships. The key contribution of our work lies in the development of a unified approach that combines the benefits of sense disambiguation and relational reasoning within a single framework. Unlike prior work that treats word senses as independent entities, our model leverages the semantic connections provided by WordNet to produce more accurate and nuanced connotation estimates. We present comprehensive evaluations on a variety of benchmark datasets, demonstrating that ConnotationWordNet significantly outperforms existing connotation and sentiment lexicons, while also exhibiting improved performance in downstream sentiment classification tasks. Domain adaptation – the ability of a machine learning model trained on one distribution of data (the source domain) to perform well on a different, but related, distribution (the target domain) – is a central challenge in natural language processing (NLP). Real-world applications often involve deploying models in environments that differ from those in which they were trained, due to variations in user demographics, topic, or data collection procedures. Ignoring these domain shifts can lead to significant performance degradation. Traditional approaches to domain adaptation have largely fallen into two categories: feature-based methods and instance-based methods (Ben-David et al., 2010). Feature-based methods aim to learn domain-invariant feature representations, while instance-based methods re-weight or select instances from the source domain to better match the target domain. More recently, adversarial training (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Ganin et al., 2016) has emerged as a powerful technique for domain adaptation, encouraging feature representations that are indistinguishable between domains. A particularly effective, yet often overlooked, line of work focuses on feature augmentation (Daumé III, 2009). This approach posits that a model should learn to *predict* the domain of an instance, and then use this prediction as an additional feature during classification. This encourages the model to learn features that are informative not only for the primary task but also for distinguishing between domains. Daumé III (2009) demonstrated significant improvements using feature augmentation with Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), particularly when dealing with sparse, binary-valued features. However, this approach has received comparatively less attention in the era of deep learning and dense, real-valued feature representations. The core motivation of this work is to bridge this gap. We investigate simple, yet surprisingly effective, neural extensions of the feature augmentation techniques proposed by Daumé III (2009) and also explore a neural adaptation of the shared structure learning framework originally proposed by Ando and Zhang (2005). Specifically, we propose a generalization of feature augmentation using multiple Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, where one LSTM captures global patterns across all domains, while the remaining LSTMs learn domain-specific representations. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the principle of learning shared structures can be adapted to the domain adaptation setting using neural networks. Our experiments on a challenging slot tagging task across 17 diverse domains demonstrate that these neural adaptations significantly outperform the original feature augmentation method applied to feature-rich CRFs. These results highlight the potential of combining classical domain adaptation techniques with the expressive power of deep neural networks, leading to remarkably simple and effective solutions.
