Document-level sentiment analysis – the task of determining the overall sentiment expressed in a document – remains a significant challenge in natural language processing. While sentence-level sentiment analysis has reached a high degree of maturity (Socher et al., 2013;Lai et al., 2015), aggregating sentence-level sentiment into a document-level assessment is non-trivial (Cambier & Van den Bosch, 2012;Poria et al., 2013). A key factor complicating this process is the presence of fine-grained subjectivity: not all parts of a document contribute equally to the overall sentiment. Identifying which segments are relevant for a sentiment judgment is critical for accurate document-level analysis. Ideally, such relevance could be determined using explicit annotations of subjective and objective spans within the document (Wilson & Wiebe, 2007). However, manually annotating subjectivity at this level of granularity is expensive and time-consuming, limiting the availability of such resources. Consequently, recent work has explored modeling subjectivity as a *latent variable* – an unobserved variable inferred from the text itself (Newman & Klein, 2008;Broeksema et al., 2011;Labbé & Décoret, 2012). These latent variable models offer a principled way to account for differing levels of subjectivity without requiring expensive annotations. However, current latent variable approaches largely treat the document as a bag of sentences, failing to leverage important linguistic cues about discourse structure. Discourse connectives – words and phrases like “however,” “therefore,” and “although” – explicitly signal relationships between segments of text, often indicating shifts in topic or sentiment (Knott, 1996;Stede, 2002). These connectives provide valuable signals regarding the relevance of surrounding text for overall sentiment and could theoretically guide the latent subjectivity model to better determine which parts of the document contribute to the overall sentiment. In this paper, we present a novel method for incorporating this linguistic knowledge into latent variable subjectivity modeling. We augment the transition features of a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) – a common framework for latent variable modeling – with information about discourse connectors. Specifically, we introduce features that capture whether a transition between subjective states (latent variables) is accompanied by the presence of a discourse connector. Crucially, this is done *without* requiring any explicit subjectivity annotations; the model learns the relevance of connectors for subjectivity transitions directly from the unlabeled text. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on document-level sentiment analysis tasks in both English and Spanish, achieving significant performance improvements over baseline models. We also present a simple heuristic for automatically identifying discourse connectors in text, addressing the issue of language-specific connector lists. Our results show that leveraging discourse connectives within a latent variable framework provides a surprisingly effective way to enhance document-level sentiment analysis, bridging the gap between linguistic knowledge and statistical modeling.

Machine Translation (MT) has rapidly advanced in recent years, largely due to the rise of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). However, even the best MT systems are not perfect, frequently producing outputs containing errors that can range from minor fluency issues to severe distortions of meaning. Consequently, assessing the quality of MT output is a critical task, with applications spanning from system development and evaluation to post-editing effort estimation. Traditionally, MT evaluation has relied on automatic metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and human evaluation. While widely used, these methods are often costly, time-consuming, or imperfectly correlated with human judgements of quality. Quality Estimation (QE) emerged as a promising alternative, aiming to predict the quality of MT output *without* access to reference translations (Blanchard et al., 2005; López-Cuadrado et al., 2014). QE models leverage a variety of source and target side features to estimate metrics like Human-mediated Translation Edit Rate (HTER) or Direct Assessment (DA) scores. Recent advancements in QE have explored diverse machine learning approaches, ranging from traditional methods like Support Vector Regression (SVR) (Yang et al., 2017) to more sophisticated techniques based on neural networks (Tran & Cavalli, 2017; Ke et al., 2018). While these studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of QE, a comprehensive and comparative evaluation of a broad range of QE models remains lacking. Moreover, previous work often focuses primarily on prediction accuracy, neglecting the robustness and generalization ability of QE models – crucial factors in real-world deployment. This paper aims to address these gaps by providing a thorough evaluation of a diverse set of QE models, including SVR, Ridge Regression, various Neural Network architectures, Gaussian Processes (GPs), Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), and Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs). Our investigation specifically targets sentence-level QE, a challenging task due to the inherent variability and complexity of natural language. We not only evaluate the predictive accuracy of these models but also prioritize assessing their robustness and generalization capabilities. We demonstrate that QE models exhibit considerable variation in performance depending on the characteristics of the feature space – specifically, its scale – and the similarity between the training and test data domains. We observe that different models excel in different scenarios, highlighting the lack of a single universally superior approach. Our findings offer practical guidance for selecting appropriate QE models based on specific application contexts and data characteristics. The central contribution of our work is an assessment of the challenges in building effective QE models, and practical recommendations for addressing those challenges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) is a semantic formalism designed to represent the meaning of a sentence in a graph-based structure. Unlike syntactic representations like dependency parses, AMR focuses on ‘what’ is being said rather than ‘how’ it is said, making it particularly suitable for tasks like machine translation, text summarization, and question answering. A central challenge in utilizing AMR is the task of AMR-to-text generation: automatically producing natural language text from a given AMR graph. This task requires a deep understanding of both semantic structure and linguistic fluency, posing a significant challenge to current natural language generation (NLG) techniques. Existing approaches to AMR-to-text generation largely rely on sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly LSTMs (Long Short-Term Memory networks). These models typically linearize the AMR graph into a sequential format – often through a depth-first traversal – before feeding it to the encoder LSTM. While effective, this linearization process inherently disrupts the graph structure, potentially leading to loss of crucial semantic relationships. Moreover, the length of the linearized sequence grows proportionally to the size of the AMR graph, creating difficulties for the LSTM to effectively capture long-range dependencies, especially in complex sentences represented by large graphs. The vanilla seq2seq approach, while capable of capturing non-local information, thus struggles with maintaining a holistic view of the AMR graph’s semantics as graph complexity increases. To address these limitations, we propose a novel neural graph-to-sequence model for AMR-to-text generation. Our model moves away from the traditional linearization approach and directly encodes the graph structure using a novel LSTM architecture designed to process graph-level semantics. Rather than converting the graph into a sequence, we leverage the inherent graph properties to directly inform the encoding process, thus preserving structural information and mitigating the issues associated with lengthy sequential representations. This allows the model to better capture semantic relations and dependencies within the AMR graph, leading to improved performance, particularly on complex sentences. The core innovation lies in how we represent and encode the AMR graph. We employ a graph-aware LSTM that iteratively processes nodes and edges, updating its hidden state to reflect the overall graph context. This approach effectively captures the relationships between concepts and their associated roles, allowing the decoder to generate more accurate and fluent text. We demonstrate, through comprehensive experiments on a standard AMR-to-text benchmark dataset, that our graph-to-sequence model achieves superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the benefits of directly encoding graph-level semantics for this task. Our results highlight the potential of graph neural networks for tackling challenging semantic generation problems. Automatic summarization has become an increasingly important task in the age of information overload, with applications ranging from news aggregation and document understanding to scientific literature review (Mani, 2001;Nenkova and McKeown, 2012). The goal of summarization is to condense a set of source documents into a shorter, coherent text that conveys the most important information. Early approaches to summarization largely focused on extractive methods, selecting and concatenating existing sentences from the source documents based on various scoring functions (e.g., sentence position, keyword frequency, sentence length) (Luhn, 1958;Salton et al., 1967). While these methods are relatively simple and efficient, they often produce summaries that lack coherence and readability, as they do not explicitly model the relationships between selected sentences. More recent approaches have explored abstractive summarization, which involves paraphrasing and synthesizing information from the source documents to generate novel sentences (Rush et al., 2015;See et al., 2017). However, abstractive methods are typically more complex and require large amounts of training data, and can sometimes suffer from factual inaccuracies. A significant challenge in multi-document summarization is maintaining coherence across the summary. Simply selecting the most salient sentences, even if they accurately represent the key information, does not guarantee a fluent and logically structured summary. Previous work has explored techniques for improving coherence by explicitly modeling discourse relations between sentences (Feng and Hovy, 2014;Marqués and Moreno, 2014), or by incorporating rhetorical structure theory (RST) (Applbaum et al., 2013). However, these approaches often require sophisticated natural language processing tools and can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose a novel graph-based method for coherent multi-document summarization that explicitly explores the links between text. Our approach represents the source documents as a graph, where nodes represent sentences and edges represent various types of relationships, including lexical overlap, semantic similarity, and rhetorical relations. We then formulate the summarization problem as finding a sequence of sentences in the graph that maximizes both informativeness and coherence. Unlike previous methods that primarily focus on salience, our approach considers both aspects equally, leveraging textual linkages to guide the selection and ordering of sentences. We evaluate our method on the Document Understanding Conference (DUC) 2004 summarization task data set and demonstrate that it achieves comparable results in terms of the ROUGE metric, while exhibiting improvements in readability according to human evaluation. Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has emerged as the dominant paradigm in machine translation over the past decade, achieving impressive results for language pairs with abundant parallel corpora (Koehn et al., 2003;Papineni et al., 2002). However, the performance of SMT systems degrades significantly when applied to low-resource language pairs, where parallel data is scarce or nonexistent. A primary challenge in these scenarios is the presence of *untranslated words* – words in the source sentence that do not appear in the target side of the training corpus (Popović, 2015). These words represent lexical gaps and prevent the model from establishing a translation correspondence, leading to reduced translation accuracy and fluency. Various methods have been proposed to address the untranslated word problem. One approach is to leverage morphological analysis and subword segmentation (Koehn & Knight, 2003; Sennrich et al., 2015) to decompose words into smaller, known units. Another strategy is to employ dictionary induction techniques to automatically expand the translation lexicon (Artetxe et al., 2017). More recently, researchers have explored the use of pivoting – translating from the source language to an intermediate language, and then from the intermediate language to the target language – as a means of augmenting the parallel training data (Chu et al., 2009; Neveau & Odijk, 2009). This allows the system to benefit from parallel corpora involving the intermediate language, indirectly improving translation for the low-resource pair. While pivoting demonstrates promising results, it relies on the availability of *additional* parallel corpora involving a third language. This requirement can be problematic, especially for languages with limited resources in multiple languages. Furthermore, the introduction of an intermediate step often leads to error propagation and reduced translation quality. Consequently, there is a need for methods that can effectively address the untranslated word problem without relying on additional parallel data or the complexities of pivoting. This paper proposes a novel approach to tackle this challenge by leveraging monolingually-derived paraphrases. Our core idea is to identify paraphrases within the target language itself, using distributional semantic similarities, and effectively expand the training data with these paraphrases. This approach sidesteps the need for parallel data or intermediate languages, providing access to vast quantities of readily-available monolingual resources – comparable and even unrelated corpora – to enhance SMT performance. We specifically integrate a collocational approach to discerning potential paraphrases and seamlessly incorporate them into a state-of-the-art, end-to-end SMT system. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first successful integration of this technique with a fully functional SMT framework. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in translation quality, particularly in a low-resource setting, validating the effectiveness of our approach. Task-completion dialogue systems aim to assist users in achieving specific goals, such as booking a restaurant or finding a movie. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown promising results in learning dialogue policies (Li et al., 2016;Zhao and Eskenazi, 2016;Nishikawa et al., 2017). However, a major challenge in applying DRL to dialogue systems is the sample inefficiency problem. Interacting with real users is costly and time-consuming, while relying solely on simulated environments may lead to policies that perform poorly in the real world due to the *reality gap* (Tobin et al., 2017). To address this challenge, model-based reinforcement learning, specifically planning algorithms such as Dyna-Q (Sutton, 1990), offer a potential solution. By learning a world model to simulate the environment, an agent can generate additional experience without interacting with the real world, thereby improving sample efficiency and learning performance. Recently, Deep Dyna-Q (DDQ) (Guo et al., 2018) successfully extended the Dyna-Q algorithm to task-completion dialogue policy learning. DDQ employs a deep neural network to learn a transition model, which simulates user behavior and environment dynamics, and uses this model to generate simulated experiences for planning. While DDQ demonstrates encouraging results, its performance heavily relies on the quality of the simulated experiences. If the learned transition model is inaccurate, the generated experiences can be unrealistic and mislead the planning process, ultimately hindering policy learning. A common problem with the learned transition model is that it cannot accurately capture the diversity and complexity of real user interactions, leading to a discrepancy between simulated and real experiences. To mitigate the limitations of DDQ, we propose a Discriminative Deep Dyna-Q (D3Q) approach. The key idea of D3Q is to incorporate a discriminator to evaluate the quality of simulated experiences and filter out those that are significantly different from real user experiences. Specifically, we introduce a recurrent neural network (RNN)-based discriminator that is trained to differentiate between simulated and real dialogue trajectories. This discriminator provides a confidence score for each simulated experience, which is then used to weight the contribution of that experience during planning. By selectively utilizing high-quality simulated experiences, D3Q reduces the negative impact of inaccurate simulations and improves the robustness of the learned policy. Our experiments demonstrate that D3Q significantly outperforms DDQ on a simulated dialogue task, specifically the CamRest task (Wen et al., 2017). Furthermore, we evaluate the robustness of D3Q in a domain extension setting where the agent needs to adapt to a slightly changed environment. The results show that D3Q exhibits superior adaptability and generalization ability compared to DDQ. These findings highlight the importance of controlling the quality of simulated experiences for effective planning in dialogue policy learning. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 details the D3Q approach, Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, and Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future work.

Event pattern extraction – the task of identifying mentions of event types and their arguments in text – is a cornerstone of information extraction (IE) and has found applications in diverse areas such as news analysis, crisis management, and knowledge base population (Grishman et al., 2013; Shaw et al., 2011; Mihalcea and Lieberman, 2006). A significant challenge in this field lies in the inherent variability in how events are expressed linguistically. The same event type can be described using countless paraphrases, leading to sparse data coverage for many event patterns and hindering the performance of traditional supervised learning approaches. For example, the event “Conflict” might be expressed as “battle,” “clash,” “fighting,” “skirmish,” or described using more elaborate phrasing. Existing approaches to tackle this paraphrastic variation often rely on large, manually annotated datasets to train models capable of recognizing these diverse expressions (Chen and Ji, 2009; Finkel et al., 2005). However, acquiring such annotated data is expensive, time-consuming, and often limited to specific domains. Distantly supervised methods offer a promising alternative by leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) and heuristics to automatically generate training data (Mintz et al., 2009; Riedel et al., 2013). While this approach can significantly reduce annotation effort, it often suffers from noise and requires careful filtering to maintain quality. More recent work has explored the use of neural networks and representation learning to capture semantic similarity between event patterns, improving generalization and robustness (Lin et al., 2018; Nguyen and Vershinin, 2018). In this paper, we introduce IDEST (Iterative Distributed Event pattern representation learning through Self-Training), a novel method for learning distributed representations of event patterns based on a new neural network architecture. Unlike previous approaches that rely heavily on labeled data or external knowledge bases, IDEST leverages a novel weak supervision signal derived from co-occurrence patterns in news articles published on the same day and mentioning the same real-world entities. The underlying intuition is that events discussed in the context of the same entities on the same day are likely to be related and can serve as positive examples for paraphrase learning. Our approach iteratively refines event pattern representations through self-training, starting from an initial set of patterns generated using a lightweight distant supervision strategy. The key innovation lies in its ability to generalize across extractions from different dates to produce a robust paraphrase model, even for rare event patterns. By learning a distributed representation for each event pattern, IDEST captures semantic similarities and allows for effective transfer learning, significantly improving performance, especially when training data is limited. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IDEST through experiments on a challenging event extraction dataset, comparing it to two state-of-the-art systems. The results demonstrate that IDEST achieves comparable quality with significantly less labeled data and highlights its superior generalization capabilities when leveraging a larger corpus of weakly supervised data.

Semantic parsing – the task of mapping natural language utterances to formal meaning representations – has witnessed significant advances in recent years, largely fueled by the proliferation of neural network architectures (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Liang et al., 2011; Dong & Lapata, 2016). These approaches often leverage syntactic information, recognizing that sentence structure provides crucial cues for understanding semantic relationships. Traditional semantic parsers routinely employ constituency or dependency parses as input features, effectively harnessing the insights encoded within syntactic trees. However, standard syntactic representations, while valuable, are not without their limitations. They often capture phenomena that are syntactically significant but semantically irrelevant, potentially obscuring the underlying meaning and hindering the performance of semantic parsers. Consider, for instance, constructions involving syntactic alternations, such as the dative alternation ("She gave the book to John" vs. "She gave John the book"). While these variations demonstrably alter the surface syntactic structure, the underlying semantic relationship – the transfer of possession – remains constant. Similarly, control and raising constructions introduce complexities in syntactic analysis that may not directly contribute to semantic interpretation. In such cases, a faithful representation of the syntactic surface can actually *impede* the parsing process, leading to spurious ambiguities and incorrect semantic assignments. This observation motivates us to explore the use of a “deeper” syntactic representation – one that intentionally abstracts away from these purely syntactic intricacies and focuses on the core structural relationships relevant to semantic interpretation. Our approach aims to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics by constructing a representation that is structurally closer to the intended meaning, effectively mitigating the influence of superficial syntactic variations. This is not merely about simplifying the syntax, but rather about re-organizing it in a way that reflects the semantic dependencies more directly. In this paper, we propose a method for generating this deeper syntactic representation and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving semantic parsing performance. We achieve this by explicitly identifying and abstracting away from syntactic phenomena known to create ambiguity for semantic analysis. The resulting representation provides a more streamlined and semantically-focused input to the parser, allowing it to concentrate on the core meaning-bearing components of the sentence. We evaluate our approach on a French corpus annotated with semantic frames, demonstrating that a semantic parser equipped with our deep syntactic input consistently outperforms one relying on traditional syntactic parses. This improvement underscores the potential benefits of moving beyond surface-level syntax and embracing representations that prioritize semantic clarity. These results demonstrate the potential for a semantic parser to operate more efficiently and accurately when fed a representation that minimizes syntactic noise and exposes the core semantic architecture of the sentence. Our work builds on the growing understanding that while syntax is undoubtedly important, a more nuanced treatment of syntactic phenomena – one that explicitly targets semantic relevance – is crucial for unlocking the full potential of semantic parsing technology. . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Machine comprehension (MC) – the task of automatically answering questions posed in natural language about a given text passage – has seen remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by deep learning models and the availability of large-scale datasets like SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). However, a critical limitation of these models is their tendency to perform poorly when applied to domains different from the one they were trained on. This lack of generalization presents a significant barrier to deploying MC systems in real-world applications where data is often sparse or unavailable for specific domains of interest. The problem of domain adaptation in machine comprehension is therefore a central challenge. Existing approaches to address this problem typically rely on either fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a small amount of labeled data from the target domain (e.g., adjusting model parameters using a few question-answer pairs), or utilizing techniques like adversarial training to learn domain-invariant representations. While fine-tuning can be effective, it requires labeled data which is often expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Adversarial methods can alleviate the need for labeled data, but often require careful hyperparameter tuning and may not always yield significant improvements. Furthermore, many approaches focus on modifying the *representation* of the input text, often overlooking the importance of adapting the reasoning capabilities of the model itself. In this paper, we propose a novel technique for transfer learning in machine comprehension that directly addresses this latter point. Our method, based on a two-stage synthesis network (SynNet), aims to *synthesize* plausible question-answer pairs in the target domain, using a high-performing model trained on a source domain (e.g., SQuAD). This synthesized data is then leveraged to guide the model's reasoning process in the new domain, without requiring any actual labeled data from the target domain. The core idea is to utilize the source model’s understanding of language and reasoning to create a bridge to the new domain, effectively mimicking expert annotations. Unlike methods that rely on domain adaptation at the representation level, our SynNet focuses on adapting the reasoning process by constructing and utilizing synthetic training examples. This allows for a more direct transfer of knowledge, leading to a significant performance boost on unseen domains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the challenging NewsQA dataset, and show that our system, initialized with a model pre-trained on SQuAD, achieves competitive performance, approaching the level of models trained directly on the NewsQA dataset, and outperforming significantly in comparison to naive out-of-domain baselines – all without using any actual NewsQA labels during the transfer phase. This demonstrates the power of our synthesis approach for effective and label-efficient transfer learning in machine comprehension. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Humans rarely consume information passively. When encountering a document, readers actively seek out concepts, entities, and topics that pique their curiosity and warrant further investigation. This selective engagement with information is a fundamental aspect of how we learn and explore the world. Motivated by this observation, we investigate the task of *predicting interestingness* – determining the degree to which a user will find various spans of text within a document compelling enough to pursue. This is a challenging problem with potential applications in areas such as personalized information retrieval, content recommendation, and adaptive document summarization. Imagine a system that could highlight or expand upon sections of a lengthy article that are most likely to resonate with a particular reader, or a search engine that could not only return relevant documents but also pinpoint the specific phrases that sparked a user’s initial interest. Existing approaches to information access often focus on relevance – identifying documents that broadly address a user’s query. However, relevance does not necessarily equate to interestingness. A user might find a document relevant but ultimately unengaging, or conversely, stumble upon a tangential concept that unexpectedly captures their attention. Our work aims to bridge this gap by directly modeling the subjective notion of “interestingness.” To address this problem, we leverage naturally occurring interest signals derived from user browsing behavior. Specifically, we analyze clickstream data – logs of user transitions from one webpage to another – to infer which text spans are likely to drive further exploration. The intuition is straightforward: if a user clicks on a link corresponding to a specific phrase within a document, that phrase likely represents an area of interest. This provides a valuable source of weakly supervised training data, allowing us to learn models of interestingness without relying on explicit user ratings or annotations. We frame the problem as a discriminative learning task, employing features derived from two primary sources: textual context and latent semantic topics. Contextual features capture the local linguistic environment surrounding a text span, providing clues about its semantic role and potential relevance. More importantly, we leverage a novel topical model to capture the semantics of the document transition. This model infers a shared, latent topic space for the source and target documents involved in a click, providing a robust representation of the underlying conceptual connection driving the user’s behavior. Crucially, this topic model is learned in an unsupervised manner, avoiding the need for pre-defined or manually annotated topic labels. We evaluate our models on a massive dataset of real-world transitions between Wikipedia documents, extracted from web browser session logs. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over several baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach and the value of incorporating latent semantic information into the prediction of interestingness. This work lays the foundation for future research into personalized information exploration and adaptive document understanding. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The automatic identification of semantic classes within text is a core task in natural language processing, with applications ranging from information extraction and text categorization to question answering and dialogue systems. Traditionally, the creation of high-performance semantic taggers has relied heavily on large, manually annotated training corpora – a costly and time-consuming endeavor, particularly when targeting specialized domains. This is especially true in fields like biomedicine, law, or engineering, where expert annotation is required, and resources are often scarce. This paper investigates a fundamentally different approach: inducing domain-specific semantic class taggers using minimal supervision, specifically leveraging only a domain-specific text collection *and* a small set of seed words for each target semantic class. Our core hypothesis is that valuable signal for semantic class identification exists within the contextual patterns of word usage in a domain, even without explicit, labeled examples. We propose a novel learning framework that exploits this signal through a multi-stage bootstrapping process. Human language understanding relies heavily on the seamless integration of lexical knowledge and syntactic structure. This interplay gives rise to a range of inferences that go beyond the literal meaning of words and sentences – what we term *lexicosyntactic inferences*. These inferences are crucial for interpreting events, understanding speaker intent, and resolving ambiguities. For example, the verb “promise” inherently carries a commitment to future action, a factuality inference triggered by both its lexical semantics and its typical syntactic context. Similarly, understanding a negated clause (“He did *not* win the race”) requires inferring the non-occurrence of an event, a factuality inference heavily reliant on the interaction between the negative particle “not” and the verb “win.” Despite recent advances in neural language modeling, it remains unclear to what extent these models truly capture such lexicosyntactic inferences. While large pre-trained models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and others demonstrate impressive performance on a wide range of NLP tasks, their internal representations and reasoning mechanisms are often opaque. Do these models merely learn statistical correlations, or do they genuinely represent the underlying logical and factual implications conveyed by language? To investigate this question, we focus on the specific task of *event factuality prediction*: determining whether an event described by a clause is likely to have actually occurred. This task serves as a valuable probe for lexicosyntactic inference because determining factuality invariably demands considering the interplay between the semantics of the verb and the specific syntactic context in which it appears. For instance, the verb “dream” typically denotes a non-factual event, even when embedded in a seemingly assertive clause. Conversely, modal verbs like “must” often indicate a high degree of factuality. In this paper, we introduce a new dataset designed to specifically assess models’ ability to perform event factuality prediction across a broad range of English clause-embedding verbs and syntactic constructions. Our dataset, which we are releasing to the community, covers all English clause-embedding verbs and a diverse set of syntactic contexts (e.g., main clauses, relative clauses, complement clauses, interrogatives). These shortcomings provide valuable insights into the challenges of building truly intelligent language understanding systems and point to promising directions for future research. By framing the investigation through the lens of factuality prediction, we aim to provide a concrete and interpretable evaluation of neural models’ capacity for lexicosyntactic reasoning. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing, serving as a crucial preprocessing step for many downstream applications such as parsing, machine translation, and information extraction. While state-of-the-art POS taggers achieve high accuracy on standard benchmark datasets, their performance often degrades significantly when applied to text from different domains or genres – a phenomenon known as domain shift. This lack of robustness limits the practical applicability of these taggers in real-world scenarios where the input text may not conform to the training data distribution. Recent work in robust generalization (Ben-David et al., 2010; Kirsch et al., 2019) and adversarial learning (Goodfellow et al., 2014) has demonstrated the importance of explicitly addressing distribution shifts during model training. The core idea behind these approaches is to minimize the expected loss not only on the training distribution but also on a range of plausible alternative distributions. However, defining a suitable set of alternative distributions is a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to learning robust structured perceptrons for POS tagging that addresses this challenge by restricting the possible target distributions to mixtures of the source distribution and random Zipfian distributions. Zipf’s law, a ubiquitous phenomenon in linguistics and information science, states that the frequency of any item is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table (Zipf, 1949). This observation suggests that Zipfian distributions naturally capture the statistical properties of language, and therefore may represent plausible distribution shifts. By augmenting the training objective to minimize average loss under these Zipfian corruptions, our model learns to be less sensitive to variations in word frequencies and overall data distributions encountered in new domains. Our approach differs from existing methods for handling domain shift in POS tagging, such as domain adaptation (Yao et al., 2011) and multi-domain training (McDonald et al., 2013). These techniques typically require access to labeled data from the target domain, or assume that a set of source domains are available during training. In contrast, our method is entirely unsupervised with respect to domain information and relies solely on the properties of Zipf’s law to generate plausible distribution shifts. Furthermore, our formulation allows us to directly optimize for robustness to distribution shifts during training, ensuring that the learned model exhibits improved generalization performance. We evaluate our algorithm on two standard POS tagging datasets: the English Web Treebank (EWT) and the Danish Dependency Treebank (DDT). Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms baseline structured perceptron models, achieving an average of 4.4% error reduction in tagging accuracy. More sophisticated formalisms, such as Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG) (Joshi et al., 1975), offer greater expressive power and the ability to model non-concatenative dependencies, making them well-suited for handling MWEs. The automatic identification of paraphrases – sentences that express the same meaning using different words – is a core problem in natural language processing. Paraphrase detection and generation have broad applications, including text summarization (Barzilay et al., 1999), machine translation (Callison-Burch et al., 2006), question answering (Riezler, 2005), and, generally, any task requiring robust semantic understanding. Early work focused on aligning sentences in comparable corpora (Ide & Véronis, 1993; Barzilay & Lee, 2003) based on lexical overlap or syntactic structure. More recent approaches utilize distributional semantics, representing words and phrases as vectors and defining similarity based on vector distance (Manning et al., 2008; Socher et al., 2013). Others employ machine translation techniques, treating paraphrase identification as a translation problem (Madnani et al., 2011). A particularly fruitful avenue for acquiring paraphrases has been the exploitation of bilingual parallel corpora, also known as bitexts. These corpora contain sentence pairs that represent translations of each other, and thus inherently contain a wealth of paraphrastic variations (Lin & Pantel, 2001; Szpektor et al., 2007). Previous work has predominantly focused on extracting *phrasal* paraphrases from bitexts – identifying pairs of phrases that are translations of each other (e.g., “butcher shop” ↔ “meat market”). However, the potential of bitexts for learning more complex *sentential* paraphrases, involving broader syntactic transformations, has remained relatively unexplored. While it might seem counterintuitive – one might assume more sophisticated paraphrases are better learned from monolingual data – bitexts offer a unique advantage: they inherently provide a strong semantic constraint. Translation demands preserving meaning, making bitext pairs excellent candidates for identifying paraphrases that go beyond simple lexical substitution. We extend existing bitext-based paraphrase extraction techniques to capture syntactic paraphrases, moving beyond simple phrase-level alignment to identify more global transformations like passivization (“The dog chased the cat” ↔ “The cat was chased by the dog”), dative shift (“He gave her the book” ↔ “He gave the book to her”), and topicalization (“As for the dog, the cat chased it” ↔ “The cat chased the dog”). Furthermore, we illustrate the versatility of our approach by adapting it to the task of sentence compression, showcasing its application to text-to-text generation and achieving competitive results with state-of-the-art systems. This paper argues that bitexts are a valuable, and largely untapped, resource for learning a broad range of sentential paraphrases with direct application to various downstream NLP tasks.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as the dominant paradigm for machine translation, demonstrating substantial improvements over traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Cho et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). Early NMT models employed an encoder-decoder framework, where an encoder compresses the source sentence into a fixed-length vector representation, and a decoder generates the target sentence from this vector. While successful, these initial models struggled with long sentences, as compressing all source information into a single vector led to information loss (Bahdanau et al., 2014). The introduction of the attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015) addressed this bottleneck by allowing the decoder to selectively focus on different parts of the source sentence during each decoding step. This dynamic alignment significantly improved translation quality, especially for longer sentences. The core idea behind attention is to calculate a weighted sum of the source hidden states, where the weights represent the relevance of each source word to the current target word being generated. However, the specific architecture of the attention mechanism itself has received relatively little attention. Most existing work has focused on applying attention as a component within a larger NMT framework, rather than systematically exploring different attentional strategies. The field of opinion mining, or sentiment analysis, has experienced remarkable progress in recent years. Driven by advances in machine learning and natural language processing, systems can now automatically identify subjective expressions in text with increasing accuracy (Pang and Lee, 2008; Liu, 2012). These systems find application in a wide range of domains, from monitoring brand reputation and predicting market trends to analyzing public opinion on political issues and understanding consumer preferences. However, despite these successes, we argue that current approaches to opinion detection are fundamentally limited in their ability to capture the full complexity of human opinion expression. This limitation stems, in part, from a lack of attention to the pragmatic dimensions of opinion, specifically the role of the system *user’s* own understanding of what constitutes an “opinion” in the first place. At its core, opinion mining seeks to distinguish between objective facts and subjective expressions. This distinction, however, is not always clear-cut. What one person considers a factual statement, another may perceive as a value judgement. Moreover, the very definition of “opinion” is itself subject to interpretation. A system trained to identify opinions based on a narrow, predefined set of features (e.g., the presence of sentiment-bearing adjectives) may fail to recognize nuanced expressions of belief, speculation, or even ironic commentary. This is not merely a question of improved feature engineering or more sophisticated algorithms; it’s a deeper issue concerning the implicit assumptions embedded within both the design and evaluation of opinion mining systems. We introduce the concept of “metasubjectivity” – subjectivity *about* subjectivity. Essentially, this refers to the user's preconceived notions about the nature of opinion itself. For instance, a user analyzing medical literature might prioritize identification of expressions of diagnostic uncertainty, while a marketing analyst might focus on consumer attitudes toward specific products. These differing priorities reflect fundamentally different perspectives on what constitutes a meaningful “opinion” within their respective contexts. Critically, these perspectives are themselves subjective and can vary widely even within a single domain. Acknowledging metasubjectivity poses significant challenges to building robust and adaptable opinion mining systems. Traditional corpus development efforts typically rely on expert annotation, yet even experts harbor biases and differing interpretations of subjectivity. Furthermore, standard evaluation metrics (e.g., precision, recall, F1-score) assume a single “ground truth” for opinion labels, failing to account for the possibility of legitimate disagreement. In this paper, we advocate for a shift in perspective. Rather than striving for a universal definition of opinion, we propose that systems should be designed to accommodate – and even elicit – the user’s own metasubjective preferences. This may involve incorporating user feedback mechanisms, allowing for customizable annotation schemas, or developing domain-specific opinion ontologies. While addressing metasubjectivity undoubtedly introduces added complexity and may require initial investment in additional resources, we believe that the long-term benefits – increased accuracy, relevance, and usability – far outweigh the costs. Ignoring this fundamental aspect of opinion risks creating systems that provide, at best, incomplete and potentially misleading insights into the world of human belief.

Query understanding is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing, enabling applications such as information retrieval, question answering, and dialog systems (Voorhees & Harman, 2000; Jurafsky & Martin, 2009). For example, the query “cheap flights from New York to London” can be segmented into “cheap flights,” “from New York,” and “to London.” Accurate query segmentation facilitates downstream tasks by enabling more precise semantic analysis and better matching of user intent. Traditionally, query segmentation has relied on rule-based approaches, statistical models trained on limited datasets, or expert annotations (Jones et al., 1999; Ko & Croft, 2004). However, these methods often suffer from limited scalability, domain specificity, or high annotation costs. The rise of crowdsourcing platforms, such as Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), has offered a potential solution to address these challenges, providing access to a large and readily available workforce capable of performing complex annotation tasks (Snow et al., 2008; Rhinehart et al., 2008). Crowdsourcing has been successfully applied to various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and relation extraction (Passoni & Tessone, 2012; Fort et al., 2011). The dream of a universal translator, a device capable of seamlessly bridging the communication gap between any two languages, has captivated scientists and science fiction enthusiasts alike for decades. While achieving true fluency remains a distant goal, the construction of comprehensive multilingual dictionaries represents a crucial stepping stone towards that vision. Existing multilingual resources, such as Wiktionary and commercially available translation dictionaries, offer significant coverage, but they remain fragmented and incomplete. Each dictionary, while valuable in its own right, represents only a partial view of the vast landscape of cross-lingual relationships. A natural question then arises: can we synergistically combine these existing resources to create a *massive*, multilingual dictionary exceeding the coverage of any individual component? This paper addresses this challenge, proposing a novel approach to compiling a large-scale multilingual dictionary from a collection of publicly available translation resources. The seemingly straightforward task of merging these dictionaries immediately reveals a complex issue: transitive inference. Consider a scenario where word ‘A’ translates to word ‘B’, and word ‘B’ translates to word ‘C’. Does this imply that ‘C’ is a valid translation of ‘A’? And if so, with what degree of confidence? The probability of such transitive relations is not necessarily high, as translations can be context-dependent and nuanced. Naively combining dictionaries without addressing this problem would inevitably lead to a significant increase in noise and a decrease in overall dictionary quality. We introduce an algorithm designed specifically to tackle this transitive inference problem. Our approach leverages probabilistic modeling to assess the reliability of transitive links, accounting for the individual strengths and weaknesses of the constituent dictionaries. This allows us to selectively incorporate inferred translations, maintaining a high level of precision while simultaneously expanding dictionary coverage. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm by applying it to a massive collection of words – over 10 million – across more than 1,000 languages. The result of this process is PANDICTIONARY, a novel multilingual dictionary. We present detailed experimental results demonstrating that PANDICTIONARY significantly outperforms existing resources in terms of coverage. Specifically, it contains more than four times as many translations as the largest publicly available Wiktionary, while maintaining high precision – 0.90. Furthermore, PANDICTIONARY boasts over 200 million pairwise translations spanning over 200,000 language pairs at a precision of 0.8. These results highlight the power of probabilistic inference for unlocking the latent potential within existing multilingual resources, bringing us closer to a comprehensive and universally accessible multilingual dictionary. This work not only advances the state-of-the-art in multilingual lexicography but also provides a valuable resource for researchers in fields such as machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and computational linguistics. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The ability to automatically detect and understand emotions expressed in text is a core task in affective computing with a wide range of applications, including customer feedback analysis, mental health monitoring, and human-computer interaction (Poria et al., 2014). A crucial component underlying many emotion classification systems is the establishment of associations between words and emotions – essentially, identifying which words tend to evoke or signal specific emotional states. Traditionally, this has been achieved through two primary avenues: utilizing pre-compiled emotion lexicons and employing measures of semantic relatedness derived from large corpora. However, both approaches exhibit limitations that hinder performance in real-world scenarios. Emotion lexicons, such as WordNet-Affect (Stone and Zhou, 2006) and NRC Emotion Lexicon (NRC, 2007), offer a seemingly straightforward solution by providing a list of words annotated with corresponding emotion labels. However, these lexicons typically cover a limited vocabulary, often focusing on a small, pre-defined set of basic emotions (e.g., anger, fear, joy, sadness). Furthermore, the granularity of emotion categories is often insufficient to capture the nuances of human emotional experience. Expanding these lexicons manually is a laborious and time-consuming process, and automated expansion techniques can often introduce noise and inaccuracies. Alternatively, emotion classification can leverage semantic relatedness measures – techniques which quantify the association between words based on their co-occurrence patterns in large text corpora. Methods such as Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA, Deerwester et al., 1990) and word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) have been applied to estimate word-emotion relatedness by assuming that words appearing in similar contexts are semantically related. However, these methods are generally designed for broad semantic relationships and do not specifically optimize for the task of word-emotion association. They often fail to capture the subtle but crucial distinctions between emotions and can be susceptible to spurious correlations. For instance, words associated with both ‘joy’ and ‘excitement’ might be given equal weight, even though they represent distinct emotional states. A key insight guiding our work is the observation that emotions often exhibit mutual exclusivity – that is, a given text segment is more likely to express one dominant emotion rather than multiple, conflicting emotions simultaneously (Ortony and Clore, 1996). This intrinsic property of emotional expression can be exploited to refine word-emotion associations. In this paper, we introduce Selective Co-occurrences (SECO), an unsupervised method designed to learn word-emotion associations by leveraging this principle of mutual exclusivity. SECO iteratively refines associations by focusing on co-occurrences that are *selective* for a particular emotion, effectively filtering out noise and enhancing the accuracy of the learned associations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SECO through extensive experiments on three diverse datasets, showing significant improvements over existing emotion lexicons and state-of-the-art word embedding models. We require only a single ‘seed’ word per emotion to initiate the learning process, highlighting the efficiency and adaptability of our approach.

Perhaps most crucially, they are often inflexible and struggle to generalize to terms that are not explicitly present in the KB, or variations in term usage. For example, a KB might list "automobile" as an ancestor of "Toyota," but might not directly recognize "Toyota Camry" as a specific instance of an automobile. A compelling way to address this limitation is through the creation of *event chronicles*. An event chronicle, distinct from a simple timeline, presents a structured narrative of significant happenings during a specified period, offering a readily accessible and coherent overview of the past. This work builds on, but significantly extends, previous efforts in event extraction, coreference resolution, and temporal reasoning, offering a novel framework for synthesizing historical narratives. Image captioning, the task of automatically generating natural language descriptions of images, has witnessed significant progress in recent years, largely fueled by advancements in deep learning. Early approaches relied on template-based methods or retrieval-based techniques, but these often lacked the fluency and adaptability required for generating diverse and accurate captions. The dominant paradigm has since shifted towards an encode-decoder framework, where a convolutional neural network (CNN) encodes the visual content of an image into a vector representation, and a recurrent neural network (RNN), typically an LSTM, decodes this representation into a sequential caption (Vinyals et al., 2015;Xu et al., 2015;Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015). This framework has yielded impressive results, but generating captions that are both detailed and comprehensive remains a significant challenge. Detailed captions require the model to focus on salient image regions and accurately describe the objects and their attributes within those regions. This is often achieved through the incorporation of visual attention mechanisms (Xu et al., 2015), which allow the decoder to selectively attend to different parts of the image while generating each word of the caption. However, visual attention alone can sometimes lead to captions that are overly focused on local details and lack a broader understanding of the scene. Comprehensive captions, on the other hand, necessitate capturing the overall context and semantic relationships within the image. Semantic attention, which focuses on extracting and representing abstract concepts or “topics” from the image, has emerged as a complementary approach (Yang et al., 2016;Lu et al., 2016). By attending to these semantic topics, the model can generate captions that are more informative and capture the essence of the scene. However, relying solely on semantic attention can result in captions that are too generic and lack the fine-grained details necessary for a truly descriptive caption. In this paper, we propose the Stepwise Image-Topic Merging Network (simNet), a novel approach that effectively integrates both visual and semantic attention within a unified framework. simNet leverages the strengths of both attention mechanisms by adaptively merging attentive information from extracted image topics and visual features at each time step of the decoding process. This allows the model to dynamically balance detailedness and comprehensiveness, generating captions that are both visually grounded and semantically coherent. The core idea is that, as the caption unfolds, the decoder progressively combines information from the image and the extracted topics based on the evolving contextual understanding. We demonstrate through experiments on two benchmark datasets (MS COCO and Flickr8k) that simNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing image captioning models in terms of commonly used evaluation metrics. Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) – the ability to quantify the degree to which two pieces of text convey the same meaning – is a core task in Natural Language Processing (NLP). It serves as a foundational building block for a remarkably diverse range of downstream applications, including information retrieval (Voorhees & Tice, 2000), question answering (Agrawal et al., 2018), paraphrase detection (Madnani et al., 2011), and machine translation evaluation (Papineni et al., 2002). Consequently, a substantial body of research has been dedicated to developing and refining STS systems. Hundreds of distinct approaches currently exist, ranging from early methods relying on lexical overlap (e.g., TF-IDF) to modern techniques leveraging advanced neural network architectures, such as transformers (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Cer et al., 2018). However, this abundance of choice presents a challenge for NLP practitioners and system designers. Determining which STS system is optimal for a *given* application is non-trivial. This is where intrinsic evaluation comes into play. Intrinsic evaluation aims to assess the quality of an STS system in isolation, typically by comparing its outputs – similarity scores – against human judgments of semantic similarity on benchmark datasets. The most widely adopted metric for this comparison is Pearson correlation (Pearson, 1895), reflecting the linear association between predicted and human scores. A higher Pearson correlation is generally interpreted as indicating a more accurate and reliable STS system. Despite its widespread use, we argue – and empirically demonstrate in this work – that relying solely on Pearson correlation for intrinsic evaluation of STS systems can be profoundly misleading. Our analysis, conducted across three representative STS-based downstream tasks (paraphrase generation, textual entailment, and duplicate question detection), reveals that Pearson correlation often fails to identify the STS system that truly performs best *in the context of the target task*. In many cases, systems with moderate Pearson correlations outperform those with considerably higher scores, highlighting a disconnect between intrinsic evaluation and real-world performance. This observation raises a critical question: how can we evaluate STS systems *effectively* and ensure that our choice aligns with the needs of our specific application? This paper addresses this question by (1) demonstrating the limitations of Pearson correlation as an intrinsic evaluation metric, (2) exploring and comparing alternative intrinsic evaluation metrics, and (3) proposing a framework for conducting task-oriented intrinsic evaluation of STS systems. This framework emphasizes the importance of understanding the characteristics of the target task and selecting evaluation metrics accordingly. We provide a rigorous methodology for assessing the validity of intrinsic evaluations and guiding the selection of STS systems for optimal downstream performance. However, standard CRFs operate at the word level, predicting a label for each individual word based on features computed from its immediate surroundings. This indirect approach often struggles to fully capture the holistic, contextual information inherent in segments, as the model’s focus remains primarily on word-level characteristics. Ad hoc information retrieval (IR) remains a central task in natural language processing, with the core goal of efficiently and effectively retrieving documents relevant to a user’s information need, expressed as a query. A longstanding technique for improving retrieval performance is query expansion (QE) (Voorhees, 1994), where the original query is augmented with related terms to broaden its scope and capture variations in terminology used by document authors. Traditional QE methods often rely on statistical co-occurrence measures derived from the corpus (e.g., Rocchio, 1971) or external lexical resources like thesauri (Voorhees, 1994). More recently, the advent of continuous space word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) has offered a promising alternative for identifying related terms. These embeddings represent words as dense vectors in a continuous space, where semantic similarity is reflected in proximity. By computing the cosine similarity between a query term and other terms in the vocabulary, one can identify candidate expansion terms. Models like word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have achieved impressive results on various NLP tasks, and their application to QE has shown initial promise (Li et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015). However, a key assumption underlying most current approaches is the use of *globally* trained word embeddings – embeddings learned from a large, general-purpose corpus, such as Wikipedia or Common Crawl. While these global embeddings capture broad semantic relationships, they may not be optimal for the specific task of IR in a particular domain or corpus. The vocabulary and term distributions of a specialized corpus can differ significantly from those of the training corpus used to generate the global embeddings. Consequently, the semantic relationships captured by global embeddings might not accurately reflect the nuances of the target retrieval task. In this paper, we investigate the impact of training locality on the effectiveness of word embeddings for query expansion. We hypothesize that embeddings trained *locally* – specifically, on the corpus being searched – will outperform globally trained embeddings for ad hoc IR. We compare the performance of QE using globally trained word2vec and GloVe embeddings with that of embeddings trained specifically on the target corpus. Our experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that locally trained embeddings consistently outperform their globally trained counterparts. Furthermore, we show that corpus-specific embeddings are more effective than traditional corpus-based expansion techniques. These findings suggest that leveraging the specific statistical properties of the target corpus through locally trained embeddings is crucial for maximizing the benefits of word embeddings in query expansion and, potentially, other IR tasks. The field of Visual Question Answering (VQA) has rapidly advanced in recent years, demonstrating significant progress in bridging the gap between computer vision and natural language processing. Initial work focused primarily on still images, with tasks such as answering questions about objects, attributes, and relationships within a single photograph (Mal-attia et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2016). The success of image-based VQA, evidenced by datasets like VQA v2 (Goyal et al., 2017) and CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017), has naturally prompted researchers to extend this paradigm to the more complex domain of video understanding. Video introduces substantial new challenges beyond those encountered in static image analysis. These include temporal reasoning – understanding events unfolding over time – the need to localize relevant segments within a longer video sequence, and integrating both visual and linguistic information from subtitles or accompanying dialogue. Despite the increased complexity, the potential benefits of video QA are immense. A system capable of accurately answering questions about videos could find application in areas such as video summarization, content-based video retrieval, and assistive technologies for visually impaired individuals. However, significant obstacles remain in realizing this potential. A key limitation hindering progress in video QA is the relative scarcity of large-scale, high-quality datasets specifically designed for this task. Existing video QA datasets, such as TGIF (Das et al., 2017) and MovieQA (Tapaswi et al., 2016), are either too small to effectively train deep learning models, or focus on relatively simple question types that do not fully exploit the rich temporal and compositional reasoning abilities that video QA demands. MovieQA, for instance, relies on long-form narratives and requires complex inference chains, however the associated questions are often ambiguous and can be answered based on common sense knowledge rather than observable content within the video. TGIF, while larger, is restricted to searching GIF clips, inherently limiting the scope of the questions that can be asked. To address this critical gap, we introduce TVQA, a new large-scale dataset for localized, compositional video question answering. Constructed from clips extracted from six widely popular television shows, TVQA consists of over 152,000 question-answer pairs spanning nearly 460 hours of video content. Critically, the questions in TVQA are specifically designed to be compositional, requiring models to jointly localize relevant temporal segments, integrate information from subtitles, and recognize specific visual concepts to arrive at the correct answer. This focus on compositionality pushes the boundaries of current video understanding capabilities and provides a more challenging and realistic benchmark than existing datasets. We believe TVQA will serve as a valuable resource for advancing research in video QA and promoting the development of more robust and intelligent video understanding systems. This paper details the construction of TVQA, performs initial analyses of its characteristics, establishes baseline performance scores, and proposes a preliminary multi-stream neural network architecture for the TVQA task.

A core challenge within semi-supervised learning lies in effectively integrating information gleaned from unlabeled data into existing supervised models. One promising avenue for tackling this challenge lies in the use of word representations. The central intuition is that words occurring in similar contexts tend to share semantic or syntactic properties. By capturing these properties in vector representations, we can provide NLP systems with valuable prior knowledge about word meaning, even in the absence of explicit labels. These representations can then be used as additional features within a supervised learning framework, effectively augmenting the information available to the model. Several methods have emerged for learning such word representations. Early approaches, like Brown clusters (Pereira et al., 2003), utilize hierarchical clustering to group words based on their distributional similarity. More recently, neural network-based approaches have gained prominence, offering the ability to learn dense, low-dimensional embeddings that capture complex semantic relationships (Bengio et al., 2003; Mikolov et al., 2013). Notable examples include the embeddings learned by Collobert & Weston (2008) and the Hierarchical Latent Dirichlet Allocation based embeddings proposed by Mnih & Hinton (2009) (HLBL). This paper investigates the efficacy of utilizing these diverse word representations as features in existing supervised NLP systems. We focus on two widely used tasks – Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Chunking – and evaluate the performance gains achieved by incorporating Brown clusters, Collobert & Weston embeddings, and HLBL embeddings. Our goal is to provide a simple, yet effective, method for improving the accuracy of existing NLP pipelines without requiring extensive modifications to the underlying architectures. We demonstrate that each of these word representations consistently improves performance, and that combining them can lead to further accuracy gains. To facilitate wider adoption, we are releasing our pre-trained word features and code publicly, allowing researchers and practitioners to easily integrate them into their own NLP systems. Additionally, we aim to quantify the practical benefit of these readily available resources, making them easily accessible to the broader NLP community. Metaphor is a pervasive feature of human language, playing a crucial role in abstract thought, creative expression, and everyday communication (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980). Identifying metaphors automatically is a longstanding challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with applications ranging from sentiment analysis and text understanding to cognitive science and computational creativity. Traditionally, approaches to automatic metaphor identification (AMI) have relied heavily on hand-crafted knowledge, such as manually defined conceptual metaphors (Martin, 1990), semantic features (Hovy, 1988), or patterns derived from linguistic theory (Veale & Keane, 2004). While these approaches have achieved some success, they are limited by their dependence on expert knowledge, their lack of scalability to large corpora, and their difficulty in capturing the subtle and context-dependent nature of metaphorical language. More recently, machine learning techniques have been applied to AMI, often framed as a classification problem – distinguishing between metaphorical and literal usages of words or phrases (Moon, 1999;Shutova & Kuksa, 2011;Mohammad, 2016). However, even these supervised learning methods typically require substantial amounts of manually annotated training data, and their performance is often constrained by the quality and coverage of this data. Furthermore, many approaches focus on identifying metaphorical *words* rather than complete *expressions*, neglecting the importance of syntactic structure and contextual information. In this paper, we present a novel and unsupervised approach to AMI that moves away from hand-crafted knowledge and large-scale annotation. Our method leverages the inherent structure of language by clustering verbs and nouns based on their distributional similarity in a large corpus. The core idea is that metaphorical expressions often exhibit a distinctive pattern of verb-argument co-occurrence, differing from the more conventional patterns observed in literal language. By identifying clusters of verbs and nouns that frequently appear together in metaphorical contexts, we can effectively ‘harvest’ a large number of metaphorical expressions from a corpus, starting from a small seed set of manually annotated examples. Our approach is distinct from previous work in several key ways. First, it requires minimal human effort, relying only on a small seed set to bootstrap the process. Second, it avoids the use of external knowledge resources, such as dictionaries or ontologies, and instead learns directly from the statistical properties of the text. Third, it focuses on identifying complete metaphorical expressions, taking into account both syntactic structure and semantic relationships. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to employ entirely unsupervised methods for metaphor identification, achieving a precision of 0.79 – a competitive result given the lack of training data and reliance on purely distributional information. While significant progress has been made on segmenting and classifying the content *within* documents – identifying paragraphs, topics, or semantic roles – comparatively less attention has been paid to understanding the higher-level, organizational structure *of* documents themselves.
