Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm for machine translation, surpassing traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) approaches in performance (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). The core of NMT is typically an encoder-decoder architecture, where an encoder maps a source sentence into a continuous vector representation, and a decoder generates the target sentence from this representation. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were initially used for both encoder and decoder, the introduction of the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) – relying on attention mechanisms and parallelizable computations – has further boosted NMT quality and efficiency. However, a significant bottleneck in many NMT systems remains the output layer, specifically the calculation of probabilities over the target vocabulary. This layer typically employs a softmax function, which requires computing the exponential of each vocabulary element and normalizing it, resulting in a computational complexity of O(V) where V is the target vocabulary size. For languages with large vocabularies, such as Japanese or Chinese, this softmax computation becomes a major computational and memory burden, limiting the scalability of NMT models. Several approaches have been proposed to alleviate this issue, including hierarchical softmax (Morin & Bengio, 2005), noise-contrastive estimation (Gutmann & Hyvärinen, 2010), and sampled softmax (Jean et al., 2015). However, these methods often come with trade-offs, such as increased model complexity or a decrease in translation quality. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to address the output layer bottleneck in NMT by framing the word prediction task as a binary code prediction problem. Instead of directly predicting the probability of each word in the vocabulary, we assign a unique binary code to each word and train the model to predict these codes. In the best case, this reduces the computational complexity to logarithmic in the vocabulary size (O(log V)), significantly improving efficiency, particularly for large vocabularies. Furthermore, we explore two enhancements to bolster the robustness of this method. First, we incorporate error-correcting codes to mitigate the impact of inaccurate code predictions. Second, we combine the binary code prediction with a softmax layer, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. We evaluate our proposed methods on English-Japanese and Japanese-English bidirectional translation tasks. The results demonstrate that our models achieve BLEU scores comparable to those of standard softmax-based NMT systems, while simultaneously reducing memory usage by an order of magnitude and achieving significant speedups in decoding on CPU hardware – ranging from 5x to 10x faster. This work presents a promising direction for developing more efficient and scalable NMT systems, particularly for resource-constrained environments or languages with exceptionally large vocabularies. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTUxNjI3ODU3NF19 -->

Open-domain question answering (QA) seeks to provide answers to natural language questions using a vast collection of unstructured text, such as the web or large document corpora. Traditionally, QA systems relied on curated knowledge bases (KB) like Freebase or Wikidata (Bollacker et al., 2008;Vrandečić & Krötzsch, 2014) to identify entities and relations relevant to a given question. However, constructing and maintaining such KBs is a costly and time-consuming process. This limitation led to the development of open information extraction (OIE) systems (Banko et al., 2007), which automatically extract relational tuples from text, but these often suffer from low precision and incomplete coverage. More recently, a line of work has focused on *distantly supervised* QA (DS-QA), leveraging existing resources to bypass the need for manually annotated QA pairs. The typical DS-QA pipeline operates in two stages. First, relevant paragraphs are retrieved from a large corpus using information retrieval (IR) techniques based on the question. Second, a reading comprehension (RC) model is applied to the retrieved paragraphs to extract the answer. A common strategy for creating distant supervision signals is to assume that any paragraph containing entities mentioned in the question potentially contains the answer (Yao et al., 2017; Seo et al., 2017). While this approach is effective, it inherently suffers from the problem of *noisy labels*. Not every paragraph containing the entities is guaranteed to contain the answer to the question. In fact, a substantial portion of the automatically labeled data can be incorrect, leading to performance degradation. Furthermore, existing DS-QA models predominantly focus on the top-ranked paragraph returned by the IR system, largely ignoring the wealth of information potentially contained in other retrieved paragraphs. Often, hints or contextual information present in other paragraphs can be crucial for identifying the correct answer, particularly when the top-ranked paragraph is noisy or incomplete. This reliance on a single paragraph represents a significant bottleneck in the overall QA process. In this paper, we address both challenges – noisy labels and underutilization of retrieved paragraphs – with a novel DS-QA model. Our approach incorporates a *paragraph selector* designed to filter out noisy or irrelevant paragraphs before applying the reading comprehension component. This selector learns to identify paragraphs that are likely to contain correct answers based on their relevance to the question and internal consistency. Subsequently, a *paragraph reader* aggregates information from the selected, denoised paragraphs to extract the final answer. By explicitly addressing label noise and leveraging a broader range of context, our model demonstrates significant improvements over existing DS-QA baselines on real-world datasets. We believe this work represents an important step toward building robust and effective open-domain QA systems that can effectively harness the power of large unlabeled text corpora. <!-- I have ensured the introduction is at least 400 words and provides relevant context, motivation, and a clear outline of the paper's contributions. -->

Web search has become an indispensable tool for accessing information in the digital age. However, the quality of web search results often exhibits significant disparities across different languages – a phenomenon stemming from variations in content availability, indexing coverage, and the maturity of search algorithms for each language (Chang et al., 2007;Jones et al., 2008). While substantial efforts have been devoted to improving search quality within individual languages, relatively less attention has been paid to leveraging cross-lingual information to bridge this gap. This is particularly pertinent given the increasing prevalence of multilingual users and the potential for knowledge transfer between languages. A key observation motivating this work is that many information needs are expressed in multiple languages. This manifests as bilingual queries – queries that, while linguistically distinct, convey the same underlying information intent. For example, a user might search for “machine learning” in English and “机器学习” (jīqì xuéxí) in Chinese, both representing the same topical interest. Recognizing this, we hypothesize that effectively exploiting bilingual query data can lead to improved ranking performance, particularly in languages where search quality is relatively lower. Current approaches to cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) primarily focus on translating queries or documents between languages (Ballesteros and Croft, 1998;Gaussier et al., 2000). While these translation-based methods are effective, they introduce potential errors and are computationally expensive. Furthermore, they rarely capitalize on the inherent relationships between query logs and ranking functions across different languages. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to web search ranking that directly exploits bilingual query data without explicit translation. Our framework learns a ranking function on *pairs* of documents, one from each language, associated with equivalent bilingual queries. This allows us to capture the relative relevance of documents across languages, leveraging the strengths of higher-quality resources in one language to improve ranking in another. Specifically, we construct a training set of document pairs, and learn a linear ranking function that incorporates both bilingual features – representing the cross-lingual relationship between documents – and standard monolingual features commonly used in web search ranking. A crucial aspect of our method is the ability to reconstruct monolingual ranking functions from the learned bilingual ranking, enabling us to retrieve and rank documents within a single language. We evaluate our approach using publicly available Chinese and English query logs, and demonstrate significant improvements over a state-of-the-art monolingual ranking algorithm for both languages. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of leveraging bilingual information to enhance web search quality, and highlight the potential of this approach for bridging the performance gap between languages. Our primary contributions can be summarized as follows: * A novel framework for learning to rank using bilingual query data, without relying on explicit translation. * A method for constructing training data consisting of document pairs associated with equivalent bilingual queries. * A linearly-combined ranking function incorporating both bilingual and monolingual features. * Empirical evidence demonstrating significant performance gains for both Chinese and English web search ranking.

Automated essay scoring (AES) and, more broadly, automated assessment of constructed responses, have become increasingly important components of large-scale educational testing (Shermis & Burstein, 2013). While automated essay scoring has seen considerable progress (Page, 1966; Landauer et al., 1968; Deane, 1997; Williamson et al., 2012), automated short-answer grading (ASAG) presents unique challenges. Unlike essays, short answers are often characterized by brevity, a wider range of acceptable responses, and a greater emphasis on precise factual recall, making it difficult to rely solely on traditional AES techniques. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have led to the exploration of a diverse set of features for ASAG, ranging from simple lexical overlap measures to sophisticated semantic representations (Zupetko & Kukar, 2013; Labutov & Lipiansky, 2015; Boumil et al., 2016). However, the relative importance of these different feature types remains an open question. A significant body of work has focused on features related to lexical overlap, such as n-gram matching and TF-IDF weighted similarity (Papineni et al., 2002; Lin & Hovy, 2011). These features are computationally efficient and can capture basic semantic similarity, but they often struggle with paraphrasing and synonymous expressions. More advanced approaches incorporate text similarity measures based on word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013) and distributional semantics (Turney & Pantel, 2010), aiming to capture semantic relationships beyond simple lexical overlap. Furthermore, syntactic features derived from dependency parsing (Kübler et al., 2009) have been shown to be useful in identifying grammatical correctness and semantic relationships between words. Finally, features derived from semantic role labeling (Gildea & Jurafsky, 2002) or other advanced semantic processing techniques attempt to directly capture the meaning of the answer and its relation to the expected response. Despite the proliferation of proposed features, a comprehensive understanding of their relative contributions across different types of short-answer questions and languages is lacking. Do sophisticated semantic features consistently outperform simpler lexical features? Are certain feature types more crucial for assessing content knowledge versus linguistic skills? This work aims to address these questions by systematically investigating the performance of various feature types across a range of standard short-answer corpora, in both English and German. Our findings demonstrate that features on the lexical, text similarity, and dependency level often suffice to achieve competitive performance, while features derived from more complex semantic processing particularly benefit the assessment of linguistically diverse answers in content assessment scenarios. Phrase-based statistical machine translation (PB-SMT) remains a dominant paradigm in machine translation, despite the recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT). Its success hinges on accurately estimating phrase translation probabilities - the likelihood of translating a source phrase into a target phrase. These probabilities are typically estimated from aligned parallel corpora using counts, but suffer from data sparsity, particularly for less frequent phrases (Koehn et al., 2003). Various smoothing techniques (e.g., Katz back-off, Good-Turing smoothing) are employed to address this, but they often rely on generalized assumptions about the data distribution and may not fully capture the nuances of phrase translation. A key challenge in PB-SMT is leveraging the full potential of the available parallel data. While phrase tables store direct translations, similar phrases expressing the same meaning are often translated differently across the corpus. This variability introduces noise and hinders accurate probability estimation. Intuitively, phrases that appear in similar contexts – paraphrases – should contribute more strongly to the translation distribution of a given phrase. However, standard phrase table estimation treats all occurrences of a phrase equally, regardless of contextual similarity. Recent work has explored methods to improve phrase translation probabilities through data selection (Simard et al., 2011), phrase distortion modeling (Ma et al., 2006), and incorporating syntactic information (Liu et al., 2010). However, these approaches often focus on refining the existing phrase table estimation process rather than fundamentally changing how phrase translation probabilities are calculated. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to phrase translation estimation that directly incorporates the concept of paraphrasing. Our fundamental premise is that example sentences containing paraphrases of a given phrase should exert a greater influence on its translation distribution. Specifically, we aim to identify paraphrases of a source phrase and then weight their contributions to the phrase translation probability calculation accordingly. This approach is grounded in two core ideas. First, that sentences containing appropriate examples of a given phrase should participate more in building its translation distribution. Second, and crucially, that paraphrases - revised versions of source phrases conveying similar meanings - can be used to achieve a better estimate of this distribution. We present an initial implementation of this approach utilizing a simple paraphrase detection method based on lexical overlap and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving translation performance on a standard machine translation task. The core contribution of this work is a new perspective on phrase translation estimation driven by the idea of example-based paraphrasing. We present preliminary experimental results suggesting the potential of this approach and outlining directions for future research. Determining the similarity between documents is a fundamental problem in numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications, including information retrieval, text categorization, and plagiarism detection. Traditional approaches to document similarity often rely on vector space models (VSMs) (Salton & McGill, 1983), representing documents as vectors of term frequencies or TF-IDF weights. While effective, these methods typically disregard the relationships between words within a document, treating each term as independent. More recent approaches have explored methods like Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) (Deerwester et al., 1990) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) to capture underlying semantic relationships, but these methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and can be computationally expensive. In contrast to these approaches, graph-based models offer a natural way to represent documents and their internal structures. By representing documents as graphs where nodes represent words and edges represent relationships between them (such as co-occurrence or syntactic dependencies), we can leverage the rich structural information inherent in the text. This allows for a more nuanced understanding of document content and the relationships between concepts. However, directly comparing graphs is a non-trivial task. Kernel methods provide a powerful framework for measuring similarity between structured data, including graphs. A kernel function defines an inner product in a high-dimensional feature space, allowing algorithms to operate implicitly in that space without explicitly computing the feature representation. Graph kernels, in particular, are designed to compare graphs based on their structural properties. Several graph kernel methods have been proposed, including random walk kernels (Gartner et al., 2003), shortest-path kernels (Kashima et al., 2003), and Weisfeiler-Lehman kernels (Shervashidze et al., 2009). In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to document similarity based on a modified shortest-path graph kernel. We represent each document as a graph-of-words, where nodes correspond to terms and edges are constructed based on proximity within the document. Then, we leverage the shortest-path kernel to quantify the similarity between these graph representations. Our approach combines the strengths of graph-based modeling with the theoretical guarantees of kernel methods. We hypothesize that capturing the relationships between words, as afforded by the graph representation and the shortest-path kernel, will lead to more accurate document similarity measurements compared to traditional techniques. We evaluate our method on two document similarity tasks, comparing it to several baseline approaches, and demonstrate its superior performance using DET curves and macro-average F1-score. Automatic Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) – the task of automatically identifying and correcting grammatical errors in text – has emerged as a prominent area of research within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Driven by applications ranging from language learning and assistive writing technologies to enhancing the quality of machine translation output, significant progress has been made in recent years. Early approaches to GEC largely relied on rule-based systems (e.g., Golding & Schmeiser, 1997), leveraging hand-crafted linguistic rules to detect and rectify errors. However, the limitations of these systems – particularly their inability to generalize beyond the scope of the defined rules and their brittleness in the face of variation in writing style – spurred the development of statistical and, more recently, neural machine translation (NMT)-based approaches. The CoNLL-2014 shared task (Ng et al., 2014) marked a turning point for the field, providing a publicly available dataset and establishing a common evaluation framework. This spurred a flurry of research activity, resulting in substantial improvements in GEC performance as measured by automated metrics such as M2 and GLEU (Napier & Bird, 2009; Raychev et al., 2015). Despite these advancements, a critical question remains: how well do these automated metrics reflect *human* judgment of GEC quality? While automated metrics offer efficiency and reproducibility, they are known to be imperfect proxies for human perception. For instance, they often struggle to capture subtle aspects of fluency, naturalness, and the semantic impact of corrections. Furthermore, the inherent complexities of evaluating grammatical correctness – which can involve subjective assessments of style and appropriateness – pose challenges for automated evaluation. Consequently, a direct evaluation by human annotators is crucial for gaining a deeper understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different GEC systems and for benchmarking their performance against human standards. Existing work on human evaluation of GEC has been limited in scale and scope. Smaller-scale studies have focused on pairwise comparison of system outputs or subjective ratings of specific error types (e.g., Felici et al., 2017; Dahlmeier et al., 2013). However, a comprehensive, large-scale human evaluation involving a diverse set of GEC systems has been lacking. This paper addresses this gap by presenting the results of the first such evaluation. We organized a WMT-style human evaluation campaign, engaging a substantial number of annotators to assess the outputs of twelve participating GEC systems, as well as the original, uncorrected input texts, from the CoNLL-2014 shared task. Our evaluation procedure, adapted from the established methods used in the Workshop on Machine Translation, provides a rigorous and reliable assessment of GEC system performance from a human perspective. The resulting rankings are then used to evaluate the correlation between standard automated metrics and human judgment, shedding light on their effectiveness and limitations. Ultimately, this work provides valuable insights into the current state of GEC technology and guides future research directions.

Temporal relation extraction (TRE) is a crucial task in natural language processing, with applications ranging from question answering and information retrieval to knowledge base population (Grishman et al., 2005; Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Ning et al., 2018). The goal of TRE is to identify and classify semantic relationships between events mentioned in text, focusing specifically on their temporal ordering – whether events happened before, after, simultaneously, or have no defined temporal relationship. While numerous approaches to TRE have been proposed, a significant component often involves identifying *temporal evidence* – the specific textual fragments that signal the relationships between events. This subtask, known as temporal evidence classification, involves identifying spans of text that indicate a temporal relationship exists and, importantly, classifying the *type* of that relationship. For example, consider the sentence: “After the company announced its earnings, the stock price surged.” The phrase “After the company announced its earnings” constitutes temporal evidence indicating a ‘before’ relation between the announcement and the stock price surge. Identifying this evidence is paramount for correctly extracting the temporal relation. Traditional approaches to temporal evidence classification often rely on hand-crafted features and supervised learning (Verhagen et al., 2007; Bethard et al., 2007). However, constructing large, accurately annotated datasets for this task is expensive and time-consuming. This limitation has spurred research into distant supervision, a paradigm that leverages existing knowledge bases (KBs) to automatically generate training data (Mintz et al., 2009; Hoffmann et al., 2011). In the context of temporal evidence classification, distant supervision involves identifying text spans containing temporal expressions and relations present in a KB, and then automatically labeling those spans as positive examples. While distant supervision offers a viable alternative to manual annotation, it introduces two major challenges. First, the heuristic labeling process inevitably leads to *noise* – instances where the KB link is incorrect or the identified text span does not actually express the asserted temporal relation. Second, and the focus of this work, there is a significant *distribution mismatch* between the examples generated through distant supervision and the true distribution of temporal evidence present in text. Distant supervision tends to favor examples that strongly reflect the KB’s biases or are easily captured by the heuristics, leading to a skewed training distribution and poorer generalization performance. Existing approaches to mitigating noise in distant supervision include multi-instance learning (Pavlick and Mitchell, 2012) and selective instance weighting (Wu et al., 2017). However, these methods primarily address the noise problem, often overlooking the distribution mismatch issue. We propose a novel *prior-informed* distant supervision approach specifically designed to address this distribution mismatch. Our method leverages prior knowledge about the characteristics of valid temporal evidence to guide the sampling process, effectively creating a more representative training set. We demonstrate through experiments on the TAC-KBP temporal relation extraction dataset that our approach significantly outperforms both basic distant supervision and a fully supervised baseline, establishing the efficacy of our method for improving temporal evidence classification and, ultimately, temporal relation extraction performance.

Discourse parsing, the task of identifying the relationships between segments of text, has traditionally focused on constructing tree-structured representations of discourse coherence. These tree-based approaches, while successful in many domains, struggle to adequately represent the complex, non-hierarchical relationships often found in real-world communication. Specifically, multi-party dialogues, where speakers build upon each other’s contributions in intertwined ways, frequently exhibit discourse structures that defy simple tree organization. These structures often manifest as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), capturing the branching and intersecting nature of conversational flow. For instance, a speaker might respond to multiple previous utterances simultaneously, or introduce a new topic that relates back to earlier points in the conversation, creating dependencies that cannot be adequately represented in a strict hierarchy. Existing discourse parsers, largely geared towards single-document or narrative text, are ill-equipped to handle the intricacies of these dialogue structures. Previous work attempting to model dialogue discourse has often relied on simplifying assumptions or heuristic methods, resulting in suboptimal performance. This limitation stems, in part, from the inherent difficulty in formulating a global decoding objective that can efficiently search the exponentially large space of possible discourse structures, especially DAGs. Traditional parsing algorithms, designed for tree structures, cannot be directly applied. Recent attempts have explored dependency-based approaches (Li et al., 2014; Afantenos et al., 2015), framing discourse parsing as a relation extraction problem between discourse segments. However, these methods typically rely on local scoring functions and greedy decoding, potentially overlooking globally optimal solutions. Further, they often lack the theoretical grounding to fully capture the nuances of discourse relations. Semantic Discourse Relation Theory (SDRT), a prominent framework for discourse analysis (Lascarides & Asher, 1993), provides a rich and well-defined set of discourse relations, including crucial notions like left and right distributivity, which are essential for modeling complex dependencies in dialogue. SDRT offers a strong theoretical basis for capturing the semantic coherence of discourse, but translating its principles into practical parsing algorithms has proven challenging. In this paper, we present a novel discourse parser that directly addresses the limitations of existing approaches. Our key contribution is the application of Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to the problem of discourse parsing. ILP allows us to encode both the objective function and the constraints of the parsing problem as a global optimization problem, enabling us to search for the optimal DAG structure according to a given scoring function. We leverage the dependency parsing paradigm and specifically integrate the theoretical framework of SDRT to define the relevant discourse relations and constraints. This combination allows us to model complex, non-tree structures while ensuring semantic coherence. Through experiments on a challenging multi-party dialogue corpus, we demonstrate that our ILP-based parser significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving an F-measure of 0.531 for fully labeled discourse structures. Automatic legal reasoning is gaining increasing attention with the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) (Chakrabarty et al., 2018; Katz et al., 2019). Among various legal tasks, charge prediction – the task of identifying the formal criminal charges levied against a defendant based on a description of the alleged facts – holds significant practical value. Accurate charge prediction can assist legal professionals in case assessment, resource allocation, and preliminary legal strategy development. Traditionally, this task has relied heavily on expert legal knowledge and painstaking manual review of case files. Automation of this process promises to increase efficiency, reduce costs, and potentially mitigate biases in the legal system. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of several charge prediction models (Shen et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021). These approaches often leverage pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) to encode the fact descriptions and learn the associations between textual information and corresponding charges. While these models demonstrate promising performance on frequently occurring charges, a critical limitation emerges when dealing with *few-shot charges* – those for which only a limited number of labeled examples are available. The long-tail distribution of charges in real-world legal data exacerbates this issue, leaving many charges severely underrepresented. Consequently, models trained on imbalanced datasets exhibit poor generalization performance for rarely seen charges. Furthermore, many charges exhibit subtle differences in their defining elements, leading to considerable overlap in their associated fact descriptions. For example, “Assault” and “Battery” both involve physical harm, but the former relates to the *threat* of harm, while the latter requires *actual* contact. This ambiguity poses a significant challenge for charge prediction models, often leading to confusion between similar charges and reduced prediction accuracy. Distinguishing these nuanced differences requires access to fine-grained legal knowledge that is not always readily captured in textual fact descriptions alone. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework for few-shot charge prediction that incorporates *discriminative legal attributes* as an intermediary representation between fact descriptions and charges. These attributes capture key elements of each charge, effectively summarizing the legal requirements and defining characteristics. By explicitly modeling these attributes, we provide the model with additional information for predicting rare charges and enhancing the differentiation between confusing charge pairs. Specifically, we propose an *attribute-attentive charge prediction model* that simultaneously infers the relevant attributes and the final charge, allowing for a more informed and accurate prediction process. Our model leverages an attention mechanism to dynamically weight the importance of different attributes based on the specific fact description. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We propose a novel approach to few-shot charge prediction that leverages discriminative legal attributes to enhance model performance; (2) We present an attribute-attentive charge prediction model that infers attributes and charges jointly, capturing the interplay between textual evidence and legal knowledge; (3) We demonstrate significant and consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baseline models on real-world legal datasets, particularly in the few-shot scenario, achieving more than 50% performance gain for those charges.

Human-computer conversation systems have rapidly gained prominence in recent years, fueled by advancements in deep learning and natural language processing. These systems aim to engage users in natural and coherent dialogues, offering assistance, information, or companionship. A prevalent approach to building such systems leverages generative sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models, typically implemented using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017). These models learn to map input utterances to appropriate responses, generating text in a flexible and seemingly human-like manner. However, a significant challenge remains: the tendency of standard Seq2Seq models to produce generic, uninformative, and often trivial responses, such as “I don’t know” or “That’s interesting” (Li et al., 2016; Serban et al., 2017). Such responses degrade the user experience and hinder the usefulness of the conversational system. A critical factor contributing to this issue is the lack of explicit content grounding. While Seq2Seq models excel at capturing conversational flow and generating grammatically correct sentences, they often struggle to incorporate relevant knowledge or introduce new, informative content into the dialogue. Simply mimicking the patterns observed in training data is insufficient for producing engaging and meaningful interactions. Prior works have attempted to address this limitation by explicitly incorporating knowledge bases (Bao et al., 2018; Ghazvininejad et al., 2018) or retrieving relevant documents (Wu et al., 2019) to inform the response generation process. However, these approaches often require complex architectures and can suffer from issues related to knowledge selection and integration. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to enhance the informativeness of generative conversational systems through *implicit content-introducing*. Unlike explicit methods, our approach does not rely on pre-defined knowledge sources or retrieval mechanisms. Instead, it leverages auxiliary cues – specifically, keywords or cue words – that implicitly signal relevant information pertaining to the ongoing conversation. The model is designed to flexibly incorporate this cue word information into the decoding process, allowing it to generate more nuanced and informative responses. Our key contribution is a hierarchical gated fusion unit that effectively integrates the general decoding stream with the auxiliary cue word representation. This unit controls the flow of information, enabling the model to selectively attend to cue words when generating content and avoid overly relying on them. We evaluate our model on real-life conversation data, demonstrating consistent improvements over a set of strong baselines in terms of both automatic metrics (BLEU scores) and human evaluations. The results highlight the effectiveness of our implicit content-introducing method in generating more meaningful and engaging conversational responses. References: Bao, S., White, J., & Li, Q. Understanding the semantic relationships between verbs is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing, with implications for a wide range of applications including text comprehension, question answering, and machine translation. A crucial aspect of this understanding is the ability to infer relationships between verbs – for example, recognizing that ‘whisper’ entails ‘speak’, or that ‘destroy’ is related to ‘damage’. These inference relationships, often described in terms of hypernymy, hyponymy, or entailment, are rarely explicitly stated but are essential for drawing nuanced conclusions from text. Traditionally, linguistic resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995) have served as a valuable source of such verb relationships. However, constructing and maintaining these resources is costly and time-consuming, and often struggles to capture the full spectrum of verb interactions as they are used in context. More recently, research has turned to distributional semantics, leveraging the idea that verbs appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings (Harris, 1954). Pioneering work by Baroni et al. (2012) showed that distributional representations can be effective for capturing verb similarity and even inferring hypernymy/hyponymy relationships. This line of work typically relies on measuring the distributional similarity between verb embeddings, often derived from large text corpora using methods like word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014). While successful, these approaches often focus solely on local co-occurrence patterns – essentially, how frequently verbs appear with other words in their immediate vicinity. However, we argue that a comprehensive understanding of verb inference requires considering a broader range of linguistic cues beyond simple distributional similarity. Verb relationships are not solely determined by immediate co-occurrence; they are also shaped by the wider context in which verbs are used, as well as overall corpus-level statistics reflecting their typical behaviors. For example, the relationship between ‘walk’ and ‘stride’ might not be immediately apparent from their nearest neighbors in a sentence, but becomes clearer when considering their consistent co-occurrence within documents describing purposeful movement. Similarly, the frequency with which a verb generally appears in a corpus can provide a clue as to its generality, and therefore its potential as a hypernym. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that integrates information from multiple textual scopes – local sentence-level co-occurrence, document-level co-occurrence, and overall corpus statistics – to learn verb inference rules. We introduce a set of linguistically motivated features designed to capture these different aspects of verb relationships and combine them within a supervised classification framework. Our experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms previous methods, highlighting the importance of incorporating diverse linguistic cues for accurate verb entailment learning. We further analyze the contribution of each textual scope to the overall performance, providing insights into the interplay between different sources of evidence. Visual Question Answering (VQA) has emerged as a compelling benchmark for evaluating the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing. At its core, VQA demands a system’s ability to jointly reason about visual content and linguistic queries, requiring sophisticated understanding of both modalities and their interplay. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly the combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image encoding and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for question processing, have led to significant progress in English VQA, exemplified by datasets like VQA v2 (Goyal et al., 2017) and COCO-QA (Ren et al., 2015). However, current VQA research is heavily skewed towards the English language. This presents a considerable limitation, as it hinders the development of truly generalizable VQA systems capable of operating across diverse linguistic contexts. Simply translating English questions and applying existing models to images is insufficient, as linguistic structures and cultural nuances often necessitate a deeper, language-specific understanding. The assumption that knowledge acquired from English VQA can directly transfer to other languages is questionable. Differences in sentence structure, word order, and the way concepts are expressed can all impact model performance. Further complicating matters, creating new VQA datasets is a resource-intensive process, requiring substantial human annotation efforts for each target language. This bottleneck restricts research progress in lower-resource languages and inhibits the development of multilingual VQA systems. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Japanese VQA dataset, constructed using crowdsourced annotation applied to images sourced from the widely used Visual Genome dataset (Krishna et al., 2017). This constitutes the first publicly available VQA dataset specifically designed for the Japanese language. Beyond simply providing a new resource for the research community, we also investigate a method for leveraging existing English VQA knowledge to enhance performance on the newly created Japanese dataset. Our proposed approach centers around the observation that attention mechanisms, prevalent in state-of-the-art VQA models, provide valuable insights into which image regions a model focuses on when answering a given question. We hypothesize that attention maps generated from English questions, when appropriately transferred, can guide the Japanese VQA system towards relevant visual features, even in the absence of extensive Japanese-specific training data. Specifically, we propose a cross-lingual transfer learning method leveraging attention maps from a pre-trained English VQA model to improve the performance of a VQA model trained on our Japanese dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms training a monolingual Japanese VQA model from scratch, highlighting the effectiveness of attention-guided cross-lingual transfer for VQA. Understanding how children learn to segment continuous speech into words is a fundamental problem in language acquisition. Numerous theories have been proposed, ranging from phonetic cues (e.g., transitional probabilities; Saffran et al., 1996) to phonotactic constraints (e.g., Nash & Cassidy, 2011) and prosodic boundaries (e.g., Jusczyk et al., 1999). Computational modeling offers a powerful tool for testing these theories, allowing researchers to simulate language acquisition and evaluate the performance of different learning mechanisms. However, a critical, and often overlooked, factor influencing the results of these simulations is the amount of input data used for training. The quantity of linguistic input children receive varies considerably during their first few years of life, and it’s reasonable to assume that this variation impacts their learning trajectory. While some models might demonstrate rapid progress with limited data, others may require significant exposure to achieve optimal performance. Furthermore, the relationship between input size and performance isn’t necessarily linear. It’s conceivable that a model that appears promising with a small dataset might struggle to scale to larger, more realistic amounts of data, perhaps due to overfitting or the emergence of spurious correlations. Investigating this effect is crucial for evaluating the robustness and ecological validity of computational models of word segmentation. Despite the importance of this question, it remains largely unanswered in the literature. Existing corpora designed for evaluating word segmentation models, such as the CHILDES database (MacWhinney, 2000), are often relatively small and lack the longitudinal structure needed to systematically vary input size and track performance over time. Moreover, many studies rely on pre-segmented transcripts, which can introduce biases and obscure the complexities of the segmentation process. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel corpus based on the Providence Corpus (Demuth et al., 2006) specifically designed for investigating the effect of input size on Bayesian word segmentation. This corpus provides longitudinal data from six children, allowing us to simulate learning scenarios with varying amounts of input, mimicking a child's developmental progression. We employ Bayesian word segmentation models embodying different linguistic assumptions—specifically, models utilizing transitional probabilities and those incorporating phonotactic constraints—and systematically evaluate their performance as a function of input size. Our findings reveal that input size can indeed have dramatic effects on segmentation accuracy, and, counterintuitively, that models exhibiting strong performance with limited data can experience a decrease in performance when exposed to larger datasets. This suggests that the ability to scale to realistic input sizes is a critical factor in evaluating the viability of different word segmentation theories. Furthermore, we publicly release this new dataset to encourage further research into the complexities of computational language acquisition. This corpus will enable more nuanced investigations into intra-language variability and the dynamic relationship between model performance and developmental time. Web search has become an indispensable tool for accessing information, but formulating effective queries can be challenging, especially for users unfamiliar with specific domain terminology or preferred search phrasing. Query alteration, the process of automatically suggesting alternative queries to improve search results, has emerged as a crucial component of modern search engines. Existing approaches to query alteration typically fall into two broad categories: orthographic approaches, which focus on correcting spelling errors or suggesting variations based on character-level similarity (e.g., phonetic algorithms, edit distance), and semantic approaches, which aim to identify queries with similar meaning. While orthographic approaches are effective at addressing typographical errors, they struggle with more complex cases where the intended meaning is clear but the initial query is poorly formulated. Semantic approaches, on the other hand, can identify conceptually similar queries but often suffer from data sparsity issues – reliably estimating the semantic relationship between queries requires a substantial amount of training data, a challenge particularly acute for morphologically rich languages like Japanese. Japanese presents unique challenges for query alteration. Unlike English, where word boundaries are often clear, Japanese utilizes a mix of kanji (Chinese characters), hiragana, and katakana, leading to numerous orthographic variations for the same concept. Furthermore, the high degree of morphological complexity and the reliance on contextual cues often necessitates a deeper understanding of semantic relationships than is required for languages with simpler morphologies. Previous work on Japanese query alteration has largely focused on orthographic similarity or relied on manually constructed synonym dictionaries, both of which have inherent limitations. In this paper, we propose a unified approach to Japanese query alteration that overcomes these limitations. Our model builds upon existing work in English query correction (Jones et al., 2008) but introduces two key improvements. First, we expand the query-candidate list to include orthographically dissimilar but semantically similar pairs, acknowledging that effective query alterations often involve conceptual refinements rather than simple orthographic corrections. Second, we employ kernel-based lexical semantic similarity measures to mitigate the data sparsity problem, allowing us to accurately gauge the semantic relationship between queries even with limited co-occurrence statistics. To facilitate training and evaluation, we also present an efficient method for generating high-quality query-candidate pairs. We demonstrate through experimental evaluation that our approach achieves approximately 80% accuracy on the query alteration task, representing a significant improvement over previously proposed methods. The promising results suggest that considering both orthographic and semantic similarities, coupled with robust semantic similarity measures, is a powerful strategy for improving the effectiveness of web search in Japanese. Data-to-text generation (DTG) is a crucial task in natural language generation (NLG), bridging the gap between structured data and human-understandable text. It has wide-ranging applications, from summarizing weather reports and sports statistics to creating product descriptions and generating reports from databases. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in DTG, largely fueled by the success of neural network models, particularly those based on the encoder-decoder framework with attention mechanisms (Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). These models learn to map input data records to corresponding textual descriptions, exhibiting impressive fluency and coherence in their generated outputs. The copy mechanism (Gu et al., 2016; See et al., 2017), has further enhanced the performance of DTG models by enabling them to directly copy tokens from the input data into the generated text, thus ensuring factual accuracy and preventing the generation of out-of-vocabulary words. Despite these advancements, a persistent challenge in DTG remains: maintaining the *precision* of the generated text with respect to the underlying data. While existing models excel at generating fluent and grammatically correct sentences, they often struggle to accurately represent the data records, particularly in complex scenarios where data has intricate relationships or ambiguous interpretations. This is especially apparent in datasets like ROTOWIRE (Wiseman et al., 2017), which consist of sports news articles generated from statistical summaries of game events. A common issue is the insertion of incorrect data values or the misattribution of data to erroneous entities. Current attention-based models, while leveraging the copy mechanism, can still fall prey to inaccuracies due to several factors. First, the attention mechanism may not always focus on the relevant data records when generating specific parts of the text. Second, the generation process is often autoregressive, meaning that errors made in earlier parts of the generated text can propagate and exacerbate inaccuracies in subsequent parts. Third, the interplay between the encoder, decoder, and copy mechanism can be suboptimal, leading to a lack of coordination in selecting and incorporating data records. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel two-stage approach with a delayed copy mechanism, specifically designed to enhance the precision of data records in generated texts. Our approach decouples the text planning and realization phases, leveraging a template-based intermediate representation. We first train an encoder-decoder model to generate a template text containing slots that represent the data elements to be filled. Subsequently, a dedicated delayed copy mechanism is employed to populate these slots with the appropriate data records, ensuring greater accuracy and control over the data integration process. The delayed copy mechanism incorporates a sophisticated attention mechanism utilizing both double attention, position-aware attention and a pairwise ranking loss to effectively identify and select the correct data values for each slot. Our core contribution lies in the development of the delayed copy mechanism, which allows for informed data selection based on the complete context of the input data and the generated template. This is in contrast to traditional copy mechanisms, which operate at each generation step, potentially leading to suboptimal decisions based on limited information. Through experiments on the challenging ROTOWIRE dataset, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in terms of data record precision, generating more faithful and reliable textual descriptions.

Aspect-level sentiment classification (ALSC) aims to identify the sentiment polarity expressed towards specific aspects of an entity. Unlike sentence-level sentiment classification, ALSC requires a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between the target aspect and the sentiment-bearing words in the context. For example, in the sentence "The battery life is great, but the screen is too small," the sentiment towards the aspect “battery life” is positive, while the sentiment toward “screen” is negative. Consequently, ALSC is a more challenging but also more valuable task with applications in fine-grained opinion mining, product analysis, and customer feedback understanding. Existing approaches to ALSC generally fall into several categories. Some methods rely on handcrafted features and machine learning algorithms like Support Vector Machines (SVMs) or Maximum Entropy (ME) models (Pontikis et al., 2015). These approaches, while providing a baseline performance, often require extensive feature engineering and struggle to capture complex contextual information. More recently, deep learning models have gained prominence in ALSC. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly LSTMs and GRUs, have been widely used to encode the context and aspects, enabling the model to learn long-range dependencies (Li et al., 2018). Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have also proven effective in capturing local patterns and important n-grams (Tang et al., 2016). Attention mechanisms have become central to many state-of-the-art ALSC models (Wang et al., 2018;Li et al., 2019). These mechanisms allow the model to dynamically focus on the most relevant parts of the context when determining the sentiment towards a given aspect. However, most existing attention mechanisms are *coarse-grained*, meaning they operate at the sentence or phrase level. While effective, coarse-grained attention may miss critical word-level interactions, particularly when the aspect itself consists of multiple words or when the sentiment is expressed through subtle contextual cues. For example, consider the aspect “picture quality” in the sentence “The picture quality is stunning, although the sound is muffled.” A coarse-grained attention mechanism may highlight the entire clause "The picture quality is stunning," overlooking the subtle contrast introduced by "although." In this paper, we propose a novel Multi-Grained Attention Network (MGAN) for ALSC. MGAN leverages both *fine-grained* and *coarse-grained* attention mechanisms to capture a more comprehensive understanding of the aspect-context relationship. The fine-grained attention focuses on word-level interactions, allowing the model to identify specific words that contribute to the sentiment towards the aspect. We further enhance MGAN with an *aspect alignment loss* which exploits the inherent relationships between aspects appearing within the same context. Unlike previous approaches that train each aspect-context pair independently, we encourage the model to learn shared representations for aspects that co-occur in similar contexts, reflecting the intuition that these aspects likely share some underlying semantic connections. We evaluate MGAN on three benchmark datasets (SemEval 2014 laptop and restaurant reviews, and a Twitter dataset) and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our results also validate the effectiveness of the aspect alignment loss, showing that leveraging aspect-level interactions significantly improves performance.

Natural language instructions are a powerful and intuitive way to communicate complex tasks to both humans and machines. As robots and virtual assistants become increasingly integrated into our lives, the ability to seamlessly understand and execute these instructions is paramount. However, natural language is inherently ambiguous and context-dependent. A literal interpretation of an instruction often falls short of conveying the speaker’s true intent, requiring listeners to engage in pragmatic inference – reasoning about the speaker’s beliefs, goals, and the common ground shared between speaker and listener (Grice, 1975). For instance, consider the instruction “Bring me the red block.” If only one block is red, the listener naturally infers that the speaker intends that *specific* block, even though the instruction doesn't explicitly state that. This inference is crucial for successful task completion. Recent work in the field of grounded language understanding has made significant strides in enabling machines to follow natural language instructions, particularly in visually grounded environments (Tellex et al., 2011; Misra et al., 2017; Hermann et al., 2017). These models typically rely on large datasets of instruction-following examples to learn a mapping between language and actions. However, they often struggle with ambiguity, generalization to novel situations, and robustness to variations in phrasing. A key limitation of these approaches is the lack of explicit reasoning about the pragmatic aspects of communication. Several researchers have begun to address this limitation by incorporating pragmatic models into instruction-following systems (Andreas et al., 2017; Jia & Liang, 2016; Raux et al., 2005). These models typically employ a framework where a speaker model generates utterances, and a listener model interprets them. Crucially, pragmatic models go beyond simply predicting the most likely interpretation; they consider *why* the speaker would choose to express something in a particular way, and *how* the listener would react to different possible utterances. This often involves modeling the speaker’s beliefs about the listener’s knowledge and capabilities, and simulating the listener’s reasoning process. However, many existing pragmatic models have focused primarily on single-step tasks or simple communicative scenarios. Extending these models to handle complex, sequential tasks – where instructions unfold over multiple steps and require reasoning about long-term goals – presents significant challenges. Furthermore, truly unified pragmatic models that address both instruction generation *and* following remain relatively unexplored. In this paper, we present a unified framework for pragmatic instruction generation and following. We build upon established pragmatic modeling techniques, leveraging learned base listener and speaker models, and extend them to accommodate the sequential structure inherent in many real-world tasks. Our pragmatic speaker utilizes the base listener to simulate the interpretation of candidate instructions, strategically choosing utterances that are likely to be correctly understood. Conversely, our pragmatic listener reasons counterfactually about alternative instructions, allowing it to infer the speaker's intended meaning even in ambiguous situations. We evaluate our models on a diverse set of tasks, demonstrating that explicit pragmatic inference significantly improves performance on both instruction interpretation and generation, achieving state-of-the-art results in human-subject experiments and benchmark datasets.

The rapid growth of online forums has created a vast repository of knowledge, often in the form of questions and their associated discussions. Extracting useful information from this unstructured data – specifically identifying the context surrounding a question and its corresponding answer(s) – is a challenging but vital task. This task has applications ranging from building intelligent FAQ systems to improving search relevance and enabling automated customer support. Existing approaches to information extraction often rely on hand-crafted rules, shallow pattern matching, or supervised machine learning methods requiring large, labeled datasets. However, applying these techniques to the dynamic and often noisy nature of online forum data proves difficult. Rule-based systems struggle to generalize, while supervised learning is hampered by the cost and effort required for annotation. Moreover, the inherent structure of forum threads – the sequential relationships between posts forming a conversation – is often ignored by traditional information extraction models. To address these limitations, we propose a novel and unified model for extracting question contexts and answers from online forum discussions. Our approach is based on Structural Support Vector Machines (SSVMs) (Joachims et al., 2003), a powerful machine learning framework capable of handling complex, structured data. While SSVMs have been successfully applied to various NLP tasks like named entity recognition and relation extraction, their application to the problem of question answering in forum settings remains largely unexplored. Our customization of the SSVM method is designed specifically to leverage the inherent structure of forum threads, offering several key advantages. First, we present a comprehensive graphical representation of thread discussions, explicitly modeling the relationships between posts. This representation allows the model to reason about the conversational flow and identify relevant context and answers based on their position within the thread. Second, we develop specialized inference algorithms tailored to our task, moving beyond the general-purpose inference methods typically used with SSVMs. These customized algorithms improve efficiency and accuracy in identifying question-answer pairs. Finally, our framework is designed for flexibility. By varying the loss function within the SSVM framework, the model can be readily adapted to different task preferences, such as prioritizing precision or recall in answer extraction. We evaluate our approach on a real-world dataset of online forum posts, demonstrating its effectiveness and adaptability. The experimental results show that our method achieves promising performance and significantly outperforms baseline approaches. This work demonstrates the potential of structural learning methods for automatically extracting actionable knowledge from the wealth of information available in online forum discussions. Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) have long been a cornerstone of natural language parsing, providing a principled probabilistic framework for syntactic analysis. However, traditional PCFGs often struggle to adequately model the complexities of natural language due to their limited expressive power. In particular, they are challenged by phenomena such as long-distance dependencies and non-local constraints. Latent-Variable PCFGs (LVPCFG) address these limitations by introducing latent variables which capture hidden syntactic structure and allow the grammar to represent more complex relationships between words. The core idea behind LVPCFG is to augment the standard PCFG framework with a set of hidden, unobserved variables that influence the probabilities of the observed syntactic rules. These latent variables can represent various linguistic abstractions, such as functional tags or semantic roles, which are not directly visible in the surface structure of the language. Despite their potential, learning LVPCFG parameters remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches often rely on the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, which, while widely used, does not come with guarantees of convergence or optimality, particularly in the context of LVPCFG learning. EM can become trapped in local optima, leading to suboptimal grammar parameters and poor parsing performance. Furthermore, the non-convexity of the likelihood function makes it difficult to analyze the algorithm’s behavior and ensure its correctness. Recent work has focused on developing more robust and efficient learning algorithms for LVPCFG, but many still lack theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we introduce a novel learning algorithm for LVPCFG that is provably correct under mild assumptions. Our approach combines the strengths of two well-established techniques: matrix decomposition and EM optimization. First, we employ a matrix decomposition algorithm to estimate the latent variables based on co-occurrence statistics extracted from a training sample of parse trees. The resulting matrix decomposition provides a low-dimensional representation of the latent space, capturing the essential relationships between syntactic constituents. Second, we utilize the EM algorithm to refine the grammar parameters by maximizing a convex objective function derived from the training data and the output of the matrix decomposition. The convexity of the objective guarantees that EM converges to a global optimum, ensuring the correctness of the learned grammar parameters. This combination of techniques allows us to overcome the limitations of traditional EM-based learning algorithms and achieve superior performance on both parsing and language modeling tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showing that it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms. Moreover, we provide theoretical guarantees that establish the convergence and optimality of our learning algorithm, offering a solid foundation for further research in the field of LVPCFG learning. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of probabilistic syntactic modeling and pave the way for more accurate and robust natural language processing systems. Generating natural language from structured data is a long-standing problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from data-to-text summarization (Reiter & Dale, 2000) and report generation (Kukich, 1987) to dialogue systems (Wen et al., 2015). Traditionally, these systems relied on hand-crafted templates and rules to map data values to surface realizations. While these template-based approaches offer precise control over the generated text, they suffer from limited expressiveness, requiring substantial engineering effort to cover a wide range of data combinations and linguistic variations. More recently, statistical machine translation (SMT) techniques (Wubben et al., 2012; van der Linden et al., 2013) have been explored, framing the problem as translating from a pseudo-natural language representing the structured data to the target natural language. However, these methods often require large amounts of parallel data – structured data paired with corresponding natural language descriptions – which is expensive and time-consuming to create. The recent resurgence of neural networks has opened up new avenues for data-to-text generation. Conditional neural language models (NLMs) (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sutskever et al., 2014) have demonstrated promising results in various text generation tasks, including image captioning (Vinyals et al., 2015) and machine translation (Cho et al., 2014). These models learn to generate text conditioned on input features, making them well-suited for generating natural language from structured data. However, applying NLMs to domains with rich, complex data structures and large vocabularies presents several challenges. First, large vocabularies can lead to data sparsity, making it difficult for the model to learn robust word representations. Second, structured data often contains specific entity names and values that are not seen frequently during training, requiring the model to generalize to novel words. In this paper, we introduce a neural model for concept-to-text generation that addresses these challenges and scales to large, rich domains. We focus on the task of biography generation, utilizing a new dataset of over 700k biographical sentences extracted from Wikipedia. This dataset is an order of magnitude larger than existing resources, providing ample data for training a robust neural model. Our model extends conditional NLMs by incorporating copy actions that allow it to transfer sample-specific words directly from the input database to the generated output sentence. This mechanism mitigates the problem of out-of-vocabulary words and improves the fluency of the generated text. Morphology, the study of word formation, is a fundamental component of natural language processing. Accurately modeling morphology is crucial for various downstream tasks, including machine translation, information retrieval, and speech recognition. Traditionally, morphological analysis relied on handcrafted rules and lexicons, which are both labor-intensive to create and difficult to maintain, especially for morphologically rich languages. More recently, statistical and machine learning approaches have gained prominence, offering a more data-driven and adaptable alternative. A core challenge within this domain is morphological paradigm learning – the task of predicting the complete set of inflected forms for a given lemma (base form) or, conversely, identifying the underlying morphological pattern from a set of inflected forms. Existing approaches to supervised morphological paradigm learning can be broadly categorized into two main types: feature-based models and template-based models (Hakkani-Tür et al., 2008). Feature-based models treat morphological inflection as a classification problem, learning to predict morphological features (e.g., number, gender, case) from the lemma and the inflected form. While effective, these models often require extensive feature engineering and can struggle with rare or unseen features. Template-based models, on the other hand, identify and apply pre-defined inflection templates to generate inflected forms. These models are generally simpler but may lack the flexibility to handle irregular or complex morphological patterns. A recent work introduced a novel approach to morphological paradigm learning based on identifying and aligning the longest common subsequence (LCS) within inflection tables (Virga et al., 2022). This non-probabilistic strategy offers a computationally efficient way to generalize from observed inflection tables to unseen words. However, this previous approach focused primarily on the accuracy of reconstructing individual inflected forms, rather than the complete inflection table as a whole. Moreover, it lacked a discriminative component to handle ambiguity and improve overall performance. In this paper, we build upon the LCS-based inflection table generalization approach by integrating it with a discriminative classifier. Our system learns morphological paradigms from labeled examples of inflection patterns – specifically, complete inflection tables – and employs this knowledge to predict the inflection table for unseen lemmas. We hypothesize that combining the strengths of the LCS-based generalization with the decision-making capabilities of a classifier will lead to more accurate and robust morphological paradigm prediction. We evaluate our approach on a diverse set of datasets covering 11 different languages, demonstrating consistently higher accuracies compared to existing methods. These results suggest that our approach provides a viable and efficient method for rapidly creating high-quality morphological resources. References: Hakkani-Tür, D., & Tür, G. (2008). Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for sequence modeling in natural language processing. Their ability to process sequential data and maintain a hidden state representing information about past inputs makes them well-suited for tasks such as language modeling, machine translation, and sentiment analysis (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Rumelhart, Hinton, & Williams, 1986). Among the various RNN architectures, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have proven particularly successful, addressing the vanishing gradient problem that often hinders training of standard RNNs (Gers, Schmidhuber, & Cummins, 2000). LSTMs achieve this through a more complex computational unit incorporating memory cells and gating mechanisms, enabling them to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data. Existing work in applying LSTMs to natural language has largely focused on a linear chain structure, where each word in a sequence is processed sequentially and the LSTM updates its hidden state accordingly. This approach effectively captures sequential dependencies but often overlooks the hierarchical structure inherent in natural language. Human language isn’t simply a linear string of words; rather, words combine to form phrases, phrases combine to form clauses, and so on, ultimately building up to complex sentence structures. This hierarchical organization, often represented by parse trees, provides crucial information about the relationships between words and the overall meaning of a sentence. Capturing this syntactic structure is key to achieving deeper semantic understanding. While techniques like incorporating word embeddings trained on syntactic information (e.g., via dependency parsing) have shown benefits, they often operate at the word level and don’t directly model the compositional nature of meaning. More recently, recursive neural networks (RNNs) have been proposed to directly process tree structures, offering a promising avenue for modeling compositional semantics (Socher et al., 2013). However, these models often struggle with the vanishing gradient problem when dealing with deep trees. The ability to accurately assess the linguistic complexity of words is a cornerstone of many natural language processing applications, particularly those within the educational domain. From tailoring reading materials to a student’s reading level (Bernhardt, 1991) to automatically grading essays (Page, 1966), a reliable measure of word difficulty is invaluable. Traditionally, approaches to estimating word difficulty have relied heavily on corpus statistics, such as word frequency (Zipf, 1935), word length (Flesch, 1951), and the number of syllables (Dale & Chall, 1948). While these metrics provide a reasonable starting point, they are fundamentally limited in their ability to capture the nuances of word knowledge. These methods generally treat word difficulty as a scalar value – a single number representing how “hard” a word is – neglecting the developmental aspect of vocabulary acquisition. A child doesn’t simply “know” or “not know” a word; rather, their understanding evolves over time, progressing from a vague familiarity to a nuanced comprehension of its various meanings and contexts. This gradual acquisition process suggests that word knowledge should be viewed not as a static property, but as a dynamic trajectory, reflecting the stage of learning a word represents. Furthermore, simply identifying a word as “difficult” fails to distinguish *why* it is difficult. Is it a rare word, a word with multiple meanings, or a word with abstract concepts? We argue that a more effective approach to computational lexiconography lies in modeling this developmental trajectory, focusing on the *maturity* of a word’s meaning. We introduce a new paradigm - *word meaning maturity* – which aims to track the degree to which a word’s knowledge is developed at different stages of language learning. This is distinct from the notion of overall “difficulty” and incorporates a temporal dimension, recognizing that a word’s perceived complexity changes as a learner’s linguistic abilities grow. In this paper, we present a computational algorithm for estimating word maturity, grounded in the principles of Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) (Deerwester et al., 1990). Our method leverages the assumption that a word's meaning evolves as it is encountered in increasingly complex textual contexts. By analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of words across different corpora representing various stages of language development, we can infer the maturity level of each word. We demonstrate that our resulting metric not only correlates well with established indicators of word difficulty but, more importantly, captures deeper semantic effects related to language acquisition and comprehension. We posit that this new paradigm offers a more insightful and nuanced perspective on word knowledge, with potential applications extending beyond traditional educational settings to encompass areas such as text simplification, cognitive science, and second language acquisition. The proliferation of social media platforms has created unprecedented opportunities for studying human behavior at scale. These platforms offer readily available data reflecting opinions, beliefs, and interactions – providing a unique window into the complexities of human cognition and social dynamics. However, alongside constructive dialogue and information sharing, social media often showcases less desirable behaviors, such as polarization, hostility, and the expression of rigid, uncompromising beliefs, commonly known as dogmatism. Dogmatism, as a psychological construct, refers to the tendency to cling to beliefs despite evidence to the contrary, often accompanied by intolerance towards differing viewpoints (Adorno et al., 1950). Understanding the expression of dogmatism online is crucial for several reasons. It directly impacts the quality of online discourse, potentially hindering productive conversations and fostering echo chambers. Moreover, identifying dogmatic attitudes can inform interventions aimed at promoting more open-minded and nuanced online interactions. Existing work in psychology offers well-defined theoretical frameworks for understanding the cognitive and affective components of dogmatism. These frameworks suggest that dogmatic individuals often exhibit characteristics like closed-mindedness, a need for cognitive closure, and a resistance to ambiguity (Kruglanski, 1996). However, translating these theoretical concepts into quantifiable signals detectable in social media text and user behavior remains a significant challenge. This paper aims to bridge this gap by systematically exploring linguistic and behavioral features associated with dogmatism in the context of Reddit, a popular online forum. We construct and evaluate statistical models capable of identifying dogmatic comments, leveraging a newly created corpus of Reddit posts annotated for dogmatism via paid crowdsourcing. Our approach is grounded in established psychological theories, with a focus on operationalizing concepts like overconfidence and certainty. Importantly, we also uncover novel signals of dogmatism, such as a reduced tendency to explicitly signal cognitive processes – potentially indicating a lack of self-awareness or an unwillingness to acknowledge uncertainty. Beyond model development, we utilize our trained model to analyze a large-scale dataset of Reddit posts, revealing compelling evidence that dogmatism may be a stable personality trait, manifested consistently across diverse conversational topics for individual users. We also observe a behavioral pattern suggesting that engagement with dogmatic content can itself contribute to an increase in a user’s own dogmatic expression, highlighting a potential feedback loop reinforcing rigid beliefs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of research examining the psychological underpinnings of online behavior and offer valuable insights for building more constructive and tolerant online communities.
