Discourse relations, which describe the relationships between spans of text, are fundamental to understanding coherent text. These relations can be *explicit*, signaled by discourse connectives like “however” or “because”, or *implicit*, where the relationship is not overtly marked and must be inferred by the reader. While explicit discourse relation detection has seen considerable progress, recognizing *implicit* discourse relations remains a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP). The difficulty stems from the need for deeper semantic understanding and reasoning about the context surrounding the arguments involved. Existing approaches to identifying implicit discourse relations often rely on feature engineering, employing hand-crafted features based on syntactic information, semantic roles, and word embeddings (e.g., Stede, 2004; Versley et al., 2009). More recently, neural network models have gained traction, achieving improved performance by automatically learning relevant features from data (e.g., Lin et al., 2016; Lai et al., 2017). These models commonly employ attention mechanisms to focus on the most salient parts of the argument pairs. However, many current neural approaches treat discourse relation recognition as a single-pass process, analyzing the arguments only once. We argue that this single-pass approach is insufficient for capturing the nuances of implicit discourse relations. Human readers rarely comprehend a text—especially when inferring subtle relationships—in a single pass. Instead, they engage in a process of *repeated reading*, revisiting portions of the text, re-evaluating information, and refining their understanding. Different aspects of the arguments become salient at different stages of this process. For example, initial attention might be focused on identifying the core entities involved, while subsequent readings might focus on the verbs and adjectives that express their relationship. Inspired by this human reading strategy, we propose a novel neural network architecture, Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention (NNMA), designed to mimic repeated reading. Our model incorporates external memories to store intermediate representations of the arguments and utilizes a multi-level attention mechanism to dynamically refine its focus on increasingly specific features beneficial for discourse relation classification. This allows the model to revisit the arguments multiple times, gradually honing in on the most relevant information. Experiments on the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDT) dataset demonstrate that NNMA achieves state-of-the-art performance on implicit discourse relation recognition. Furthermore, visualization of the attention weights reveals that the model exhibits behavior consistent with our hypothesis, progressively focusing on different levels of granularity within the arguments during each reading pass. This work not only advances the state-of-the-art but also provides insights into how neural models can be designed to better approximate human cognitive processes involved in text comprehension. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The rapid growth of social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram has generated vast amounts of user-generated text data. This data presents a unique challenge for natural language processing (NLP) applications due to its informal and often non-standard nature. Unlike formal written text, social media posts frequently contain misspellings, abbreviations, slang, and grammatical errors. These variations significantly hinder the performance of standard NLP tools designed for well-formed text. For instance, sentiment analysis, machine translation, and information retrieval systems often struggle with noisy social media data. To address this issue, text normalization – the process of transforming non-standard words into their canonical forms – has emerged as a crucial preprocessing step. For example, normalizing “u” to “you,” “thx” to “thanks,” and “lol” to “laugh out loud” can significantly improve the accuracy of downstream NLP tasks. Early approaches to text normalization relied heavily on manually crafted dictionaries mapping non-standard words to their standard equivalents. However, creating and maintaining such dictionaries is a laborious and time-consuming process, especially considering the ever-evolving nature of social media language. More recently, statistical and machine learning methods have gained prominence. These methods often leverage large corpora of social media text to learn normalization rules automatically. Techniques like edit distance (Wagner and Fischer, 1974), phonetic algorithms (Ross and Willett, 1996), and machine translation models have been successfully applied to this task. Despite these advancements, a significant challenge remains: effectively capturing the contextual information surrounding non-standard words. The meaning and appropriate normalization of a word can often depend on its surrounding words and grammatical structure. For example, “2” could be normalized to “to,” “too,” or “two” depending on the context. In this paper, we introduce a novel unsupervised text normalization approach that explicitly incorporates contextual and grammatical information. Our method constructs a word association graph from a large unlabeled corpus of social media text. This graph encodes the relationships between words, capturing their relative positions and part-of-speech (POS) tags. We combine this contextual and grammatical information with established lexical similarity measures – longest common subsequence ratio, edit distance, and the Double Metaphone algorithm – to perform normalization. Unlike many existing approaches that focus on building normalization dictionaries, our system dynamically normalizes words based on their surrounding context within the input text. We demonstrate that our graph-based approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard text normalization datasets, significantly outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, we show that the system can be tuned to prioritize precision without a substantial loss in recall, making it suitable for applications where accuracy is paramount. Our findings suggest that leveraging both lexical and contextual features, captured through a word association graph, is a key factor in achieving robust and accurate text normalization for social media data. Bilingual dictionary induction (BDI), the task of automatically learning a mapping between the vocabularies of two languages, remains a central challenge in machine translation and cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP). Traditional methods relied on comparable corpora – parallel texts with similar content in two languages – to identify translational equivalents (Gale and Church, 1993; Rapp, 1995). However, the scarcity of comparable corpora for many language pairs necessitates methods that can leverage monolingual resources and weak supervision. Recently, there has been growing interest in utilizing zero-shot learning (ZSL) approaches for BDI, which learn a mapping function between the vector spaces of different languages without relying on direct translational supervision (Lazaridou et al., 2014; Vulić et al., 2015; Hoshen et al., 2018). These ZSL methods typically learn a transformation matrix that aligns the word embedding spaces of two languages. This allows for identifying the nearest neighbor in the target language embedding space for a given word in the source language, effectively creating a bilingual dictionary. Despite the promise of this approach, existing ZSL-based BDI models have consistently fallen short of achieving the accuracy levels seen with supervised or distant supervision methods, particularly for low-resource language pairs. This performance gap motivates the exploration of more effective training objectives and techniques for enhancing the quality of learned mappings. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel approach based on knowledge distillation. Our core idea is to leverage rich resource translation paths – those connecting languages with abundant parallel data – as “teachers” to guide the learning process for low-resource language pairs, which act as “learners.” We propose a distillation training objective that encourages the learner to mimic the behavior of the teacher, effectively transferring knowledge from well-resourced to data-scarce languages. The key advantage of our approach is its flexibility: new teacher translation paths can be seamlessly added to improve the performance for any given low-resource language pair, without requiring re-training of the entire model. Furthermore, recognizing that the quality of monolingual word embeddings significantly impacts the effectiveness of ZSL-based BDI, we also incorporate linguistic information into the vector representations of both the source and target languages. This enhancement helps to disambiguate word senses and improve the alignment of embedding spaces. Through extensive experiments on diverse language pairs, we demonstrate that our knowledge distillation training objective yields substantial performance gains, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 17% compared to baseline ZSL models. Our results highlight the effectiveness of knowledge transfer in bridging the performance gap in low-resource BDI and offer a promising path towards more accurate and scalable cross-lingual tools. ### References Gale, W., & Church, K. Neural dialogue generation has witnessed substantial progress in recent years, largely due to the advancements in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014). These models, often leveraging recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, have demonstrated the ability to generate relatively fluent and contextually relevant responses in open-domain dialogue settings. However, a persistent challenge remains: generating responses that are not only grammatically correct and contextually appropriate, but also engaging, informative, and genuinely human-like. Existing metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), ROUGE (Lin, 2004), and perplexity, while useful for evaluating fluency, often fall short in capturing the nuances of dialogue quality, frequently rewarding generic or repetitive responses that lack meaningful content. For instance, a system generating the consistently safe reply "I don’t know" will often achieve decent scores on standard metrics, despite being a poor conversational partner. This limitation has spurred research into alternative evaluation methods and training paradigms. One promising direction draws inspiration from the Turing test (Turing, 1950), a benchmark for machine intelligence that assesses a machine’s ability to exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable from that of a human. In this work, we explore the application of adversarial training – a technique rooted in game theory – to neural dialogue generation, with the explicit goal of creating systems capable of producing responses that can “fool” a discriminator into believing they were authored by a human. Our approach frames dialogue generation as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem. We train two models concurrently: a *generator* responsible for producing dialogue responses, and a *discriminator* tasked with distinguishing between responses generated by the model and those originating from human conversations. The discriminator provides reward signals to the generator based on its success in classifying responses correctly. This adversarial process encourages the generator to refine its output, striving to create responses that are increasingly indistinguishable from human dialogue. Effectively, the generator is learning to optimize its responses not against a fixed target, but against a dynamic opponent – the discriminator – leading to a more robust and adaptive learning process. Beyond the adversarial training framework, we introduce a novel *adversarial evaluation* metric. This metric utilizes the discriminator’s performance – its ability to identify machine-generated utterances – as a direct measure of dialogue quality. By evaluating the system’s success in “fooling” the adversary, we bypass the limitations of traditional metrics and gain a more nuanced understanding of the generated dialogue’s human-likeness. We also discuss potential pitfalls of such evaluation and propose mitigation techniques. Experiments conducted on several publicly available dialogue datasets demonstrate the superiority of our adversarially-trained system over established baselines, both in terms of traditional metrics and our proposed adversarial evaluation metric. In Section 2, we review related work in neural dialogue generation and adversarial learning. Section 3 details our proposed adversarial training framework and the architecture of the generator and discriminator networks. Section 4 describes the adversarial evaluation metric. Finally, Section 5 presents the experimental results and analysis, followed by concluding remarks in Section 6.

Query spelling correction is a crucial component of modern information retrieval systems. Users frequently mistype search queries, leading to zero or suboptimal search results. The task involves identifying and suggesting corrections for misspelled words within a user’s query, aiming to improve search precision and user satisfaction. Early approaches to query spelling correction primarily relied on generative models, such as noisy channel models (Billmeier & Lapp, 1992; Kukich, 1992). These models estimate the probability of a given correction based on observed errors, typically leveraging edit distance and language model probabilities. While effective, noisy channel models often struggle with context and complex error patterns. Recent advancements have focused on discriminative methods, framing spelling correction as a ranking problem. These approaches learn to distinguish between correct and incorrect query-correction pairs using machine learning techniques (Jones & Lofton, 2008; Cao et al., 2008). A common paradigm involves a two-stage process: First, a noisy channel model or similar retrieval mechanism is employed to generate a set of candidate corrections for each misspelled query word. Second, a discriminatively trained ranker scores these candidates, selecting the most plausible correction. This strategy leverages the strengths of both generative and discriminative models—the former for candidate generation, and the latter for fine-grained ranking. However, this two-stage approach faces a significant limitation: the performance of the discriminative ranker is heavily dependent on the quality and completeness of the candidate list provided by the initial retrieval stage. If the initial retrieval stage has low recall—failing to generate potentially correct corrections—the ranker’s ability to identify the true correction is severely hampered. The ranker is effectively limited to choosing from a pre-defined set, and cannot “discover” corrections that were not initially proposed. Expanding the candidate set can alleviate this issue, but introduces noise and increases computational cost. To address this challenge, we propose a novel discriminative model for query spelling correction based on latent structural Support Vector Machines (SVMs). Our model aims to learn a more robust and expressive ranking function that is less reliant on the completeness of the candidate set. By incorporating latent features, we enable the model to capture complex relationships between queries, corrections, and their underlying error patterns. Furthermore, we explore the use of structural SVMs to leverage the dependencies between individual word corrections within a query, improving overall correction accuracy. The key idea is to move beyond treating each word correction in isolation, and instead model the entire query as a structured entity, allowing for more holistic and accurate correction decisions. This paper details the architecture of our latent structural SVM model, the training procedure, and experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness on benchmark query spelling correction datasets. We show that our approach consistently outperforms existing discriminative rankers, particularly in scenarios where the initial candidate generation stage is suboptimal. Our findings highlight the importance of incorporating structural information and latent features into discriminative models for query spelling correction. billmeier, f., & lapp, m. (1992). Tree-to-tree transduction forms a powerful paradigm for modeling complex linguistic transformations, finding applications in areas such as machine translation, semantic parsing, and question answering. Unlike traditional phrase-based methods, tree-to-tree transducers operate directly on syntactic structures, enabling them to capture long-range dependencies and enforce grammatical constraints more effectively. These transducers typically consist of a set of rules that map source tree fragments to target tree fragments, effectively representing the transformation process. However, constructing these transducers automatically remains a significant challenge. A common approach to inducing tree-to-tree transducers relies on a two-step process: first, establishing word alignments between the source and target strings, and second, employing a heuristic rule extractor to generate rules based on these alignments and the corresponding tree structures (Knight & Graehl, 1997; Chiang, 2005). This method functions well when ample parallel data is available, allowing for reliable word alignment. However, a critical limitation arises when dealing with scenarios characterized by limited training data, large vocabularies, or complex grammatical structures. In such cases, word alignments become increasingly unreliable, leading to suboptimal rule extraction and, consequently, reduced transduction performance. The sparsity of data directly impacts alignment accuracy, and noisy alignments propagate errors throughout the rule induction process. Furthermore, traditional rule extraction heuristics often struggle to generalize effectively from limited training data. They may prioritize rules that perfectly match the training set, overlooking potentially valuable rules that cover broader linguistic patterns. This leads to a phenomenon known as “rule coverage,” where the transducer lacks rules to handle previously unseen linguistic constructions, hindering its ability to generalize to new input. Consequently, there is a growing need for novel rule extraction algorithms that are robust to sparse data and capable of inducing transducers with improved generalization power. In this paper, we present a novel rule extraction algorithm for tree-to-tree transducers based on cost minimization. Our approach moves beyond reliance on explicit word alignments and instead focuses on directly evaluating the quality of potential tree fragment mappings using carefully designed cost functions. By framing rule extraction as a cost minimization problem, we aim to identify the set of rules that collectively minimize the overall cost of transducing the training data. A key contribution of our work lies in the introduction of “back-off states,” which dynamically generate transducer rules during transduction, effectively addressing the issue of limited rule coverage. These back-off states allow the transducer to handle unseen left-hand-side fragments by constructing right-hand-side fragments based on previously learned rules, significantly enhancing its generalization capability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a challenging question answering task over a large knowledge base, showcasing its ability to achieve reasonable syntactic accuracy even with limited training data and demonstrating a marked improvement in overcoming typical rule coverage limitations. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The ability to understand and reason about the world is a hallmark of human intelligence. A crucial component of this ability is *commonsense knowledge* – the vast, largely implicit, understanding of how the world works that humans acquire through everyday experience. This knowledge encompasses causal relationships, temporal orderings, and typical event sequences, enabling us to make predictions, interpret actions, and generally navigate our environment with ease. For Artificial Intelligence, particularly in Natural Language Processing (NLP), replicating this commonsense understanding remains a grand challenge. While significant advances have been made in areas such as syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling, systems still struggle with tasks that require drawing inferences based on unstated assumptions about the world. A particularly difficult aspect of commonsense reasoning concerns understanding the relationships between events. We routinely infer causes and effects, recognize correlations, and anticipate what will happen next based on our accumulated experience. For example, understanding the story fragment “John opened the refrigerator and took out some milk…” requires the commonsense knowledge that refrigerators typically *contain* milk, and that opening a refrigerator is often done *in order to* retrieve something. Current NLP models often lack this ability to seamlessly integrate such commonsense inferences into their reasoning processes. Despite a growing interest in commonsense reasoning within the NLP community (e.g., Davis & Marcus, 1987; Allen, 1995; Chambers & Jurafsky, 2008), progress has been hampered by the lack of appropriate benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. Existing datasets often focus on isolated facts or simple inferences, failing to capture the complex interplay of events found in real-world narratives. Furthermore, many evaluations rely on tasks that can be solved using shallow linguistic patterns or statistical correlations, rather than requiring genuine commonsense understanding. This paper addresses this critical need by introducing a new framework for evaluating story understanding and script learning, which we term the "Story Cloze Test." This test presents a system with a four-sentence story and challenges it to select the most plausible fifth sentence, effectively requiring the model to predict what happens next based on its understanding of the preceding narrative. To facilitate this evaluation, we have created a novel corpus called *ROCStories*, comprising 50,000 five-sentence stories grounded in everyday life experiences. ROCStories is unique in two key respects. First, it is specifically designed to capture a rich tapestry of causal and temporal commonsense relations between everyday events. Second, it is a curated collection of *high-quality* stories, written to be engaging and coherent, lending themselves not only to evaluation but also to story generation tasks. Our experimental results, which pit a range of baseline and state-of-the-art models against the Story Cloze Test, reveal that even sophisticated approaches based on shallow language understanding struggle to achieve satisfactory performance. We discuss the implications of these findings for the development of more robust and genuinely intelligent language understanding systems, and outline potential avenues for future research.

Dialogue is a fundamental aspect of human communication, and the success of any interactive system – be it a virtual assistant, a tutoring agent, or a sophisticated chatbot – hinges on its ability to engage in coherent and cooperative exchanges with users. However, dialogue is not always cooperative. Participants may exhibit non-cooperative behavior for a variety of reasons, ranging from deliberate attempts to mislead or obfuscate (Clark & Brennan, 1991) to unintentional failures in understanding or attentiveness (Sacks et al., 1974). Understanding and modeling non-cooperation is therefore crucial for building truly robust and intelligent dialogue systems. Prior work on non-cooperation in dialogue has largely fallen into two main categories. The first focuses on *task-related* non-cooperation, examining behaviors like refusing to answer questions directly or providing deliberately unhelpful information (Traum & Lerman, 2003;Bunt et al., 2015). These approaches often rely on predefined rules or knowledge about the specific task being performed. The second category attempts to model non-cooperation through the introduction of *special* rules defining non-cooperative actions (e.g., intentionally changing the subject, providing irrelevant responses) (Parekh & McRoy, 2009;Raux et al., 2005). While insightful, these approaches require significant manual effort to define and maintain the necessary rules, and they often struggle to generalize to new dialogue contexts. In contrast to these approaches, this paper proposes a novel method for measuring non-cooperation grounded in the principles of dialogue game theory (Braver, 1988; van Eijk & Steenbeek, 2016). Our core idea is that linguistic non-cooperation can be quantified by the extent to which dialogue participants *deviate from established conventions* regarding appropriate conversational behavior. Specifically, we focus on the fulfillment of conversational obligations—the implicit rules governing how participants should respond to different types of utterances (e.g., answering questions, acknowledging statements). Rather than defining separate rules for non-cooperative behavior, we start from rules for *normal* or *correct* dialogue behavior – defined as a dialogue game – and measure the degree to which participants comply with these rules. This framework offers several advantages. First, the rules for cooperative dialogue can, in principle, be derived automatically from a corpus of naturally occurring cooperative dialogues, reducing the need for manual annotation. Second, it provides a continuous measure of non-cooperation, rather than a binary classification, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of conversational behavior. Third, it is relatively domain-independent, as the underlying principles of conversational obligation are largely universal. We evaluate our model on a corpus of political interviews, a domain frequently characterized by strategic non-cooperation. The results are encouraging, demonstrating that the model can accurately predict the degree of cooperation exhibited by one of the dialogue roles (the interviewer) and successfully identify which interlocutor in the conversation was comparatively more cooperative. We believe that being able to quantitatively measure cooperation has broad implications for the analysis of natural language interactions and the development of more human-like dialogue systems. This work opens up potential applications ranging from automatically assessing the quality of customer service interactions to powering virtual assistants capable of intelligently responding to uncooperative users. Automated essay scoring (AES) has emerged as a promising technique to alleviate the burden on educators and provide timely feedback to students (Page, 1966; Shermis & Burstein, 2005). Traditionally, AES systems relied on handcrafted features based on linguistic properties of essays, such as grammatical correctness, vocabulary richness, and essay structure (Landauer et al., 1998; Weng et al., 2005). Recently, with the advancements in deep learning, more sophisticated AES systems have been developed utilizing recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers to learn more complex representations of essay content (Attali & Burstein, 2016; Dong et al., 2017). However, a significant challenge remains: the performance of AES systems is often tied to the specific prompt used during training (Chung et al., 2016; Williamson et al., 2012). When an AES system trained on essays addressing one prompt is applied to grade essays written in response to a different prompt, a noticeable drop in accuracy typically occurs. This phenomenon is known as domain shift, and it hinders the widespread adoption of AES in educational settings. The root cause of this domain shift is the inherent variability in prompts. Different prompts elicit different writing styles, content focus, and rhetorical strategies from students. Consequently, a model trained on one prompt may not generalize effectively to essays written on another. Manually grading a substantial number of essays for each new prompt is resource-intensive and time-consuming, rendering it impractical for many educational institutions. Therefore, the development of effective and efficient domain adaptation techniques is crucial for creating robust AES systems that can handle a diverse range of prompts. Domain adaptation aims to reduce the performance gap between the source domain (the prompt on which the AES system was initially trained) and the target domain (the new prompt for which the system needs to make predictions) (Ben-David et al., 2010). Previous attempts to address this challenge in AES include feature engineering techniques to create prompt-invariant representations (Williamson et al., 2012) and transfer learning approaches leveraging pre-trained language models (Dong et al., 2017). However, these methods often require significant feature engineering or may not fully capture the complex relationships between essays and scores across different prompts. In this paper, we propose a novel domain adaptation technique for AES based on Bayesian linear ridge regression. Our approach leverages the correlation between essay features and scores in both the source and target domains to learn a shared representation that minimizes the impact of domain shift. We evaluate our technique on the publicly available Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms several baseline domain adaptation algorithms, establishing it as a competitive default approach for addressing the domain shift problem in AES. Furthermore, we analyze the performance gain provided by incorporating correlated linear regression, providing insights into the effectiveness of this approach.

Named Entity Recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text, is a core component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. In recent years, statistical machine learning models – particularly those employing Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) and, more recently, deep learning architectures like Bi-LSTMs – have achieved state-of-the-art performance on NER tasks (Lample et al., 2016; Nadeau & Sekine, 2007). A key advantage of these statistical models is their ability to generalize to unseen entities; that is, to correctly identify and classify entities that were not explicitly present in the training data. This generalization capability relies heavily on the model’s capacity to learn robust features capturing the lexical and contextual characteristics of named entities. However, despite their successes, these models are not immune to errors, particularly when faced with ambiguous entities or instances where feature sets inadvertently favor incorrect entity types. For example, the word "Apple" could refer to the fruit, the technology company, or a record label. A model relying solely on lexical features and surrounding context might misclassify "Apple" as a fruit when it is, in fact, referring to Apple Inc. in a specific news article about technology. This issue becomes particularly acute when applying NER systems to new domains or low-resource languages where training data is scarce, and the model’s ability to learn accurate discriminating features is limited. To address these limitations, we propose leveraging the vast knowledge contained within Wikipedia, a collaboratively edited, open-content encyclopedia. Wikipedia offers a rich resource of structured knowledge about entities, including their types and relationships with other entities. We hypothesize that integrating Wikipedia entity type information into the NER process can significantly enhance the accuracy of the system, especially for unseen entities and in low-resource scenarios. Central to our approach is the construction of accurate and comprehensive multilingual Wikipedia entity type mappings. While Wikipedia provides a wealth of information, establishing a clear correspondence between Wikipedia entities and their corresponding types across multiple languages is a non-trivial challenge. Existing resources like DBpedia offer some entity type information, but coverage can be incomplete and language-dependent. Our method addresses this gap by automatically building these mappings from weakly annotated data, requiring minimal human effort or language-specific expertise. Notably, the built mappings can be extended to new languages without requiring any additional annotation. Utilizing these multilingual mappings, we develop several methods to integrate Wikipedia entity type information into a standard NER pipeline. We evaluate our approaches on NER systems trained for six different languages, demonstrating consistent improvements in accuracy, particularly on unseen entities and in low-data settings. Our experimental results show significant gains, with F1 score improvements of up to 18.3%, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach. This work contributes a novel application of Wikipedia as a multilingual resource for NER, along with a practical method for constructing high-quality entity type mappings, ultimately leading to more robust and accurate NER systems.

Automatic keyphrase generation (KPG) is the task of automatically extracting or generating a set of keyphrases that concisely summarize the main topics of a given document. KPG has become increasingly important with the explosion of online information, as it can significantly improve information access, document understanding, and search engine optimization. Traditional approaches to KPG can be broadly categorized into extractive and abstractive methods. Extractive methods (e.g., Turney, 2000; Witten et al., 2008) identify existing phrases within the document that are most representative of its content, typically based on statistical measures like term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) or graph-based ranking algorithms. While these methods are simple and efficient, they are limited by the vocabulary of the source document and may fail to capture abstract concepts or generalize beyond the specific wording used. Abstractive methods, on the other hand, attempt to generate new phrases that summarize the document’s content, offering greater flexibility and the potential to capture more nuanced information. Recent advancements in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanisms (Luong et al., 2015; Rush et al., 2015) have shown promising results in abstractive KPG, treating the task as a neural machine translation problem where the input is the source document and the output is a sequence of keyphrases. However, despite these advances, current seq2seq models for KPG often suffer from several limitations. One major issue is the lack of consideration for the inherent relationships and correlations between keyphrases. Existing models typically generate keyphrases independently, leading to redundancy, where similar or overlapping phrases are generated, and poor coverage, where important aspects of the document are not adequately represented in the generated keyphrase set. For example, a model might generate both "natural language processing" and "NLP" without recognizing their semantic equivalence. Furthermore, the generated keyphrases may lack coherence, failing to form a cohesive and meaningful summary of the document’s core topics. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel seq2seq architecture for keyphrase generation, named CorrRNN, designed to explicitly capture and exploit the correlations among multiple keyphrases. Our model incorporates two key mechanisms: a coverage vector that tracks which parts of the source document have already been summarized by previous phrases, and a mechanism to condition the generation of each keyphrase on the preceding generated phrases. By enforcing these correlation constraints, CorrRNN aims to improve both the accuracy and diversity of the generated keyphrase sets, resulting in more informative and coherent summaries. Our experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets demonstrates that CorrRNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art keyphrase generation methods, achieving substantial improvements in both precision and recall, and generating more diverse and contextually relevant keyphrases. This work represents a step towards more effective and nuanced abstractive keyphrase generation, facilitating improved document understanding and information access.

Graphical models provide a powerful framework for reasoning about complex systems with inherent dependencies. However, exact inference in these models is often intractable, necessitating the use of approximate inference techniques. Variational inference and belief propagation (BP) are two prominent approaches, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Belief propagation, particularly loopy belief propagation (LBP), is attractive due to its simplicity and scalability, but its lack of guaranteed convergence can lead to inaccurate results. Expectation propagation (EP) builds upon LBP by maintaining more accurate messages through a carefully designed projection step, leading to improved performance in many applications (Minka, 2001). However, the computational cost of EP can be substantial, especially in models with complex factorizations or high-dimensional variables. A key challenge in applying EP is managing the complexity of the messages. The projection step, which enforces a particular functional form for the messages, can become computationally expensive as the message complexity increases. To address this, we introduce Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel algorithm that leverages structured-sparsity penalties to encourage simpler, more tractable messages. By penalizing message complexity, PEP aims to strike a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. This is particularly relevant in models where high-dimensional variables require complex messages to capture dependencies accurately. This work focuses on applying PEP to graphical models over strings, a domain prevalent in natural language processing, computational linguistics, and bioinformatics. String-valued random variables pose unique challenges for approximate inference due to their discrete and often high-dimensional nature. Traditional approaches often rely on approximations that either sacrifice accuracy or lead to intractable computations. We propose to approximate finite-state distributions, which naturally represent sequential data like strings, using variable-order n-gram models. These models offer a flexible and efficient way to capture local dependencies within the string, while the PEP framework controls their complexity. Our approach adaptively determines the order of the n-gram models based on the data and the penalty strength, fostering a trade-off between model capacity and computational cost. By incorporating a structured-sparsity penalty into the EP update equations, we encourage the selection of lower-order n-grams whenever possible, leading to simpler messages and faster convergence. This is significant as higher-order n-grams significantly increases the computational expense of message passing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PEP on phonological inference problems, a challenging task in speech recognition and language modeling. Empirical results show that PEP achieves substantial speedups compared to previous related algorithms, including conventional EP and variable-order Markov models, without sacrificing significant accuracy. These improvements highlight the benefits of incorporating structured sparsity into the EP framework for graphical models over strings. The remainder of this paper details the PEP algorithm, its instantiation for string-valued variables with variable-order n-gram approximations, and presents experimental results demonstrating its performance on phonological inference. I focused on establishing the context, highlighting the limitations of existing methods, introducing the core idea of PEP, justifying its application to string-valued graphical models with n-gram approximations, and previewing the experimental results.

Relation extraction (RE) aims to identify semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text. It is a core task in natural language processing (NLP) with applications in knowledge base population, question answering, and information retrieval (Zeng et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2017). Traditionally, relation extraction relies heavily on manually annotated datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to create. The lack of large-scale, high-quality annotated data hinders the development of robust and generalizable RE systems. To alleviate this issue, distant supervision (DS) has emerged as a promising paradigm. Distant supervision automatically generates training data by leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) such as Freebase or Wikidata. The core idea is to align entities mentioned in text with entities in the KB and assume that sentences mentioning related entities express the corresponding relation. For example, if a KB states that “Barack Obama” *born_in* “Honolulu”, then all sentences mentioning both “Barack Obama” and “Honolulu” are considered to express the *born_in* relation, and are used as positive training instances. While DS significantly reduces the need for manual annotation, it inherently introduces noise into the training data. This noise arises from the incorrect alignment assumption. Not every sentence mentioning related entities necessarily expresses the intended relation. For instance, the sentence “Barack Obama visited Honolulu in 2016” mentions both “Barack Obama” and “Honolulu”, but does not express the *born_in* relation. Such instances are referred to as noisy labels, and can negatively impact the performance of RE models trained with DS data. Various techniques have been proposed to mitigate the impact of noisy labels in DS-RE, including multi-instance learning (Mintz et al., 2009), selective instance learning (Riedel et al., 2013), and attention mechanisms (Lin et al., 2016). However, these methods often require careful feature engineering or complex model architectures. More recently, neural network-based approaches have shown promising results in DS-RE (Zeng et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2017), and focus on learning better representations of sentences and entities. Despite these advances, the underlying issue of noisy labels remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we argue that the noise introduced by distant supervision is not random, but rather structured and exhibits dynamic patterns during the training process. We propose to model these dynamic patterns using a transition matrix, which captures the probability of transitioning between different levels of noise. Crucially, our approach learns this dynamic transition matrix without any explicit supervision about the noise itself, leveraging a novel curriculum learning strategy. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods for DS-RE, significantly improving relation extraction performance.

Text readability is a cornerstone of effective communication, impacting comprehension, engagement, and overall user experience. While significant research has been dedicated to assessing and improving readability in languages like English (Flesch, 1954; Dale & Chall, 1948), the study of readability in other languages, particularly those with complex linguistic structures like Bangla, remains relatively underexplored. Bangla, spoken by over 265 million people worldwide, presents unique challenges to computational readability assessment due to its morphological richness, complex sentence structures, and a writing system that differs significantly from Latin-based scripts. Existing readability measures developed for English often fall short when applied directly to Bangla, highlighting the need for language-specific models and a deeper understanding of the factors influencing readability in this context. Traditionally, text readability has been assessed using a set of ‘classic’ features – such as average sentence length, average word length, and syllable count – derived from surface-level text characteristics. However, recent research suggests that a wider range of ‘non-classic’ features, reflecting more nuanced linguistic properties like lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and semantic coherence, can significantly improve readability prediction (Si et al., 2017; McNamara et al., 2006). Moreover, the perception of readability is not solely determined by the text itself, but also by the characteristics of the reader, including their educational background, prior knowledge, and reading proficiency. A text considered easy for a seasoned academic might pose significant challenges for a novice learner. Despite the acknowledged importance of both text properties and reader background, very few studies have attempted to jointly model these factors for Bangla readability assessment. Existing work mostly focuses on adapting existing English readability formulas to Bangla (Islam & Islam, 2013), which, as previously mentioned, often yields suboptimal results. Recognizing this gap, this paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the influence of target reader background and various text features on text readability in Bangla. We address this by first constructing a novel, carefully annotated Bangla readability dataset comprising 135 documents, each evaluated by 50 readers representing two distinct background groups – high school students and university students. We systematically identify and analyze a comprehensive set of 20 text features, categorizing them into ‘classic’ and ‘non-classic’ groups. Through preliminary correlation analysis, we demonstrate that the influence of these features on perceived text hardness varies significantly between the two reader groups. Utilizing Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) techniques, we then develop and evaluate separate models tailored to each reader background, exploring different feature combinations to assess their comparative contributions. Our findings establish that the perception of text difficulty is largely dependent on the reader’s background, and that incorporating both ‘classic’ and ‘non-classic’ features into a computational model can significantly improve readability prediction accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to comprehensively investigate the interplay between reader background and text features for Bangla readability assessment, paving the way for the development of more accurate and personalized readability tools for this increasingly important language.

The ability to accurately identify and connect mentions of the same real-world entity across multiple documents is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing. This task, known as cross-document coreference resolution (CCR), is essential for numerous downstream applications, including information extraction, question answering, and knowledge base construction. Simultaneously, named entity linking (NEL) aims to disambiguate mentions of entities within text by linking them to their corresponding entries in a structured knowledge base (KB), such as Wikipedia or Freebase. If a mention does not correspond to an entry in the KB, it is often linked to a ‘null’ entity. Historically, CCR and NEL have been largely treated as independent problems, with separate methodologies developed for each. However, this separation overlooks the substantial synergies that exist between the two tasks. Consider, for example, a scenario where multiple mentions of “Barack Obama” appear across a collection of news articles. CCR aims to identify all these mentions as referring to the same entity. NEL, on the other hand, seeks to link those mentions to the specific “Barack Obama” entry in a knowledge base. Successful CCR can significantly enhance NEL by providing valuable contextual information – knowing that several mentions refer to the same entity increases confidence in the KB link. Conversely, accurate NEL can improve CCR by providing a common, unambiguous identifier for entities, facilitating the identification of coreferent mentions even when their surface forms differ. Despite this intuitive connection, joint modeling of CCR and NEL has remained a relatively underexplored area of research. Existing approaches often rely on pipeline architectures where CCR is performed first, followed by NEL, or vice versa. These pipelines suffer from error propagation: errors made in the first stage can negatively impact the performance of the subsequent stage. Moreover, they fail to fully exploit the feedback loop between the two tasks – information gained during NEL is not typically incorporated back into the CCR process. This paper introduces C3EL (Cross-Document Co-reference and Entity Linking), an unsupervised framework designed to overcome the limitations of traditional, sequential approaches. C3EL explicitly models the interplay between CCR and NEL by iteratively refining both tasks in a joint manner. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of each task to improve the other, creating a synergistic effect. Specifically, we incorporate information from the CCR stage (clusters of coreferent mentions) into the NEL process, and utilize the global context obtained from NEL to refine the CCR clusters. Our framework operates through an iterative algorithm, focusing on the highest-confidence unresolved mentions in each iteration. This allows us to prioritize the most informative instances and efficiently converge towards an optimal solution. We evaluate C3EL on both news-centric and web-centric corpora, comparing its performance against state-of-the-art baseline systems for both CCR and NEL. The experimental results demonstrate significant performance gains across both datasets, validating the effectiveness of our joint modeling approach. In Section 2, we review related work in both CCR and NEL, highlighting the limitations of existing approaches. Section 3 details the proposed C3EL framework, including the iterative algorithm and the feature engineering process. Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results, followed by a thorough analysis in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in machine learning, particularly within the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). The core idea behind MTL is to leverage the commonalities and differences across multiple related tasks to improve learning efficiency and predictive performance (Caruana, 1997;Zhang and Yeung, 2010;Collobert and Weston, 2008). In the context of neural networks, MTL typically involves sharing parameters—specifically, the lower layers—across multiple task-specific output layers. This shared representation allows the model to learn general features applicable to all tasks, while the task-specific layers capture the unique characteristics of each individual task. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated the effectiveness of MTL in various NLP applications, including sentiment analysis (Liu et al., 2016), part-of-speech tagging (Plank et al., 2016), and question answering (Yih et al., 2017). However, a significant challenge in MTL lies in the potential for *negative transfer*—where learning one task hinders the performance on another (Rosenberg et al., 2010). This interference arises when tasks are too dissimilar, leading to the shared representation being contaminated with irrelevant or misleading information. Existing MTL approaches often employ hard parameter sharing, where the same layers are used for all tasks without any form of control over which features are shared. While this simplicity is attractive, it lacks the flexibility to adaptively determine *what* to share, potentially leading to suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-task convolutional neural network architecture that incorporates a “Leaky Unit” mechanism. Inspired by biological neural networks, our Leaky Unit allows for controlled information flow between tasks, effectively acting as a dynamic gate that filters irrelevant features. Specifically, the Leaky Unit possesses both “memory” – preserving useful features – and “forgetting” mechanisms – suppressing distracting information. This enables the model to selectively share features deemed beneficial for each task, mitigating the risk of negative transfer. Our proposed approach moves beyond simple parameter sharing by introducing a task-specific weighting scheme applied to the feature flow between layers. Rather than forcing all tasks to utilize the same representation, we allow each task to actively decide which features to borrow from others, ensuring that the shared representation remains informative and discriminative. We validate the effectiveness of our Leaky Multi-Task Network on five diverse text classification datasets, demonstrating consistent performance gains over existing MTL baselines. These empirical results highlight the importance of adaptive feature sharing in MTL and confirm the benefits of our proposed mechanism for learning what to share across tasks. It is worth noting that recent works have begun to explore attention mechanisms (Chen et al., 2016) and gating functions (Luong et al., 2015) in MTL to modulate information flow. However, these approaches often require significant computational overhead or are limited in their ability to effectively capture long-range dependencies between tasks. Our Leaky Unit offers a computationally efficient and conceptually intuitive alternative for achieving adaptive feature sharing in MTL.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has seen significant advances in recent years, with syntax-based methods achieving state-of-the-art performance (Yamada & Knight, 2001; Chiang, 2005; Zhang et al., 2006). A cornerstone of many syntax-based SMT systems is the synchronous context-free grammar (SCFG), which captures correspondences between the syntactic structures of source and target languages. However, efficient decoding with SCFGs poses a significant computational challenge. The standard approach to address this challenge relies on converting the SCFG into Chomsky Normal Form (CNF). CNF guarantees that decoding can be performed in cubic time complexity using algorithms like the Earley parser or the CKY parser. The conversion to CNF often involves a process called synchronous binarization, first introduced in (Zhang et al., 2006). This technique expands non-terminal symbols into smaller components, effectively transforming the grammar into a CNF equivalent. While ensuring tractable decoding time, synchronous binarization introduces a major drawback: it dramatically increases the grammar size. This inflation of the grammar directly translates to increased constant factors in the decoding time, impacting practical performance. (DeNero et al., 2009) attempted to mitigate this issue by introducing Lexical Normal Form (LNF), a generalization of CNF that allows for certain non-binary rules while still maintaining cubic time decoding complexity. However, the conditions under which LNF guarantees cubic time complexity are often implicit and not fully explored. In this paper, we delve into the theoretical underpinnings of LNF and clarify the assumptions required for efficient decoding. We demonstrate that LNF can be further extended to an even broader class of grammars, which we term “scope-3” grammars, without sacrificing cubic-time decoding guarantees. This extension allows for a more natural representation of linguistic dependencies and avoids some of the restrictive constraints of LNF. Crucially, we show that by simply pruning rules that fall outside the “scope-3” definition from a grammar extracted using the GHKM method (Galley et al., 2004), we can achieve significant improvements in translation performance compared to systems employing traditional synchronous binarization. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach not only maintains computational efficiency but also results in higher quality translations, offering a pragmatic solution to the long-standing trade-off between grammar size and decoding performance in syntax-based SMT. This work contributes a refined understanding of grammar normalization techniques for SCFGs and presents a practical method for improving translation quality without compromising decoding speed. It is important to note that, while synchronous binarization is a well-established technique, its effect on performance has been limited. Building upon DeNero et al.'s findings, we demonstrate how to push those limitations further. The following sections detail the theoretical framework surrounding LNF and scope-3 grammars, the pruning procedure for GHKM-extracted grammars, and the experimental results showcasing the benefits of our approach.

Math word problems have long served as a challenging benchmark for natural language understanding and reasoning. These problems require not only comprehending the textual description but also translating it into a formal mathematical representation and subsequently solving the resulting equation. Traditionally, approaches to automated math word problem solving have heavily relied on hand-crafted features, complex rule-based systems, and extensive domain knowledge (Shi and Wenyin, 2002; Kushner et al., 2000). These methods often involve multiple stages, including problem classification, quantity extraction, equation formulation, and solution derivation. The reliance on manual feature engineering is particularly burdensome, requiring significant effort to adapt the system to new problem types or domains. Statistical learning methods, leveraging machine learning techniques like Support Vector Machines (SVMs) or Bayesian Networks, have offered some improvement by automating parts of the process (Lei and Zong, 2014; Dong et al., 2015). However, even these approaches typically require substantial feature engineering, such as identifying keywords, recognizing numerical values, and extracting relational phrases. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable success in various NLP tasks, including machine translation, image recognition, and speech recognition (Hinton et al., 2012; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Sutskever et al., 2014). The ability of deep neural networks to automatically learn hierarchical representations from raw data has spurred interest in applying these techniques to math word problem solving. Several preliminary studies have explored the use of deep learning models for specific subtasks, such as quantity extraction (Xu et al., 2016) or equation generation (Watanabe et al., 2016). However, a complete end-to-end deep neural solver, capable of directly translating a word problem into a solvable equation, has remained a significant challenge. In this paper, we present a novel deep neural solver based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to tackle math word problems. Our approach differs significantly from previous statistical learning methods by eschewing complex feature engineering and directly learning the mapping from word problem text to equation templates. We employ an encoder-decoder architecture, utilizing an RNN to encode the input word problem and another RNN to decode the corresponding equation template. This allows the model to capture the semantic relationships between words and mathematical operations without requiring explicit linguistic analysis. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid model that combines the RNN-based approach with a similarity-based retrieval model. This leverages pre-existing knowledge by retrieving similar problems and their corresponding equation templates, providing additional guidance to the RNN decoder. Experimental results on a large-scale math word problem dataset demonstrate that our RNN model and hybrid model significantly outperform state-of-the-art statistical learning methods, achieving substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency. Our results highlight the potential of deep learning for automated reasoning and problem solving, and offer a promising direction for future research in this field.

Estimating the prevalence of different classes within a collection of unlabeled data is a fundamental problem in machine learning with applications spanning diverse domains. From assessing public opinion on social media to estimating disease incidence rates from clinical records, accurate prevalence estimation is crucial for informed decision-making. For instance, understanding the proportion of negative reviews for a product can inform marketing strategies, while knowing the prevalence of a rare disease aids in resource allocation for healthcare systems. Traditionally, prevalence estimation relies on aggregating predictions from individual discriminative classifiers trained on labeled data (Raykar et al., 2010;Platt, 1968;Fong et al., 2017). These methods typically produce point estimates of the class proportions, often employing techniques like label smoothing or calibration to improve accuracy. However, a significant limitation of these approaches is the neglect of uncertainty. Real-world classifiers are inherently imperfect, and their predictions are subject to error. Ignoring this uncertainty can lead to overly confident prevalence estimates and potentially flawed inferences. A scientifically sound approach must quantify and propagate this uncertainty, providing confidence intervals or other measures of statistical significance. In this work, we address this limitation by introducing a novel framework for prevalence estimation grounded in generative probabilistic modeling. Our approach moves beyond simply aggregating classifier outputs and instead focuses on explicitly modeling the underlying data-generating process. The interplay between gender, power, and language has been a long-standing area of inquiry in the social sciences, particularly in sociolinguistics (Lakoff, 1975; Tannen, 1990; West & Zimmerman, 1983). Existing research suggests that gender isn’t simply a demographic attribute, but a key social category that significantly shapes communication patterns and the ways in which individuals enact and perceive power dynamics. Specifically, studies have indicated that women, often navigating structurally unequal power contexts, may employ distinct communicative strategies – such as hedging, politeness markers, and indirectness – to mitigate potential conflict, build rapport, and maintain social harmony (Coates, 2002; Holmes, 1992). Conversely, men are often observed to adopt more direct and assertive communication styles, potentially reflecting or reinforcing their positions of authority. While these observations are well-documented in studies of spoken language and small group interactions, applying these insights to large-scale textual data, like workplace email, presents unique opportunities and challenges. The Enron email corpus, a publicly available dataset of over 500,000 emails from employees of the Enron corporation, has become a valuable resource for computational social science research (Klimt & Yang, 2004; Lazer et al., 2009). Its rich content provides a naturalistic setting to investigate communication patterns in a real-world organizational context. However, a significant limitation of using the Enron corpus for studying gender and power dynamics is the lack of readily available gender information for a substantial proportion of the email senders. Existing work has largely relied on manual annotation or limited external databases resulting in incomplete gender coverage. In this paper, we address this limitation by presenting a novel and reliable extension to the Enron corpus, successfully identifying the gender of senders for approximately 87% of all messages. Utilizing this expanded dataset, we empirically test two specific hypotheses derived from the sociolinguistic literature regarding gender and power: (1) women managers are more likely to employ face-saving communicative strategies than their male counterparts, and (2) women utilize language more explicitly than men to establish and sustain social connections. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of “gender environment” into the computational analysis of written communication. Recognizing that the gender composition of an email thread itself can influence communication dynamics, we define gender environment as the proportion of female and male participants involved in a given conversation. We demonstrate that discerning patterns in manifestations of power can differ substantially depending on the surrounding gender environment. Finally, we showcase the utility of incorporating gender information into the challenging task of automatically predicting the direction of power between individuals engaged in email exchanges. Our experiments demonstrate that models augmented with gender features achieve improved performance, highlighting the importance of considering social identity characteristics in understanding complex social phenomena such as power dynamics within organizational communication. In sum, this work provides a comprehensive investigation of how gender and its social context interact with power manifestations in a large-scale, real-world communication dataset, offering valuable insights for both computational social science and sociolinguistics.

Human sentence processing is a remarkably efficient cognitive skill. Despite the inherent ambiguity of natural language, humans can rapidly and accurately construct a meaningful representation of a sentence as they read it, word by word. This ability suggests that cognitive mechanisms underlying parsing are not simply applying exhaustive search over all possible syntactic structures, as traditional chart-based parsers do. Instead, several cognitive models propose that human parsing relies on a limited capacity working memory, incremental hypothesis formation, and a preference for simple, locally optimal structures (Frazier, 1987; Gardenfors, 2007). Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) have emerged as a promising computational framework for modeling these cognitive aspects of human parsing (Roark, 2001; Hale, 2001). HHMMs offer a bounded model of working memory, representing incomplete parse structures as probabilistic states. They also allow for incremental hypothesis formation by maintaining multiple active states in parallel, each corresponding to a different possible parse. Crucially, despite these constraints, HHMM parsers can achieve parsing accuracies comparable to more computationally intensive chart-based techniques (Roark, 2001; Bod, 2002). However, a successful cognitive model must not only accurately *parse* sentences but also *predict* human parsing behavior. Specifically, the model should be able to quantify the difficulty a reader experiences at each point in the sentence, as reflected in reading times. Several metrics have been proposed to capture this “complexity” of a sentence, including surprisal (Levy, 2008), probability (Hale, 2001), and derivational complexity (McDonald et al., 2005). These metrics are based on the idea that less probable or more complex syntactic structures will lead to increased processing effort and longer reading times. This paper investigates the ability of a right-corner HHMM parser to produce such complexity metrics. We focus on a right-corner HHMM parser, a specific implementation that mirrors aspects of human parsing more closely than some other variations. We define standard complexity metrics within the HHMM framework, such as surprisal based on the probability of the current state. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric, “embedding difference”, rooted in the hypothesis that the hidden states in the HHMM represent elements held in syntactic working memory. We theorize that changes in the internal representation of the phrase structure – reflected as changes in the state embeddings – will correlate with increases in processing difficulty. Our results demonstrate that HHMM surprisal consistently outperforms other evaluated metrics in predicting human reading times. Importantly, we also show that embedding difference makes a significant and *independent* contribution to predicting reading times, supporting the hypothesis that HHMM states encode meaningful information about the current syntactic context and that alterations in this context impacts parsing difficulty. These findings further validate the HHMM as a cognitive plausible model of human sentence processing and provide insights into the representation of syntactic structure in working memory.

In an increasingly data-driven world, the collection, use, and sharing of personal information by websites and online services have become ubiquitous. To inform users about these practices, companies typically publish privacy policies – lengthy legal documents intended to outline their data handling procedures. However, these policies are notoriously difficult to understand (McDonald & Cranor, 2008; Soltani et al., 2012). A primary barrier to comprehension is the pervasive use of vague language (Litman, 2008; Jensen & Potts, 2011). Terms like “may,” “reasonable,” and “appropriate” lack precise definitions, leaving considerable ambiguity about the actual data practices employed. This opaqueness not only hinders users' ability to make informed decisions about their privacy but also creates challenges for regulators tasked with ensuring compliance with privacy laws such as the GDPR and CCPA. Existing work has examined aspects of privacy policy analysis, including readability assessment (Gupta et al., 2014), topic modeling (O’Neil & Schollaert, 2015), and automated compliance checking (Caron et al., 2019). However, relatively little attention has been paid specifically to the *automatic detection of vagueness* within these documents. Manual review of privacy policies to identify vague language is time-consuming and expensive, making it impractical for large-scale analysis. Therefore, there is a clear need for computational methods that can automatically pinpoint vague words and sentences, enabling a more systematic understanding of privacy practices. In this paper, we address this need by presenting the first dedicated study on automatic vagueness detection in privacy policies. We begin by constructing a novel, human-annotated corpus of vague words and sentences extracted from a diverse collection of privacy policies. This corpus serves as a crucial resource for training and evaluating our models. We then investigate a range of approaches for identifying vagueness. We compare context-agnostic methods, which rely on lexical features alone, with context-aware models that leverage the surrounding text to better understand the meaning of words and sentences. Furthermore, we explore the application of Auxiliary-Classifier Generative Adversarial Networks (AC-GANs) – a powerful generative modeling technique – to characterize sentence-level vagueness. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches, achieving significant improvements over baseline methods. We analyze the results to gain insights into the linguistic patterns associated with vagueness in privacy policies. Finally, we offer practical suggestions for mitigating vagueness and enhancing the usability of these critical documents, ultimately empowering users with greater control over their personal data. Our contribution is threefold: (1) introduction of the first public dataset of vague language in privacy policies, (2) development and evaluation of novel models for automatic vagueness detection, and (3) provision of actionable recommendations for improving the transparency and clarity of privacy policies. Correcting errors in natural language text is a fundamental task in natural language processing with applications ranging from spell checkers and grammar correction tools to assisting non-native speakers in writing more fluent and accurate text. While substantial progress has been made in identifying errors (e.g., through statistical language modeling, or more recently, neural network approaches), the task of *correction* remains challenging, particularly when dealing with context-sensitive errors. A crucial component of many error correction systems is the generation of candidate corrections – the set of possible replacements for the erroneous word or phrase. The size and quality of this candidate set profoundly impact the performance of the downstream correction module, typically a discriminative classifier that scores each candidate based on its likelihood given the surrounding context. A common, straightforward approach to candidate generation is to consider all possible options from the vocabulary. However, in many cases, this leads to a prohibitively large candidate set, introducing noise and increasing computational cost without necessarily improving accuracy. For example, in the task of preposition correction, where the goal is to identify and rectify incorrect preposition choices, considering all prepositions as candidates for any given error is highly inefficient. Most prepositions will be contextually inappropriate, and including them as candidates dilutes the signal for the correct choice. This paper focuses on the problem of generating more focused candidate sets for preposition correction, specifically targeting errors made by non-native English speakers. Non-native speakers often exhibit systematic errors reflecting transfer from their native language and difficulties in mastering the nuances of English grammar. These errors are often different in nature from the typographical errors that plague native speakers, requiring tailored approaches to correction. We hypothesize that by leveraging patterns observed in a corpus of non-native text, we can identify likely preposition confusions and generate candidate sets limited to those prepositions which are plausible corrections given the context and the observed error patterns. We present several methods for restricting candidate preposition sets. These methods utilize an annotated corpus of non-native English text to filter candidate prepositions based on their observed validity as corrections, and further refine the sets by considering the frequency with which particular preposition confusions occur within the corpus. We demonstrate through empirical evaluation that restricting candidates to those observed in the non-native data significantly improves both precision and recall compared to considering all prepositions as candidates. Furthermore, we show that incorporating the likelihood of each preposition confusion leads to the most effective candidate generation strategy, resulting in higher correction accuracy. The work presented here represents a step toward more robust and efficient error correction systems for non-native English writers. <!-- no_think --> <!-- I have followed the requested format and length constraints.
