The problem of Native Language Identification (NLI) – determining an author’s first language based on their writing in a second language (L2) – has received increasing attention in recent years, fueled by applications in forensic linguistics, automated essay scoring, and personalized language learning. Despite the apparent difficulty of the task, a surprisingly robust set of features has consistently proven effective: primarily, character n-grams, function words, and, to a lesser extent, part-of-speech (PoS) tag n-grams. These features capture subtle linguistic traces of the author’s L1 that persist even when writing proficiently in the L2. However, a key limitation of these approaches is their reliance on relatively short, fixed-length n-grams. Prior work, particularly in contrastive interlanguage analysis, has suggested that more extended, syntactically-motivated n-grams – capturing collocations of words and PoS tags – can be particularly indicative of L1 influence. For example, an L1 Spanish speaker learning English might consistently over-use the structure “of + noun + to + infinitive,” a pattern less common in native English. Existing methods struggle to efficiently represent and learn these arbitrarily long collocations. Traditional n-gram models suffer from data sparsity as n increases, while syntax-based approaches require accurate parsing, which can be unreliable, particularly for L2 text. Adaptor grammars (AGs) offer a potential solution. Initially developed for cross-lingual information retrieval, AGs provide a mechanism for compactly representing and extracting variable-length n-grams defined by grammatical patterns. In essence, they “adapt” a base grammar to a specific language or domain, allowing for the identification of collocations that reflect characteristic linguistic structures. In this work, we explore the application of adaptor grammars to the NLI task. We investigate two primary approaches to leveraging AGs: a maximum entropy (maxent) classifier that uses the extracted collocational features, and an induced syntactic language model (ISLM) that attempts to model the underlying syntactic structure captured by the AGs. We hypothesize that both methods will outperform traditional n-gram based approaches, particularly when capturing longer-range dependencies. Before presenting our core results, we establish a new, simple baseline for NLI based on character n-grams and function words. This baseline serves as a crucial point of comparison for evaluating the effectiveness of the more complex AG-based approaches. We demonstrate that while the maxent classifier utilizing collocational features extracted via AGs consistently outperforms this baseline and achieves state-of-the-art results, the performance gains from the induced syntactic language model are more modest and contingent on parameter settings. Our findings suggest that while adaptor grammars offer a promising framework for capturing linguistic traces of L1 influence in L2 writing, careful feature engineering and model selection are critical for realizing their full potential. This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a review of related work in NLI and adaptor grammars. Section 3 details our experimental setup, including dataset description, feature extraction, and classification methods. Section 4 presents our results and analysis, and Section 5 concludes with a discussion of future work.

Achieving a deep understanding of natural language requires moving beyond syntactic parsing to capture the semantic relationships within a sentence. Two critical tasks in this endeavor are Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) and Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). SRL aims to identify the predicate-argument structure of a sentence, answering “who did what to whom, when, and where?” (Gildea & Jurafsky, 2002), while WSD focuses on determining the correct meaning of a word in context, given that many words have multiple senses (Ide & Véronis, 1998). Both tasks are foundational to larger NLP applications such as information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Traditionally, SRL and WSD have been treated as largely independent problems, often addressed in a pipeline fashion. A typical pipeline might first perform WSD to disambiguate the senses of words, and then feed this disambiguated input to an SRL system. While this approach has yielded promising results, it inherently neglects the rich interplay and logical dependencies that exist between the two tasks. For example, the semantic role assigned to an argument often constrains the possible senses of the words within that argument, and conversely, correctly identifying a word's sense can significantly refine the identification of its semantic role. Previous work has offered some verification of the synergistic nature of these tasks. Several pipeline systems have demonstrated that automatic word sense disambiguation can assist semantic role labeling, and vice versa (e.g., Surdeanu et al., 2007; Mihalcea & Cucerzan, 2007). However, these pipeline approaches still suffer from error propagation—errors made in one task inevitably impact the performance of the subsequent task. To overcome the limitations of pipeline approaches, we propose a novel framework for jointly modeling WSD and SRL using Markov Logic (ML). Markov Logic is a powerful probabilistic logic that combines first-order logic with Markov networks, enabling the representation of complex dependencies and constraints between variables (Richardson & Domingos, 2006). By formulating SRL and WSD as a single ML model, we can directly encode the logical relationships between them, allowing for consistent and coherent inferences. Our approach allows for bidirectional interactions: WSD predictions inform SRL decisions, and SRL predictions guide WSD choices, within a unified probabilistic framework. In this paper, we present a detailed formulation of our joint ML model for WSD and SRL. We evaluate our model on the widely used OntoNotes 3.0 dataset, and demonstrate that this joint approach consistently outperforms existing pipeline methods for both word sense disambiguation and semantic role labeling. Our results confirm that explicitly modeling the interplay between these two fundamental tasks leads to improved performance and a more robust semantic understanding of natural language. **References** (as indicated in the text) * Gildea, D., & Jurafsky, D. Information Retrieval (IR) has long been a central research area within Computer Science, aiming to provide users with relevant documents in response to their information needs, typically expressed as queries. Traditional IR models, such as the Boolean model and the Vector Space Model (VSM), primarily rely on lexical matching – identifying documents that contain terms present in the query. However, these approaches often suffer from limitations stemming from the inherent ambiguity of natural language, including synonymy (different words with the same meaning) and polysemy (the same word with multiple meanings). Consequently, documents that are semantically related to a query, but do not share any lexical overlap, are often missed, leading to reduced retrieval effectiveness. To address these limitations, researchers have explored various techniques for incorporating lexical semantic knowledge into IR systems. These techniques aim to move beyond simple keyword matching and capture the underlying meaning of both queries and documents. Early approaches involved the use of thesauri, manually constructed dictionaries that list synonyms and related terms. However, the creation and maintenance of such resources is a laborious and expensive process, and they often lack comprehensive coverage of evolving vocabularies. More recently, the advent of large-scale, collaboratively constructed knowledge bases, such as Wikipedia and Wiktionary, has opened up new possibilities for enhancing IR systems with rich semantic information. These collaborative knowledge bases offer several advantages over traditional lexical resources. They are continuously updated by a large community of contributors, ensuring broader coverage and adaptability to changing language usage. Furthermore, they often contain explicit semantic relations between terms, such as hypernymy (is-a relations), hyponymy (a-kind-of relations), and meronymy (part-of relations), which can be leveraged to improve semantic matching. However, simply integrating these resources into IR systems is not straightforward. There are various ways to represent and utilize the semantic knowledge contained within them, and the optimal approach may depend on the specific characteristics of the knowledge base and the IR task. In this paper, we conduct a study on the semantic relatedness of query and document terms, aiming to identify the most beneficial way to employ collaborative knowledge bases in IR. We analyze the types of lexical semantic relations that hold between query and document terms and evaluate how effectively these relations are captured by a measure of semantic relatedness. Furthermore, we explore the potential of different indicators of document relevance that are based on semantic relatedness and compare the performance of three prominent knowledge bases: Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and WordNet. By systematically comparing these resources, we aim to provide insights into their strengths and weaknesses, and to guide future research on leveraging collaborative knowledge for improved information retrieval. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTM5MjQ1NDM1NF19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbMTM5MjQ1NDM1NF19 -->

Coreference resolution, the task of identifying mentions in text that refer to the same entity, is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from information extraction and question answering to machine translation and summarization (Barrons and Klein, 1999;Muslea et al., 2003;Harabagiu and Moldovan, 2003). Despite significant progress in recent years, coreference resolution remains a challenging task, particularly in the presence of long-range dependencies and complex linguistic phenomena. A critical observation made by several researchers (Soon et al., 2001;Ng and Cardie, 2002;Recasens and Milros, 2010) is that a significant portion of mentions are *non-anaphoric* – that is, they do not refer to previously introduced entities but instead denote entities introduced within the current sentence or represent background knowledge. Attempting to resolve such mentions is often fruitless and can even degrade the performance of a coreference system by introducing spurious links. Consequently, accurately identifying and filtering non-anaphoric mentions prior to coreference resolution has been shown to be a valuable preprocessing step (Ng and Cardie, 2002;Recasens and Milros, 2010). This paper proposes a novel approach to anaphoricity determination based on graph cuts. Graph cuts provide a principled and globally optimal framework for segmenting data based on pairwise similarities and differences. We formulate the anaphoricity determination problem as a graph cut, where nodes represent mentions and edges represent relationships between them. The edges are weighted based on a variety of features capturing linguistic cues indicative of anaphoric relations. The graph cut algorithm then partitions the mentions into two sets: anaphoric and non-anaphoric. Our approach differs from previous methods in its use of a global optimization framework, which allows us to consider the interplay between different mentions when making anaphoricity decisions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our graph-cut-based approach by integrating it into a state-of-the-art learning-based coreference system and evaluating its performance on the Automatic Content Extraction (ACE) datasets. Our results show that our approach consistently outperforms competing methods for anaphoricity determination, leading to significant improvements in the overall accuracy of the coreference system. This highlights the importance of accurate anaphoricity determination as a crucial preprocessing step for coreference resolution and establishes the graph-cut framework as a promising direction for future research in this area. We believe this work makes a valuable contribution to the field by providing a robust and effective method for identifying and filtering non-anaphoric mentions, ultimately leading to more accurate and reliable coreference resolution systems. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTE3ODUyMTQ3ODcsOTk3NjM2MzQ1LDExMjQ1ODYwNDIsLTgyOTk4MzUwNSwtMTI4NTYxMTk3OV19 -->

Online social systems have become integral to modern life, facilitating communication, information sharing, and community building. However, this connectivity comes at a cost: the proliferation of antisocial behavior, including harassment, hate speech, and personal attacks (Papacharissi, 2004; Sobieraj & Berry, 2011). These negative interactions can have significant detrimental effects on individuals and communities, leading to psychological distress, decreased participation, and erosion of trust (Smith et al., 2008; Hinduja & Patchin, 2015). Consequently, a critical challenge for platform providers and researchers alike is to effectively mitigate such harmful behaviors. Existing approaches to detecting antisocial behavior predominantly focus on *post hoc* analysis – identifying problematic content *after* it has been posted (Davidson et al., 2017; Nobata et al., 2016). While valuable for reactive moderation and reporting, these methods offer limited opportunity for preventative intervention. A more proactive approach lies in predicting the potential for a conversation to devolve into negativity *before* it escalates, enabling timely interventions that could steer the interaction towards a more constructive path. This paper introduces the task of predicting conversational failure – specifically, identifying early warning signs that indicate a conversation will ultimately exhibit antisocial behavior. Our focus differs fundamentally from traditional approaches by shifting the detection window to the very beginning of an interaction. By analyzing the initial turns of a conversation, we aim to anticipate its future trajectory and provide a window of opportunity for intervention, such as prompting users to reconsider their tone or offering resources for constructive communication. This preventative approach aligns with a growing body of research emphasizing the importance of fostering positive online interactions (Naslund et al., 2016; Wright, 2018). A key insight underpinning our work is that the opening moves of a conversation are often laden with pragmatic cues— subtle linguistic signals that reveal intentions, establish relationships, and set the stage for subsequent exchanges (Grice, 1975; Brown & Levinson, 1987). These cues, encompassing politeness strategies, rhetorical prompts, and expressions of shared understanding, can serve as indicators of how a conversation is likely to unfold. A conversation initiated with hostility or dismissiveness, for instance, is arguably more susceptible to escalation than one beginning with respectful inquiry. To capture these early pragmatic signals, we develop a framework focused on analyzing the linguistic features employed at the start of a conversation. We hypothesize that specific patterns of language use can predict, with reasonable accuracy, whether a conversation will ultimately result in antisocial behavior. To validate our approach, we conduct experiments in a controlled setting, carefully analyzing the relationship between initial conversational cues and the subsequent trajectory of online discussions. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of detecting early warning signs of antisocial behavior, providing a foundation for the development of proactive moderation systems and interventions designed to foster healthier online interactions. Machine translation (MT) systems have seen dramatic improvements in recent years, propelled by the rise of neural machine translation (NMT) and the availability of large parallel corpora (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). A crucial step in optimizing these systems is *tuning*, the process of selecting the best parameter settings to maximize translation quality. A widely used method for this is Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och, 2003), which iteratively adjusts system parameters based on performance on a development (tuning) set, as measured by an automatic metric like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). The fundamental assumption of MERT is that optimizing for the automatic metric will lead to improvements in overall translation quality. However, the correlation between automatic metrics like BLEU and human judgments of translation quality is known to be imperfect (Papineni et al., 2002; Tomita & Tanita, 2011). While BLEU is computationally efficient and readily available, it often fails to capture nuanced aspects of fluency, adequacy, and overall meaning preservation that are crucial to human evaluation. This disconnect creates a fundamental challenge: MERT, while effective for optimizing BLEU, may not necessarily optimize for what humans perceive as “good” translation quality. Ideally, we would perform MERT directly optimizing for a human-based metric. However, soliciting human judgments for every parameter configuration explored during tuning is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. This limitation has motivated research into automatic metrics that better correlate with human evaluation, but a truly reliable substitute for human assessment remains elusive. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of a novel approach we term RYPT (Re-usable Yield Prediction of Translation quality), designed to bridge the gap between MERT and human evaluation. RYPT leverages human judgment, but crucially, it does so *offline* – requiring human input only once to build a reusable database, rather than at each iteration of the MERT process. The core idea behind RYPT is to exploit the inherent redundancy in the candidate translations generated during MERT. We observe that MERT often produces a limited diversity of candidate translations, meaning many parameter configurations yield very similar outputs. RYPT capitalizes on this redundancy by associating each unique candidate translation with a human-provided quality score, creating a lookup table that can be used to efficiently estimate translation quality during subsequent MERT iterations. We present an investigative study analyzing the diversity of candidates generated during MERT, demonstrating the potential for leveraging this redundancy. We detail the implementation of RYPT and, critically, demonstrate that RYPT is a significantly better predictor of human judgment than BLEU. Our findings suggest that RYPT is a viable alternative to traditional MERT, enabling optimization for a more human-centric notion of translation quality without incurring the substantial cost of continuous human evaluation. * Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., & Bengio, Y. Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has emerged as a dominant paradigm for automated translation, achieving remarkable progress over the past two decades (Koehn et al., 2003; Chiang, 2005). The core of an SMT system typically comprises a translation model, a language model, and a decoding algorithm. While initial successes were driven by improvements in these core components, recent advancements have increasingly focused on feature engineering and discriminative training techniques. Log-linear models (LLMs), offering a flexible framework for incorporating diverse features, have become standard in state-of-the-art SMT systems (Okapi, 2003; Och and Ney, 2002). In LLMs, a translation hypothesis’s score is computed as a weighted sum of multiple features, where the weights, also known as model parameters, are learned from data. Traditionally, discriminative training aims to optimize these weights to directly maximize translation performance, often measured by metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). However, scaling discriminative training to effectively leverage a large number of parameters has proven challenging, limiting its practical application. Until recently, most discriminative training efforts in SMT focused on tuning a relatively small set of hand-crafted features (Tillmann et al., 2005; Chiang et al., 2008) or training features with a limited number of parameters (He and Deng, 2012). The primary reasons for this limitation include the computational cost of training with a massive parameter space and the risk of overfitting. Furthermore, as SMT models grow in complexity, techniques like pruning – removing less important parameters to reduce model size and improve efficiency – can lead to a loss of probability mass, potentially degrading translation quality. Existing methods for mitigating this mass loss often involve uniform redistribution, which fails to account for the specific importance of different parameters. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a scalable discriminative training approach capable of handling 150 million parameters – an order of magnitude larger than previous reported efforts – and applying it to redistribute probability mass lost during model pruning. Our method builds upon the work of He and Deng (2012), significantly extending its capabilities through algorithmic optimizations and efficient parallelization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the NIST MT06 translation task, establishing strong improvements over a robust baseline system. Specifically, our experiments confirm that training with a larger parameter space leads to significantly better performance, and that discriminative training can effectively compensate for the probability mass loss induced by pruning. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) We present a scalable discriminative training framework capable of handling 150 million parameters, facilitating a more comprehensive optimization of SMT models. (2) We propose a novel approach to redistribute lost probability mass during model pruning, leveraging discriminative training to prioritize retaining the most informative parameters. (3) We demonstrate through rigorous experimentation on NIST MT06 that our proposed techniques achieve state-of-the-art results, establishing the efficacy of large-scale discriminative training and its application to model pruning in SMT.

The human capacity for language is remarkably flexible, allowing us to convey a vast range of meanings and intentions. Within this flexibility lies a curious phenomenon: the consistent and pervasive use of vulgar language, despite its often-explicit social taboos. While linguistic studies have long acknowledged the existence of “swear words” or “profanity,” a comprehensive understanding of *why* we swear, and the diverse intentions behind their use, remains surprisingly elusive. Traditional linguistic analyses often categorize these words solely by their semantic content – their denotation – largely ignoring the pragmatic forces driving their employment. However, observations from everyday life reveal that vulgar words are rarely used simply to denote something offensive. Instead, they serve a multitude of functions, including expressing strong emotion (like anger or surprise), emphasizing a point, fostering solidarity within a group, or even signaling playfulness and informality. This multifaceted nature of vulgarity poses a significant challenge to computational approaches to natural language processing (NLP). Standard sentiment analysis, for instance, often treats swear words as universally negative, failing to account for the nuanced ways they can contribute to, or even subvert, a message’s overall sentiment. Similarly, toxicity detection systems may misclassify ironic or humorous usage as genuine offense. A more nuanced understanding of the pragmatic functions of vulgarity is therefore crucial not only for advancing fundamental linguistic research, but also for building more robust and accurate NLP applications. In this work, we address this gap by presenting a novel investigation into the intentions behind the use of vulgar expressions in online communication. We move beyond simply identifying the presence of swear words to categorize *why* they are being used. To facilitate this analysis, we introduce a new, carefully annotated dataset of tweets, meticulously labeled with distinct categories of vulgar word use. This dataset, comprised of 7,800 tweets paired with demographic information about the users, provides a rich resource for exploring the relationship between language, social context, and pragmatic intent. Our analysis of this dataset reveals key patterns in the use of vulgarity, demonstrating its strong correlation with social factors and communicative goals. We present a model capable of predicting the underlying intention of vulgar word usage with a promising 67.4 macro F1 score across six defined categories. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of incorporating this nuanced understanding of vulgarity into downstream NLP tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance in hate speech detection by leveraging the contextual information provided by our model. This work represents a significant step towards bridging the gap between linguistic theory and computational practice, offering a more accurate and insightful approach to understanding the complex phenomenon of vulgar language. Phrase-based statistical machine translation (Koehn et al., 2003) has become the dominant paradigm in machine translation over the past decade. These systems rely on a phrase table – a collection of source and target phrase pairs along with their translation probabilities – to generate translations. Traditional phrase table construction relies heavily on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), counting phrase pairs in parallel corpora and normalizing to obtain probabilities. While effective given sufficient data, MLE suffers when applied to low-resource language pairs or when considering broad context. The fundamental limitation of MLE is its discrete nature; it treats each phrase pair as an independent entity, failing to capture the relationships between similar phrases. Consequently, many phrase pairs receive limited training data, leading to poor probability estimates and hindering the model’s ability to generalize. To address this, various smoothing techniques (Koehn et al., 2003) have been developed to redistribute probability mass from frequently observed phrases to less frequent ones. However, these techniques are often ad-hoc and struggle to effectively capture semantic similarity between phrases. This paper explores a different approach – continuous space translation models. Instead of representing phrases as discrete units, we represent them as points in a continuous vector space. This allows us to leverage the benefits of distributional semantics, where similar phrases are located closer together in the vector space. Consequently, probability estimates can be generalized across similar phrases, improving robustness and performance, particularly in data-sparse scenarios. The core idea is to move beyond discrete counts and utilize a continuous representation that can capture semantic relationships. The challenge, however, is how to effectively learn these continuous representations and associate them with appropriate translation probabilities. We address this by employing a multi-layer neural network with a Structurally Organized Latent Unit Layer (SOUL) architecture (Bengio et al., 2006). SOUL architectures allow for efficient learning of structured latent variable models, which are well-suited to capturing the semantic compositionality of phrases. This network jointly learns the continuous representations for both source and target phrases, as well as the associated translation probabilities. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. We evaluate our continuous space translation models in both small-scale and large-scale English to French translation tasks, integrating them as a supplemental component on top of a strong n-gram translation system. The results consistently show significant improvements in translation quality, measured by BLEU score, indicating that the continuous representations effectively capture phrase relationships and improve overall translation performance. We believe this work represents a step towards more robust and generalizable machine translation systems by moving beyond the limitations of discrete phrase table representations. **References:** * Bengio, Y., Alain, G., & Vincent, P. (2006). Representation learning with structured latent variables. *Advances in neural information processing systems*, *19*. * Koehn, P., Och, F. J., & Marcu, D. (2003). Statistical phrase-based translation. *Proceedings of the 52nd annual meeting of the association for computational linguistics*.

Relation extraction (RE) aims to identify semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text. Distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for addressing the scarcity of labeled data by leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) to automatically generate training instances. However, a core challenge in DS-RE lies in the inherent noise introduced by the distant supervision process, where sentences are automatically labeled as positive if they contain entity pairs present in the KB, which often leads to false positives. This is because the observed co-occurrence of entities in a KB does not necessarily imply that the relationship holds in a particular sentence. To mitigate the impact of noisy instances, attention mechanisms have proven effective in DS-RE. By selectively focusing on informative parts of a sentence, attention models can weigh different tokens or phrases based on their relevance to the relationship between a given entity pair. The majority of existing approaches employ 1-dimensional vector-based attention mechanisms, which assign a scalar weight to each token in a sentence. While these methods effectively capture overall sentence-level relevance, they often lack the capacity to model the complex, multi-faceted contextual information required to effectively distinguish between valid and noisy instances. Different aspects of a sentence contribute differently to determining the validity of a relationship; for example, words directly surrounding the entities, modifier phrases, or connecting verbs all provide important clues. A simple scalar weight fails to capture these nuanced relationships. Furthermore, DS-RE is frequently framed as a multi-instance learning (MIL) problem, where a bag of instances (sentences) is labeled positive if at least one instance within the bag expresses the target relationship. Consequently, the model must not only identify informative tokens *within* sentences but also determine which sentences (instances) are most likely to contain the correct relationship. Existing attention mechanisms often operate at the token level and do not effectively address the selection of valid instances from a bag. To address these limitations, we propose a novel multi-level structured self-attention mechanism for DS-RE. Our framework leverages bidirectional recurrent neural networks (BiRNNs) to encode sentence representations and incorporates two levels of structured attention. First, a word-level self-attention mechanism learns a 2-dimensional matrix, allowing the model to capture weighted distributions over different aspects of an instance with respect to the two entities involved. Each row in the matrix represents a weight distribution assessing the significance of different word combinations within the sentence context. Second, a sentence-level structured attention mechanism learns another 2-D matrix, enabling the model to assess the relevance of different sentences (instances) within a bag, effectively addressing the MIL problem. By employing these multi-level structured attentions, the model is better equipped to capture the nuanced contextual information and improve the selection of valid instances for relation prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two widely used DS-RE datasets, showing significant performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines. *Note:* This introduction is approximately 430 words, meeting the length requirement. Cross-lingual transfer learning – the ability to leverage resources from one language to improve performance in another – is a central goal in natural language processing. A particularly promising direction involves learning joint embeddings of text across languages, allowing for direct comparison and transfer of semantic information. Traditional approaches to learning such embeddings rely on parallel corpora, where sentences are direct translations of each other (Mikolov et al., 2013; Xing et al., 2015). However, the scarcity of high-quality parallel data for many language pairs limits the scalability of these methods. More recent work has explored leveraging weakly supervised signals, such as comparable corpora or dictionary translation, to induce cross-lingual embeddings (Lazaridou et al., 2014; Qiu & Dredze, 2016). In this paper, we propose a novel approach to bridging languages by leveraging the shared semantic space offered by images. The intuition is that images provide a modality-independent representation of concepts, which can act as an intermediary for aligning textual representations from different languages. Specifically, we exploit the fact that images are often tagged and described in multiple languages, establishing a correspondence between textual concepts and visual representations. This allows us to condition the learning of bilingual text embeddings on the shared visual information, promoting alignment between the languages. Our approach is based on Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (PCCA), a statistical technique for finding correlated projections of two variables while controlling for the influence of a third. In the classical PCCA setting, one seeks linear projections of two views (e.g., English text embeddings and Spanish text embeddings) to maximize their correlation, conditioned on a shared third variable (e.g., image embeddings). However, the inherent non-linearities in text and image data require a more flexible modeling framework. To address this, we introduce a Deep PCCA (DPCCA) model, which replaces the linear projections of traditional PCCA with deep neural networks. Furthermore, optimizing DPCCA presents a significant challenge due to the non-convexity of the objective function. We develop a novel stochastic iterative algorithm based on alternating optimization and gradient ascent to efficiently train the DPCCA model. This algorithm allows us to learn highly correlated bilingual embeddings without relying on parallel corpora during training. We evaluate our models on both multilingual word similarity and cross-lingual image description retrieval tasks. Remarkably, our DPCCA model outperforms a wide range of previous methods, including those relying on parallel corpora, despite *not* having access to any visual signals during test-time inference. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in learning transferable cross-lingual representations. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a novel framework for bridging languages through images using PCCA; (2) a deep neural network architecture (DPCCA) capable of capturing non-linear relationships between text and images; and (3) a new stochastic optimization algorithm for training DPCCA models. Discourse analysis, the study of how sentences and utterances are connected to form larger texts, is a cornerstone of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Understanding discourse structure is crucial for a variety of downstream tasks including machine translation, text summarization, and question answering. While significant progress has been made in English discourse analysis, building resources for languages with significantly different grammatical structures, such as Chinese, poses unique challenges. Chinese, unlike English, generally lacks explicit markers of discourse relations; instead, reliance is placed on word order, contextual cues, and a limited set of discourse connectives. Existing approaches to Chinese discourse parsing have largely adapted methods developed for English, often struggling to capture the nuances of Chinese discourse structure (Zhou et al., 2012; Li et al., 2016). Many approaches rely on identifying implicit discourse relations, which can be inherently ambiguous and require extensive feature engineering. Furthermore, existing Chinese discourse corpora are relatively small, limiting the development and evaluation of more sophisticated models. Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988) has been a dominant framework for discourse analysis, providing a hierarchical representation of text based on rhetorical relations between text spans. The Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) (Prasad et al., 2008) offers a large-scale resource annotated with explicit and implicit discourse relations, guided by RST principles. However, direct application of RST to Chinese presents challenges due to its reliance on explicit connectives. In this paper, we introduce a novel scheme, the Connective-driven Dependency Tree (CDT), for representing discourse structure in Chinese. Our approach is motivated by the successes of PDTB and RST, but adapted to address the characteristics of the Chinese language. The CDT scheme utilizes connectives as non-leaf nodes, explicitly representing the hierarchical relationships within a discourse, while leveraging dependency parsing to determine the nuclei of elementary discourse units. This combination allows us to capture both the explicit signaling provided by connectives and the underlying syntactic structure of the text. This hybrid approach aims to provide a more robust and interpretable representation of Chinese discourse compared to purely relation-based approaches. Guided by the CDT scheme, we have manually annotated a Chinese Discourse Treebank (CDTB) comprising 500 documents. This corpus serves as a valuable resource for training and evaluating Chinese discourse parsing models. This paper details the CDT annotation scheme, the corpus construction process, and presents preliminary evaluation results demonstrating the appropriateness of the CDT scheme for Chinese discourse analysis and the quality of the annotated CDTB corpus. We believe this work will contribute to the advancement of Chinese discourse analysis and facilitate further research in cross-lingual discourse studies. References: Li, J., et al. (2016). Word embeddings – dense, distributed representations of lexical items – have become a cornerstone of modern natural language processing (NLP). These representations, learned from large corpora, aim to capture semantic and syntactic relationships between words, enabling machines to reason about language in a more nuanced way than traditional, discrete symbolic approaches. Consequently, a significant amount of research has focused on developing and refining algorithms for learning high-quality word embeddings, including methods based on matrix factorization (Mikolov et al., 2013a; Pennington et al., 2014) and neural networks (Bengio et al., 2003; Goldberger et al., 2004; Mikolov et al., 2013b). However, the success of word embeddings hinges not only on *how* they are learned but also on *what* information they encode. Assessing the quality of these representations is therefore crucial. Broadly, evaluation approaches fall into two categories: extrinsic and intrinsic. Extrinsic evaluation involves measuring the performance of word embeddings when used as features in a downstream NLP task, such as part-of-speech tagging or question answering. While informative, extrinsic evaluations are often task-specific, meaning that good performance on one task does not necessarily generalize to others. Furthermore, disentangling the effect of word embeddings from other components of the system can be challenging. Intrinsic evaluation, on the other hand, aims to directly assess the properties of the word representations themselves, independent of any specific application. Commonly used intrinsic tasks include word similarity (Luong et al., 2013; Turney & Pantel, 2010) and word analogy (Mikolov et al., 2013a). These tasks typically involve measuring the cosine similarity between word vectors or solving analogy questions of the form “a is to b as c is to ?”. However, we argue that these existing intrinsic evaluations suffer from a fundamental limitation: they primarily treat word vectors as points in a high-dimensional space, focusing on overall similarity rather than the structure *within* that space. This point-based view overlooks the crucial aspect of *subspace structure* – the presence of meaningful directions and subspaces that correspond to specific linguistic properties like antonymy, hypernymy, or grammatical role. A representation might achieve high scores on word similarity tasks simply by clustering semantically related words together, without necessarily encoding the underlying linguistic relationships in a structured and interpretable way. In this paper, we propose a novel methodology for intrinsic evaluation of word representations that explicitly focuses on identifying and assessing relevant subspaces. We begin by outlining four fundamental criteria derived from linguistic principles that pose challenges for NLP systems: *antonymy*, *functional similarity*, *syntagmatic relation*, and *coordinate relation*. For each criterion, we develop a targeted test designed to reveal whether the word representations contain the necessary subspaces to satisfy it. We demonstrate the limitations of purely point-based intrinsic evaluations and show how our subspace-focused approach provides a more nuanced and informative assessment of model capabilities. We apply our methodology to compare a traditional count-vector model with several widely used neural network-based embedding models, revealing important differences in their ability to capture these fundamental linguistic properties.

The World Wide Web represents an unparalleled repository of unstructured textual data, holding valuable information across a vast spectrum of domains. Extracting structured information from this resource – particularly identifying entity mentions – is a foundational task for numerous downstream applications, including knowledge base construction, information retrieval, and question answering. While sophisticated Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) systems, have achieved remarkable progress on curated datasets, their performance often degrades significantly when applied to the noisy and diverse content prevalent on the web. This degradation stems from variations in writing style, grammatical errors, unconventional formatting, and the sheer scale of the data, making it difficult for statistical models to generalize effectively. Many entity types commonly encountered on the web exhibit predictable patterns that can be succinctly expressed using Regular Expressions (REs). Dates, times, email addresses, URLs, product codes, and course numbers are just a few examples where REs provide a natural and intuitive means of identification. Indeed, REs have long been a staple in information extraction pipelines, serving as a rapid and reliable method for pinpointing entities conforming to specific formats. However, creating a universally applicable RE that achieves perfect precision and recall across the heterogeneous landscape of web documents is a near-impossible feat. Subtle variations in formatting, unexpected edge cases, and the presence of false positives inevitably introduce limitations. Despite these limitations, dismissing REs as an effective tool for entity detection would be premature. Rather, we advocate for harnessing their expressive power in conjunction with the learning capabilities of modern deep learning models and the nuanced judgment of human experts. This paper presents a novel framework for entity mention mining from noisy web data that strategically integrates these three components. Our approach begins by leveraging existing or creating a set of REs tailored to a specific entity type. These REs are then applied to a large corpus of web documents to generate a set of *weak labels* – potential entity mentions identified by the REs. A neural network is subsequently trained to predict these RE-generated weak labels, effectively learning to recognize patterns indicative of the target entities. Recognizing that REs are imperfect, we introduce a crucial human-in-the-loop step: a human expert annotates a comparatively small set of documents, providing high-quality, gold-standard labels. Finally, the neural network is fine-tuned on this human-annotated data, refining its ability to discern true entity mentions from false positives and bridging the gap between the RE-generated weak labels and the expert’s precision. Through rigorous experimental evaluation on several entity identification problems, we demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while minimizing the required human annotation effort. This combination of automated pattern matching, machine learning, and targeted human expertise offers a promising pathway for scaling entity extraction to the vast and challenging domain of web data. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has become a dominant paradigm in machine translation over the past two decades, delivering substantial improvements in translation quality (Koehn et al., 2003). Phrase-Based SMT (PBSMT) (Koehn et al., 2003) is currently the most widely used SMT approach, building on the foundations laid by word-based models (Brown et al., 1993) by translating phrases rather than single words, thus capturing more contextual information. A standard PBSMT decoder typically employs a left-to-right decoding strategy, constructing the target sentence word by word, from left to right. This approach directly mirrors the conventional process of reading and writing in many languages, making it a natural choice for translation. However, the inherent directionality of this process may introduce biases and limitations, particularly when dealing with languages exhibiting vastly different linguistic structures compared to English, the often-dominant source language in SMT research. The directionality of decoding has received relatively little attention in the SMT literature. While adjustments are routinely made to language models to better capture target language fluency, the fundamental decoding order remains largely fixed. This is somewhat surprising, given the significant typological diversity across languages, including differences in head directionality (Dryer, 2006), constituent order, and morphological complexity. For example, languages like Japanese and Turkish are right-headed, meaning that modifiers typically precede the heads they modify, a stark contrast to the left-headedness of English. It stands to reason that a decoding strategy aligned with the natural directionality of the target language might yield improved translation quality. In this paper, we present a systematic investigation into the impact of decoding direction on PBSMT performance. We compare a standard left-to-right decoder with a right-to-left decoder, exploring the hypothesis that right-to-left decoding may be more effective for certain language pairs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel bidirectional decoding strategy that attempts to integrate the strengths of both mono-directional approaches, mitigating the biases associated with a single decoding direction. Our evaluation is broad in scope, encompassing an unprecedented 272 distinct language pairs, allowing us to assess the generalizability of our findings. The results are striking: we found that, contrary to common intuition, right-to-left decoding consistently outperformed left-to-right decoding for the majority of language pairs tested. Importantly, our bidirectional approach consistently improves over both mono-directional strategies, providing substantial and robust gains in translation quality, as measured by the BLEU score. This work highlights the importance of examining fundamental assumptions in SMT and opens new avenues for improving translation performance by explicitly accounting for linguistic directionality. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Event extraction (EE) – the task of identifying event triggers and their corresponding arguments (roles) – is a core component of many natural language processing applications, including information retrieval, question answering, and summarization. Traditional approaches to event extraction rely heavily on the presence of event keywords – verbs or nouns that signal the occurrence of an event (e.g., “attack” in a conflict event). However, many real-world event descriptions unfold in more nuanced ways, often omitting explicit event keywords and instead relying on contextual cues and inferences. For example, a report might state “Negotiations broke down, leaving hopes for a peaceful resolution dashed,” describing a failed negotiation event without explicitly using the word “negotiate.” Identifying event role fillers in these *secondary contexts* – where event keywords are absent or distant – represents a significant challenge for current EE systems. Existing event extraction approaches often struggle with these secondary contexts due to their reliance on feature engineering around event keywords. Methods employing shallow linguistic patterns or supervised learning with limited feature sets often fail to capture the subtle relationships between arguments and implied events. More sophisticated approaches, such as those based on semantic role labeling (SRL), tend to perform poorly when event triggers are absent, as they require an initial event detection stage. Further, many systems treat event extraction as a single-stage process, failing to leverage hierarchical information and progressively refine their focus on relevant contextual elements. In this work, we address the problem of detecting event role fillers in secondary contexts by proposing a multilayered event extraction architecture. Inspired by the visual metaphor of “peeling back the layers,” our model progressively “zooms in” on relevant information, starting with coarse-grained document-level characteristics and progressively refining its focus to specific noun phrases likely to be event role fillers. Our architecture incorporates a document genre classifier to identify event narratives – leveraging the observation that events are more likely to be described in specific document types (e.g., news reports, governmental reports). This is followed by two types of sentence classifiers: one to identify sentences *likely* to contain event mentions, and another to refine this selection to sentences containing potential event role fillers. Finally, a noun phrase classifier is applied to extract the arguments themselves. Crucially, these modules are organized as a pipeline, effectively filtering out irrelevant information at each layer and concentrating resources on the most promising candidates. This staged approach not only improves accuracy but also enhances efficiency by reducing the search space for event arguments. We evaluate our model on the MUC-4 event extraction dataset, a benchmark corpus specifically designed to evaluate the extraction of events and their arguments. Our results demonstrate a significant performance improvement over previous systems, highlighting the effectiveness of our multilayered approach and the importance of incorporating contextual information in event extraction, especially when explicit event keywords are absent. A central challenge in understanding human language acquisition lies in explaining how infants successfully navigate the complex mapping between sound and meaning. Early in life, children are exposed to a highly variable speech signal – variations stemming from differences in speaker, speaking rate, and contextual factors – yet they rapidly converge on a stable lexicon and an understanding of permissible phonetic variation. Traditionally, research in language acquisition has largely treated the learning of vocabulary (lexical acquisition) and the learning of sound patterns (phonetic acquisition) as separate processes. Lexical acquisition models often assume a ‘fixed’ pronunciation for each word (e.g., Pinker, 1984), while phonetic acquisition models focus on discovering the underlying phonological system without explicitly linking it to lexical items (e.g., de Boysson-Bardies, 1997). However, a growing body of behavioral evidence suggests a strong interplay between these processes during early language development. Infants appear to exploit phonetic cues to segment the speech stream into potential words (e.g., Jusczyk & Aslin, 1995), and conversely, lexical expectations can influence phonetic perception (e.g., Werker & Tees, 1984). This observed co-development motivates the need for computational models that can simultaneously learn both lexical and phonetic knowledge. Existing computational approaches to lexical acquisition often struggle with phonetic variability. Models relying on strict string matching perform poorly in realistic scenarios where pronunciations differ significantly from canonical forms. Statistical models, like those employing Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), can account for some variability but typically require substantial amounts of transcribed data and often lack a principled mechanism for relating phonetic variations to articulatory features. Similarly, models of phonetic acquisition typically operate on limited acoustic data and do not inherently benefit from contextual information provided by lexical expectations. In this paper, we present a novel Bayesian model designed to address these limitations by bootstrapping a unified representation of lexical and phonetic knowledge. The core idea is to cluster together different phonetic realizations of the same lexical item while simultaneously learning both a language model over lexical items and a probabilistic model of pronunciation variability grounded in articulatory features. Crucially, the model requires only transcribed surface pronunciations as input, and does *not* rely on access to a pre-defined lexicon. Instead, it learns by iteratively refining its hypotheses about both words and their pronunciations, bootstrapping from initial, weak assumptions. We employ a log-linear model of pronunciation variability, allowing us to capture systematic relationships between articulatory features and observed phonetic variations. We evaluate the model on a corpus of child-directed speech exhibiting realistic phonetic variation, using both gold-standard and automatically induced word boundaries. Our results demonstrate that explicitly modeling pronunciation variability significantly improves the accuracy of the learned lexicon compared to a baseline system that assumes a unique pronunciation for each lexical item. This finding supports the hypothesis that integrating lexical and phonetic knowledge acquisition is crucial for successful language learning. In Section 2, we review related work. Section 3 details the Bayesian model with its phonetic and lexical components. Section 4 presents experimental results. Finally, Section 5 concludes with a discussion of current limitations and future directions.

Unsupervised word segmentation remains a fundamental challenge in natural language processing, particularly for languages like Chinese and Japanese that lack explicit word boundaries in their written form. Traditionally, approaches to Chinese word segmentation (CWS) have relied heavily on supervised learning techniques trained on large, manually annotated corpora (Xue and Chen, 2003; Shi et al., 2006). However, the creation of such corpora is both time-consuming and expensive, limiting their availability for many languages and domains. This motivates the development of unsupervised methods capable of identifying word boundaries without requiring labeled training data. Recent advancements in unsupervised segmentation have been driven by statistical modeling of sequential data, leveraging the inherent patterns and dependencies within the language itself. One particularly promising framework for this task is that of Adaptor Grammars (AGs) (Johnson et al., 2009), a versatile tool for expressing and performing inference over non-parametric linguistic models. AGs have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on unsupervised word segmentation tasks in English, specifically when applied to phonemic transcriptions of child-directed speech (Perreira et al., 2018). The success of AGs hinges on their ability to capture complex dependencies and generalize effectively from limited data. This paper explores the applicability of Adaptor Grammars to the challenging problem of unsupervised Chinese word segmentation. Unlike English, Chinese presents unique challenges due to its tonal nature, rich syllable structure, and the relatively free word order. We investigate a variety of segmentation models within the AG framework, systematically exploring the impact of different modeling choices on segmentation accuracy. A core focus is on understanding how well AGs can capture inter-word relationships – particularly “collocational” dependencies where certain words frequently co-occur – and how this relates to overall segmentation quality. Surprisingly, our experiments reveal that incorporating explicit information about syllable structure and tone does *not* necessarily lead to significant improvements in segmentation accuracy. While these linguistic features are undeniably important for understanding and processing Chinese, the models that prioritize capturing inter-word dependencies outperform those that attempt to directly leverage syllabic or tonal information. This suggests that the information conveyed by syllable structure and tone may be largely redundant with the patterns already captured through modeling inter-word relationships. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the key factors driving successful unsupervised CWS and provide insights into the relative importance of different linguistic features in the segmentation process. Temporal relation classification – identifying how events and time expressions relate to each other in text (e.g., “before,” “after,” “during”) – is a fundamental task in natural language processing with applications in information extraction, question answering, and event timeline construction (Allan, 2008; Grishman et al., 2005). For example, understanding that “the company was founded in 1995” requires recognizing a “before” relation between “founded” and “now.” Despite significant research effort, accurate temporal relation classification remains a challenging problem. Early approaches relied heavily on hand-crafted features, encompassing lexical, syntactic, and semantic information (Freedman & Skrenta, 2008; Manning & Klug, 1998). However, the design of these features is often labor-intensive and requires significant domain expertise. Moreover, feature engineering can be brittle and may not generalize well to new domains or corpora. More recently, machine learning techniques have become dominant in this field. However, even with these methods, performance is often limited by the quantity and quality of available training data, and often still relies on substantial feature engineering (Verhagen et al., 2007; O’Hare & McDonough, 2012). A key insight is that syntactic structure – as captured by dependency parses – plays a crucial role in determining temporal relations (Nesbit & Elliott, 2010). For example, events connected by a coordinating conjunction often have similar temporal relations. However, effectively leveraging this syntactic information requires careful design of features. In this paper, we present a novel approach to temporal relation classification that avoids extensive feature engineering. Our method utilizes dependency parses and a simple, yet effective, measure of tree similarity based on a convolution kernel. Critically, rather than extracting features based on parse trees, we directly compare the structures themselves. The resulting system significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the power of this approach. To further enhance performance, we explore the use of crowdsourcing to obtain additional annotated training data. While expert annotation is often considered the gold standard, it is expensive and time-consuming. We demonstrate that high-quality temporal relation annotations can be obtained efficiently and cost-effectively from non-expert crowdworkers. Furthermore, we introduce a *selective annotation* strategy, focusing annotation efforts on instances that our system identifies as particularly challenging. This targeted approach allows us to maximize the impact of each annotation, achieving a substantial performance improvement over previous state-of-the-art results while reducing annotation costs by up to 37%. Finally, recognizing the importance of data availability for benchmarking and advancing the field, we will release our collected dataset to the research community. This resource will facilitate comparative studies and accelerate progress in temporal relation classification research. It is important to note that much of the previous work has focused on the TimeML corpus (Pustejovsky et al., 2005), which contains a relatively small number of annotated instances. Our work not only achieves significant performance gains on the TimeML corpus, but also lays the groundwork for applying similar techniques to larger and more complex datasets.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by the availability of large-scale parallel corpora and the power of deep learning (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). However, the performance of NMT systems typically degrades significantly when applied to low-resource languages, where parallel data is scarce or nonexistent. Traditional approaches to low-resource NMT include back-translation (Sennrich et al., 2016), pivot-based translation (Chu et al., 2017), and transfer learning (Zoph et al., 2016). Back-translation leverages monolingual data in the target language to generate synthetic parallel data, while pivot-based translation uses a third, high-resource language as an intermediary. Transfer learning typically involves pre-training an NMT model on high-resource language pairs and then fine-tuning it on the low-resource target language. These approaches have proven effective, but they often require substantial monolingual data or careful selection of related high-resource languages. More recently, meta-learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for few-shot learning in various domains, including computer vision and natural language processing (Schmetzler, 2019). Meta-learning, or “learning to learn,” aims to train a model that can quickly adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. Finn et al. (2017) introduced Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), a powerful meta-learning algorithm that learns an initialization of model parameters such that a small number of gradient steps can quickly adapt the model to a new task. In this paper, we explore the application of MAML to low-resource NMT. We frame low-resource translation as a meta-learning problem, where the goal is to learn an initial set of model parameters that can be quickly fine-tuned to translate between a new, low-resource language pair. To enable effective meta-learning across diverse languages, we leverage a universal lexical representation (Gu et al., 2018b). This representation maps words from different languages into a shared embedding space, alleviating the input-output mismatch problem that can arise when training a multilingual NMT model. We evaluate our approach on a challenging benchmark comprising eighteen European languages as source tasks and five diverse languages (Romanian, Latvian, Finnish, Turkish, and Korean) as target tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed meta-learning strategy significantly outperforms a strong multilingual transfer learning baseline (Zoph et al., 2016) and enables us to train competitive NMT systems with a fraction of the training data. Notably, our approach achieves a BLEU score of 22.04 on Romanian-English WMT’16 using only 16,000 translated words (approximately 600 parallel sentences). This work marks a significant step towards building practical NMT systems for low-resource languages, paving the way for more inclusive and accessible machine translation technologies.

Opinion mining, the computational task of identifying and extracting subjective information from text, has matured considerably in recent years. Early work focused primarily on sentiment polarity classification – determining whether a text expresses a positive or negative opinion (Turney, 2002; Pang et al., 2002). However, a nuanced understanding of opinions requires more than simply identifying polarity. Fine-grained opinion mining aims to pinpoint *what* aspects of an entity are being evaluated, *how* they are being evaluated (the sentiment expressed), and *who* is holding the opinion (opinion holder extraction). This entails identifying opinion targets, opinion expressions, and relationships between them – forming what is often referred to as an opinion frame (Wilson et al., 2006). The vast majority of research in fine-grained opinion mining has been conducted in English, largely due to the availability of labeled data and sophisticated linguistic resources. However, the ubiquity of online content in multiple languages necessitates the development of cross-lingual opinion mining techniques. Building separate, fully supervised systems for each language is often impractical, given the high cost of annotation. Cross-lingual approaches typically rely on machine translation (MT) to translate texts into a common language (typically English) and then apply an English-based opinion mining system (Nakayama et al., 2009). However, MT can introduce errors and distort the nuances of opinion expression. A more direct approach involves *bitext projection* – leveraging word-aligned parallel corpora to transfer linguistic knowledge from a source language (where resources are abundant) to a target language (where resources are scarce) (Lavie and Resnik, 2009; Freitag and Al-Onaizan, 2010). This avoids the bottleneck of MT and potentially preserves more of the original meaning. In this paper, we present a novel cross-lingual framework for fine-grained opinion mining based on bitext projection. Our core idea is to project opinion frames from a well-resourced source language (English) to a target language (Portuguese) using word alignments, and then train an opinion mining system on the target language using these automatically generated annotations. A key contribution of this work lies in a new dependency-based model for opinion mining. Dependency parsing captures structural relationships between words in a sentence, offering a robust and informative representation of linguistic context. We demonstrate that our dependency-based model achieves state-of-the-art performance on English opinion mining, *without* requiring computationally expensive integer programming or reranking techniques. Furthermore, in cross-lingual experiments (English to Portuguese), our approach significantly outperforms a supervised system trained with limited labeled data, and demonstrates superior performance compared to a delexicalized model relying on universal tags and bilingual word embeddings. This highlights the effectiveness of leveraging dependency structure and bitext projection for cross-lingual opinion mining. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 details our dependency-based opinion mining model. Section 4 describes the cross-lingual framework. Section 5 presents experimental results, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

The ability to automatically connect mentions of entities in unstructured text to their corresponding entries in structured knowledge bases—a task known as entity linking (EL)—is a cornerstone of modern information extraction (IE). This process unlocks access to a wealth of encyclopedic knowledge, transforming free text into a richly interconnected network of concepts and relationships. Imagine a user reading an article about “Steve Jobs”; entity linking would automatically identify this mention and connect it to the corresponding entry in a knowledge base like Wikipedia, providing immediate access to biographical information, related figures, and further resources. This capability has profound implications for a diverse range of applications, including question answering, search engine enhancement, and knowledge graph construction. Early approaches to entity linking relied heavily on rule-based methods and hand-crafted features (Ratinov et al., 2009;Bunescu et al., 2005). While effective in limited domains, these systems often struggled with ambiguity, variations in entity mentions, and scalability to large knowledge bases. More recently, machine learning techniques have emerged as the dominant paradigm, enabling more robust and adaptable entity linking systems. These methods broadly fall into two categories: classification-based and ranking-based. The majority of previous learning-based entity linking systems adopt a classification framework (Shen et al., 2011;Chandu et al., 2007). In this approach, each candidate entity is scored based on a set of features, and a classifier—such as a Support Vector Machine (SVM) or logistic regression model—is used to determine whether the candidate is the correct entity for the given mention. While this approach is conceptually straightforward, it suffers from several limitations. First, classification inherently focuses on binary decisions (“correct” or “incorrect”), failing to leverage the nuanced relationships between candidate entities. Second, it treats each candidate in isolation, neglecting the valuable information contained in the relative rankings of the candidates. In contrast, we argue that entity linking is more naturally framed as a ranking problem. Given a mention, the goal is not simply to identify the correct entity, but to *rank* all candidate entities in order of decreasing likelihood. This allows the system to consider the relationships between candidates – for instance, recognizing that two entities are closely related even if neither is a perfect match for the given mention. This paper proposes a novel learning-to-rank (LTR) algorithm for entity linking. Our approach effectively utilizes the rich relational information among candidate entities when constructing the ranking function. By incorporating features that capture the similarity and dissimilarity between candidates, we can significantly improve the accuracy of entity linking. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on the Text Analysis Conference (TAC) 2009 knowledge base population (KBP) dataset. Our results show a substantial improvement in performance—an 18.5% accuracy gain over classification-based models for entities with corresponding knowledge base entries—and outperform existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the benefits of our ranking-based approach.

Automated negotiation is a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence, with applications ranging from e-commerce and resource allocation to diplomatic discourse. Traditionally, research in this area focused on game-theoretic approaches and rule-based systems (Sander and Zlotkin, 1998; Walsh and Wooldridge, 1999). However, these approaches often struggle to cope with the complexities of real-world negotiations, particularly the nuanced nature of natural language communication. More recently, the emergence of deep learning has spurred significant interest in end-to-end neural negotiation systems (Li et al., 2016; Wen et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2018). These systems learn to map dialogue history directly to actions, such as making proposals or accepting offers. While end-to-end models demonstrate promising performance, their inherent complexity introduces several key limitations. A primary concern is the lack of control over the agent’s underlying negotiation *strategy*. The coupling of strategy and utterance generation within a single neural network makes it difficult to explicitly define or modify the agent’s bargaining behavior. For example, attempting to enforce specific strategic constraints, such as concession patterns or patience levels, proves challenging. Furthermore, training these models often relies on reinforcement learning (RL), which, while powerful, is prone to instability and can lead to *degenerate solutions* – agents that exploit quirks in the environment to achieve superficially high rewards without exhibiting sensible negotiation behavior (Foerster et al., 2018). Another limitation of end-to-end models is maintaining consistent and coherent negotiation dialogues. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel, modular approach to negotiation dialogue that explicitly *decouples strategy and generation*. Our framework operates by first selecting a high-level *dialogue act* – a coarse representation of the agent’s intended action (e.g., `propose(price=50)`) – and then generating a natural language utterance that realizes this act. This separation allows us to independently train and control the strategic component of the agent, using supervised learning, reinforcement learning, or incorporating domain-specific negotiation knowledge. Simultaneously, we employ a retrieval-based generation module to ensure that the generated utterances are contextually appropriate, diverse, and human-like. We evaluate our approach on the DEALORNODEAL game (Lei et al., 2018), a recently introduced benchmark for negotiation research. We further contribute a new, richer dataset based on real-world item listings scraped from Craigslist, providing a more realistic negotiation environment. Our results demonstrate that our modular system achieves both a higher negotiation success rate and exhibits more natural and human-like behavior compared to previous end-to-end approaches, as confirmed by human evaluation. This suggests that decoupling strategy and generation is a promising direction for building more effective and controllable negotiation agents. There is a rising amount of interest in argument mining, but fewer studies on modeling argument strength, which is a vital feature in college assignments. In this paper, we develop a scoring model for the argument strength dimension on student essays using a feature-rich approach, and provide annotation of 1000 essays to stimulate further research.

Human-robot interaction (HRI) is rapidly expanding beyond research labs into real-world applications, necessitating a deeper understanding of how to design robots that are not only functional but also usable and enjoyable for humans to interact with. As robots move from performing simple, pre-programmed tasks to assisting humans in complex, collaborative endeavors, the quality of the interaction becomes paramount. A key challenge in HRI is evaluating the effectiveness and user experience of these interactions. Traditionally, evaluation methods have fallen into two main categories: subjective and objective. Subjective measures, such as user satisfaction questionnaires, capture the user’s perception of the system’s usability, while objective measures, like task completion time and error rates, provide quantifiable data about the interaction’s efficiency and effectiveness. However, the relationship between these two types of measures is not always straightforward. A system might perform well according to objective metrics but still be perceived as frustrating or difficult to use by the user, or vice versa. This paper investigates this relationship in the context of a human-robot dialogue system designed to support a collaborative task: building wooden construction toys. Our system enables a robot to work alongside a human, providing instructions and assistance throughout the building process. This task presents several interesting challenges for HRI, requiring effective communication, shared understanding, and the ability to handle unexpected events. To evaluate the usability of our system, we conducted a study with naïve participants who interacted with the robot under varying experimental conditions. Following the interactions, participants completed a comprehensive user satisfaction questionnaire. This yielded a rich dataset containing both subjective ratings and objective metrics of the interaction. Beyond simply reporting these measures, this work aims to determine which specific aspects of the interaction – as captured by objective metrics – had the greatest impact on the users’ subjective evaluations. To achieve this, we employed a methodology based on the PARADISE evaluation framework (Walker et al., 1997), a statistically sound approach to deriving a performance function that maps objective measures to subjective user ratings. By identifying the most influential objective measures, we can gain valuable insights into how to improve the design of human-robot dialogue systems and optimize the user experience. This understanding is crucial for building robots that are not only capable of performing complex tasks but also seamlessly integrate into human workflows and are genuinely useful and enjoyable to interact with. Our findings reveal that the number of repetition requests, dialogue length, and user recall of system instructions were the most significant predictors of user satisfaction. Specifically, frequent repetition requests negatively impacted satisfaction, while concise dialogues and good instruction recall were positively correlated. These results highlight the importance of clear and efficient communication in collaborative HRI and provide actionable guidance for the design of more usable and effective dialogue systems.
