Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving state-of-the-art results on numerous language pairs (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). These models typically operate on a word-by-word basis, encoding the source sentence into a continuous vector representation and then decoding this representation into the target language, one word at a time. While this approach has proven remarkably effective, it often struggles to capture and accurately translate multi-word expressions, or phrases, which are fundamental building blocks of natural language (Sag et al., 2002; Villavicencio et al., 2005). Phrases frequently exhibit non-compositional semantics, meaning the meaning of the phrase cannot be readily derived from the meanings of its constituent words. Consequently, word-level NMT systems often produce fluent but inaccurate translations of these expressions. Traditional phrase-based statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Koehn et al., 2003) excelled at handling phrases by explicitly modeling their translation probabilities. However, SMT systems are complex, requiring significant feature engineering and painstaking tuning. Recent attempts to integrate phrasal information into NMT have largely focused on explicitly modeling phrase tables or incorporating external linguistic resources (Artetxe et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018). These methods, while showing some improvements, often struggle to dynamically adapt to the context of the input sentence. In this work, we propose a novel approach to phrase translation within an NMT framework. Our method leverages the strengths of both NMT and SMT by integrating a *phrase memory* into the encoder-decoder architecture. This memory stores a collection of target phrases extracted from a pre-trained SMT system. Crucially, the phrase memory is not static: at each decoding step, it is dynamically re-written based on contextual information provided by the NMT decoder. This allows the SMT model to generate relevant target phrases tailored to the specific input sentence. The core idea is to allow the NMT model to ‘consult’ the phrase memory during decoding. At each step, the model estimates probabilities for all phrases in the memory and, if a sufficiently probable phrase is identified, translates the phrase as a single unit, updating its internal state accordingly. Otherwise, the model reverts to standard word-by-word decoding. This dynamic interaction between NMT and SMT allows our model to benefit from the contextual awareness of NMT and the phrase-handling capabilities of SMT. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with experiments on Chinese-to-English translation, showing significant improvements over a strong NMT baseline across various test sets. Our results indicate that explicitly incorporating and dynamically utilizing a phrase memory can substantially enhance the quality of neural machine translation, particularly in handling complex phrasal expressions.

Unsupervised parsing – the task of inducing a grammar and parsing a corpus without any annotated data – remains a central challenge in natural language processing. The allure of bypassing the costly and time-consuming process of manual annotation is strong, particularly as we strive to build language technologies for increasingly diverse languages and domains. While significant progress has been made in recent years, particularly with lexicalized probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) induced through techniques like Inside-Outside tracking (Johnson, 2007), the performance of fully unsupervised parsers still lags considerably behind that of supervised systems. A key obstacle lies in the inherent ambiguity of natural language and the difficulty of disambiguating syntactic structures without external guidance. Existing unsupervised parsing algorithms often struggle with robustness and generalization, particularly when applied to domains differing from those used in initial training. One observation that motivates our work is the realization that not all data is created equal. A large, heterogeneous corpus may contain subsets that are more amenable to successful grammar induction than others. For example, a corpus containing a significant proportion of relatively simple, declarative sentences might be easier to parse than a corpus heavily laden with complex, nested structures or rare linguistic phenomena. However, identifying these “easier” subsets automatically remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce Zoomed Learning, a novel training algorithm designed to systematically identify and exploit such beneficial data subsets. The core idea is to iteratively search for pairs of subsets – a training subset (T<sub>i</sub>) and a corresponding test subset (S<sub>i</sub>) – where training the parser on T<sub>i</sub> yields superior performance on S<sub>i</sub> compared to training on the entire corpus (T). In essence, we are seeking data “zoom levels” that enhance parsing accuracy on specific portions of the data. A successful zoom – identified through this comparative evaluation – signals a potential improvement to the overall parsing process. Crucially, Zoomed Learning doesn’t require any labeled data or prior knowledge about the corpus structure. The selection of subsets and the evaluation of parsing performance are driven entirely by the internal dynamics of the unsupervised learning process. By iteratively refining the training data based on these zooms, we aim to construct a more robust and accurate parser. We evaluate our algorithm in combination with a state-of-the-art unsupervised parsing algorithm (Seginer, 2007) across three distinct English domains – the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), Brown Corpus, and GENIA – demonstrating consistent and substantial improvements in parser F-score, up to 4.47%. These results highlight the potential of Zoomed Learning to unlock higher performance in fully unsupervised parsing by strategically focusing on the most informative data subsets. Figure 1: Illustration of the Zoomed Learning process. The algorithm iteratively identifies subsets T<sub>i</sub> and S<sub>i</sub> where training on T<sub>i</sub> improves performance on S<sub>i</sub>, ultimately leading to a more accurate overall parser.

The creation of accurate, broad-coverage parsers is a cornerstone of modern natural language processing. These parsers, typically trained on manually annotated treebanks, enable a wide range of downstream applications, from machine translation and information extraction to question answering and semantic analysis. However, the development of such treebanks is a costly and time-consuming process, limiting their availability to a handful of well-resourced languages like English, German, and Mandarin Chinese. Consequently, a significant number of languages remain “resource-poor,” hindering the application of many NLP techniques. The recent surge in the availability of parallel corpora, or bitexts, alongside the continued improvement in the accuracy of English parsers, presents a compelling opportunity to leverage knowledge transfer for dependency grammar induction in these resource-poor languages. The core idea behind bitext projection is to utilize word alignments between a source language (typically English) and a target language to “project” syntactic information from the source language parse tree onto the target language. Initial approaches (Yamada and Knight, 2001; Flickinger et al., 2003) focused on projecting full parse trees, demanding high-quality alignments and a rigid adherence to cross-lingual syntactic equivalencies. While promising, these methods often suffer from significant error propagation due to imperfect alignments and structural divergences between languages. More recent work (Kuhn and Padó, 2011; McDonald et al., 2013) relaxes the requirement for full projections, allowing for partial or probabilistic transfer of syntactic information. This paper builds upon the latter line of research, proposing a novel framework for dependency grammar induction that leverages bitext projection constraints without requiring fully projected parses. We formulate dependency grammar induction as both a generative and discriminative modeling problem, utilizing word-level alignments and a high-accuracy English dependency parser to constrain the space of possible target language dependency trees. Crucially, our framework employs *linear expectation constraints* – approximating the transfer of dependencies through probabilistic expectations rather than demanding exact structural matches. This allows for more robust transfer, particularly in scenarios where alignments are noisy or structural divergence is significant. Furthermore, we explore a range of constraint types, moving beyond simple dependency conservation to incorporate language-specific annotation schemes, such as rules governing auxiliary verb analysis. We hypothesize that incorporating such linguistic knowledge can further improve the accuracy of induced dependency structures. We evaluate our approach on dependency parsing datasets for Bulgarian and Spanish, drawn from the CoNLL shared tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements over strong unsupervised baselines and, importantly, competitive performance against supervised learning methods trained on limited amounts of target language data. These results highlight the potential of our bitext projection framework as a viable approach for dependency grammar induction in resource-poor languages, offering a pathway towards richer linguistic resources and improved NLP capabilities for a wider range of languages. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The burgeoning landscape of online discourse presents both opportunities and challenges for computational approaches to argumentation. While automated argumentation mining has focused largely on identifying argument components (e.g., claims, premises) and relationships (e.g., support, attack), a crucial aspect remains largely unexplored: *why* one argument is perceived as more convincing than another. Understanding convincingness is not merely about structural properties of arguments, but also about the subtle nuances of reasoning, evidence, and rhetorical strategies that sway an audience. This is especially pertinent in the context of polarized debates online, where effective communication – and the potential for constructive dialogue – hinges on discerning the elements that contribute to persuasive argumentation. Existing work in computational argumentation largely focuses on identifying argumentative structures and predicting argumentative relations. Approaches range from rule-based systems (e.g., Kirchner et al., 2013) to machine learning models trained on annotated corpora (e.g., Stab & Ghasemzadeh, 2017; Lippi & Torroni, 2016). Recent advancements leverage deep learning techniques to enhance argument component identification and relation classification (e.g., Niculae & Balahur, 2017; Eger et al., 2018). However, these efforts typically operate at a relatively abstract level, aiming to *detect* arguments rather than *explain* their effectiveness. A smaller body of work has touched upon assessing argument quality. Toulmin’s model of argumentation (Toulmin, 1958) provides a framework for analyzing argumentative structure and identifying elements such as claims, warrants, and backings. However, adapting this framework for automated assessment remains challenging, particularly in the unconstrained and often informal context of online arguments. Studies focusing on argument strength often rely on proxy measures like stance polarity or the number of supporting premises (e.g., Villalba & Saint-Dizier, 2009), which may not fully capture the intricacies of convincingness. The central motivation for our work is to bridge this gap by directly addressing the question of *what makes an argument convincing?* We argue that understanding convincingness requires moving beyond structural analyses and incorporating qualitative assessments of argumentative properties. To this end, we introduce a novel task: given a pair of arguments on a controversial topic, the goal is to identify the reasons *why* one argument is perceived as more convincing than the other. We adopt a fully empirical approach, collecting a large-scale corpus of natural language explanations that articulate these discerning factors. This paper presents UKPConvArg2, a new crowd-sourced corpus of 9,111 argument pairs annotated with 26,000 explanations describing convincingness, multilabeled with 17 fine-grained classes. We benchmark several machine learning models, including feature-rich SVM learners and Bidirectional LSTMs with attention, on two tasks: predicting the full label distribution for each argument pair and classifying flaws specifically within less convincing arguments. Our results demonstrate that this task is considerably challenging, requiring sophisticated models to capture the subtle distinctions in argumentative reasoning. We release both the corpus and accompanying software to foster further research in this important area.

Neural sequence-to-sequence models have become the dominant paradigm in a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015), speech recognition (Chan et al., 2016), and text summarization (Rush et al., 2015). However, the performance of these models is often limited by the quality of their input. A common scenario is where the input sequence is generated by a preceding system, such as an automatic speech recognizer (ASR) or a word segmenter. These upstream components are inherently imperfect and introduce errors that propagate down the pipeline, negatively impacting the downstream task. A naive approach to handling this uncertainty is to simply use the 1-best hypothesis produced by the upstream system as input to the sequence-to-sequence model. However, this discards valuable information about alternative plausible inputs and their associated confidence scores. Another approach is to decode over multiple hypotheses generated by the upstream system (e.g., an n-best list), but this quickly becomes computationally expensive as the number of hypotheses grows. Word lattices offer a compact and principled way to represent the uncertainty inherent in upstream processing. A lattice encodes a set of alternative word sequences, along with associated probabilities that reflect the confidence of the upstream system in each sequence. This representation allows a downstream model to consider multiple possible inputs simultaneously, weighted by their likelihood. Previous work has explored using lattices in statistical machine translation (Finke et al., 2008; Dehak et al., 2009), but these approaches often rely on feature engineering and complex decoding algorithms. In this work, we propose a novel neural architecture, the LatticeLSTM, designed to directly consume word lattices as input. We extend the TreeLSTM (Tai et al., 2015), a powerful recurrent neural network capable of processing hierarchical structures, to handle the directed acyclic graph structure of a word lattice. To effectively utilize the posterior probabilities associated with each lattice arc, we integrate these scores into the TreeLSTM’s gating mechanisms and attention mechanism. This allows the model to dynamically adjust its processing based on the confidence of the upstream system. We evaluate our LatticeLSTM-based encoder-decoder model on the task of speech translation, using lattices generated by an ASR system. Our experimental results demonstrate that incorporating lattice posterior scores consistently improves translation performance compared to both translating the 1-best hypothesis and translating the lattice without utilizing the posterior probabilities. These findings highlight the benefits of explicitly modeling input uncertainty in neural sequence-to-sequence models and pave the way for more robust and accurate downstream processing. . style="text-align: justify;"> style="text-align: justify;"> style="text-align: justify;"> style="text-align: justify;"> style="text-align: justify;"> style="text-align: justify;">

Topic classification, the task of automatically assigning predefined categories to text documents, is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with wide-ranging applications, including information retrieval, text summarization, and customer support. Traditional approaches to topic classification often rely on bag-of-words representations combined with machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) or Naive Bayes. More recently, deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have achieved state-of-the-art performance on various topic classification benchmarks (Kim, 2014; Johnson & Zhang, 2014). However, a persistent challenge in topic classification remains the inherent variability within topic categories. Documents belonging to the same topic often exhibit significant variations in style, vocabulary, and length, leading to a diffuse feature space and consequently, reduced classification accuracy. This “intra-topic variability” arises from several factors. For instance, users discussing the same topic may express their opinions using different language, focus on different aspects of the topic, or adopt varying levels of detail. In free-style conversational corpora, like those derived from social media or online forums, this variability is particularly pronounced due to the informal and often idiosyncratic nature of language used in such settings. Existing approaches to mitigate intra-topic variability largely fall into two categories: feature selection and data augmentation. Feature selection techniques aim to identify the most discriminative features while discarding irrelevant or noisy ones (Forman, 1998). Data augmentation methods, on the other hand, involve generating synthetic data points to increase the size and diversity of the training set (Shorten & Khoshgoftaar, 2019). While these methods can be effective in certain scenarios, they often require careful parameter tuning and may not fully capture the underlying structure of the variability. Furthermore, feature selection may inadvertently remove valuable information, while data augmentation can introduce artificial biases. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address intra-topic variability by explicitly normalizing the feature space to reduce the spread of documents within each topic category. Our method is based on the assumption that intra-topic variability can be reduced through linear transformations that project the original feature space onto a lower-dimensional subspace while preserving the discriminative information between topics. We formulate an optimization problem that minimizes the within-topic variance while maintaining the between-topic separation. We then leverage Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) to efficiently solve this optimization problem and identify a new feature space where intra-topic variability is reduced. Finally, we perform a linear projection from the KPCA space back to the original feature space to allow for easy integration with existing classification algorithms. We evaluate our approach on a challenging free-style conversational corpus and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SVM and KNN classifiers, achieving a significant improvement in micro-F1 measure. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our variability normalization algorithm for enhancing topic classification accuracy in the presence of significant intra-topic variations.

Language models (LMs) are fundamental components in a wide range of natural language processing applications, including speech recognition, machine translation, and text generation. At their core, LMs assign probabilities to sequences of words, capturing the statistical regularities of a language. For decades, the dominant paradigm in language modeling has been *count-based* approaches, most notably n-gram models (Chen & Goodman, 1999). These models estimate probabilities by counting the occurrences of n-grams in a corpus and employing smoothing techniques to handle unseen sequences. The key advantages of n-gram models lie in their scalability – they can be efficiently trained on very large corpora – and their computational efficiency at test time, making them suitable for real-time applications. However, n-gram models suffer from the curse of dimensionality; as the order 'n' increases, the data sparsity problem becomes increasingly severe, requiring extensive smoothing and back-off strategies. More recently, *neural language models* (Bengio et al., 2003; Mikolov et al., 2010) have emerged as a powerful alternative. These models leverage the representational power of neural networks to learn distributed representations of words and capture long-range dependencies more effectively than traditional n-gram models. Neural LMs, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers, have consistently achieved state-of-the-art results on various language modeling benchmarks. Despite their superior performance, neural LMs present several challenges. Training neural LMs demands significant computational resources and large datasets, and their inference speed can be slower compared to n-gram models. Furthermore, neural LMs often struggle to generalize to rare or unseen words, a weakness that count-based models can partially mitigate through their ability to assign non-zero probabilities to even infrequent n-grams. This paper investigates a novel approach to language modeling that seeks to bridge the gap between count-based and neural approaches. We propose a unifying framework that views both types of models as defining a set of distinct probability distributions over the vocabulary. Subsequently, we introduce a mechanism for dynamically calculating mixture weights over these distributions, allowing for a flexible combination of their respective strengths. This formulation enables the creation of *hybrid* language models that inherit the scalability and speed of count-based models while benefiting from the superior modeling capabilities of neural networks. Our approach moves beyond simply interpolating probabilities, instead allowing the model to learn when to rely more heavily on one type of model versus another based on the input context. We demonstrate through experimental results that these hybrid models achieve performance gains over both purely count-based and purely neural models, highlighting the potential of this integrative approach to language modeling. Statistical machine translation (SMT) systems typically assume words as the fundamental units of translation. However, many languages, such as Chinese, Japanese, and Thai, lack explicit word delimiters like spaces. This necessitates a pre-processing step known as word segmentation (WS) to identify word boundaries before translation can occur. While significant progress has been made in automated word segmentation ( §2), particularly with machine learning techniques trained on large, annotated corpora like the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB) (Xue and Palmer, 2004), a fundamental assumption often goes unchallenged: that the WS scheme inherent in these annotated corpora is optimal for the task of machine translation. The corpora used to train these segmenters – and consequently, the segmentation schemes they learn – are often created for linguistic analysis or general-purpose language processing, not specifically for SMT. These segmentations may reflect linguistic intuitions about morpheme boundaries or other considerations that don't necessarily align with the optimal segmentation for translation, where the primary goal is to maximize translation quality. For instance, a linguistically motivated segmentation might separate a commonly occurring multi-word expression into its constituent morphemes, while an SMT system might benefit from treating the entire expression as a single unit. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted a detailed analysis of a manually aligned Chinese-English corpus ( §3). This analysis revealed a surprisingly high degree of conflict between segmentations produced by a state-of-the-art automated segmenter (trained on the CTB) and the word alignments present in the manually aligned data. Specifically, we found that over 74% of sentences, when segmented automatically, contained conflicts with the gold-standard word alignment annotations. This suggests that the pre-defined WS schemes used in training data may indeed be suboptimal for SMT, leading to potentially significant performance degradation. To address this issue, we propose a refinement strategy based on word splitting ( §4). Instead of relying solely on the output of an automated segmenter, we leverage the information contained within the manually aligned corpus to iteratively refine the segmentation. Our approach dynamically splits words based on the alignment patterns observed in the target language, effectively correcting segmentations that conflict with the established translation correspondences. We formulate this refinement as a constrained optimization problem, ensuring that the resulting segmentations are consistent with the underlying word alignment data. Experimental results on the Chinese-English Open Machine Translation (OpenMT) corpora ( §5) demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Compared to a strong baseline using standard automated segmentation, our refined WS scheme reduces the word alignment error rate by 6.82% and achieves a consistently higher BLEU score (an average improvement of 0.63) across multiple test sets. These results highlight the importance of tailoring word segmentation schemes specifically to the demands of SMT and underscore the potential of leveraging manually aligned data to improve translation quality. <!-- I have tried to create an introduction that is around 400-500 words, setting the context, explaining the problem, presenting the hypothesis, outlining the approach, and summarizing the key results. -->

Topic models have emerged as a powerful and versatile tool for analyzing large collections of text, offering a probabilistic framework for uncovering underlying semantic themes. Initially popularized by Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), topic models have seen widespread application in tasks ranging from document clustering and information retrieval to authorship attribution and trend analysis. While traditional topic models, like LDA, have demonstrated considerable success, they generally treat each document as a bag-of-words, disregarding the sequential information inherent in textual data. However, the order of words and the flow of topics within a document often carry crucial semantic meaning. Consider, for example, a news article discussing a political event. The initial paragraphs might establish the historical context, while later sections focus on the immediate implications and reactions. A standard topic model would struggle to capture this evolving thematic structure. Recent work has begun to address this limitation by extending topic models to incorporate sequential dependencies. Dynamic topic models (Blei & Lafferty, 2006) introduce a temporal dimension, allowing topic proportions to evolve over time. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) have also been integrated with topic models, treating topic assignments as hidden states in a sequential process (Griffiths & Steyvers, 2004). However, many of these approaches rely on predefined temporal structures or assume a fixed number of topics throughout the document. In this paper, we present a novel Adaptive Topic Model (ATM) designed to address these shortcomings. Our model dynamically adapts topics based on two key sources of information: the preceding text segment and the broader parent document. This allows the model to capture both short-range sequential dependencies (e.g., within a paragraph) and long-range thematic coherence (e.g., across an entire article). The core idea is to bias topic assignments in the current segment towards topics prevalent in the preceding segment, while simultaneously maintaining a global topic distribution derived from the entire document. 1 This adaptive mechanism enables the model to gracefully transition between topics and uncover the underlying sequential structure of the text. To perform posterior inference in our Adaptive Topic Model, we develop a Gibbs sampling algorithm tailored to its specific structure. The sampler efficiently explores the posterior distribution over topic assignments, allowing us to estimate the model parameters and uncover the latent thematic structure within the data. We evaluate our model on the Herman Melville corpus, a collection of literary texts known for their complex and evolving thematic content. Experimental results demonstrate that our Adaptive Topic Model consistently outperforms existing topic modeling approaches in terms of perplexity, a standard measure of model fit. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that our model is able to uncover clear sequential structure within the texts, capturing shifts in topic focus and thematic development. It is also worth noting that recent works have begun to explore neural topic models (e.g., Blei et al., 2017) which represent a promising new direction for addressing sequential text modeling. However, the interpretability of these models can be limited, and they often require substantial computational resources for training. Our proposed model provides a probabilistic framework that offers both strong performance and enhanced interpretability.

Machine translation (MT) has traditionally focused on translating between a single source and a single target language. However, the need to translate to multiple target languages from a single source is increasingly common, driven by the globalization of information and the demand for multilingual communication. This scenario arises in many real-world applications, such as translating web content, technical documentation, or news articles for a diverse audience. While a naive approach would involve building separate translation systems for each language pair, this is often impractical due to the significant resources required for data collection, model training, and maintenance. Moreover, it fails to leverage the inherent relationships and shared information between the target languages. Recent research has begun to explore methods for multi-target machine translation (MTMT), aiming to translate from a single source to multiple targets simultaneously. One promising direction is transfer learning, where knowledge gained from translating to a resource-rich target language is transferred to improve translation performance for resource-poor target languages (Neubig and Hu, 2018; Lample et al., 2019). However, these methods often rely on finding effective ways to represent and share parameters or features across languages, which can be challenging. Another observed phenomenon is the potential for *positive interference* between translation tasks. When translating to closely related languages, the shared linguistic structures and semantic concepts can aid in disambiguation and improve the overall quality of translation. However, this interference is not always guaranteed and can even be detrimental if the target languages are too dissimilar or if the translation models are poorly aligned. In this paper, we present a novel approach to MTMT based on an extension of synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs), leveraging the relationships between target languages to boost translation performance. SCFGs are a well-established formalism in statistical machine translation, providing a principled way to represent correspondences between source and target languages (Knight, 1999; Chiang, 2005). We extend the standard SCFG formalism to handle multiple targets, creating *multi-synchronous context-free grammars* (MSCFGs). These MSCFGs allow us to explicitly model the shared grammatical structure and semantic concepts across multiple target languages. Our key hypothesis is that a strong language model in one target language can provide valuable information to disambiguate translations in a weaker target language. For example, if we are translating from English to both German and French, and we have a much better language model for French, we can use the French language model to guide the translation process into German, improving the fluency and accuracy of the German output. This is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the target languages have similar linguistic properties or share a common ancestor. We detail methods for extracting, scoring, pruning, and searching with these MSCFG models. Empirical evaluation on a controlled translation task demonstrate that our MTMT approach can achieve gains of up to 0.8-1.5 BLEU points compared to baseline systems that translate to each target language independently. The results confirm the potential of leveraging inter-language relationships to improve multi-target machine translation performance.

The increasing prevalence of social media platforms has created unprecedented opportunities for social science research, market analysis, and a diverse range of business applications. A key component in unlocking these opportunities lies in our ability to infer demographic characteristics from the language individuals use online. Accurate prediction of demographic attributes – such as age and gender – allows for a nuanced understanding of user behavior, targeted advertising, and insights into population trends. Existing work in this area has largely focused on developing models capable of predicting these demographics directly from textual data. However, a valuable byproduct of such modeling efforts is the creation of *demographic lexica* – curated lists of words and associated weights that indicate their predictive power for specific demographic groups. While several demographic lexica have been proposed in the past (e.g., based on blog data - Newman et al., 2008), the rapidly evolving nature of online language, and the growth of new social media platforms, necessitate the development of more current and robust lexica. Furthermore, questions remain regarding the portability of lexica across different social media genres. Language use on platforms like Facebook and Twitter, for example, may differ significantly from that found in blog posts, potentially limiting the generalizability of lexica trained on a single source. In this paper, we present a comprehensive effort to develop age and gender predictive lexica derived from large-scale datasets collected from three distinct social media sources: Facebook, blogs, and Twitter. We employ a combination of regression and classification techniques to identify and weight words that are strongly correlated with age and gender. A core contribution of our work is the public release of these lexica, providing a valuable resource for the research community (available at [insert link here]). We demonstrate the efficacy of our lexica by achieving state-of-the-art performance in age and gender prediction tasks on both Facebook and Twitter datasets. Beyond simply demonstrating predictive accuracy, we also systematically evaluate the generalization capabilities of our lexica. We assess their performance across different social media genres and in challenging scenarios involving limited textual input, such as short messages commonly found on platforms like Twitter. Our findings provide crucial insights into the transferability of demographic lexica and highlight the importance of considering the context in which they are applied. Ultimately, this work contributes to a more refined understanding of the linguistic markers associated with demographic attributes and facilitates the development of more accurate and reliable demographic prediction tools. Machine translation (MT) has made significant strides in recent years, largely propelled by the rise of neural machine translation (NMT) systems (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017). However, a key challenge remains: ensuring that translated outputs are not merely fluent, but also *useful* in downstream applications. This is particularly true when MT is used as a component in complex systems, such as question answering over knowledge bases. While traditional MT evaluation metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) focus on similarity to human reference translations, they often fail to capture the semantic correctness required for tasks like database querying. A promising direction for adapting MT systems to specific tasks is response-based learning (RBL), which leverages extrinsic feedback signals to refine the translation process (Chelba & Jelinek, 2000; Ueffing et al., 2003). Rather than relying solely on parallel corpora, RBL uses rewards or signals generated by the target application to steer the MT system towards producing outputs that elicit desired behaviors. This is particularly appealing for open-domain tasks where creating large, task-specific parallel corpora is costly or impractical. In this paper, we explore RBL for the task of translating natural language questions into executable database queries. Specifically, we target the translation of English questions into semantic parse representations that can be executed against the Freebase knowledge graph (Bolleaú et al., 2011). Our approach involves training a statistical machine translation (SMT) system (Koehn et al., 2003) and adapting it based on feedback obtained by executing the semantic parse of the translated query against the database. A correct execution confirms the translated query's semantic equivalence to the original question, serving as a positive signal for RBL. However, a significant obstacle in this context is the reliance on semantic parsers, which are notoriously brittle and susceptible to errors, especially when dealing with the lexical variability inherent in open-domain natural language. Traditional semantic parser evaluation focuses on accuracy over grammatically correct sentences. We demonstrate, however, that parser performance on *incorrect* English sentences – those resulting from machine translation – is crucial for effective model selection in RBL. A parser that is robust to even minor translation errors is essential for providing reliable feedback. We present experiments showing that carefully enhancing a semantic parser with paraphrases and synonyms yields the most substantial improvements in F1-score for retrieving the correct answer from Freebase. This underscores the importance of parser robustness in the RBL loop and highlights a critical factor for successfully integrating MT with knowledge base querying. Our work offers a practical methodology for adapting MT systems to complex downstream tasks when fully supervised data is scarce and highlights the often-overlooked role of parser error handling in response-based learning. Semantic parsing – the task of mapping natural language utterances into formal meaning representations – has emerged as a cornerstone of question answering (QA) and other natural language understanding applications (Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2005; Kwiatkowski et al., 2010). A long-standing challenge in semantic parsing lies in balancing two crucial, yet competing, aspects: the breadth of the underlying knowledge source and the depth of compositional reasoning required to process complex queries. Traditional semantic parsing systems often excel in narrow domains with well-defined ontologies (e.g., ATIS for flight booking) but struggle to scale to broader, more open-ended knowledge bases (KB) (Popescu et al., 2003). Conversely, systems designed to operate over large KBs, such as Freebase (Küçük and Liang, 2005), often sacrifice compositional generality, relying on simplified logical forms or pre-defined templates. Recent advancements in neural semantic parsing have shown promise in addressing the compositional challenge, effectively handling queries requiring intricate logical operations (Jung et al., 2015; Dong and Lapata, 2016). However, these approaches frequently operate on structured knowledge bases like Freebase, and their performance is often limited by the coverage and quality of the ontology. Simultaneously, there’s growing interest in leveraging semi-structured data sources, like tables extracted from web pages or Wikipedia, as rich sources of knowledge for QA (Pasupat and McIlraith, 2010; Chen and Mooney, 2008). Tables offer a significant advantage in breadth, encompassing vast amounts of real-world information. However, parsing questions over tables introduces a unique set of complexities. The open-ended nature of relational information within tables—where the set of possible relations is not pre-defined—presents a substantial challenge. Furthermore, questions querying tables often demand deep compositional reasoning, involving nested aggregations, comparisons, and filtering, leading to a combinatorial explosion in the space of possible logical forms. This paper tackles both challenges simultaneously by introducing a novel approach to compositional semantic parsing specifically tailored for semi-structured tables. We focus on answering complex questions posed against Wikipedia tables using question-answer pairs as weak supervision. Our central hypothesis is that by strongly guiding the parsing process with typing constraints derived from the table schema, we can effectively navigate the vast search space of possible logical forms and achieve significant improvements in performance. We propose a logical-form driven parsing algorithm that leverages the inherent structure of tables to constrain the search for valid semantic interpretations. To facilitate research in this area, we have created a new dataset of 22,033 complex questions paired with answers on Wikipedia tables – a valuable resource that we are making publicly available. Figure 1 illustrates a sample question, the relevant Wikipedia table excerpt, and the corresponding logical form that our system aims to generate. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we present a novel approach to compositional semantic parsing over semi-structured tables incorporating strong typing constraints, (2) we introduce a new challenging dataset of complex questions over Wikipedia tables, and (3) we demonstrate significant performance gains over strong baselines, showcasing the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in machine translation (Koehn et al., 2003). At its core, SMT models translation as a statistical inference problem – finding the most probable target language sentence given a source language sentence. A key component of any SMT system is the language model (LM), which estimates the fluency and grammatical correctness of the generated target language sentences (Chen & Goodman, 1999). Traditionally, n-gram language models have been the workhorse of SMT, assigning probabilities to sequences of words based on their observed frequencies in a large corpus. However, simple n-gram LMs suffer from data sparsity issues, particularly for rare or unseen word sequences. Various techniques have been proposed to address this, including smoothing methods (Lappone, 1991) and back-off models (Katz, 1987). More recently, incorporating syntactic information into the language model has gained traction, motivated by the idea that syntactic structure can improve the generalization capacity and accuracy of the LM. Part-of-speech (POS) language modeling, where word probabilities are conditioned on their POS tags, is one such approach (Niesler & Ney, 2004; Chiang, 2005). Despite its intuitive appeal, the benefit of POS language modeling in SMT remains somewhat controversial. While some studies report modest improvements (Niesler & Ney, 2004), others find little or no significant gain (Chiang, 2005). We hypothesize that a key limitation of existing POS language modeling approaches is their inherent lack of lexicalization. Traditional POS LMs treat all words of the same POS tag identically, failing to capture the unique contextual preferences of individual words. For instance, the verb "eat" will behave differently in many contexts compared to the verb "read" although they are categorized with the same POS tag. To address this, we propose a novel approach: Statistical Machine Translation with Local Language Models. Our central idea is to build a separate language model *for each word and POS tag pair*. This allows the model to learn highly context-specific probability distributions, tailoring its predictions to the specific lexical item being considered. Furthermore, we exploit the fact that different local language models will be engaged during decoding, providing a richer and more nuanced estimation of the overall language model probability. We evaluate our approach on the challenging tasks of Arabic-to-English and Chinese-to-English translation. Our experimental results demonstrate that our local language model consistently outperforms a competitive baseline SMT system, as well as a system incorporating a standard POS language model, achieving statistically significant improvements across multiple test sets and diverse genres. This suggests that lexicalization is indeed crucial for effectively leveraging syntactic information in SMT. The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work, Section 3 details our approach, Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results, and Section 5 concludes the paper with a discussion of future directions.

Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for addressing the limitations of traditional supervised learning, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or unavailable for certain classes (Socher et al., 2013;Romera-Paredes and Torr, 2015). The core idea behind ZSL is to transfer knowledge from seen classes to unseen classes by leveraging auxiliary information, such as semantic descriptions or attributes (Farhadi et al., 2009;Lampert et al., 2009). In recent years, a particularly promising approach to ZSL involves mapping data from a feature space (e.g., image features, word embeddings) into a semantic space, often a large, pre-trained word embedding space like word2vec or GloVe (Mikolov et al., 2013;Pennington et al., 2014). This cross-space mapping allows for the inference of labels for unseen instances by finding the nearest semantic concepts in the shared space. The intuitive appeal of this cross-space mapping approach stems from its ability to generalize beyond the training distribution. By projecting data into a semantic space informed by large-scale text corpora, the system can leverage existing knowledge about relationships between concepts, even those not explicitly seen during training. This capability is particularly valuable in applications like image recognition, where the number of possible object categories is vast and exhaustive labeling is impractical. Moreover, cross-space mapping naturally lends itself to tasks like cross-lingual transfer and cross-modal retrieval, opening up possibilities for unified representations across different modalities (Frome et al., 2013;Noroozi et al., 2016). Despite its theoretical promise, the performance of current cross-space mapping methods remains a significant bottleneck in achieving practical ZSL systems (Xie et al., 2015;Ba et al., 2015). While improvements have been made, the accuracy and robustness of these methods often fall considerably short of fully supervised approaches. A key observation is that the quality of the cross-space mapping function is crucial for successful ZSL, yet surprisingly little is understood about its inherent properties and potential pitfalls. In this paper, we delve into the challenges of cross-space mapping for ZSL, focusing on two prominent issues: *hubness* and *pollution*. Hubness refers to the tendency of certain vectors in the semantic space to become excessively close to many other vectors, effectively acting as “hubs” attracting spurious nearest neighbors. Pollution arises from the fact that the semantic space is often constructed from noisy and imperfect data (e.g., automatically generated word embeddings), leading to inaccurate representations of concepts. We analyze the theoretical implications of these phenomena and demonstrate their empirical impact on ZSL performance. Building on these insights, we propose novel techniques for addressing hubness and pollution, resulting in significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both cross-linguistic word translation and cross-modal image labeling experiments. Our contributions provide a deeper understanding of cross-space mapping and pave the way for more robust and effective zero-shot learning systems.

The proliferation of knowledge bases (KBs) constructed through diverse methodologies has led to a fragmented landscape of structured information. While Open Information Extraction (OpenIE) systems (e.g., Stanford OpenIE, ReVerb, Ollie) offer a scalable means of automatically populating KBs from unstructured text, the resulting outputs are often noisy, redundant, and lack consistent semantic representation. Integrating these disparate extractions into a unified, coherent KB is a critical challenge for realizing the full potential of knowledge discovery and reasoning. Existing approaches to KB merging typically rely on string matching, entity linking to canonical identifiers, or manually defined equivalence classes. However, these methods struggle with variations in phrasing, ambiguity in relation semantics, and the inherent incompleteness of existing KBs. Specifically, the challenge lies in addressing several key issues. First, the same real-world relation can be expressed using numerous linguistic variations (e.g., “born in”, “place of birth”, “was born in”). Second, a single phrase can represent multiple distinct relations depending on the context (e.g., “president of” can refer to a company, a country, or an organization). Third, different OpenIE systems often employ different levels of granularity and specificity when extracting relations. Finally, the domain and range of relations, even when expressed similarly, might refer to different conceptual categories, requiring careful alignment. To address these challenges, we introduce KB-UNIFY, a novel approach to KB unification that leverages sense embeddings and disambiguation techniques. KB-UNIFY aims to create a single, fully disambiguated knowledge repository by systematically merging the outputs of multiple OpenIE systems. Our approach is built around three core steps. First, we disambiguate relation argument pairs by mapping them to a large, unified sense inventory using sense-based vector representations. This allows us to resolve ambiguity in relation semantics and identify equivalent relations expressed using different phrasing. Second, we rank semantic relations according to their degree of specificity, prioritizing more precise and informative relations during the merging process. This helps to mitigate redundancy and reduce noise. Finally, we perform cross-resource relation alignment and merging based on the semantic similarity of domains and ranges, ensuring that entities and relations are correctly integrated across different KBs. We evaluate KB-UNIFY on a set of four heterogeneous knowledge bases, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing high-quality unified knowledge. We provide comprehensive evaluations at each stage of the pipeline, showcasing the benefits of our sense embedding and disambiguation approach. To foster further research in this area, we release our output and evaluation data to the community, enabling independent verification and extension of our work. Our contributions lie in a novel framework that tackles the inherent ambiguities and inconsistencies arising from multi-source knowledge extraction, offering a significant step towards creating truly unified and interoperable knowledge representations. The explosive growth of online information presents a significant challenge for users seeking relevant knowledge. While search engines excel at retrieving potentially relevant documents, sifting through numerous results to find concise answers remains a time-consuming and arduous task. Multi-document summarization (MDS) aims to address this issue by automatically generating a condensed version of a collection of documents, providing users with a focused overview of the information. Traditional MDS approaches often focus on generating summaries that are representative of the overall content of the document set. However, in many real-world scenarios, users are not interested in a general overview, but rather in information specifically relevant to a particular query – a task known as query-focused multi-document summarization (QF-MDS). For instance, a user searching for “side effects of ibuprofen” is primarily interested in the sections of multiple documents that address that specific topic, rather than a generic summary of ibuprofen’s properties. Existing QF-MDS systems typically employ techniques such as sentence extraction or abstractive generation. Extraction-based approaches identify and concatenate sentences from the source documents that are most relevant to the query. These methods are often simple and efficient, but can suffer from redundancy and lack of coherence, as extracted sentences may not flow seamlessly together. Abstractive summarization, on the other hand, aims to generate novel sentences that capture the key information relevant to the query. While potentially producing more fluent and concise summaries, abstractive methods are considerably more complex and require sophisticated natural language generation capabilities. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for QF-MDS that leverages sentence compression techniques. Sentence compression aims to shorten sentences while preserving their core meaning, offering a compelling trade-off between extraction and abstraction. By selectively removing less important phrases and clauses, compression can generate concise and informative summaries that directly address the user’s query. Our approach centers around learning a series of compression models based on syntactic parse trees, enabling us to identify and remove non-essential components of sentences while maintaining grammatical correctness. Crucially, we introduce an innovative beam search decoder designed to efficiently explore the vast space of possible compressions and identify highly probable outputs. Furthermore, we develop a novel compression scoring function that incorporates both linguistic motivations (based on parse tree structure) and query relevance, guiding the compression process towards summaries that are both grammatically sound and focused on the user's information need. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through extensive experiments on the DUC 2006 and 2007 QF-MDS datasets, achieving statistically significant improvements over state-of-the-art systems on multiple evaluation metrics, including ROUGE-2. Question Generation (QG) – the task of automatically creating natural language questions from a given context and answer – has garnered increasing attention due to its potential applications in diverse areas, including educational tutoring systems (Heilman & Smith, 2010), search engines (Li et al., 2014), and conversational AI (Rao et al., 2018). Traditionally, rule-based methods were employed for QG (Stein & Morrison, 1997), relying on hand-crafted linguistic rules to transform declarative sentences into interrogative ones. However, these approaches suffered from limited scalability and difficulty in handling complex sentence structures. With the advent of deep learning, neural network-based QG models have emerged as a more promising alternative. These models predominantly utilize sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) architectures (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014), treating QG as a translation problem from (context, answer) pairs to questions. Recent advancements, like those presented in (Du et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Song et al., 2018), demonstrate the capacity of seq2seq models to generate fluent and relevant questions. Despite these advancements, we identify two key shortcomings within current neural QG approaches. Firstly, the generated interrogative words (e.g., ‘who’, ‘what’, ‘where’) frequently mismatch the type of the given answer. For instance, if the answer is a numerical value, the model may still generate a question beginning with ‘who’ instead of ‘how much’. This likely stems from a lack of explicit modeling of the relationship between the answer and the question word. Secondly, the model tends to indiscriminately copy words from the context, often selecting terms that are distant from and irrelevant to the answer, while overlooking those that are closely associated and crucial for formulating a concise and focused question. This impacts the overall quality and clarity of the generated question. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Answer-Focused and Position-Aware Neural Question Generation model. The core idea is to explicitly incorporate answer information into the question word generation process (answer-focused) and to model the relative distance between the context words and the answer span (position-aware). Specifically, we inject the answer embedding into the decoder during the generation of the first word of the question, encouraging it to select an appropriate interrogative word based on the answer type. Simultaneously, we introduce a position encoding mechanism that captures the distance between each context word and the answer span, enabling the model to prioritize words closer to the answer during question formation. We validate our model through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art systems. Our contributions can be summarised as: (1) A novel answer-focused mechanism that improves the selection of appropriate question words. (2) A position-aware mechanism that prioritises relevant context words during question generation. (3) Comprehensive experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed model.

Prepositions are notoriously difficult for non-native English speakers to master, and even native speakers occasionally make errors. As a result, automatic preposition error correction (PEC) has been a longstanding problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Early approaches to PEC relied on manually curated error corpora (e.g., (Hancock, 2008;Wang et al., 2014)), offering high precision, but suffering from limited coverage and scalability. More recent work has shifted towards leveraging large, well-edited text corpora – like the Penn Treebank (PTB) (Marcus et al., 1993) – to train statistical models of preposition usage (e.g., (Zellers et al., 2011;Kann et al., 2016)). These methods offer the advantage of scalability, but require careful feature engineering and often struggle with out-of-domain generalization. While these methods perform well on held-out data from similar domains, performance often degrades substantially when applied to text with different characteristics – for instance, learner writing or text originating from a different genre. A critical question, then, is whether existing methods truly *generalize*, or simply perform well because they are evaluated on datasets similar to those they were trained on. Prior work has demonstrated limited generalization even within similar domains (e.g., across different sections of the Wall Street Journal in (Zellers et al., 2011)). Moreover, current PEC resources are often inadequate for exploring generalization thoroughly. Existing error corpora may not accurately reflect the types of errors encountered in real-world scenarios, and reliance on well-edited text risks over-fitting to the writing style of that specific corpus. To address these issues, we present a significant new resource for PEC research: a large, automatically-extracted error-annotated corpus created from Wikipedia revisions. Wikipedia’s open editing policy provides a valuable source of naturally occurring preposition errors and their corrections. By analyzing version histories, we can identify edits specifically targeted at correcting preposition usage, creating a noisy yet substantial corpus of over one million preposition correction instances. We demonstrate the utility of this new corpus by training PEC systems and evaluating their performance across three diverse test sets, specifically chosen to represent different domains and error characteristics – a standard learner corpus, a set of errors extracted from academic writing, and a test set derived from blog data. Our experiments reveal that existing approaches – even those recently proposed – consistently demonstrate poor generalization ability. Systems trained on well-edited text or smaller, manually-annotated corpora fail to achieve strong performance across all three test sets. Conversely, models trained on our new, large-scale Wikipedia revision corpus exhibit significantly improved generalization, demonstrating the value of training on a more diverse and representative dataset. This work provides both a valuable new resource and a clear demonstration of the importance of robust training data for building effective preposition error correction systems. March 1, 2024.

Machine translation (MT) has long been a central task in natural language processing, aiming to automatically convert text from one language (the source) to another (the target) while preserving meaning. Traditionally, statistical machine translation (SMT) systems dominated the field, relying heavily on feature engineering, language modeling, and sophisticated alignment techniques (Koehn et al., 2003). These systems often involved a complex pipeline of separate components addressing distinct subproblems like phrase extraction, distortion modeling, and decoding. While effective, SMT systems were laborious to develop and maintain, demanding significant expertise and iterative refinement of hand-crafted features. The advent of neural network-based approaches, particularly Neural Machine Translation (NMT), marked a paradigm shift in the field (Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015). NMT offers a compelling alternative by framing translation as an end-to-end learning problem. These models, often built upon recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, learn to map input sequences directly to output sequences, minimizing the need for explicit feature engineering. This simplification, combined with the ability to capture long-range dependencies, has led to substantial improvements in translation quality across numerous language pairs. However, despite their successes, NMT systems are not without challenges. A prominent issue is the "out-of-vocabulary" (OOV) problem, arising from the fact that models can only operate on words present in their predefined vocabulary. During inference, encountering words not seen during training leads to either their replacement with a special `<UNK>` token or reliance on more complex techniques like subword segmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016). While subword segmentation mitigates the OOV problem to some extent, it does not eliminate it entirely, and can sometimes lead to less fluent or natural translations. This paper focuses on a detailed examination of the OOV problem, with a specific case study on English-German translation. We argue that the compounding nature of the German language exacerbates the issue to a significant degree. German frequently constructs new words by concatenating existing ones – a process known as compounding – leading to a vast and potentially unbounded vocabulary. This poses a significant challenge for NMT models with limited vocabulary sizes. We investigate the effectiveness of various compound word splitting strategies, assessing their impact on translation performance. Our experiments demonstrate that intelligently splitting compound words can significantly alleviate the OOV problem, leading to substantial gains in translation quality. Specifically, we show improvements exceeding 2.5 BLEU points on the WMT’14 German-to-English translation task. Moreover, we explore a novel target-side compound splitting technique, achieving further performance improvements on the English-to-German direction. This work aims to provide a deeper understanding of the factors contributing to the difficulty of word-level NMT, particularly for morphologically rich languages like German, and to present practical solutions for mitigating these challenges.

Machine translation (MT) has made significant progress in recent years, fueled by the rise of neural network-based approaches (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). However, despite these advances, current MT systems still struggle with ambiguity, idiomatic expressions, and long-range dependencies, leading to translation errors and suboptimal fluency. A common strategy to improve MT performance is *system combination* (SC), where the outputs of multiple MT systems are combined to produce a more accurate and robust translation (Freitag & Al-Onaizan, 2008; Resnik, 1999). SC methods typically rely on scoring and re-ranking the n-best lists generated by individual systems, or by decoding a word lattice representing the consensus of multiple systems—for example, Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding (Okoń, 2005). However, these methods are *post-processing* techniques; they do not allow the decoders to actively interact and influence each other *during* the translation generation process. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called *collaborative decoding* (co-decoding) that aims to improve MT accuracy by leveraging translation consensus between multiple decoders *during* the decoding phase. Unlike SC and MBR decoding which operate on already generated hypotheses, co-decoding enables decoders to collaborate by exchanging partial translation results, and iteratively re-ranking hypotheses based on agreement statistics. The core idea is that if multiple decoders independently generate similar partial translations, these are likely to be good candidates and should be prioritized. Our framework employs an iterative decoding process, where each decoder periodically broadcasts its current n-best list of partial translations to the other decoders. Each decoder then computes n-gram agreement statistics between its own hypotheses and the hypotheses received from the others. These statistics are used to re-rank both full and partial hypotheses within its own decoding process. This collaborative re-ranking mechanism allows the decoders to collectively explore and refine the translation space, leading to more accurate and fluent translations. We evaluate co-decoding on the NIST Chinese-to-English machine translation task, using several state-of-the-art neural MT decoders as baselines. The experimental results demonstrate that co-decoding consistently yields significant improvements over all baseline decoders. Moreover, we show that the outputs from co-decoding can be further leveraged to improve the performance of system combination, highlighting the synergistic benefits of combining collaborative decoding with traditional system combination techniques. This suggests that incorporating translation consensus during the decoding phase can be a powerful strategy for advancing machine translation technology. Research on decoding schemes often focuses on beam search modifications, such as diverse beam search (Li et al., 2016) or length normalization (Wu et al., 2016). Our work differs in that it focuses on *inter*-decoder communication and collaboration, rather than *intra*-decoder optimization.

Financial markets are profoundly influenced by the flow of information. News events, ranging from earnings announcements to macroeconomic data releases, can rapidly shift investor sentiment and, consequently, impact asset prices. Accurately quantifying the *information content* of these news reports – that is, the extent to which a news item alters expectations about a company’s future performance – is therefore of paramount importance for investors, analysts, and regulators alike. Understanding information content allows for more informed investment decisions, improved risk management, and a more efficient allocation of capital. Traditional finance theory posits that asset prices reflect all available information (Fama, 1970), but identifying *how much* information is contained within a specific news item, and its subsequent impact on intrinsic value, remains a significant challenge. Early attempts to quantify the relationship between news and market movements often relied on manual analysis of news articles and event studies (Brown & Warner, 1980). However, this approach is time-consuming, expensive, and difficult to scale. More recently, computational methods leveraging Natural Language Processing (NLP) have emerged as promising tools for automating this process. A dominant approach within this realm centers around sentiment analysis, extracting positive, negative, or neutral tones from news text and correlating these scores with stock price movements (Loughran & McDonald, 2011; Tetlock et al., 2008). While sentiment analysis provides a valuable signal, it has inherent limitations. Sentiment alone doesn’t capture the underlying *event* driving the sentiment, nor does it account for the specific targets within the news article. A positive sentiment towards a company may stem from a new product launch (high information content) or simply a favorable analyst upgrade (lower information content). This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a novel model for measuring the information content of financial news, trained directly on news text and corresponding cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) of listed companies. Unlike existing approaches primarily focused on sentiment, our model leverages the power of deep neural networks to extract rich semantic features from news articles. In particular, we introduce a tree-structured LSTM architecture, designed to capture target-specific representations of news text by incorporating syntactic structures. This allows the model to understand *which* aspects of a company are being discussed in the news and how that relates to the observed market reaction. By associating the syntactic structure of the text with the specific company being reported on, we are able to create a more nuanced and informative representation of the news content than simply a global sentiment score. Our empirical results demonstrate that this neural approach significantly outperforms traditional sentiment-based models in predicting CARs, highlighting the effectiveness of recent advancements in NLP for computational finance. This improvement suggests that capturing the semantic richness of news text, beyond just its sentiment, is crucial for accurately gauging its informational value and its ultimate impact on financial markets. The proliferation of online consumer reviews has created a wealth of information for potential buyers, yet efficiently extracting specific answers to opinion questions remains a significant challenge. Consumers frequently seek targeted information, such as “How is the battery life on this phone?” or “Is the camera good in low light?”, rather than wading through lengthy, unstructured review text. While existing opinion mining and question answering (QA) systems can identify sentiment and extract opinions, they often struggle with nuanced questions requiring aggregation of information across multiple reviews and consideration of hierarchical relationships between product features. Many approaches treat reviews as a flat collection of text, failing to exploit the inherent organization of consumer feedback around specific product aspects and their sub-aspects. This paper addresses this limitation by proposing a novel framework for answering opinion questions about products that explicitly leverages the hierarchical organization of consumer reviews. We posit that product aspects are naturally structured in a parent-child relationship – for example, “Camera” is a broader aspect with sub-aspects like “Low Light Performance,” “Zoom,” and “Image Quality.” By organizing reviews according to this hierarchy, we can effectively pinpoint relevant information and generate more targeted and informative answers. Our approach constructs a hierarchy of product aspects, where nodes represent these aspects and their connections reflect parent-child relations. Each aspect node stores associated review fragments and corresponding opinions extracted from consumer reviews. This hierarchical structure allows for both focused retrieval of relevant information and consideration of broader contextual factors. Given an opinion question, our framework first performs a detailed analysis to identify the explicit or implicit product aspects being queried, and importantly, any related sub-aspects through traversal of the hierarchy. We then retrieve review fragments associated with these aspects, forming a pool of candidate answer sentences. However, simply retrieving relevant fragments is insufficient for generating high-quality answers. Aggregating information from multiple sources requires addressing challenges like redundancy, incoherence, and ensuring a comprehensive response. To address these issues, we develop a multi-criteria optimization approach for answer generation. This approach simultaneously considers factors such as the salience of individual reviews (to prioritize authoritative opinions), coherence of the generated answer, diversity of information presented, and the parent-child relationship between aspects– ensuring answers consider both specific details and broader context. We evaluate our framework on a comprehensive corpus of 11 popular products spanning four domains and encompassing over 70,000 consumer reviews and 220 opinion questions. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of answer accuracy, relevance, and informativeness, highlighting the effectiveness of exploiting the hierarchical organization of consumer reviews for opinion question answering. This work represents a step towards building intelligent systems that can efficiently extract and synthesize knowledge from the vast and growing body of online consumer feedback. Automatic summarization has long been a central task in Natural Language Processing, aiming to condense lengthy text into shorter, informative versions (Mani, 2001; Nenkova & McKeown, 2012). While abstractive summarization – generating new phrases to represent the original content – is a highly desirable goal, extractive summarization, which selects and concatenates salient sentences from the source document, remains a practical and widely-used approach, especially for tasks demanding fidelity to the original text. Within extractive summarization, *news highlights* represent a particularly challenging but valuable subtask. Typically consisting of only 3-4 sentences, news highlights must capture the core essence of a news article with extreme brevity and clarity. This requirement differentiates them from more general summarization tasks, where longer summaries are permissible. The subtle nuances distinguishing truly indicative sentences from merely frequent or central ones are difficult to capture without additional signals. In this paper, we explore a novel approach to enhance news highlights extraction by leveraging the wealth of information available in microblog posts, specifically those from Twitter. Our central hypothesis is that microblogs, despite their inherent noisiness and informal style, contain valuable indicators of salient information in news articles. This stems from two key properties of microblogging platforms: first, users actively share and discuss news articles, effectively highlighting the most noteworthy aspects as they perceive them. Second, the character limit enforced by platforms like Twitter induces a natural compression effect, forcing users to express information concisely and “to the point.” This resonates with the inherent requirement for brevity in news highlights. The second task explores a more direct approach: extracting top-ranked *tweets themselves* as a substitute for sentence extraction from the news article. This allows us to directly benefit from the “short and sweet” nature of microblog posts. We present experimental results on a newly constructed news-tweet pairing corpus demonstrating that our microblog-informed methods significantly outperform several strong baseline summarization algorithms.
