The pursuit of truly multilingual natural language processing (NLP) systems – those capable of seamlessly processing and understanding text across a wide range of languages – is a central goal within the field. A core tenet of this ambition is the development of language-agnostic architectures, neural networks or statistical models that operate independently of the specific linguistic properties of any given language. The underlying assumption is that, with sufficient data and model capacity, a single, universal system can be built which generalizes across all languages. However, this aspiration frequently encounters significant hurdles. While the dream of a truly universal grammar has captivated linguists for decades, the reality is that the world’s languages exhibit a remarkable degree of variation in their structural and semantic characteristics. This variation, systematically studied by the field of linguistic typology, presents a fundamental challenge to the development of truly language-independent NLP systems. Linguistic typology focuses on classifying languages based on their shared structural features, ranging from word order to morphological complexity. These typological distinctions are not merely superficial; they reflect deep-seated differences in how information is encoded and conveyed across languages. For example, languages can differ dramatically in whether they rely on word order (e.g., English) or morphological marking (e.g., Finnish) to signal grammatical relations. Some languages are highly isolating, with minimal morphology (e.g., Mandarin Chinese), while others are highly agglutinative, stringing together multiple morphemes into single words (e.g., Turkish). These differences impact the statistical properties of language, creating distinct challenges for modeling. In this work, we investigate the relationship between linguistic typology and the performance of language models (LMs), particularly in a multilingual setting. We present a large-scale study of both traditional n-gram based LMs and state-of-the-art neural LMs across 50 typologically diverse languages. By centering on full vocabulary language modeling, that is predicting the next word in a sequence without subword segmentation, we aim to assess the limits of current modeling approaches when faced with morphological complexity. Our findings demonstrate a clear correlation between a coarse-grained typology of morphological systems and absolute LM performance. Specifically, languages with richer morphologies systematically exhibit lower LM perplexities, suggesting that these languages are more difficult to model. Furthermore, we examine more fine-grained typological features – such as exponence (the number of morphemes per word), flexivity (the number of grammatical categories expressed per word), fusion (the degree to which morphemes blend together), and inflectional synthesis (the complexity of inflectional systems) – and demonstrate their impact on the proliferation of low-frequency word forms. These low-frequency phenomena pose a significant challenge for statistical architectures, leading to poor generalization. Our results underscores the necessity of incorporating typological considerations into the design of next-generation language-agnostic LM architectures, particularly for effectively handling morphologically rich languages like Tamil or Korean. In essence, this paper argues that ignoring linguistic typology is not a viable path towards truly multilingual NLP. A greater engagement with typological insights is critical for developing models that can effectively capture the nuanced variations across the world’s languages.

The automatic identification of opinions expressed in text – often referred to as opinion mining or sentiment analysis – has become a central task in natural language processing (NLP) with applications ranging from market research and brand monitoring to political analysis and public opinion tracking (Liu, 2012). A core subtask within this broader field is *opinion expression extraction*, which aims to pinpoint the specific phrases in a text that convey subjective information, beliefs, or evaluations. These expressions can take various forms, including adjectives (“a *fantastic* movie”), adverbs (“*surprisingly* good”), nouns (“a *disaster*”), and even entire clauses (“I *strongly believe* that…”). Traditionally, opinion expression extraction has been approached as a sequence labeling problem. Given a sentence, the task is to assign a label to each token, indicating whether it belongs to an opinion expression or not (e.g., using BIO tagging – Beginning, Inside, Outside). Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) have emerged as the dominant modeling technique for this task, effectively capturing dependencies between neighboring labels and incorporating a rich set of features derived from the text (Lafferty et al., 2001). However, standard CRFs operate at the token level, and thus struggle to fully capture the inherent segmental nature of opinion expressions. Opinion expressions often span multiple tokens and frequently align with syntactic constituents – phrases like noun phrases or verb phrases. Ignoring this structural information can lead to suboptimal performance. While incorporating syntactic features into token-level CRFs can help, it doesn’t directly model the boundaries of opinion expressions as segments. Recent work, such as the semi-CRF model proposed by Sarawagi and Cohen (2004), offers a promising alternative by performing sequence labeling at the segment level. This allows the model to directly learn segment boundaries and leverage information about the internal structure of the segments themselves. In this paper, we build upon the semi-CRF framework to develop a more effective approach to opinion expression extraction. We extend the original semi-CRF model to handle arbitrarily long opinion expressions, a limitation of previous implementations. Crucially, we integrate syntactic parse information into the segment boundary modeling process, allowing the model to prioritize segmentations that align with likely syntactic constituents. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough evaluation of our approach on two publicly available opinion expression datasets. Unlike prior sequence labeling methods, we systematically investigate the contribution of segment-level syntactic features to the task. Our experimental results convincingly demonstrate that our semi-CRF-based approach, leveraging syntactic information, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for opinion expression extraction, confirming the importance of modeling opinion expressions as segments and incorporating syntactic knowledge into the extraction process. Image captioning, the task of automatically generating textual descriptions of images, has witnessed tremendous progress in recent years. Driven by advances in deep learning, particularly the combination of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for visual feature extraction and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for sequence generation, state-of-the-art models now produce captions that are often remarkably fluent and contextually relevant (Vinyals et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015; Karpathy et al., 2015). However, despite these advancements, a persistent and concerning issue remains: the tendency of these models to “hallucinate” objects – to describe elements that are not actually present in the input image. This phenomenon is not simply a matter of generating inaccurate details; it fundamentally undermines the trustworthiness and reliability of image captioning systems. For example, a model might caption an image of a dog in a park as "a dog is playing with a frisbee," when no frisbee is visible. Such errors can have serious implications in applications requiring accurate and faithful scene understanding, such as assistive technology for the visually impaired or automated image indexing. Existing evaluation metrics for image captioning, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and CIDEr (Vedantam et al., 2015), primarily focus on measuring the similarity between generated captions and human-provided ground truth captions. While these metrics are useful for assessing fluency and overall relevance, they are not specifically designed to detect and quantify object hallucination. A caption can achieve a high score on these metrics even if it contains hallucinatory objects, as long as the overall phrasing and semantic content are similar to the ground truth. This limitation motivates the need for new evaluation methods that are more sensitive to image fidelity. In this work, we take a closer look at the problem of object hallucination in image captioning. We propose a novel image relevance metric, grounded in veridical visual labels, specifically designed to assess the rate at which models generate descriptions containing objects not present in the image. We utilize a large-scale, manually annotated dataset to identify commonly hallucinatory objects and establish a more reliable benchmark for evaluating and comparing captioning models. Furthermore, we analyze the architectural and learning characteristics that contribute to object hallucination, investigating whether errors stem from misclassification of image content or are driven by biases inherent in the language model component. Through a comprehensive analysis of a diverse set of models trained on the standard MSCOCO dataset, we aim to shed light on the underlying causes of this pervasive problem and offer insights towards developing more trustworthy and reliable image captioning systems. Our results reveal surprising findings, including instances where models with superior performance on conventional metrics exhibit higher rates of object hallucination, and a strong correlation between hallucination and reliance on language priors. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving state-of-the-art results on numerous language pairs (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015). However, this approach can struggle when dealing with morphologically rich languages (MRLs) – languages like German, Turkish, Finnish, and Russian, where words are often formed by combining multiple morphemes, each carrying specific grammatical or semantic meaning. A key challenge when translating from MRLs is the inherent complexity of their word structure. A single word in a source MRL can often correspond to multiple words, or even an entire phrase, in the target language. Traditional word-based NMT models, which treat words as atomic units, may fail to capture the internal structure of these morphologically complex words (MCWs), leading to suboptimal translation quality. This is because the surface form of a word can obscure the underlying semantic and grammatical components, hindering the model's ability to accurately map it to the corresponding target representation. Several approaches have been proposed to address this issue. Subword segmentation techniques, such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2015), aim to decompose words into smaller, more frequent units, thereby reducing the vocabulary size and allowing the model to handle unseen words. Character-level models (Lee et al., 2017) take this a step further, operating directly on the character sequence, which eliminates the need for segmentation but introduces challenges in capturing long-range dependencies. While these methods have shown some success, they often fail to fully exploit the hierarchical structure inherent in MCWs. In this work, we propose a novel NMT architecture specifically tailored for translating from MRLs. Our approach, building upon the encoder-decoder framework, is designed to provide richer information on the encoder side and redesign the decoder to effectively utilize this information. We introduce a “double-channel encoder” that processes the input sentence at both the word and the character levels and a “double-attentive decoder” that leverages both representations during the decoding process. The core idea is to allow the model to simultaneously capture both the holistic meaning of a word and its internal morphological structure. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms existing subword- and character-based NMT architectures on the translation of German, Russian, and Turkish into English. The improvements observed across these diverse MRLs highlight the effectiveness of our approach in capturing the complexities of morphological variation and producing more accurate and fluent translations. This work represents a step towards more effective NMT systems for languages where morphology plays a crucial role in meaning construction.

Natural language processing (NLP) models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ranging from information extraction and question answering to machine translation and sentiment analysis. A core component of many of these systems is the ability to assign probabilities to possible linguistic structures – for example, the probability of a particular parse tree, the likelihood of a specific named entity tag, or the confidence in a predicted relation between entities. However, while much research focuses on maximizing the accuracy of these models – that is, minimizing overall error rates – comparatively little attention has been paid to the *quality* of the probabilities themselves. Are these probabilities well-calibrated, meaning do they accurately reflect the true likelihood of the predicted structures being correct? And, crucially, how can we leverage this information, either to improve our models or to inform users about the reliability of the NLP analysis? We argue in this paper that assessing the calibration of NLP models is not merely a theoretical concern, but a critical step toward building trustworthy and robust systems. A well-calibrated model provides probabilities that can be directly interpreted as degrees of confidence. For example, if a model assigns a probability of 0.9 to a particular parse tree, we should expect that, across many similar sentences, approximately 90% of the time that parse tree will be the correct one. When models are *miscalibrated* – as is often the case in practice – this interpretation is invalid. Overconfident models may report high probabilities for incorrect predictions, leading to unwarranted trust and potentially costly errors. Underconfident models, conversely, may mask correct predictions with low probabilities, hindering their usefulness. Beyond the direct evaluation of model calibration, we propose that understanding uncertainty in NLP can enable more informative exploratory data analysis. Traditionally, qualitative analysis of NLP output relies on manual inspection and expert judgment. However, even skilled annotators are susceptible to bias and can be misled by confidently presented, yet incorrect, analyses. By quantifying uncertainty and providing confidence intervals for NLP predictions, we can guide users toward areas of the data that require closer scrutiny and help them identify patterns that might otherwise be overlooked. In this work, we present a methodology for analyzing calibration in NLP models, applying it to a comparative study of several commonly used systems. We demonstrate that many state-of-the-art models exhibit significant miscalibration, highlighting the need for techniques to improve probability estimation. Furthermore, we contribute a novel coreference sampling algorithm tailored for political event extraction, which allows us to generate confidence intervals for extracted events and provide a quantifiable measure of uncertainty in the analysis. This work demonstrates a path toward building NLP systems that not only perform well, but also honestly communicate their limitations. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Existing typological databases, such as WALS (Dryer & Haspelmath, 2011) and AutoTyp (List, 2014), provide a rich source of information, but remain incomplete, particularly for under-represented language families and geographically remote regions. Secondly, translating *into* English encourages the NMT system to encode cross-linguistic generalizations in a shared representation space. This suggests that the NMT system is learning genuinely linguistic characteristics, rather than simply relying on areal or historical correlations. This work represents a step towards bridging the gap between neural NLP and linguistic theory, offering a novel methodology for accelerating typological research and expanding our understanding of the world’s linguistic diversity.

Distributed word representations, or word embeddings, have become a cornerstone of modern Natural Language Processing (NLP). Techniques such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), and FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) learn to map words to dense, low-dimensional vector spaces, capturing semantic and syntactic relationships between words. These embeddings have demonstrated remarkable success across a wide range of downstream NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, machine translation, and question answering. However, it’s been observed that the performance of word embeddings is highly sensitive to the specific task at hand (Pilehvar et al., 2018; Neelakantan et al., 2015). For instance, embeddings trained on different corpora or using different algorithms often exhibit varying strengths in capturing nuanced semantic differences or handling rare words. This suggests that individual word embedding methods capture *complementary* aspects of lexical semantics, rather than a single, universally optimal representation. Motivated by this observation, a growing body of research has focused on combining multiple pre-trained word embeddings into “meta-embeddings” (Faruqui et al., 2015; Neelakantan et al., 2015; Levy et al., 2015). The goal is to leverage the unique strengths of each source embedding to create a more robust and informative representation. Early approaches often relied on simple averaging or concatenation of embeddings, while more sophisticated methods employ techniques like orthogonal Procrustes analysis to align the embedding spaces (Faruqui et al., 2015). Despite these advancements, creating effective meta-embeddings remains a challenging problem. Many existing methods require careful tuning of hyperparameters or rely on assumptions about the underlying embedding spaces that may not always hold true. In this paper, we present a novel approach to learning word meta-embeddings based on the principle of autoencoding. We formulate the problem as learning a lower-dimensional “meta-embedding space” that can accurately *reconstruct* all of the source embeddings simultaneously. This compels the meta-embedding space to capture the shared and complementary information present in the original embeddings, effectively creating a coherent common embedding space. We hypothesize that by forcing the meta-embedding to represent all source embeddings well, we can learn representations that generalize better to downstream tasks. We explore three distinct variations of our autoencoding approach, each guided by different criteria for what constitutes a good meta-embedding – specifically emphasizing reconstruction accuracy, sparsity, and robustness to noise. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed autoencoded meta-embeddings consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art meta-embedding techniques across a diverse set of benchmark evaluation tasks, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach in capturing complementary semantic information. . Natural language exhibits substantial variation, a persistent challenge for robust and generalizable natural language processing (NLP) systems. The challenge is further complicated by the often-continuous nature of dialect boundaries. Rather than sharp divisions, dialects tend to exist along a gradient, with subtle shifts in linguistic features as one moves across geographic space. Existing discretized dialect maps, while valuable resources, often represent approximations of this continuous reality, imposed by pre-defined administrative or regional boundaries. A more nuanced approach would be to represent dialects as continuous variations, capturing the complex interplay of linguistic features across geographic space. In this work, we explore representation learning as a means to automatically capture these continuous regional linguistic distinctions. Specifically, we leverage the Doc2Vec algorithm (Le & Mikolov, 2014) to learn distributed representations of cities based on a large corpus of geotagged online text. This approach avoids the need for hand-engineered features and allows the model to discover relevant linguistic variables directly from the data. To further enhance the geographic coherence of these representations, we introduce a retrofitting technique (Faruqui et al., 2015) that incorporates explicit geographic information. We then apply agglomerative clustering to these retrofitted representations, allowing us to recover dialect areas at varying levels of granularity. They typically fail to capture the intricate interplay of various simplification techniques—splitting, dropping, reordering, and substitution—that are often necessary to achieve substantial simplification. The availability of large-scale, high-quality parallel data is a critical bottleneck in the development of effective simplification models. This dataset provides a valuable resource for learning robust simplification patterns from real-world text. We evaluate our model on standard simplification benchmarks and demonstrate that it achieves improved readability scores compared to a set of competitive baseline systems. This observation motivates the field of *personalized summarization*, which aims to tailor summaries to individual user needs. Recent advancements in user modeling and preference elicitation have fueled progress in this area, however, most personalized summarization systems rely on explicit user profiles—information directly provided by the user—which are often sparse, inaccurate, or simply unavailable. A promising alternative lies in leveraging the wealth of implicit information available in social networks. Social context, encompassing a user’s connections, activities, and shared interests, provides a rich and readily accessible source of user preference data. By analyzing a user’s social interactions—such as posts, likes, and shares—we can infer their interests without requiring explicit input. This approach is particularly well-suited for social media platforms where user-generated content and social connections are pervasive. However, effectively integrating social context into personalized summarization remains a complex problem. Existing approaches typically focus on either incorporating local document information and user profiles individually, or perform simple keyword matching between document sentences and user interests. These methods often fail to capture the nuanced relationships between document content, user interests, and the broader social landscape. This paper proposes a novel unsupervised approach to context-enhanced personalized social summarization, aiming to overcome the limitations of existing methods. Our framework leverages enhanced social context to simultaneously achieve document expansion, user expansion, and implicit induction of a user's interest aspects through a fuzzy tripartite clustering algorithm. This allows the system to identify not only keywords relevant to the document and the user, but also the underlying thematic dimensions that connect them. Furthermore, we introduce a unified ranking process that integrates both the informativeness of individual sentences and their alignment with the inferred user interest aspects. We evaluate our approach on a social tagging dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating personalized summaries that are both informative and relevant to individual users. Our contributions lie in the novel application of fuzzy clustering for integrated context modeling and the development of a unified ranking framework that balances informativeness and personalization. This work represents a significant step towards more intelligent and user-centric summarization systems capable of navigating the overwhelming flood of online information. The question of what makes a novel “successful” has captivated authors, publishers, and literary critics for centuries. While artistic merit is often cited as a primary driver, the market realities of book sales and sustained readership suggest a more complex interplay of factors. Could it be that underlying, quantifiable characteristics of *how* a story is written—its style—play a significant, and perhaps predictable, role in determining its fate? This question motivates our investigation into the relationship between writing style and literary success. Traditional literary analysis often focuses on thematic content, character development, and narrative structure to assess a novel’s quality. However, these assessments are inherently subjective. In contrast, stylometry—the quantitative study of literary style—offers a data-driven approach to analyzing the linguistic features that characterize an author’s or a genre’s writing. Previous applications of stylometry have largely focused on authorship attribution (Mosteller & Wallace, 1963), genre classification (Argyle & Galbraith, 1994), and tracing influence between authors (Ryder, 2007). To our knowledge, no prior work has systematically investigated the predictive power of stylistic features in identifying novels destined for commercial or critical success. We hypothesize that stylistic patterns, even if unconsciously employed by authors, correlate with a novel’s reception. This correlation could reflect audience preferences, readability factors impactful to broader consumption, or even subtle cues that signal quality to readers. This work aims to rigorously test this hypothesis. We compile a large corpus of novels spanning a variety of genres, paired with objective measures of success—namely, sales figures, award nominations, and sustained presence on bestseller lists. We then extract a comprehensive suite of stylistic features from these novels, encompassing lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and characteristic word usage. Using machine learning techniques, we evaluate the extent to which these features can discriminate between successful and less successful literary works. Our results demonstrate, surprisingly, that statistical stylometry *can* be remarkably effective at predicting success, achieving accuracies up to 84% in our model. Furthermore, our analyses reveal novel insights into the stylistic characteristics prevalent in successful literature—insights that challenge some commonly held beliefs about “good” writing style and readability. These findings contribute a new quantitative perspective to the long-standing debate concerning the determinants of literary success, with potential implications for authors, publishers, and readers alike. --- **References (Placeholder - would be filled in a full paper):** * Argyle, R., & Galbraith, W. The notion that English orthography, despite its widely acknowledged irregularities, is “near optimal” has persisted within linguistic circles for over half a century. This assertion, prominently made by Chomsky and Halle (1968) in *The Sound Pattern of English*, has largely gone unchallenged, becoming a frequently cited, though rarely rigorously examined, tenet of linguistic discussion. The claim, stemming from a generative phonological framework, suggests that the seemingly haphazard nature of English spelling is, in fact, a historically contingent but ultimately justifiable outcome of competing pressures towards phonemic representation and morphological transparency. However, with the advent of readily available computational resources and advancements in algorithmic design, the opportunity arises to subject this long-held belief to empirical scrutiny. This paper aims to do just that. We argue that English orthography is demonstrably *not* “close to optimal,” and that a spelling system constructed with explicit goals of maximizing both phonemic transparency – the degree to which spelling reflects pronunciation – and morphological consistency – the degree to which spelling reflects word structure – can significantly outperform the conventional system. Our investigation departs from traditional linguistic analysis by adopting a computational approach. Rather than relying on qualitative arguments about historical development or underlying linguistic principles, we implement an algorithm designed to *generate* an orthography based on explicitly defined optimality criteria. This algorithm utilizes a modern pronunciation dictionary and a morphological lexicon to construct spellings that minimize ambiguity in both sound-symbol correspondence and morpheme boundaries. By generating a “best-case” orthography based on these principles, we establish a benchmark against which the existing English spelling system can be objectively evaluated. The core of our methodology hinges on defining quantifiable metrics for both phonemic transparency and morphological consistency. We utilize established measures of edit distance to assess the similarity between spellings and their phonetic transcriptions, and employ morphological parsing techniques to quantify the degree to which spellings reflect constituent morphemes. The algorithm then iteratively optimizes spellings, seeking to maximize these combined metrics. The resulting orthography, presented and analyzed in detail, consistently outperforms English orthography across both metrics. The implications of our findings are significant. While acknowledging the historical complexities that shaped the current English spelling system, we demonstrate that a significant improvement in both readability and learnability is readily achievable. Our work challenges the prevailing view of English orthography as a historically contingent but justifiable system, providing evidence that a more rational and efficient system is not only possible, but demonstrably superior. Machine Translation (MT) evaluation remains a central challenge in the field of Natural Language Processing. While automatic metrics such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) have become the standard for evaluating MT systems due to their efficiency and reproducibility, they are known to correlate imperfectly with human judgements (Lin and Och, 2004;Callison-Burch et al., 2006). This is largely because these metrics primarily focus on n-gram overlap and do not explicitly capture higher-level linguistic phenomena such as fluency, adequacy, and discourse coherence. Recent research has explored incorporating linguistic features into MT evaluation, including syntactic information (Chen and Zhao, 2014) and semantic role labeling (Owczarzak et al., 2007). However, relatively little attention has been paid to leveraging discourse structure – the way ideas are organized and connected in text – for this purpose. Discourse structure is crucial for understanding the meaning and coherence of a text. Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988) provides a framework for analyzing discourse relations, identifying how clauses and sentences relate to each other to form a coherent whole. We hypothesize that capturing discourse relations can improve MT evaluation by providing a more nuanced assessment of translation quality, going beyond surface-level lexical matching. A good translation should not only accurately convey the meaning of individual sentences, but also preserve the underlying discourse relationships between them. In this paper, we explore the use of discourse structure for improving MT evaluation. We introduce two novel discourse-aware similarity measures based on all-subtree kernels applied to RST discourse parse trees. These measures quantify the similarity between the discourse structures of a candidate translation and a reference translation. We then demonstrate that incorporating these measures as features into existing MT evaluation metrics, both at the segment level (evaluating individual sentences) and the system level (evaluating the overall translation), leads to improvements in correlation with human judgements. Our approach differs from previous work in that we do not aim to replace existing evaluation metrics with a single, new metric based solely on discourse. Instead, we argue that discourse information is *complementary* to current state-of-the-art metrics. Our results support this claim, showing that combining discourse-aware features with metrics like BLEU consistently yields improved performance. This suggests that future development of MT evaluation metrics should prioritize the integration of richer linguistic information, including discourse structure, alongside traditional n-gram-based approaches. We believe this work represents a step towards more accurate and reliable automatic evaluation of machine translation systems, ultimately accelerating progress in the field. The World Wide Web has become an indispensable resource for information seeking, yet navigating its vastness remains a significant challenge. Hyperlinks are fundamental to this navigation, enabling users to traverse related content. Crucially, the *anchor text* – the visible, clickable text of a hyperlink – plays a vital role in conveying the destination of a link and guiding user expectations. Well-chosen anchor text provides context and improves the overall user experience. However, constructing effective anchor text is often a manual and time-consuming process, frequently resulting in generic phrases like “click here” or repurposing document titles, which offer limited semantic value. Existing approaches to automated anchor text generation often rely on techniques like extracting key phrases from the target document or leveraging the surrounding text in the linking document. However, these methods often fail to capture the nuanced relationship between the two documents, leading to anchor text that is either overly general or irrelevant to the specific connection being established. We argue that a more effective approach requires considering the *localized similarity* between specific sections or passages of the two documents, rather than treating them as monolithic entities. In this paper, we present a novel approach to automatic anchor text generation that exploits this localized similarity. Our method ranks segments within the linking document based on their relevance to the target document, utilizing a suite of information retrieval and natural language processing techniques. This ranking identifies the portions of the original document that are most closely related to the linked document, allowing us to extract or synthesize anchor text that accurately reflects the connection. We adapt and evaluate several existing methods for measuring document similarity, including term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and latent semantic analysis (LSA), within the framework of localized similarity assessment. The core innovation lies in applying these methods not to the documents as a whole, but to smaller, overlapping segments or windows of text. This allows us to pinpoint the most relevant sections and generate more meaningful anchor text. To rigorously assess the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a series of experiments using a corpus of web documents. We compare automatically generated anchor texts with the original anchor texts present in the documents, using both manual evaluation by expert annotators and crowdsourcing for a larger-scale assessment of relatedness and clarity. The results demonstrate that our best-performing methods achieve a level of precision that rivals the quality of the baseline – the originally authored anchor texts – suggesting a viable path towards automated and intelligent hyperlink creation. Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text – is a core component of many information extraction (IE) systems and a crucial step toward building knowledge graphs. Traditional approaches to RE have relied heavily on supervised learning, requiring substantial amounts of manually annotated data to train effective models (Zheng and Gelbukh, 2008; Eriksson et al., 2011). The creation of these labeled datasets is costly, time-consuming, and, critically, domain-dependent. The most prominent benchmark dataset for relation extraction, the Automatic Content Extraction (ACE) evaluation, focuses on a limited set of relation types defined specifically for news articles (Voorhees and Mitchell, 2000). Models trained on ACE-style datasets often fail to generalize to other domains or to novel relation types, hindering their applicability in broader IE tasks. To address these limitations, we explore a paradigm shift: distant supervision. Our approach leverages existing knowledge bases (KBs) – large collections of structured data representing facts and relationships – to automatically generate training data for relation extraction, circumventing the need for manual annotation. Instead of relying on human-labeled examples, we exploit the inherent relational information embedded within the KB to identify candidate instances of relations in unstructured text. Specifically, we utilize Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), a massive, collaborative knowledge base containing information on a wide range of entities and their relationships. The central idea is to assume that if two entities are related in Freebase, then any sentence that mentions both entities is likely to express that relationship. For example, if Freebase states that ‘Barack Obama’ *born_in* ‘Honolulu,’ then every sentence containing both ‘Barack Obama’ and ‘Honolulu’ is considered a potential positive example for the *born_in* relation. This process allows us to generate a large, albeit noisy, training dataset from readily available resources. Our approach combines the strengths of both supervised and unsupervised IE techniques. Like supervised IE, we employ a probabilistic classifier with a rich set of features derived from the text, including lexical, syntactic, and semantic information. However, unlike traditional supervised methods, we do not rely on manually labeled data, enabling us to scale to a much larger number of relation types and leverage corpora of arbitrary size. Furthermore, we embrace the benefits of unsupervised IE by extracting potentially millions of relational instances from vast unlabeled text collections. In this work, we present a practical implementation of this distant supervision framework. We demonstrate its effectiveness on a large-scale relation extraction task, applying it to over 100 relation types from Freebase. Our experiments demonstrate the ability to extract 10,000 instances of 102 relations at a precision of 67.6%, showcasing the potential of this approach for building large-scale knowledge graphs. We also present an analysis of feature performance, highlighting the crucial role of syntactic parse features in accurately identifying relations, particularly those that are semantically ambiguous or lexically distant from their trigger words. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed overview of related work. Section 3 describes our distant supervision framework and feature engineering process. Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results. Section 5 includes a discussion of feature performance and error analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in machine translation, achieving remarkable progress over the past two decades (Koehn et al., 2003; Och and Ney, 2003). Traditional phrase-based SMT (Koehn et al., 2003) models perform translation by segmenting sentences into phrases, and aligning these phrases between source and target languages. While effective, these models often struggle to capture long-range dependencies and non-local reordering phenomena, particularly when dealing with languages that exhibit significant structural differences. To address these limitations, syntax-based machine translation models were proposed (Knight & Graehl, 1997; Chiang, 2005). These models leverage the syntactic structure of sentences, represented as tree structures, to guide the translation process. They operate on tree sequences, which are contiguous sequences of subtrees, effectively modeling the hierarchical relationships between phrases. However, the inherent assumption of contiguity within tree sequences restricts their ability to handle non-contiguous phrases – phrases that are syntactically disjoint but semantically related. This limitation is particularly problematic when translating between languages where non-syntactic or idiomatic phrases are common, or when dealing with languages lacking strict word order. Recent work has explored methods to overcome this limitation by allowing for controlled violations of syntactic boundaries. For example, the contiguous tree sequence based translation model (Zens et al., 2008) relaxes the strict requirement of contiguity, permitting some degree of flexibility in phrase segmentation. While representing an improvement over purely syntactic models, this approach still struggles to effectively capture relationships involving large gaps between phrases. In this paper, we present a novel translation model based on non-contiguous tree sequence alignment. Unlike previous approaches, we explicitly allow for gaps within the tree sequence, representing a sequence of subtrees and gaps. This “non-contiguous tree sequence” provides a more flexible representation, enabling the model to accurately handle non-contiguous phrases with potentially large gaps. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm tailored for decoding with non-contiguous constituents, addressing the challenges posed by this increased flexibility. The core idea is to systematically explore possible tree sequence alignments, allowing for insertions of gaps to best match the semantic and structural relationships between the source and target sentences. Our experiments, conducted on the NIST MT-05 Chinese-English translation task, demonstrate that the proposed model significantly outperforms baseline systems, including both phrase-based and contiguous tree sequence-based models. These results highlight the effectiveness of our non-contiguous alignment approach in capturing nuanced phrase relationships and improving translation quality. Document-level sentiment classification, the task of determining the overall sentiment expressed in a long piece of text, remains a challenging problem in natural language processing. While traditional approaches relied heavily on handcrafted features and lexicons (Turney, 2002; Pang et al., 2002), recent advancements in deep learning, particularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have demonstrated the ability to automatically learn effective representations, significantly improving performance (Socher et al., 2013; Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), a specialized type of RNN, have become particularly popular due to their ability to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem, allowing them to capture long-range dependencies in sequential data. However, a critical limitation arises when applying LSTMs – and RNNs in general – to long documents. Standard LSTMs, while better equipped than simple RNNs to handle long sequences, still struggle to retain crucial sentiment information across extended contexts. The “forgetting” mechanism, integral to the LSTM’s operation, while enabling it to dynamically adjust its memory content, can inadvertently discard sentiment-bearing signals relevant to the document’s overall polarity. This is especially problematic in document-level sentiment classification where understanding the global context is crucial for accurate prediction. For example, a document might contain both positive and negative sentiments, and correctly gauging the dominant sentiment requires remembering and integrating information from across the entire text. Several approaches have been proposed to address this issue. Attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015) allow the model to focus on the most salient parts of the input sequence, but they don't necessarily guarantee the preservation of long-range contextual information. Hierarchical RNNs (Yang et al., 2016) divide the document into sentences and then model the interactions between sentences, but this approach might lose finer-grained sentiment cues present within sentences. Memory Networks (Weston et al., 2014) introduce an external memory component, but require separate learning procedures for reading and writing to memory. In this paper, we introduce a novel architecture, the Cached Long Short-Term Memory (CLSTM) network, designed to specifically address the challenge of capturing long-range sentiment information in document-level classification. CLSTM enhances the standard LSTM by incorporating a cache mechanism. This mechanism divides the LSTM’s memory cell into several distinct groups, each assigned a different forgetting rate. By strategically assigning slower forgetting rates to certain memory groups, CLSTM can selectively preserve sentiment-relevant information over longer distances, leading to improved performance on document-level sentiment analysis tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that CLSTM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models on three publicly available datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach. <!-- I've included additional introductory context and extended the concluding remarks to create a more complete introduction. -->

Understanding relationships between entities is fundamental to natural language understanding. Humans effortlessly grasp nuanced connections – “John *works for* Acme Corp,” “Mary *is a friend of* Susan” – and leverage this understanding to interpret meaning and draw inferences. Replicating this ability in machines requires effective methods for representing and reasoning about relations. Recent advances in distributional semantics have shown that representing words and phrases as dense vectors (distributed representations) can capture semantic similarity and enable downstream NLP tasks (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). Consequently, significant effort has been devoted to learning distributed representations of relational patterns, aiming to encode the semantic meaning of relations themselves. These representations are crucial for tasks such as relation extraction, relation classification, and knowledge base completion (Bordes et al., 2013; Socher et al., 2013). A key challenge lies in defining what constitutes a "good" representation of a relational pattern. While existing work has often relied on existing datasets and evaluation metrics designed for relation *classification* (e.g., predicting the relation type between two given entities), these tend to focus on discriminative power rather than capturing the inherent *semantic similarity* between different relational patterns. For example, the patterns “is married to” and “is a spouse of” are semantically very similar, but a relation classification task might treat them as distinct categories if they are associated with different entity pairs in the training data. To address this limitation, and facilitate more rigorous evaluation of relational pattern representations, this paper introduces a new dataset specifically designed to measure the semantic similarity between relational patterns. We augment the dataset from Zeichner et al. (2012) by collecting multiple similarity ratings for every pair of relational patterns. This allows for a more granular and nuanced assessment of how well different representation learning methods capture semantic relationships. Furthermore, we conduct a comprehensive comparative study of various encoder architectures for composing distributed representations of relational patterns. These include simple additive composition, recurrent neural networks (RNNs), long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), and gated recurrent units (GRUs). In addition, we propose a novel enhancement to additive composition, termed Gated Additive Composition, which integrates a gating mechanism to selectively emphasize or suppress different components of the input. Our experiments demonstrate that the newly created dataset provides a valuable benchmark for analyzing and comparing different relational representation learning methods. Critically, we find a strong correlation between the performance of these representations on the semantic similarity task and their success in the downstream relation classification task, suggesting that the new dataset serves as a reliable gauge for predicting performance in real-world applications. This work contributes both a new resource and a rigorous evaluation framework for advancing the field of relational representation learning. Understanding natural language often requires grounding linguistic concepts in the real world. While significant progress has been made in areas like image captioning and visual question answering, a core challenge remains: bridging the gap between language’s abstract semantic representations and the concrete visual elements that realize them. A crucial component of this bridging process is semantic role labeling (SRL), which identifies the arguments of a predicate (typically a verb) and labels them with their semantic roles – Agent, Patient, Instrument, etc. – detailing *who* did *what* to *whom*. Traditional SRL operates on text, but extending this capability to visual data – visual Semantic Role Labeling (vSRL) – presents a compelling and largely unexplored opportunity. In vSRL, the goal is to identify the visual counterparts of these semantic roles within an image. For example, given an image depicting a person riding a horse, a vSRL system should identify the ‘person’ as the Agent and the ‘horse’ as the Patient of the ‘riding’ action. This task requires not only object recognition but also a deeper understanding of the relationships between objects and the event they participate in. However, creating a large-scale, annotated dataset for vSRL is a prohibitively expensive undertaking. Manually labeling image regions with semantic roles requires substantial human effort, limiting its feasibility. Existing approaches either rely on small, carefully curated datasets or transfer knowledge from text-based SRL, which can suffer from a domain gap between language and vision. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to vSRL that mitigates the need for extensive, costly image annotations. We leverage the abundance of image captions paired with automatically generated linguistic SRL annotations to learn a vSRL model. Specifically, we employ a linguistic SRL system to annotate captions with semantic role information, and then automatically project these roles onto corresponding image regions identified via object detection. While this process introduces noise, we demonstrate that it provides a surprisingly effective training signal for learning to ground semantic roles in images. Our approach centers on rendering candidate participants as image regions corresponding to detected objects, and training a model to learn associations between these regions and their corresponding semantic roles. Beyond simply identifying roles, our model implicitly learns frame-semantic visual representations—visual patterns associated with particular event types (frames). We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments, showing that it achieves competitive performance on vSRL tasks despite relying on automatically generated, noisy data. Further, we compare our induced visual representations to those learned in previous work on supervised visual verb sense disambiguation, finding that our approach yields superior results. This suggests a potential synergy between vSRL and other visually-grounded language understanding tasks. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: * We introduce a novel, weakly-supervised approach to visual semantic role labeling that avoids the need for expensive, manual image annotations. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing noisy data extracted from image captions and linguistic SRL systems for training a vSRL model. * We show that our model learns meaningful frame-semantic visual representations, which outperform previous approaches to visual verb sense disambiguation.

The organization of knowledge into hierarchical taxonomies—systems that classify concepts based on generalization and specialization (e.g., “dog” is a *kind of* “mammal” which is a *kind of* “animal”)—is fundamental to human cognition and vital for many natural language processing applications. Such taxonomies underpin information retrieval, question answering, and semantic reasoning, providing a structured backbone for efficient knowledge representation and access. Traditionally, constructing these taxonomies has been a laborious manual process, reliant on expert knowledge and extensive annotation efforts, as exemplified by the creation of resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995) and the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS). However, the scale and dynamism of modern knowledge demands automated approaches to taxonomic learning. Recent years have seen significant progress in automated taxonomy induction, largely driven by distributional semantics and machine learning techniques (Lin et al., 1998;Soroa et al., 2009;Dowman & Shwartz, 2018). These approaches typically leverage the statistical co-occurrence patterns of words in large text corpora. The underlying intuition is that concepts appearing in similar contexts are likely to be semantically related, and hierarchical relationships can be inferred from these patterns. However, these text-based methods often struggle with ambiguity and polysemy – the fact that words can have multiple meanings – and can miss important perceptual information that’s implicit in the concept itself. Crucially, much of our understanding of concepts is grounded in visual experience. We readily categorize objects based on their appearance, and visual features often provide strong cues for identifying hierarchical relationships. For example, even without knowing the definition of a “corgi,” a person can likely infer that it's a type of “dog” based on its visual characteristics. Despite this, existing taxonomy induction methods largely *ignore* the wealth of information encoded in visual data. There have been some attempts to incorporate visual features, but these typically rely on carefully engineered features and are often limited in scope (e.g., focusing on a specific domain). In this paper, we address this gap by presenting a novel probabilistic model for taxonomy induction that *jointly* leverages textual and visual data. We propose an end-to-end approach that learns distributed representations of both images and words, eliminating the need for manual feature engineering. Our model is discriminatively trained using a small set of existing ontologies as supervision and is capable of constructing full taxonomies from scratch for collections of unseen conceptual labels accompanied by their corresponding images. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on the WordNet hierarchies, substantially outperforming previous approaches. The results demonstrate the significant benefits of incorporating visual information into the taxonomy induction process, paving the way for more robust and comprehensive knowledge organization systems. We believe that our work represents a step toward truly understanding conceptual hierarchies in a manner that’s more aligned with human cognition. Negative constraints and learning from limited supervision are also discussed within the paper.

Semantic parsing – the task of mapping natural language sentences to formal meaning representations – has emerged as a critical component in a wide range of natural language processing applications, including question answering, dialogue systems, and program synthesis (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Wong & Mooney, 2006; Liang et al., 2011). A particularly successful paradigm for semantic parsing leverages Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) (Steedman, 2000), a mildly context-sensitive grammar formalism that provides a natural and powerful framework for compositional semantics. CCG’s ability to explicitly represent both syntactic and semantic information in a unified manner has led to state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets (Kuhn & Dehto, 2010; Zettlemoyer et al., 2013). However, despite its success, traditional CCG-based semantic parsing systems often rely on hand-crafted or painstakingly curated lexicons that map words and phrases to their corresponding syntactic and semantic categories. These lexicons tend to be large and inflexible, and can become a bottleneck in scaling semantic parsing to new domains or languages. Further, they often suffer from redundancy: the same word often appears with multiple lexical entries, differing only in minor semantic details. For example, the word “run” might have separate entries for the verb “run” in “I run quickly” and the noun “run” in “a morning run.” This redundancy not only increases the size of the lexicon, but also hinders generalization to unseen data. To address these limitations, we propose a new approach to learning CCG grammars for semantic parsing that incorporates *lexical generalization*. Our key innovation lies in the introduction of *factored lexicons*, which decompose lexical entries into two components: *lexemes*, representing the core meaning of a word, and *templates*, capturing systematic variations in its usage. This factorization allows us to share semantic information across related lexical items, reducing redundancy and improving generalization. For instance, both instances of “run” mentioned above could share a common lexeme representing the general concept of “motion,” while employing different templates to specify its syntactic category (verb vs. noun) and any subtle semantic adjustments. We present an algorithm for learning these factored CCG lexicons from data containing sentences paired with logical-form meaning representations. Our learning process leverages a probabilistic model that simultaneously infers the lexemes, templates, and CCG grammar rules. Furthermore, we incorporate a parse-selection model that combines probabilistic grammar with features that favor parses consistent with the learned lexicon. Our experimental results on benchmark semantic parsing datasets demonstrate that our approach learns highly accurate CCG parsers, and that the generalization performance of these parsers is significantly improved by the lexical factoring. These results suggest that factored lexicons offer a promising direction for addressing the scalability and adaptability challenges in CCG-based semantic parsing. The crux of our work is to empower the machine to capture semantic similarity between words, whereas traditional systems don’t allow for this generalization.

The task of generating structured text, such as computer code, from a combination of natural language descriptions and formal specifications presents a unique challenge to current sequence-to-sequence models. Traditional approaches often struggle when presented with multiple, heterogeneous input sources – a natural language prompt alongside structured data like API call sequences or data schemas. While attention mechanisms offer some capacity to focus on relevant input, they typically operate with a fixed, predefined set of inputs, and don’t easily accommodate varying degrees of context granularity or the implicit selection of relevant information. Moreover, effectively training such models can be computationally expensive, particularly when dealing with large input spaces and complex dependencies. Our work addresses these limitations by introducing Latent Predictor Networks (LPNs), a novel neural network architecture designed for generating output sequences conditioned on an arbitrary number of input functions. The key innovation of LPNs lies in the introduction of a latent variable that governs *both* the selection of relevant conditioning context *and* the granularity at which the generation process operates. This allows the model to dynamically determine which aspects of the input are most important, and whether to generate the output at the character, token, or even larger unit level. By marginalizing over this latent variable during training, we achieve a scalable and effective approach to learning complex conditional generation tasks. The core idea behind LPNs draws inspiration from variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma & Welling, 2013), where a latent variable is used to encode and decode data. However, unlike VAEs which primarily focus on unsupervised learning, we use the latent variable to mediate the interaction between the input and output spaces, effectively allowing the model to learn *which* input features are relevant for generating each part of the output sequence. This adaptability is crucial for code generation, where the precise relevance of natural language descriptions or structured specifications can vary greatly depending on the specific code being generated. To evaluate the effectiveness of LPNs, we focus on the challenging problem of generating programming code from a mixed natural language and structured specification. We realize this through two novel datasets constructed from the collectible card games Magic: The Gathering (MTG) and Hearthstone – environments that require precise reasoning and code generation to simulate game actions. We also evaluate our model on a preexisting code generation corpus. Our experiments demonstrate that marginalizing over multiple predictors within the LPN framework consistently outperforms strong baseline models, showcasing the benefits of our approach in handling complex conditional generation tasks. Moreover, we present analysis showing the model’s ability to implicitly learn which input features are most informative, further validating the utility of the latent predictor mechanism. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details the architecture of Latent Predictor Networks. Section 3 describes the construction of the MTG and Hearthstone datasets used for evaluation. Section 4 presents the experimental results and comparisons with baseline models. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work. (Kingma, D. P., & Welling, M. (2013). Auto-encoding variational bayes. *arXiv preprint arXiv:1312.6114*.)

Multi-document summarization (MDS) aims to condense information from a collection of related documents into a concise and coherent summary. This task is increasingly important in the age of information overload, where users are bombarded with vast amounts of text data from diverse sources. Traditional MDS approaches often rely on generic sentence scoring methods, evaluating sentences based on factors like term frequency, sentence position, and similarity to other sentences in the document set (Mani, 2001;Radev et al., 2002). While these techniques can identify salient sentences, they often fail to capture the nuanced relationships and contextual information that are crucial for producing high-quality summaries. A significant limitation of many current MDS systems is their lack of awareness of the overarching theme or category to which the documents belong. Documents within a specific category – such as “sports,” “politics,” or “technology” – tend to share common vocabulary, entities, and concepts. Exploiting this category-specific information can significantly improve the relevance and coherence of the generated summaries. For example, a sentence mentioning “touchdown” is likely more important in a summary of a football game than in a summary of a political debate. This insight motivates our exploration of *category-specific importance* (CSI), a concept that quantifies the relevance of a sentence within the context of its associated category. We hypothesize that by incorporating CSI into the sentence scoring process, we can enhance the quality of automatically extracted summaries. This work demonstrates that leveraging category-specific information, even without sophisticated external knowledge, offers a simple yet effective means of improving MDS performance. We introduce two novel features that quantify CSI based on readily available information within the document set itself, eliminating the need for external resources like ontologies or knowledge bases. Furthermore, we investigate the benefits of automatically categorizing document sets when manually-curated category mappings are unavailable, demonstrating that even approximate categorization can lead to performance gains. The contributions of this paper are threefold: first, we formalize the concept of Category-Specific Importance and demonstrate its utility in extractive summarization. Second, we propose two new features for computing CSI without relying on external knowledge. Third, we show that automatic categorization improves summarization performance even when manual category assignments are not available. We have implemented these techniques in SWING, a freely available and open-source extractive summarization system. Notably, SWING achieved state-of-the-art results in the TAC-2011 guided summarization task, outperforming all other participating systems as measured by automated ROUGE scores (Lin, 2004), validating the effectiveness of our approach.
